ELAN still trades at ~21x FY26 EPS, but recent quarters suggest “No One Really Wants to Be There.”  Once the “Second Derivative” clearly turns, Presenter expects remaining Holders “Will Run for the Exits,” and warns some of these companies, particularly ELAN and ZTS, “Might NEVER Grow Again.”

• Lastly, another Participant adds that Tractor Supply [TSCO] carries leverage to the same Pet Theme, while AI Tools now help Consumers switch Trupanion [TRUP] Pet Insurance Policies to LESS expensive alternatives.

DiaMedica Therapeutics Inc. [DMAC]

Multiple “Shots on Goal” via Fetal Growth Restriction [FGR] + Preeclampsia Readouts

• DMAC is a Clinical-stage Biopharmaceutical company focused on improving the lives of people suffering from severe Ischemic diseases.

• Presenter describes DMAC as a Pre-Revenue Biotech with “Multiple Shots on Goal” via its DM199 Protein, which has several potential indications, and expects Mgmt. to ultimately pursue a Sale of the company following the Efficacy Data.

• DM199 lowers Blood Pressure and is used “Pretty Regularly” in China for Stroke Management but has NOT yet received Approval in Western Medicine.  The largest opportunity lies in Preeclampsia, a serious Pregnancy Complication with NO approved Treatments that spikes Blood Pressure and can force early Delivery.  Formal Data is due next year, but POSITIVE Investigator-sponsored Results have already emerged, and the drug is in use for Preeclampsia in a few International Markets.  Fetal Growth Restriction [FGR] represents another large Market, with Interim Results expected at an October 23rd Key Opinion Leader [KOL] event.

• Short Interest is elevated at ~20%, as “Nearly Every Stroke Drug Fails” amid notoriously difficult Enrollment, Statistical Hurdles, and Patient Mortality.  Stroke Interim Data arrives in 1Q27, and while Presenter concedes uncertainty around the results, he contends a negative outcome will NOT “Break the Thesis.”  DMAC itself frames Preeclampsia and FGR as the “Main Events,” and positive FGR Data should shift focus away from Stroke.

• Presenter values Preeclampsia at ~$25/share, FGR at ~$15/share, and Stroke at ~$15/share, for a SOTP Total of $55/share (~560% Upside).  Following positive DM199 Data, he believes DMAC could be worth $75/share (~800% Upside) in a Takeout.

Convatec Group PLC [CTEC.LN]

Patch Pump Shift + Eroding Infusion Business Amplifies “Air Pocket” Risk

• CTEC manufactures Medical and Surgical Equipment for the management of Chronic conditions across 4 major product categories: 1) Advanced Wound Care [AWC] (~30% of Revenues); 2) Ostomy Care [OC] (~30%); 3) Continence Care [CC] (~20%); and 4) Infusion Care [IC] (~20%).

• Presenter sourced CTEC through Forensic Accounting Screens and contends Mgmt. will NOT hit the Medium-term Algorithm set in April, calling for 6% – 8% Topline Growth and “Double-digit%” EPS and FCF Growth at ~25% EBIT Margins.  Consumables for Chronic Conditions account for over 90% of Revenue while Wound Care and Ostomy are mature, LOW-Growth (i.e., 2% – 4%) Categories exposed to Price Competition from Chinese Manufacturers, leaving CTEC heavily reliant on Infusion Care.

• Importantly, Diabetes anchors ~85% of the Infusion business, and Presenter flags 2 Structural Headwinds:

1)      GLP-1 Uptake suppresses NEW Insulin Pump Starts; and

2)      Innovation is “Disintermediating the Crown Jewel” Consumable Revenue stream.  New Extended-wear Infusion Sets from Medtronic [MDT] and others can cut Annual Sets per patient in HALF.  Compounding matters, newer Patch Pumps attach directly to the skin, eliminating the need for CTEC’s Infusion Sets altogether.  Beta Bionics [BBNX] received FDA clearance for its Patch Pump on 9/14/26, with MDT and Tandem Diabetes Care [TNDM] launching in late 2026 – 2027.  Presenter expects Patch Pumps to capture ~HALF of the Pump Market over the next 5 – 10 years.  TNDM, CTEC’s 2nd-largest Customer, also acquired its own Infusion Set Technology, creating real “Insourcing Risk.”

• Additionally, Margin Pressure is emerging in a “Business with NO Pricing Power.”  With COGS at ~40% of Sales and Plastics (an Oil derivative) the dominant input, Presenter models 100bps – 200bps of pressure EACH from Plastics and Freight, only partly offset by periodic Price Increases under Multi-year Contracts.

• Presenter doubts the current Mgmt. Team can navigate these pressures.  Then-CFO Jonny Mason (former Finance Exec at UK Retailers Halfords and Dixons Carphone) took the helm after the CEO passed away in October 2025, but “Is NOT an Operator or MedTech Exec.”  Consolidating an R&D Center in Manchester adds a “Hiccup” in Product Development, while Cost Cuts weigh on morale.  With the Board already searching for a new CFO with “More Public Markets Experience” after promoting the Controller, Presenter flags a potential “Air Pocket” in Guidance.

• He frames CTEC as a “Show-Me Story as the Ice Cube Melts,” with the 2H26 Bar “Exceedingly High.”  Revenue Growth must accelerate from ~5% in 1H26 to 7% – 8% in 2H to meet Full-year Guidance.  FCF reached just $22M in 1H, making the guided 2H Ramp “Beyond Anything CTEC has Done” in 10 years as a Public Company.  Inventory grew ~14% y/y in 1H26 vs. ~5% Revenue Growth, pushing DSI’s UP ~8% y/y.  Net Leverage of ~2.3x remains manageable, but Mgmt. has “Fired Its Bullets” with a $200M Buyback ending in a few months.

• Presenter is confident Mgmt. will cut the FY27 Algorithm during the November 3Q Trading Update, or early next year.  Forecasting FY27 EBITDA of $690M (~10% BELOW Consensus), he applies a compressed ~8x Multiple (from ~9x) given the Structural Issues, arriving at a Price Target of £1.50/share (~32% Downside).  Conversely, his Risk Price is £3.00/share (~35% Upside) assuming ~12x Bull Case EBITDA.

• RISKS: 1) New Infusion Sets for Parkinson’s (~3% of Sales) may offset weakness elsewhere; 2) Takeout Potential as shares screen “Cheap” on P/E; 3) Type-2 Diabetes Pump Penetration still in the Single digits, while Pump Makers face high Switching Costs.

CSL Limited [CSL.AU]

“Sandbagged” Guidance + Immunoglobulin G Yield Step-Up to Spark “Re-Rating”

• CSL.AU develops, manufactures, and markets Pharmaceutical and Diagnostic products derived from Human Plasma, operating through 3 segments: 1) CSL Behring (Plasma-derived Therapies); 2) CSL Seqirus (Influenza Vaccines); and 3) CSL Vifor (Iron Deficiency & Nephrology).

• Presenter describes CSL as the “Crown Jewel” for Australian Investors and a “High-Quality Industrial Manufacturer” that historically traded ABOVE 35x EPS, delivering a ~25% Annualized TSR [Total Shareholder Return] for ~25 years until COVID.  The company runs ~300 Plasma Centers, extracting Proteins to make Lifesaving Therapies with NO Patent Cliff, NO Most-Favored-Nation [MFN] Risk, and NO Genericization.

• Presenter explains that COVID created a “Highly Unusual” Disruption as Donor Fees “Exploded” amid collapsing Blood Collections, driving Margins sharply LOWER.  Mgmt. attempted to “Plug the Problem” with the 2022 Acquisition of Specialty Pharma company Vifor Pharma, which “Blew Up Right Away” and has since triggered $4.1B of FY26 Impairments, including a $1.7B Goodwill Write-down, with FY27 Revenue guided DOWN ~25%.  Meanwhile “Vaccine Fatigue” in the US compounded the Operating Deleverage.  After the CEO was ousted, Mgmt. “Kitchen-sinked” FY26 and “Absolutely Sandbagged” Guidance, setting up the next CEO to BEAT a Low Bar.

• The “Hook” is a NEW Manufacturing Process that DOUBLES the ~4 grams of Immunoglobulin G [IgG] CSL currently extracts per liter of Plasma, an uplift Presenter refers to as “Pure Gross Profit.”  Additional Catalysts include an imminent CEO Announcement, stabilization read-throughs from Peers Takeda Pharmaceutical [TAK] and Grifols [GRF.SM], and rotation out of AI into large, liquid GARP names, as ResMed [RMD] and Cochlear [COH.AU] leave “Nothing to Own” in Australia.  CSL is also “Massively Under-owned” for a former “Pension Fund Favorite.”

• Lastly, Presenter forecasts a “HSD%” Revenue CAGR and “MDD%” EPS Growth, while CSL trades at 19x – 20x, or just ~15x on “Normalized” Margins.  Adjusting for the IgG Yield Upgrade, a pure “Execution Bet” with NO Reimbursement or Pricing Risk, Investors are effectively paying just 12x – 13x.  Applying a ~25x Multiple to his FY28 EPS Estimate of ~A$10.00 (vs. A$9.59 Consensus), Presenter arrives at a Price Target of A$250/share (~36% Upside).

Abivax [ABVX]

Renewed Takeout Potential amid “Middle Innings” Pharma M&A Cycle

• ABVX is a Clinical-stage Biotechnology company developing therapeutics that harness the body's natural regulatory mechanisms to stabilize the Immune Response in patients with Chronic Inflammatory diseases.

• Presenter frames ABVX as a “Pre-Commercial Biotech” whose sole drug, Obefazimod, targets BOTH forms of Inflammatory Bowel Disease [IBD].  The company already holds POSITIVE Phase 3 Data in Ulcerative Colitis [UC], with Crohn’s Disease [CD] Data still pending, and is ~1 year from generating Revenues.  Presenter describes Obefazimod as a “Highly Differentiated” drug in an attractive Commercial Market, and as a result, views ABVX as a potential Acquisition Target.  He contends Large Pharma must keep striking Deals to offset Patent Cliffs and expects the robust pace of M&A Activity in the space to persist.

• IBD is a chronic, “Indefinite-Treatment” Market where existing drugs work only ~20% of the time and often stop working completely.  Presenter explains Obefazimod offers equal or BETTER Efficacy vs. AbbVie’s [ABBV] Rinvoq WITHOUT Rinvoq’s Side Effects, along with MORE convenient Oral dosing.  It has also shown “Really Exciting” Data in Patients who failed other Therapies, and a differentiated “Mechanism of Action” positions Obefazimod as a strong candidate for Combination Therapy.

• Following Press reports of a potential acquisition by Eli Lilly [LLY] in Late 2025, ABVX shares sold off significantly when a Deal failed to materialize.  Presenter’s Base Case remains that ABVX “Eventually Gets Bought,” pointing to CEO Marc De Garidel’s “History of Selling Companies,” and he believes the “De-Risked” UC Indication alone justifies today’s Valuation, if not HIGHER.  Applying “Transaction Comp” Multiples of 5x – 7x, he believes ABVX is worth AT LEAST $172/share (~95% Upside) in a Takeout – BEFORE any ex-US or CD contribution.

• Reporting quality described as "somewhere between terrible and nefarious" — e.g., flashing 99% monthly retention which is actually dollar-based net expansion

• No near-term catalyst; controlling share sunset in ~2 years noted as a potential future trigger

• MasTec (MTZ) — Infrastructure services company; stock ~50% off highs due to multiple compression from misses in adjacent telecom and solar names• Core business has grown backlog every quarter for 8 straight quarters; M&A deal improving ROIC from 10% to 16%

• 2028 EPS estimated $16–$17; stock trading at ~13.5x that vs. historical range of 17–20x

• Data center exposure <10% with Latin America upside optionality; 40–50% upside to $300+ by end of next year

• Trades at ~35x EBITDA vs. Datadog at ~70x and CrowdStrike at ~120x, despite being within spitting distance on growth rates

• Interim CEO (original founder/builder) stepped back in; stock seen as an attractive entry on the CEO-departure dislocation

ideas.2026-10-01-bofa-brian-fen-fenske-tmt-ide:
Raj — Short UBER

Thesis: Bears have cut 2028 and 2029 numbers but not 2027 and 2028 enough. Tesla's Austin robotaxi data looks very positive with no incidents, so it will likely ramp faster than expected and investors will extrapolate to other cities, pressuring Uber pricing. Waymo may exit its Uber arrangement early (exclusivity runs to 2028), pay to break it, and build its own app, leaving Uber in a Lyft-like position competing on price and take rate. Agentic AI (Muse) raises the question of what ride-share and delivery apps are worth. Uber's own driverless launch with Lucid and Nuro in 1H27 is at risk given Lucid's struggles and Nuro being 2.5 to 3 years behind Waymo. Waymo's reported share loss in San Francisco reflects repositioning and testing, not lost demand.

Valuation / Target: Downside to $45 to $50. Street 2028 EPS around $4.57; presenter is 6% to 7% lower for 2028 and a bit less for 2027, with the bigger issue being the multiple.

Catalysts: Next leg down over the next couple of quarters as robotaxis ramp and the narrative shifts to Waymo leaving Uber.

Risks: Insurance tailwinds this year and next. The stock has already sold off and is now traded by hedge funds; long-onlys need to see driverless supply in cities. The host added private autonomy as a further long-term bear point, possibly with test cases in late 2027 or 2028.

Participant — Long U

Thesis: AppLovin, Unity's main competitor, is suing Unity over data extraction; the presenter reads that as evidence AppLovin is losing share. Unity should crush Q3, growing about 30% vs. the Street at about 20% (guide was 23%), with numbers going up by double digits.

Valuation / Target: About $3 of fiscal 2028 EPS vs. consensus around $1.25; 20x implies about $60.

Risks: Historically an investor favorite that over-promised, so it must convince new investors. The host was strongly bearish on AppLovin itself, calling its model story overhyped and comparing it to Yahoo's casual games dominance, and asked for a non-conspiracy short case by email.

(Joe Flaum's preface: "Moore Cap is pitched U long funded by APP." Ideas list: "Participant — Long: U (APP funded)")

Participant — Short TDC

Company: Teradata, a legacy data warehouse still used by large banks.

Thesis: LLMs have compressed data migration timelines from two to three years to about nine months, and that will keep improving, which helps Databricks, Snowflake and hyperscalers take the installed base. The new Autonomous Knowledge Platform (July) and AI Data Factory (on-prem, for data sovereignty) are catch-up products with six to nine-month sales cycles. Management missed its $1B public cloud ARR target (now around $600M) and has shifted to guiding total ARR, growing an anemic 2% to 4%. No new logos; cloud growth is only migration of existing customers. Hyperscalers can offer credits (Azure, Fabric) to win migrations.

Valuation / Target: About 5x to 6x free cash flow on an EV basis, with $300M to $350M of FCF. Target around $20.

Risks: Cheap stock and a CFO-turned-CEO seen as a cleanup hire could mean a sale, though the presenter thinks no one needs the installed base. An acquisition could add terminal value. The host noted tech M&A of small assets rarely gets credit.

Devin (Rockefeller Capital Management) — Long MSFT

Thesis: The most underappreciated part of Microsoft is that about 80% of its cloud infrastructure is CPU-based, and CPUs are repricing. The latest generation came in about 30% higher when new generations are typically flat. Dell and HPE traditional server revenue is up about 100% year over year with margins up about 9 points, so they are passing through memory inflation and more. The existing cloud fleet has not repriced yet; as one, two and three-year contracts renew over about three years, a 30% reprice is essentially all margin and roughly doubles profitability on that infrastructure. AMD says it is running out of CPUs. Agentic tool use (Muse and others) is driving the demand. This partly explained the big Amazon and Microsoft beats last quarter and builds as an accelerating tailwind.

Second participant add (M365): Another participant's favorite stock is MSFT for the Office side: the E3 to E5 to E7 upgrade cycle, recent price increases, and consumption-based pricing through Copilot and Cowork, where early adopters pay about double on a monthly basis vs. subscription. That could add 4 to 5 points to M365 growth over the next couple of years, making MSFT the first real software winner from AI.

Valuation / Target: Host math: about $30 of EPS in fiscal 2028 at about 25x implies roughly $750.

Catalysts: Quarterly beats driven by CPU repricing; the host thinks a 10% to 15% EPS revision would be materially positive because good revisions are scarce outside semis and hardware.

Risks: Azure expectations are already high; if Azure is only in line, the rest may not matter. Too early to model consumption Copilot fully. A participant questioned how all mega-cap stocks can work at current market caps.

Jared Donson (High Valley) — Short MRVL

Thesis: Marvell will not be a custom accelerator maker; it will be a customized memory controller, CXL and XPU-attach business. The Street reads the warrant disclosures as implying a custom accelerator win (roughly $18B of revenue) and treats that as the floor. The presenter sees that as the ceiling. Published compression work (TurboQuant-style KV cache compression, pointing the model to where to look) lets customers use lower-tier DRAM and pooled memory rather than a custom SRAM chip, so there is little evidence a custom accelerator is needed. Broadcom is procuring capacity at Samsung and MediaTek announced the same, while Marvell has no leverage with its supplier on a custom chip.

Valuation / Target: An attach and CXL chip carries about a $1,000 ASP vs. roughly $20,000 for a custom accelerator, so the attach opportunity is closer to $5B than $18B. The presenter cited a wide range of outcomes. Without the warrant business, it is a much smaller business that should not trade at a 40x-plus multiple.

Catalysts: Investor event postponed to Tuesday, where Marvell should guide to fiscal 2031. A guide implying $11B to $12B would imply a custom accelerator; a number closer to $5B would support the short. Optical pressure also cited: lost Amazon business, and better optics and CPO reduce transceiver needs.

Risks: Management is very salesy and could announce a custom chip at the event. The host noted Marvell has become a momentum name in AI compute, Asia investors like it, and Jensen's trillion-dollar comment adds to the narrative. The host's own read from a meeting was that the CEO is backing away from big accelerator sockets after the Trainium experience hurt the multiple, and is emphasizing attach and networking.

Participant — Long MDB

Thesis: OLTP application databases have a real secular tailwind from agents and computer use. The presenter was hesitant earlier in the year because Postgres (Neon, Supabase and others) was growing faster, but came away impressed from the user conference by Atlas agent engine, similar to Snowflake's Cortex, which lets customers build agents on data already in Mongo with governance and controls. Snowflake and Databricks show two vendors can grow in a good subsector. The key change is pricing: the core storage product is low ASP and cluster-priced (between subscription and consumption), while the new runtime and retrieval offering is pure, unbounded consumption at higher ASPs. OpenAI uses Mongo for agent conversational memory and JPMorgan is testing the new product.

Valuation / Target: About 7x revenue vs. Datadog and Snowflake around 15x; narrowing to 10x to 12x is doable.

Catalysts: Growth above 13% as the agent engine ramps, possibly over the next few quarters into next year.

Risks: Postgres competition, including Muse running on Postgres and Google's new Postgres-based database. The host noted big bank tech budgets (around $15B) tend to stick with vendors they like, which supports retention.

Joe Flaum (Newbrook Capital) — Long LION

Company: Lionsgate, a pure-play film and TV studio with a roughly 20,000-title library that generates cash, plus a current slate. Starz was spun out about a year ago.

Thesis: The industry is consolidating and Sony is the most logical buyer. With Warner Bros. and Paramount settled and closing next week, there is more urgency for remaining studios to combine, and Lionsgate could not credibly run a sale while that deal was in limbo. The company has finally gotten its house in order: Starz spun, the Pay-1 deal redone with Amazon, and a strong slate. EBITDA has gone from about $200M to about $400M and is heading higher. A buyer could remove large G&A and marketing overlap; the company has historically been bloated.

Valuation / Target: About a $3B market cap and $5B EV, stock around $11 (it was $16 with takeout speculation that has since come out). MGM went to Amazon at high-20s EBITDA; mid to high teens would be close to a double, $15 to $20+. Downside view is dead money rather than large losses; JPM recently initiated underweight with a DCF near $7, which Joe does not think is how it trades.

Catalysts: Spin anniversary passed, so no tax consequences. Expect a formal sale process to launch in the next couple of months, hopefully this year, otherwise Q1. Hunger Games prequel in November, a sequel to Michael, and a good slate over the next couple of years. Roughly two years left in the Trump administration creates a finite window.

Risks: Higher rates could stall large M&A, though at a $5B EV it is digestible for Sony or Amazon. Without a process the stock is dead money. Other potential buyers: Amazon, with Netflix likely to look once a process is announced.

Participant — Long ESTC

Company: Elastic, across three end markets: search, observability and security (SIEM).

Thesis: Partner checks show significant acceleration; subscription growth of 17% should move above 20%. In search, vector and hybrid search for agent recall can cut token usage by 60% to 70%, with heavy experimentation at large enterprises; large customer growth is 16% and search is growing over 20%. Observability has lost share to Datadog, but the market is growing double digits and Elastic has fixed its metrics gap; agent actions (browser actions, timeouts, captures) need heavier, context-rich logs. Security is seeing competitive displacements and should grow in the mid 20s. RPO is up 29%.

Valuation / Target: About 3.8x revenue and 16x to 17x free cash flow; 20%-plus growth should not trade there.

Catalysts: Next quarter's subscription growth close to 20%, then higher. Positioned as a shorter-term, roughly two-quarter idea.

Risks: CEO Ash Kulkarni has sold a lot of stock. Customer count has not grown much; growth is coming from expansion within existing customers rather than AI-native logos.

Participant (Wind Advisors) — Long ASTS

Company: AST SpaceMobile, satellite direct-to-mobile connectivity.

Thesis: The spectrum it acquired about two years ago (NPV of payments over roughly 40 years) is worth $13B to $15B today by the presenter's estimate, and about $20B by the company's, close to the entire market cap. Spectrum valuations are up at least 10x in recent months (Amazon, EchoStar spectrum sales including to SpaceX, Iridium). Revenue build: AT&T and Verizon TAM of about 500M subscribers at a 10% attach and about $2.50 per subscriber, MOUs covering about 2.5B subscribers globally at a 5% contribution, plus government and Golden Dome revenue that adds a floor. Roughly $3B of revenue in 2029.

Valuation / Target: Market cap about $23B; presenter has been buying in the mid to high $50s and below $60. Space communications stocks have traded north of 13x; that supports $110 to $120. If half the assumptions are wrong, $70 to $80.

Risks: SpaceX is the main risk; a carrier could sign with SpaceX. The Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile JV is seen as carriers protecting themselves, and they are investors in ASTS. The host cautioned that spectrum is a trophy asset with no cash flow: Straight Path went up about 10x when Verizon and AT&T bid, but DISH destroyed many hedge funds that owned it on transaction-based marks.

Participant — Long U

Thesis: AppLovin, Unity's main competitor, is suing Unity over data extraction; the presenter reads that as evidence AppLovin is losing share. Unity should crush Q3, growing about 30% vs. the Street at about 20% (guide was 23%), with numbers going up by double digits.

Valuation / Target: About $3 of fiscal 2028 EPS vs. consensus around $1.25; 20x implies about $60.

Risks: Historically an investor favorite that over-promised, so it must convince new investors. The host was strongly bearish on AppLovin itself, calling its model story overhyped and comparing it to Yahoo's casual games dominance, and asked for a non-conspiracy short case by email.

(Joe Flaum's preface: "Moore Cap is pitched U long funded by APP." Ideas list: "Participant — Long: U (APP funded)")

Participant — Long 2383 TT (Elite Material)

Company: Taiwan-listed supplier of high-end copper clad laminate with 65% to 70% share.

Thesis: EPS compounding at about 70%, supply-constrained through 2028. PCB content rises about 200% from Blackwell to Rubin as boards get larger and more layered, and each material generation (M7, M8, M9) roughly doubles in price. A key enabler for high-end networking and baseboards.

Valuation / Target: About 14x, cheap mainly because it is listed in Taiwan.

ideas.2026-09-28-monness-crespi-mch-industrial:
The presenter would like to discuss Sensient Technologies as a long.

Sensient has a $5.5 billion market cap / $6.3 billion EV. It is currently levered 2.8x, but they will be de-levering rather quickly due to a peaking investment cycle. For context, it trades at ~20x 2028 consensus earnings of $6.

In terms of the setup, the presenter believes the story is underfollowed / under-the-radar. Roughly a third of EBIT is derived from flavors and extracts. It is essentially a specialty chemical company, with flavors and extracts selling to food, beverage, pharmaceutical, and personal care companies. They generally sell to small to midsize CPG, so they are selling to smaller, upstart, growing businesses, which is why their business is growing mid-single digits, with high-teens EBITDA margins. The company thinks they can get that to the low-to-mid 20%s over time.

The crux of the thesis is that they sell color into companies as an ingredient. That is approximately half of the EBIT, and the crux of the thesis. They produce both natural and synthetic colors in foods, beverages, pharmaceuticals, personal care, etc. They sell that to both large and small companies. There has been a large push, which was started by the MAHA (Make American Healthy Again) movement, moving away from synthetic dyes to using only natural colors. It started as a voluntary pledge by the industry, but it is more commercial and societal pressure that is driving the change now.

They have $100 million of synthetic color revenue in the US that they think will convert to $1 billion dollars of revenue over the next several years. The reason why there is that uplift is that if you take Red 40, and you want to make a Skittle that is red, they know it is one part. In order to do that with natural colors, you need to use beets, carrots, and other natural ingredients from the ground – so it is more volume and at higher prices.

They are one of the only companies, possibly in the world, but definitely in the US, that can do this. There are other companies that do it, but do not have the same breadth of offerings. Some of them only have certain color offerings. What is unique about Sensient is that they are already working with all of these companies, and they are assisting them with the transition. So they are in a pole position to win.

We are kind of in the bottom of the first inning. The presenter would say the transition is being triggered by, at the start of 2027, Walmart says that all of their own private label needs to be (or will be) natural colors. All new products going into Walmart need to be natural colors. Target, all cereals in their stores today are natural colors. There is other state legislature for K-12 schools and others that starts in 2028, so there is a massive push there. What is interesting is that it is kind of difficult to do this from a supply-chain perspective, both on the Sensient side (and why they are well ahead from a CAPEX and working-capital perspective) but also from the company perspective. To say you are only going to do it for K-12 is really difficult to do from an R&D, supply chain, and manufacturing process perspective. The presenter has done a lot of work on this, and when you speak to large CPG companies, they are essentially doing all of this at the same time.

In the third quarter of 2025, they invoiced $1 million of this $1 billion. Then it went to $5 million, then it went to approximately $10 and $15 million. So, the company has invoiced $45 million of the $1 billion opportunity. That should accelerate in the back half of this year, and then again through 2027.

At this early stage, the presenter believes that they have both the supply chain and the technical skills to achieve this, by working alongside the likes of General Mills, Campbells, Nestlé, and Conagra. And they front-loaded many of the OPEX investments. The CAPEX and working-capital investments will be over a couple of years. But from here, incremental margins should be a lot better than what we have seen to date.

And the fieldwork has come back so universally positive that this is not going backwards. Things could change quarter to quarter, but it is universally positive that Sensient is in pole position to win. Guidance feels like it is in a good place. The presenter thinks management likes to be conservative. They feel like they have better visibility on the top line than the middle of the P&L, only because there are investments that they are making. But to date, they have beaten expectations.

The presenter thinks we see continued quarter-over-quarter growth in the conversion from synthetic to natural. The presenter thinks earnings power is $7 to $8 in 2028, versus the Street at low $6s. The presenter thinks there is still an opportunity to compound from there. They have said, at a recent conference, they think they can get to a $1 billion run-rate in the first half of 2028 (that would be upside to the presenter's numbers).

If you think about this business relative to Givaudan, Symrise, or IFF - if you roll forward what this is going to look like from 2026 to 2028 and then some, it is going to have faster revenue growth, faster EBITDA growth, faster earnings growth, and margins that are very similar to those peers that are trading at 25x. And they will still be in the early-to-mid innings, because there is still an opportunity in the US, still opportunity in personal care, makeup and cosmetics, as well as in pet.

The stock is currently trading at ~$130. The presenter thinks it could easily be a $175 to $200 stock as we exit next year and investors think about what the earnings power could be in 2028, which will continue to ramp. It is also not out of the realm of possibility that it could be acquired.

The presenter would like to discuss Resideo as a long.

Resideo is a residential products company. The stock currently trades at $18 per share and the presenter thinks it could be worth over $30.

It is a residential products company mostly exposed to oligopoly markets, with 40%-plus gross margin, 20%-plus EBITDA margin, with 3% to 5% top-line growth. It is trading in the low 8x on 2026 EBITDA and low 9x EBITDA minus CAPEX.

In terms of the business, 30% is air, which is thermostats / indoor air quality with approximately 50% market share in this segment. 23% is safety, which consists of fire alarms, CO2 alarms, fire suppression with approximately 50% market share in this segment. 20% is global climate solutions, which are products for boilers, water heaters, furnaces, and heat pumps. 16% is security, which is intrusion panels, sensors, and cameras. 11% is water, which is valves and heads for water control, plumbing, and heating.

For context, the private equity bid for each of these businesses is between 10x to 12x, and we have seen a number of recent acquisitions in the space. Lone Star bought Kidde, which is the other oligopolistic player in the fire alarm market, for a bit north of 10x, and the presenter believes they are eventually going to look to IPO somewhere in the double digits to low teens (which might be hard, given that their closest comp is trading at 8x). Reliance Worldwide is a company that is getting taken out by Brookfield for just shy of 13x. Emerson carved out Copeland and sold it to Blackstone for mid-12x.

The presenter thinks there is an earnings improvement story here, a rebuilding-credibility story, and it can re-rate and grow by itself. However, the presenter thinks there is an interesting activist or take-private, sum-of-the-parts story as well. The story in the past has been very difficult to invest in, and they have cleaned it up a lot. They used to pay out $140 million per year due to a Honeywell environmental liability. After they spun out from Honeywell, that is now gone. They spun out a more volatile piece of their business in ADI Global Distribution, which increased earnings volatility and dragged down the organic growth of the business. That is now out. It is a touch levered, at 3.2x net debt, but the presenter thinks they can de-lever to 2x by mid-2028 and start buying back stock. Then with execution (the presenter is in line to slightly above Street numbers), they think the stock can re-rate from here.

Post-Investor Day, in the first-quarter reporting as a standalone company, there were a couple of very minor headwinds, about 5% on second-half EBITDA, that hurt their credibility / poor communication which ultimately dragged down the stock. But the presenter thinks those factors will be proof that in the next couple of quarters as being not too much of an issue, while the earnings growth formula is still intact.

The presenter would like to discuss RBC Bearings as a long.

The market cap is $16 billion. They are a manufacturer of highly engineered precision bearings, motion control products, and valves. For reference, 55% of their revenue is tied to industrial end markets and approximately 45% is tied to aerospace and defense (as well as a space business).

What separates this company from other bearings manufacturers like Timken or Regal is that they focus on highly specialized pieces, which get co-designed with their customers early in the design phase, and get spec'd into long-duration programs, which lends itself to attractive pricing power and economics relative to these other players. So they have compounded earnings at a much higher rate than peers over the last 20 years; so, structurally it is a very good business.

There are three key factors as to why the presenter thinks it is interesting today. One, within the industrial business, you are seeing this ongoing positive inflection in short-cycle industrials, which the presenter thinks will accelerate their organic growth to high singles to low doubles over the next few quarters, which is slightly above where the Street is. But the most interesting piece of the business is in the aerospace and defense segment, where you have three new growing businesses - space, missile, and marine defense. Collectively, these businesses are a low double-digit percent of total revenue and very difficult to model because they are so nascent; as a result, the presenter believes investors will not find them in any sell-side models. But there is very good demand visibility over the next few years to potentially doubling or tripling these businesses in the medium term. The presenter thinks that presents a pretty attractive upside toggle that is not priced into industry estimates. That is really interesting on top line.

And then on margins, you have this attractive story where, over the next 6 to 12 months, approximately 40% of their commercial OEM LTAs are getting repriced, and in some cases by as much as 35% to 40% in terms of step-ups. If you put these pieces together, the presenter thinks the business should be growing earnings over 20% over the next three years, versus the Street that is only assuming mid-teens growth.

In summary, the presenter believes this is a really interesting setup where you have a great business with multiple ways to win, and with the pullback in A&D multiples recently, you have a more attractive, reasonable entry point today.

The presenter models ~30% upside over the next 12 months. The thinking there is, the presenter is high single digits above the Street on earnings, and then you assume the multiple remains flat from here.

The presenter would like to discuss OpenLane as a long.

OpenLane has a $4 billion (unlevered) EV.

OpenLane operates a virtual used car auction.

The simple way to think about the company is, they generated $300 million of EBITDA last year going to $500 million in 2028. They are a beneficiary of declining used car pricing and a beneficiary of virtual auctions taking share from physical auctions. The timely piece of news is that a much smaller competitor of theirs, ACV, based up in Rochester, was recently bought for $2 billion or 15x EBITDA, by Copart.

There is a long entanglement of companies here. For context, OpenLane used to be KAR Auction Services. They sold their physical auction business to Carvana. Ritchie Brothers is a competitor to Copart. They might view virtual auctions as something they might need to get into, and the presenter thinks OpenLane would be an obvious strategic target for them. The company did a secondary and a co-lead investor, a private equity firm, sold stock. The stock took a hit and never really recovered. The company bought back stock in the deal. The CEO bought stock in the open market after. Roughly, call it $400 million of EBITDA, $250 million of free cash flow, and 100% of free cash flow to buy back stock. The presenter thinks it is a clean / simple story where you do not have to think about AI. The presenter’s price target is $60, or 15x $500 million, and then investors can discount that back however you would like.

The presenter would like to discuss MasTec as a long.

MasTech has a market cap of $16 billion, with $4.2 billion in debt, generating approximately $500 million of free cash flow per year and growing.

In terms of the setup, the stock is down ~60% in the last two to three months. The pitch is simple, this is a business that is going to grow. The top line is compounding at 15%+ plus deals with leverage to the bottom line. In the presenter’s opinion, there were a lot of generalist investors in the E&C space and they seem to have all exited the stock. You now have a business that is trading around 8x 2028 EBITDA, which is back to the pre-AI low end of the EBITDA range.

Why did the stock sell off so much? The presenter would say, if you benchmark MasTec to best in breed, which is Quanta - Quanta is down approximately 30% from its peak - that is the industry component of the sell off. The idiosyncratic part is they have two businesses. One is 15% of the top line and 14% of EBITDA in communications, where half is wireless, half is wireline where they had a slight pushout of a project. The presenter would simply say that the communications segment is not the most exciting part of the story, while the balance of the business (80%+) is far more interesting. The presenter thinks the communications business is fine where it is, with 8% margins, but the presenter is not underwriting that getting materially better.

The presenter will lead with why the business is growing so much. It is simply the dynamic with utilities, where utilities have had flat budgets. Utilities give you 10-year capital plans. They have been flat for 20+ years. They inflected two years ago. They will be growing for the next eight to ten years based on their 10-year forecasts, and MasTec is tied to that, as is Quanta and others.

The 80%+ of sales and EBITDA that are tied to that, should double from last year through 2028, compounding organically 15% +, in addition to the acquisitions that they are making as they de-lever.

The presenter does not think that they have a large EBITDA discrepancy versus the Street, but they would argue that you have had a material de-rating to the tune of 60%, and the presenter thinks you are now back to the low end of the EBITDA range for a business that legitimately grows. Effectively, nothing has changed in terms of the risk profile of the business. In the presenter’s opinion, there were a lot of investors in the stock that did not appreciate the dynamics and volatility of an engineering company.

The presenter would like to discuss Madison Air as a long.

The presenter’s price target is $40 which equates to 23x 2027 EPS of $1.75.

For background, the stock is down 50% off its highs.

The presenter thinks the interesting / idiosyncratic piece here is their recent acquisition of German fan and motor maker ebm-papst that was announced in mid-August. Today, Modine was on a sell-side call talking about tightness in the supply chain, largely within this fan segment that has been tight across the chiller space more broadly. The presenter believes that there is an opportunity here for massive pricing and more LTAs for MAIR.

If you layer that on top of what will be 20% of the business that is data-center-exposed, the presenter thinks you have the potential for numbers upside next year. Of the equity needed to close the deal, the CEO came in with, the presenter thinks, $600 million out of $2.5 billion - so meaningful confidence in the deal from the CEO.

The presenter would like to discuss IDEX Corporation as a long.

IDEX is an industrial conglomerate with a $17 billion market cap, levered at a little less than 1x based on the presenter's numbers.

The presenter thinks the part of the story that is well understood is that they have a lot of short-cycle industrial businesses, plus a semis business, in addition to a Bloom Energy tie-up from their core power business. The additional upside now is what is happening in the biopharma markets - particularly with the life science tools companies like Agilent, Waters, Danaher, and Thermo Fisher. They have basically been on the road for two straight months telling you that there is a real tailwind to their businesses, particularly on the liquid chromatography/mass spectrometry cycle, because AI infrastructure integrated into drug discovery labs, particularly wet labs, is actually driving an incremental pickup in the amount of drug discovery processes that they can run.

Consequently, what is happening is that there is a major tug on an already inflecting liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry equipment spending cycle, and that is accelerating the fundamentals for all of these companies. You can see it in the commentary from Agilent and Waters. You can see it from the underlying tone of the companies, as well as their stock price reactions.

Why this matters for IDEX is that they have a large mass spectrometry business that comprises a meaningful percentage of their HST business. If that inflects meaningfully, it layers on top of a pre-existing bull thesis. The presenter thinks the bulls underwrite an acceleration of 5% to 6% organic growth to approximately 8% next year. Layering this on top of that could yield closer to low double digits growth.

IDEX has commanded a high 20s multiple in terms of its P/E multiple historically. If it gets to high 20s on the presenter's numbers, that would equate to 30% upside by year end when this all gets realized. In the presenter’s opinion, this creates a positive tug on the backlog as well, which the company clearly trades on going into year end.

The presenter would like to discuss GXO as a long.

GXO is an outsourced contract warehouse and logistics operator (it spun out of XPO pre-COVID). The pandemic was the mother of all booms for outsourcing warehousing, as everyone needed to build inventories because the supply chain was so broken. Their business boomed. A lot of contracts were signed. And given that they have a fair amount of exposure to Europe, that bust has been extremely painful, but the presenter thinks we are finally through the worst of it.

The bust was exacerbated by a few management mistakes. First, they got hurt by an acquisition that they made in Europe which froze their sales force. Second, they bid on low-risk contracts, mostly in Europe, where it is a more competitive market.

Important to note, this is a greenfield opportunity with only 20% to 30% of Europe being outsourced. In the US, it is closer to 10% to 15%, so there is an enormous greenfield opportunity, and the cost curve has steepened with material growth ahead.

In terms of the management team, they fired their CEO, and subsequently brought in the head of DHL Logistics, who the presenter thinks is considered a superstar. He has been in the position for approximately one year but investors are growing impatient because it takes a little while to turn the Titanic. He is focusing on higher-margin, stickier business where they can add more value. Think of it as the following - if Kohl's only has eight pairs of size 10 shoes on the store floor, it is a problem. If the Boeing actuator does not show up to the plant for just-in-time inventory, it is an existential problem. So they are moving into higher-value-add aerospace, biotech, AI data center management, etc.

Investors have been waiting for this backlog to materialize but the presenter acknowledges that it does take time. This past quarter, the actual backlog and billings booked really inflected. The CEO is out there insisting that this trend is accelerating. However, their organic growth slipped to 3.5% from the guided 4% to 5%. The presenter thinks you have long-only accounts (back from the pandemic days) that are fed up. You have investors that follow the CEO that are losing confidence, because this is taking a bit more time. And then you have all the passive investors in industrials that likely got out as well (fears around diesel, etc.).

The presenter strongly suspects that a contract had slipped, which indicates to the presenter that the third quarter should be strong. The presenter believes that the CEO sounds really confident about the quarter. Important to note, they have an Analyst Day after this quarter. Should this trajectory on new wins continue and they start to print 6%, 7%, or 8% organic growth, the presenter believes this goes from 12x P/E today and 7x EBITDA to 14x to 18x EBITDA and 20x to 30x P/E very quickly, as the compound story here is very powerful.

The presenter would like to discuss Generac as a short.

Generac is the marginal provider of power equipment for backup for data centers. Two weeks ago, they announced a monster deal with Amazon: $2.4 billion over the next two years and $8 billion through 2030. Amazon gets 2% of the business for that.

The presenter thinks this deal is going to be the last one they announce, because they think there are three factors that will work against the company. One, you have a lot of supply coming online from higher-tier players like Caterpillar and Cummins. Two, you have Amazon now influencing control of the company and directing capacity. And three, the engine manufacturer for their gensets is Weichai - a Chinese company - and the presenter thinks the United States is going to require the Chinese to need a permit. Even if they do not, the presenter thinks the price for these gensets is only going to go one direction, particularly if the Chinese start getting more deals.

The presenter also thinks the stock is expensive, trading at 16x 2027 P/E for a highly cyclical business that used to depend on hurricanes to grow revenue and will have a much worse profitability profile / business going forward, even if the $8 billion data center deal goes through. The presenter thinks it is worth 35% less than it is currently, using a 12x multiple instead of 16x consensus. As soon as investors see that capacity come online for the other players, the multiple compresses.

The presenter would like to discuss GFL as a long.

The company has an $18 billion market cap and $25 billion EV.

For context, GFL is the third largest waste management company in North America. They recently closed on the deal to acquire Secure Waste. They are doing business in Canada and in the US (the stock is dual listed). But the single most important factor about the story currently is, on the last call, the CEO said that he was open to taking the company private. For reference, he has a 27% voting interest in the stock.

The presenter thinks it is unusual that the CEO has been so open about this. They formed a strategic committee. There have been articles written that there are up to six PE firms bidding on it. The two leaders supposedly are Blackstone and KKR (who have teamed up), and then Brookfield has also been a rumored suitor. For background, this company has already been private twice before.

The presenter thinks the CEO's frustration is that he wants to run this business at 7.5x leverage, and he sees a real ramp to organically grow it. And in the public markets, no investor wants him to be over 3.5x leverage. Every time they do, they get penalized for it. The presenter thinks he is tired of it. He has taken a lot of money off the table (several hundred million dollars off the table). He wants to roll, and the presenter thinks something happens.

When you think about potential buyers, it makes a lot of sense. This is a crown jewel asset that, if you have a continuation vehicle, you want to be able to roll this out to all future investors. It is not expensive. It is trading at approximately 12x EBITDA (11x using the presenter's numbers, because they think people have underestimated the synergies with Secure). The stock is currently trading at $41. The presenter would not be surprised if the stock is well above $50, between $50 and $55, in the next three months.

The presenter would like to discuss Eaton as a long.

The presenter believes there are really two drivers to the thesis. The first is price-cost and margins, and the second is just organic growth. On the price-cost side, if you look at Electrical Americas (EA), wage and commodity inflation have been a 450 to 500-basis point margin headwind in that segment for each of the last four quarters, and roughly 80% of that is commodity inflation.

During the CFO transition last fall (in November), their price-cost simply got away from them during that period of time. The presenter thinks it was, on a dollar basis, in EA roughly a $300 million headwind in the first half, and on a gross dollar basis, something like $600 million in EA for the year when you roll through commodity pricing through the back half. The new CFO started in early March, and he has made it a clear priority to be recouping that. So they took price in April, they took price again in August, and they have stated that they intend to be dollar-neutral on a full-year basis, with more price earning in Q4 relative to Q3. Investors can do that math in terms of dollars that they are going to get. The presenter thinks they put some of this - but not all of it - in their second-half margin bridge. Then you have a similar dynamic, but on a smaller scale, playing out in EG as well. Where the presenter thinks it looks interesting is into 2027, where inflation will start to lap, but you will get the full-year benefit of the pricing actions. The presenter thinks that is not modeled in consensus. The presenter thinks the clearest way to see that is in incremental margins, where at their investor event in 2025, they guided to a framework for the combined global electrical business that implied a 35% incremental margin (2030 over 2024 as your base year). When you look at consensus for 2027 over 2024 (2024 is a clean base, and 2027 would be the year that you fully lap the price-cost headwinds) consensus has a 27% incremental margin. So the dollar basis there between the 27% incremental and the 35% incremental is about $800 million. The presenter thinks that is $800 million effectively of price that is unrecouped in consensus numbers. So the Street is modeling the headwind going away but does not incorporate the price impact on earnings. That is the thesis as it relates to margins. If you zoom out, Eaton is in a position where the two pain points in industrials (either price-cost or manufacturing ramps), are accelerating out the other end of the tunnel on both of those as you go into next year. Then the second piece is on organic growth, where they have been chasing numbers up all year. They are implying in their guidance a deceleration in the second half in both EA and EG. The presenter thinks they are likely to beat that. If you put everything together - margins and organic growth - looking to next year consensus is less than $16 EPS while the presenter thinks they can earn $18 EPS. If you hold the current multiple, roll that forward on $18 next year, it would equate to a $525 stock price.

The presenter would like to discuss CECO Environmental as a long.

It has a $4 billion market cap, levered 2.5x, and trades approximately $50 to 60 million per day.

The story here is that they did a transformative acquisition six months ago. They bought a company called Thermon, which focuses on heat tracing (cables and wires). The presenter believes standalone CECO is very interesting, but investors were questioning why they were doing this deal.

The core business has doubled backlog from $800 million to $1.6 billion in the last two quarters, because they are essentially a year behind GE Vernova and Siemens in terms of the power generation cycle. They sell scrubbers, products that reduce noise and reduce emissions. They have 70% market share for their products on turbines 200 megawatts and up. The presenter thinks their content per megawatt can grow substantially. The presenter believes that they are a year behind GE Vernova and Siemens in the order cycle. All the big orders that those companies started to book two years ago, CECO is starting to see that now. According to a sell-side note, the big project they just won is $350 million of content on Project Kilby, the big data center in Texas with Microsoft and Chevron.

The story here is that the backlog has doubled and they are now seeing good operating leverage. They are mostly contract manufactured, so they do not have to add all this capacity to capitalize on this demand. They can simply serve the orders when they get them. The presenter thinks they can generate $2 billion of revenue next year while the Street is at $1.8 billion. This year they are likely going to book $3 billion of orders. If you think about how these turbine orders have occurred over the last two years, they likely book another $3 billion next year. They are going to exit 2027 with $3 billion of backlog and potentially $3 billion of revenue. Typically they convert backlog over 12 to 18 months.

The presenter believes it is a situation where Street numbers are materially too low. It is not a well-trafficked company as it is only covered by approximately five analysts. A new sell-side analyst just picked up coverage two months ago, and it has started to generate more buzz / attention. But the presenter thinks the story is that power generation is 30% of revenue and will be growing to 50% or 60% over the next two years. They also have a lot of exposure to gas pipeline and midstream; that is another 20%. The rest is a mix of other oil & gas markets and general industrial. They have some semiconductor manufacturing exposure as well. The non-power-gen business is mostly focused on filtration and dust collection. These are sleepy industrial businesses but the presenter thinks the entire company can grow 20% to 30% organic for the next four years.

Based on the presenter's numbers, the stock trades at ~12x 2027 EBITDA. The presenter thinks there is a meaningful discovery-value situation occurring, where investors are figuring out that this company / opportunity exists, and numbers should go materially higher. Obviously, there is an AI angle to the story as well. Investors want to say that we are at peak gas turbine orders, but because of the timing of when CECO books orders, the presenter does not think you are going to see that peak until 2028 or maybe even into 2029. In summary, it is an undiscovered story with material numbers upside. The company does a lot of marketing. They were at Laguna, and they were at a sell-side conference. They are trying to get more sell-side coverage. EBITDA margins are going from 10% to 20% over the next three years. And as it relates to Thermon, they share a lot of the same end markets, and they have a lot of the same customers. So, there are a lot of cross-selling opportunities that are already being booked. In the presenter’s opinion, it is not in the deal assumptions. They are already tracking ahead on the cost synergies. The presenter thinks the earnings power of the combined business is materially higher.

The presenter would like to discuss Buzzi as a long.

It is a €37 stock, €6.7 billion market cap. There is €900 million of net cash, and they also own a third of a Mexican cement company called Moctezuma that is worth €1.2 billion. The EV is approximately €4.8 billion. The stock is very cheap. It trades at 4.3x EBITDA and 7x P/E ex cash. The JV income from Mexico sits below the EBITDA line.

The stock is down ~30% year to date on concerns regarding pricing power in the US cement market and European regulatory dynamics coming into focus once again. The company is largely a cement supplier with some concrete and aggregates exposure. For context, 40% to 50% of their EBITDA is in the US, approximately 10% is in Brazil, and then 40% to 50% is in Europe.

In the US, cement prices have been flat to down 1% year to date, which is causing margin pressure across the industry, given rising input costs, particularly diesel. At the same time, demand has been weak, as construction markets remain soft. The weak pricing backdrop, especially in the face of higher energy costs, is driving the narrative that the cement industry pushed too much pricing during the 2022 to 2024 time frame. There is also heightened competition from imports, which the presenter does not believe to be the primary driver. Imports as a share of total industry volumes rose from 2013 to 2022, but they have stagnated since 2022 to roughly 20% to 21% share. The presenter thinks weak pricing is more a function of volume declines and they expect better price realization and cost recovery in 2027. Outside the US, the competitive dynamics are better. The company reported slight EBITDA growth ex-US in the first half, despite all of the energy pressures. But there is renewed investor focus on the EU's planned phase-out of free carbon credits to the cement industry over the next decade, which will gradually increase the fee paid per ton of cement produced. Bearish investors think Buzzi is in a worse position than peers, because they have not been as quick to spend capital on decarbonization projects or carbon capture plants. The presenter thinks Buzzi is simply taking a different approach, where they are not committing significant capital before it is clear how the economics will play out. Given this is an industry-wide issue, the presenter sees cement pricing across Europe increasing in response to higher environmental costs, which is similar to what happened during the energy crisis following the Ukraine war.

Stepping back, there is a lot of focus on year-to-date profitability, but this is a business that has dramatically increased profitability and improved its balance sheet over time. If you look at historical results, you can see that EBITDA consolidates around a certain level for a few years and then increases significantly. From 2016 to 2018, EBITDA was in the €500 to €600 million range. Then from 2019 to 2021, it was in the €700 to €800 million range. The company has been in the €1.15 to €1.25 billion range since 2023. At the same time, the business used to have over one turn of leverage, but they have generated a lot of free cash flow and now sit with €900 million of net cash, which they can use for acquisitions and share buybacks. The presenter thinks just showing some level of EBITDA growth from here can drive a significant re-rating. Looking out to 2028, if the presenter puts 7x on €1.25 billion of EBITDA - which is approximately 11x P/E ex-cash - and a 6% free cash flow yield - the stock would be worth €61, or over 60% upside. It is worth noting that in the presenter's price target, it excludes the Russia business, which likely has no value following the fallout from the Ukraine war.

The presenter would like to discuss Air Canada as a long.

Air Canada has a $12.5 billion EV, $6.6 billion market cap, and a little less than $6 billion net debt including leases. It trades over $75 million per day. It is the number one Canadian airline, with over 40% domestic market share. The top two players have over 70% share, so it is a true oligopoly, but with a better structure compared to the US market.

Aside from the top two players, every single other airline in Canada took money from the Canadian government because of fuel prices. The only two players that did not were WestJet and Air Canada, and they are the only ones that can make the business work. It is a different form of what happened in the US, with the low-cost carriers going bankrupt (i.e. Spirit). This is very different from the pandemic, when the Canadian government forced every airline to issue shares. Air Canada took part in that during the pandemic, where they issued shares. Prior to that, there were ten years where the share count had not moved. Now, since Q4 2024, they have retired a third of the shares outstanding. They issued a normal course issuer bid in the fourth quarter of 2024, and bought back 10% of their stock. They settled some converts in May of 2025. They did another normal course issuer bid.

Recently, they closed on a 10% share buyback of the company, but they still have a lot of cash on the balance sheet. Over 100% of market cap is in cash, and they are less than two turns net levered. The presenter thinks they will potentially do another normal course issuer bid for another 10% in November. So they are massively under-levered, they are asset rich, they own over 80% of their fleet, and they have agreements to sell $2 billion of their fleet over the next 18 months - again, versus a sub-$7 billion market cap.

The most recent / interesting component to the story - they own Aeroplan, which is the largest loyalty program in Canada. They sold a 25% stake to Blackstone and a consortium for a $10 billion implied value. They are able to buy back that 25% stake at a 6.5% IRR to Blackstone. The value of Aeroplan is being marked by private equity at $10 billion against a $13 billion EV. They also have pension assets - net surplus funding that is $4 billion or so - and then the actual planes that they own, which the presenter estimates are worth over $10 billion in terms of book value.

Worth noting, last year WestJet received an investment from Delta and others that valued the company at 6x EBITDA, which is higher than where United trades currently. In 2024, Air Canada put out a plan to generate $5 billion of EBITDA by 2028. The Iran war obviously throws a wrinkle into that most likely, but even if they generate $4 billion or so, which is conservative, the presenter thinks the stock is on a path to doubling over the next 18 months.
