UNIT — Uniti Group — LONG — Sagar Gupta, Anson Funds

• Disclosure first. He runs an activism strategy, but this is not an activist position.

• The asset. A fiber company — “fiber is an incredibly scarce and strategic asset.” Two sides, simplified: residential fiber, and enterprise/dark fiber. A leading player at $2.5 billion market cap and $12.5 billion EV, so $10 billion of net debt on top — but stable, high-quality businesses.

• Why it gets sold. Elliott owns 20%. This used to be two companies — Uniti owned the assets and Windstream operated them — and they have now combined, eliminating a lot of intercompany cost and complexity. Elliott's board representative is a former Elliott executive whose compensation agreement, visible in the proxy, pays him more if the company is sold.

• The approach that already happened. Media reported a joint bid from T-Mobile and TPG, splitting the company — T-Mobile taking residential fiber, TPG the enterprise/dark fiber side. TPG is quasi-strategic, having bought Crown Castle's fiber business. The sector precedent is clear: AT&T bought Lumen's business, and Verizon bought Frontier after a Jana push.

• Why it is available now. M&A speculation came out of the stock after the recent earnings call with no deal announced. But the CEO spoke at a recent Cowen conference and more or less confirmed they will sell at some point and remain in M&A discussions.

• The math. Non-core assets worth roughly half a billion to a billion on top of a simple sum of the parts get him to a $17 or $18 takeout against $10 today.

• On timing, and reading the last approach. They needed to complete the Windstream combination and get the operating cadence going first. By year end the fundamentals should all point the right way, including residential fiber — they want to sell with wind behind them and get full credit for the non-core assets. When approached, the stock went from $8 to $12; if the bid was in the low double digits and they thought it insufficient, asking for time makes sense. It is back to $10 now and the company has grown since. The reported approach is what makes the timing real rather than theoretical.

• Other buyers. Other telcos or larger cable companies for residential; private equity and infrastructure funds for dark fiber. His own precedent: a campaign at Cincinnati Bell that ended in a bidding war between Brookfield and Macquarie Infrastructure — “heavy demand for these types of assets.”

Transcript:

UNIT — Uniti — Long — Sagar Gupta, Anson Funds

Sagar Gupta: For transparency, I do run an activism strategy — however, this is not an activist position, so there shouldn't be any compliance concerns. The name is Uniti, ticker UNIT. I figured we don't have enough Elliott names discussed on this call, so here's another one: they own 20% of this company.

Sagar Gupta: It's a fiber company, and fiber is an incredibly scarce and strategic asset. There are two sides of the business, to overly simplify: the residential fiber side and the enterprise and dark fiber side. They're a leading player with a $2.5 billion market cap and $12.5 billion EV, so $10 billion of net debt on top. But these are incredibly stable, high quality businesses.

Sagar Gupta: Elliott owns 20%, so this company needs to get sold. I think everybody's more or less known that was eventually the plan. Going back, this used to be two companies — Uniti and Windstream, where one owned the assets and leased them to the other to operate them. Those two have combined, and a lot of the intercompany cost and complexity has been eliminated. The person now on the board of the pro forma company as Elliott's representative is a former Elliott executive, and you can go into the proxy statement and find that his compensation agreement has him getting paid more if the company gets sold. So now that it's a fully combined, clean company, we think this sale is actually quite feasible.

Sagar Gupta: The media reported the company was approached by a joint bid from T-Mobile and TPG. T-Mobile would take the residential fiber side, TPG the enterprise dark fiber side — and TPG is quasi-strategic since they bought the fiber business out of Crown Castle before. Then you have AT&T, which bought Lumen's business, and Verizon, which bought Frontier after a push from Jana. So we think the deal is inevitable. A bunch of the M&A speculation has come out of the stock following the recent earnings call since a deal wasn't announced, but the CEO spoke at a recent Cowen conference and more or less confirmed that yes, they will sell it at some point and they're still in M&A discussions. There are also non-core assets worth about half a billion to a billion on top of a very simple sum of the parts. That gets me to a $17 or $18 stock price in a takeout versus $10 today.

Nico: What's your view on timing, or on when the street may appreciate it more? Some people have thought the thesis was that it'd be sold for a while now.

Sagar Gupta: You first had to do the combination with Windstream and really get the operating cadence in motion. I think by the end of this year you'll have the basic fundamentals all pointing in the right direction, including on the residential fiber side. They just want to sell with wind behind their sails and get full credit for the non-core assets as well. When they were approached, the stock was around eight bucks and it shot to twelve. If I made up numbers — maybe they got approached in the low double digits and didn't think it was good enough. So I wouldn't be surprised if they said, give us some time, get the business in better shape, and then we'll sell, and we want credit for the non-core stuff too. The stock went from eight to twelve, now it's back to ten, and the company has grown a bit since. The news of them being approached makes the timing a lot more real rather than theoretical.

Nico: Do you have a feel for who the potential acquirers would be?

Sagar Gupta: The approach was from T-Mobile and TPG, reportedly a joint bid where they'd split the company in half. You could have the other telcos or larger cable companies interested in the residential fiber side, and a number of private equity or infrastructure private equity firms interested in the dark fiber side. I long ago ran a campaign at Cincinnati Bell that got into a bidding war between Brookfield and Macquarie Infrastructure — a great outcome for shareholders. There's heavy demand for these types of assets.

SNPS — Synopsys, paired against CDNS — LONG / PAIR — Andres Menocal, Nomura

• The trade, stated up front. $84 billion market cap, $870 million average daily value traded, 2.5x net leverage. He thinks it is a $530 stock within a year, roughly 20% higher, as margins converge on Cadence. September 30 is when you find out. If you must run a hedge book, own it dollar for dollar against a short in Cadence — the other half of the duopoly.

• The industry. Chip design software (EDA). Every chip you have heard of is designed and tested in these tools before a fab will touch it. Two companies hold roughly 60% of the market and dominate the certified checks a design must pass before TSMC will manufacture. Switching costs are enormous and the bill is small — about 2% of a customer's revenue — while one failed tape-out costs $50 to $100 million. Nobody leaves and nobody cuts spend. 25 to 30 cents of every dollar becomes free cash flow.

• The event. In June, Jesse Cohn of Elliott took a board seat. On September 30 the board hosts an investor day, where he expects hard margin targets. Cadence already runs 40 to 45% operating margins against the 41.5% Synopsys just guided to, and Synopsys closed four points of the gap this year on its own. Two days ago they beat by 6.5% and raised full-year guidance, especially on free cash flow.

• Why the event is cheap. The stock is up about 8% since the print and sits roughly 7% below his risk-weighted value, so today's 5% pullback is the entry. Options price September 30 as a 3% move; he thinks a hit is a 5 to 10% move.

• The base rate. Of five comparable Elliott campaigns of this size — AT&T, Salesforce, Texas Instruments, Workday and one other — four ended with financial targets on the table, Workday the exception. He handicaps hard numbers landing on September 30, and the market paying up, at about one in three within five weeks.

• Why hedge at all. Cadence trades roughly 42x forward earnings against 30x for Synopsys — a 40% premium for the other toll booth on the same highway. September 30 only answers for Synopsys. The hedge covers a sell-off, a sector scare and China risk; it does not cover an AI melt-up or Cadence outrunning Synopsys, but that costs little over five weeks.

• The risk-reward. If the day delivers: five to ten points higher on the way to $530, and the pair keeps four to five of it. If it is a dud: drift to $415, and the pair loses three points before he is out within two sessions. So risk 3% to make 4 to 5% at near-even odds with no net market exposure — about 67% annualized on the pair, 50% on the outright. He prefers the pair because the stock can gap: it fell 8% in a single session in July, and from $526 to $373 with the Elliott agreement already signed.

• The exit rule. If they reveal targets with a timeline, let it run. If they present without numbers, out at the stop.

• Q&A — the AI disintermediation fear. He just returned from an Asia technology tour across Taiwan, Korea and Japan, sitting with about 30 companies in the semi supply chain. GUC told him chip companies like Google are increasingly using Synopsys and Cadence tools, so he sees in-housing as a muted risk. What caused the 8% drop a month ago was the Kimi/Moonshot model provider claiming it could do what Cadence and Synopsys do — but its technical report two weeks later showed it running on outdated, stale infrastructure. And TSMC is not going to let a design house switch to an open-source model at the last minute when failure costs $50 to $100 million.

• Q&A — what the targets will be. He expects them focused on the margin gap, which is the perennial overhang and why Elliott is involved. Possibly some framing on monetizing the agentic opportunity, and possibly a lift to organic growth assumptions from mid single digits to low double digits or mid teens — but he is playing for the margin pathway.

Transcript:

SNPS long vs. CDNS short — Pair — Andres Menocal, Nomura

Andres Menocal: My idea today is long Synopsys, SNPS — $84 billion market cap, $870 million average daily value traded, two and a half times net leverage as of the latest quarter. • Q&A — immigration and the CEO change. On Canada's immigration clampdown: possibly a sentiment impact, not fundamental — six-freedom traffic is a structural tailwind, Canadian population still outgrows the US, and Canadian air traffic is still recovering faster than the US off a lower base. • Story one — the cyclical and self-help core. Global analog and power semis are about three months into an upcycle after a four-year downturn. Rohm's operating margins are in the low single digits, which is the central restructuring opportunity. A new CEO and an American CFO have targeted ¥500 billion of sales and ¥100 billion of EBIT by 2028 — and even half of that is essentially just getting the loss-making silicon carbide business to breakeven, plus some cost cuts and pricing. He gets to ¥300 per share of core earnings, worth ¥4,200 to ¥5,000 at the 14–17x analog peers trade on.

• Story two — the Toshiba power analog deal. Could be announced as early as September. Context: a party attempted to acquire all of Rohm in April 2026 and was rejected, and Rohm preserved its Toshiba relationship in the wake of that. Mitsubishi Electric has also signaled interest in consolidation. He thinks Rohm is in talks for Toshiba's power analog unit, fundable with cash and very cheap debt, and 40% accretive — adding ¥130 per share of earnings and roughly ¥2,000 of cumulative value.

• Story three — the hidden asset. A 14% stake in now-private Toshiba, which he thinks is misunderstood: it owns a large stake in Kioxia and the third-largest HDD business behind Seagate and Western Digital. Marking their financials to listed peers and applying a heavy discount, he gets an after-tax value of ¥3,000 to ¥5,000 per share — against a stock that touched ¥4,000 at the recent lows. A Toshiba IPO expected in 2027 forces that value into the open.

• Sum of the parts. Core ¥4,200–5,000, plus M&A accretion to ¥7,200–10,000, plus the Toshiba stake at ¥3,000–5,000 — call it ¥9,000 to ¥12,000 against ¥4,830 today. Three independent catalysts.

Transcript:

SIRI — Long — Steve Scherr, Shames Partners (Millennium)

I'll go first. Steve Scherr, we're at Shames Partners, a unit within Millennium; we're long-short. I'll pitch a long today: Sirius Satellite. $9.8 billion market cap, 19% short interest, ticker SIRI.

Historically I've been a short seller for 20 years, and in the last few years we started taking over the long book. One of the classifications we look for in longs is businesses that are broken, because a category of names that would hurt us as consensus shorts were the ones with a potential change agent.

Quick bull case. Sirius has been a secular decliner for 20 years — subscriptions down to about 33 million from north of 50 million. But it has stabilized: churn has come in a bit, or at least it's getting matched by new adds. People are somewhat excited about the spectrum sale opportunity; I don't really care that much. I think it takes a long time to unlock and I don't think it's an immediately feasible catalyst.

What gets us excited is that Google has picked Sirius to manage its entire audio advertising platform, because of their expertise in the space. We think it fundamentally becomes a different business over the next two to three years. The street right now sees potential for $2 billion of revenue and $300 million of EBITDA from that business by 2028. We've done about 15 calls, including with the world's largest podcasting company and a bunch of others, and it seems like the story grows faster than that. It fundamentally changes the business model from a slowly decaying music delivery mechanism into an advertising platform where they have real domain expertise.

It currently trades at about 7x EBITDA. We think 10x on 2028 EBITDA of about $3 billion — or at least a $3 billion run rate by 2028 — is 100% upside if the growth manifests with Google the way we think. Bear case is 6x on flat to modestly negative growth persisting, which is probably 35% to 40% downside from here. So we really like the risk-reward.

The nice thing is the massive short interest. It feels right now like if we're wrong it's not a clearing event, and if we're right everybody figures it out at the same time. One other thing, if anyone wants to reach out offline: there's commentary about whether they'd buy iHeartRadio, which is taking leverage and putting more leverage on top of it. I think the iHeart deal is unlikely, even though there are some compelling reasons an acquisition would work. They've been doing bolt-on acquisitions, which suggests to me they're leaving that aside. I'll leave it there — fast, short, sweet.

KBR — LONG — Daniel, Kettle Hill

• The company. Engineering, technology and government services. About $8B of sales across two businesses, STS and MTS, each doing roughly $500M of EBITDA. $4.7B cap, ~$6.7B EV, ~$37 per share, $65M ADV — roughly 7x EBITDA, 9x earnings, double-digit free cash flow yield.

KBR — Long — Daniel, Kettle Hill

Daniel from Kettle Hill. I'm pitching KBR long. KBR is an engineering, technology and government services business doing around $8 billion of sales. It has two different businesses, STS and MTS, and they both do around $500 million of EBITDA. FTAI Aviation — LONG — Ari Friedman

• Position context. Around $200 per share and roughly $20–30B enterprise value. Probably the most volatile name in his portfolio; owned since about $17 a share and traded around since. He thinks the setup is the best it has ever been.

• Segment 1 — jet engine remanufacturing (the core). Lead provider on the CFM56, now global, and the lowest-cost provider because its private label parts are the only FAA-approved ones. Big airlines are noticing. 14% share of remanufacturing today against an interim target of about 25%, which he thinks can go higher. • Segment 2 — turbine power. Their edge over everyone else piling into turbine power: they can rebuild jet engines at the end of their aviation lives and use them for data center power. Moving the fleet off balance sheet into SPVs with a sliver of firm equity and third-party capital. $6B in the first fund, another ~$6B this year, potentially an $18–20B AUM business. • Why it is available. The stock “blew up because they got everybody too excited,” with some chop on the call, but fundamentals look intact. The Fortress history is a perceived overhang; he argues they have done what they said and the accounting has proven clean. Sees the stock doubling from $200.

FTAI Aviation — Long — Ari Friedman

I'm going to pitch FTI Aviation as a long. It's about 200 bucks right now — probably the most volatile stock in my portfolio — with maybe a $20, $30, $40 billion enterprise value. These guys have three businesses and the company has been in transition. We've owned this thing since it was around 17 bucks a share and we keep trading it, but I think the setup here is probably the best it's ever been.

The core business is remanufacturing jet engines. They're the lead on the CFM56. They're now global and are going to be the lowest-cost provider, because they have private label parts that are the only ones FAA approved — so they can do this cheaper. Big airlines have started noticing. They have about 14% share of remanufacturing right now, with an interim target of about 25% of the global market, and I think it could go well higher over time. That business does around $2 billion of EBITDA next year, hopefully with a pathway to doubling or tripling.

The second part is turbine power — and who isn't getting into turbine power? Why do they have a leg up? They can take old engines after their useful lives on airplanes, rebuild them, and use them for data center power. This is a new business. They have their first major contract, which I believe is somewhere between 15 and 60 turbines, rumored to be with SpaceX, and I believe they'll announce a couple more in this segment over the next year or so. They've guided to $450 million of EBITDA in that segment next year, just assuming the contracts they have in the bank. If they do 100 turbines, which was their original target, it could be upwards of $750 million of EBITDA — and that's the starting point. These aren't stopgap solutions; they're 10-year contracts with a service tail. So a lot of growth in front of it.

The third segment is the old aviation leasing business. They're moving it off balance sheet to create what they call an asset management business. Who knows if it actually gets an asset management multiple, but they're putting in a little firm equity, raising third-party equity, and putting it into SPVs. They did $6 billion in the first one, they'll do $6 billion again this year, and next year we'll see how much they can do. You could have an $18 to $20 billion asset management business they're taking fees off. And when they take fees, it's not just a management fee on the equity like a hedge fund — they take a management fee on the whole kit and caboodle, equity and debt. So it ends up being a pretty juicy fee stream.

The company just blew up because they got everybody too excited. There was some chop on the call, but everything seems totally fine and the fundamentals seem totally intact. FELE — Franklin Electric — LONG — Dennis Vishni, Ararat Capital

• The setup. An old-world industrial best known for residential groundwater well pumps, run by a conservative CEO for two decades. • Leg 1 — data center. The new CEO's enclosures background is in cooling distribution units. Franklin is leveraging its pumps, motors and drives expertise to get spec'd into hyperscalers' next-generation CDU designs and into OEMs. Work began with those OEMs in Q4 2025 and the company is fairly certain of orders by year end. Vontier, the largest competitor, is forcing a replacement cycle at the end of life of its monitoring product. Transcript:

FELE — Long — Dennis Vishni, Ararat Capital

My name is Dennis Vishni, chairman analyst at Ararat Capital. The stock I'm pitching long is Franklin Electric, ticker FELE, $4.5 billion market cap.

Franklin is a bit of an old-world industrial business, best known for water pumps that go into residential groundwater systems — think a well in your backyard. The company was run by an older, conservative CEO for two decades, but he was replaced at the end of 2024 by the president of nVent's enclosures business. That guy, Joe, has come in and changed up a lot within the business.

The thesis has three parts. First, given Joe's background in the enclosures business, which is focused on cooling distribution units, he came to Franklin to leverage their experience in pumping systems — pumps, motors and drives — to sell into the data center, specifically to get designed into hyperscalers' next-generation CDU models and into OEMs. I've done a bunch of work, spoke to the CFO several times, spoke to people in the industry including somebody currently at nVent. Franklin started working with those OEMs in Q4 of 2025 to get spec'd into their next generation. The company is pretty certain they'll get orders by the end of this year. The opportunity is significant if you're familiar with the CDU market, and I don't think it's reflected in sell-side estimates or priced into the stock at all.

The second piece is the company's energy systems business — pumping systems for the forecourt of a gas station, everything under the pump that pumps into your car. About 30% of that segment is software. The largest competitor is Vontier, and they're currently forcing a replacement cycle based on the end of life of their monitoring product. Franklin is going to that installed base with a full monitoring software and hardware system at the same price as the module replacement Vontier is pushing, to gain market share and win more software revenue — cheaper price to get the recurring revenue. Another opportunity not really reflected in street numbers, and the company has only started to talk about it.

The third is a significant margin opportunity from unintegrated acquisitions and, as I said, the previous sleepy old management team. They're having an investor day in March 2027 to outline all of this. I think there are several hundred basis points of margin opportunity in every segment. The data center opportunity is about a dollar of EPS in 2028 above the street, energy systems is something like 50 cents, and the margin opportunity plays into some of that $1.50 of upside as well. That's the idea in a nutshell.

COMP — Compass — LONG — Mitch Shapiro, Clearline Capital

• The company. Largest residential real estate brokerage, about $11.50 per share, $9.5B market cap, $12B EV. Merged with Anywhere in January; roughly 80,000 agents.

• The obvious case. Torque to an existing-home recovery. They are outperforming the overall housing market by about 1,000 basis points every quarter, largely because high-end luxury keeps outgrowing a weaker broad market.

• The actual thesis. You do not need a big housing recovery — the cost and margin story is what matters.

• Synergies and sandbagging. Still targeting $420M of OpEx synergies through 2028, with about $150M in the bank through 2026. Management has intimated upside to the targets while saying the pace slows — comments he reads as cutting against each other and setting up another guidance raise in H2 or early 2027.

• The street's error. 2027 and 2028 OpEx looks way too high. Management guides core pre-synergy OpEx growth of 3–4%; grow 2026's $2.8B at 3.5% and subtract $120–150M of synergies and you get flat to slightly down, versus the street up 3%.

• Gross margin. The broader brokerage market is turning more rational and legacy Compass gross margins are actually improving as one-time per-transaction agent fees and programmatic advertising layer in — despite very negative mix as the highest-performing agents keep outperforming. Last quarter had an outsized California benefit from AI wealth creation.

• Targets. $15 on 2027 numbers; roughly $22 through-cycle, or about 100% upside. Previously bucketed as an AI loser by Citrini, now turning into a winner.

Transcript:

COMP — Long — Mitch Shapiro, Clearline Capital

Mitch here from Clearline Capital, pitching Compass long, ticker COMP. About $11.50 today, $9.5 billion market cap and about $12 billion EV. Most of you know Compass, so I don't need much detail — it's the largest residential real estate brokerage. They merged with Anywhere in January and now have about 80,000 agents on the platform.

The obvious case is that it's a great way to play the existing-home recovery, with great torque to the housing market. They continue to outperform the overall housing market by about a thousand basis points every quarter, largely because high-end luxury homes continue to outgrow the overall market — the broad-based housing tracks are a little weaker, but luxury continues to outperform.

What I really like is that you don't need a big housing recovery for the thesis to play out. The more interesting side is the cost and margin story. They're still targeting $420 million of OpEx synergies through 2028, with about $150 million in the bank through 2026. They've intimated there will be upside to these synergy targets over time, though the pace will slow. A lot of these comments cut against each other, and I think management is setting themselves up for another guidance raise in the back half of the year or early 2027.

I think street OpEx looks way too high in 2027 and 2028. Management talks about core OpEx growth pre-synergies of 3% to 4% a year. Do the math on 2026 OpEx of $2.8 billion, grow it at 3.5%, subtract $120 to $150 million of synergies, and you get flat to slightly down OpEx — versus the street up 3%.

One of the interesting things is that the broader brokerage market is becoming a bit more rational, and legacy Compass gross margins are actually improving as they layer on additional one-time transaction fees for agents — even though the mix has been extremely negative because the highest-performing agents continue to outperform. Last quarter had an outsized benefit in California due to everybody getting rich on AI. They're starting to roll out more of these transaction fees, so you're getting a little more margin accretion over time.

On 2027 numbers I have about a $15 price target, and through the cycle, a bit more normalized, I get to about 100% upside or a $22 price target. I think it was bucketed as an AI loser by Citrini, and now it's turning into a winner. That's it for me.

Close — Eric Ritter

Thanks, Mitch, really appreciate that. I think that's it — it's 2:54 and I've got a bunch of ideas. Thank you everyone for being on. If you have any questions please reach out, and we'll do this again soon. Again, we'll have notes if you'd like them.

AZUL — Azul — LONG — Ben Ziff, Black Barn

• The pitch, self-aware. One of three commercial passenger airlines in Brazil. Historically a low-double-digit grower doing $1.5B of EBITDA at a 34% margin, against a $1.4B market cap — 4x P/E and roughly 3x 2027 consensus EBITDA. He opened by acknowledging how few people would pitch a recently restructured Brazilian airline equity in 2026.

• Why Brazil is not the US. Where relentless US competition drives economic profits to zero, this is a moated business with a fresh balance sheet in an underpenetrated market — the strongest per-liter unit profitability in the Americas.

• The moat. There is not enough demand on regional Brazilian routes to serve them with large Airbus and Boeing aircraft. Over the last decade Azul built an unusual mixed fleet running from seven-seaters up to 300-plus-seat A330s, so the other two carriers cannot fly its routes profitably. Result: 82% of Azul routes are a monopoly and it is the leading provider on more than 90%.

• Post-reorg state. Restructured in 2025, emerged in Q1 2026 with the youngest fleet in the Americas and renegotiated below-market leases. Historically a premium multiple name.

• Why the discount exists. A tough post-reorg technical, lost sell-side coverage during the filing (under-followed), H1 2026 results that were strong but noisy with non-recurring restructuring items, and a planned fleet reduction misread as a demand problem.

• What changes it. Those planes come back in H2 2026, when Latin American airlines generate essentially all their cash flow. Near-term catalysts: quarterly index inclusion, analyst initiations, discounted stock and bond buybacks (running the LATAM post-reorg playbook from 2023), and the Hormuz fuel headwind turning into a tailwind as they sell at higher prices and face market fuel cost months later.

• Valuation. A 25% levered free cash flow yield and a greater than 50% discount to peers GOL and LATAM.

Transcript:

AZUL — Long — Ben Ziff, Black Barn

I'll be pitching Azul equity, A-Z-U-L, one of three commercial passenger airlines in Brazil. To orient folks: historically a low-double-digit grower doing $1.5 billion US of EBITDA at a 34% margin. That's against a $1.4 billion market cap, trading at 4x P/E and about 3x 2027 EBITDA on consensus.

Who on planet earth is crazy enough to pitch a recently restructured Brazilian airline equity in 2026? Two answers. Number one, me — I'm that crazy, and I forgot to take my antipsychotics today, so you're stuck with this one. Number two, more importantly, it's decently interesting and more nuanced.

The short and sweet of it: unlike US airlines, where relentless competition drives economic profits to zero, Brazil is a very different setup. We think this is a very moated business with a fresh balance sheet in an underpenetrated market. They have the strongest per-liter unit profitability across all of the Americas. Despite that, they trade at a 25% levered free cash flow yield and a greater than 50% discount to all the relevant peers, GOL and LATAM.

Prior to the 2025 restructuring they were a premium name. Our view is that today's discount is driven by a tough post-reorg technical and a complex story — Hormuz, the Brazilian election coming up, and so on in this exact moment. But fundamentally we think there's really nothing wrong with the business, and there's a lot of convexity and upside levers to be pulled as those headwinds roll off.

On the moat: Azul is a regional provider in Brazil, one of three carriers. There simply isn't enough demand to serve those markets with giant Airbus and Boeing planes. Over the last decade they developed a frankly bizarre mixed fleet, carrying planes as small as seven-seaters all the way up to A330s with 300-plus seats. As a result, the other two competitors really cannot fly the routes Azul flies profitably at the density Azul has. So we've seen a rational market: today 82% of Azul's routes are a monopoly, and they're the leading provider by market share on over 90%.

They restructured in 2025 and emerged recently, in Q1 2026, with the youngest fleet across the Americas and renegotiated below-market lease deals — a great outcome fundamentally. On the technical side: they lost sell-side coverage when they filed, so it's been under-followed. The first half of 2026 was frankly very strong but very noisy with non-recurring and restructuring one-offs. And they lost part of their fleet, which I think the market misunderstood as a demand issue — but it was planned, and they get those planes back in the back half of the year, when Latin American airlines really generate all their cash flow anyway.

So: the business is exceptionally cheap and it's a great business. Over the months ahead we think there's quarterly index inclusion and analyst initiations. I think the company will pursue discounted stock and bond buybacks, running the LATAM Airlines post-reorg playbook from 2023. And at some point this Hormuz headwind turns into a tailwind, as you sell at higher prices and then face the market cost of fuel months later.

ASTS — AST SpaceMobile — SHORT — Paul (Holwick)

• The business. Building a constellation of roughly 65 very large satellites to enable direct cell-phone-to-satellite voice connectivity. Stock has run up substantially on space-sector hype.

• Execution. Satellites appear to cost over $100M each. One was written off at a loss of more than $100M about six months ago after being deposited at the wrong altitude.

• Launch is the binding constraint. Key launch partner Blue Origin suffered a catastrophic explosion at its launch pad and is sidelined for about a year. Additional SpaceX slots run out past October. Service therefore looks unlikely before mid-calendar 2028 at the earliest.

• Financials. Quarterly cash burn above $500M against roughly $25.5B enterprise value, with a fair amount of insider selling.

• Demand risk even if built. Most people are already well served by terrestrial networks and are not in dead zones for long. Direct-to-satellite has latency issues, weak signal strength, and does not work indoors.

• The analogy. “I think this is Iridium Part 2.” One of their favorite shorts.

Transcript:

ASTS — Short — Paul (Holwick)

My apologies, I'm a little disorganized today. We had a couple of those education companies, Universal Technical Institute and Lincoln, that both blew up recently, so it seems like a fertile area.

I was going to pitch AST SpaceMobile short. This company has run up quite a bit over the last couple of years on hype in the space sector. They're trying to put in place a constellation of satellites — I think they need 65 — to enable cell-phone-to-satellite connectivity for voice communications.

They've had all sorts of obstacles getting the constellation into space. These are really large satellites, and the cost of each seems to be over $100 million — because they had one that had an accident, which they had to write off because it was deposited at the wrong altitude in space. They ended up taking over a $100 million loss on that satellite, I think about six months ago.

More recently they've had further obstacles with Blue Origin having that catastrophic explosion at their launch pad. Blue Origin is their key partner for getting satellites into space, and with Blue Origin sidelined for the next year or so, they're really kind of stuck. They've been able to get a number of additional satellites up on SpaceX, but I think once you go past October they won't have additional launch slots on SpaceX for quite a long time. So they're not going to get this constellation up and running and ready to deliver service until probably mid-calendar 2028 at the earliest.

In the meantime the company is spending a ton of money building satellites. Quarterly cash burn is over $500 million. The enterprise value is around $25.5 billion. There's been a fair amount of insider selling.

And at the end of the day, even if they get the constellation up and running, it's not clear to us anyone is really going to use it to any meaningful degree, simply because most people are already well served with terrestrial cell phone service. The large wireless carriers have set-it-and-forget-it customers; most people are not in dead cell zones for long periods. And there are other limitations to direct-to-satellite service: a latency issue, a signal strength problem, and you can't be indoors — you have to be outside.

So bottom line: huge financial obstacles to get the constellation running, and once they get there, no guarantee they'll ever have meaningful revenues to support the business. It's one of our favorite short ideas. The industry has had quite a few bankruptcies over the years — I remember Iridium quite well in the early 2000s. I think this is Iridium Part 2.

3a. Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD) Merger Arb — Long the spread

Joe Flaum, Newbrook Capital

• Setup: Paramount/Skydance–WBD deal has cleared federal and international antitrust approval. Only remaining obstacle is a California state AG lawsuit.

• Recent developments: Judge granted a short preliminary-injunction window and a March trial date — seen as favorable to the state, which pushed the spread/stock toward $25 and the timeline out to March. Since then: California’s current governor and the leading gubernatorial candidate have both publicly voiced support for a settlement; unions have written in favor of the deal closing; movie theater chains support it (with committed theatrical release minimums).

• View: Deal likely settles in 2026 (post-election) or before the March trial; if it goes to trial, the state’s legal merits are seen as weak with little precedent on its side. Ticking fee protects downside while waiting. Implied deal probability discussed as ~60–65%.

• Risk: The presiding judge’s rulings so far have leaned favorable to the state.

Transcript:

3. Warner Bros. Discovery / Spotify — Joe Flaum, Newbrook Capital

“Two ideas — I’ll be quick on the first since it’s a hard-catalyst play. We like the Warner Bros. Discovery deal closing — still a double-digit spread. What’s changed in the last few weeks: we’ve cleared basically everything — federally approved, internationally approved. The only thing left is a state AG lawsuit in California.

The stock initially traded down toward $25 when the judge granted a short window toward a preliminary injunction ruling, which suggested bias since it didn’t give the companies a chance to present a defense. The companies then said they wouldn’t close until the AG matter is settled. Subsequently, the judge was also favorable to the states and set a March trial date — pushing expectations of a September close out to March, which is roughly where the spread bottomed.

Since then we’ve gotten some things going the other direction. We think either way this settles in March — the merits of the case are, frankly, fairly weak — but the practical reality is that everyone, including the current California governor and the leading gubernatorial candidate in the upcoming election, has publicly said they favor a settlement. Several unions have written letters wanting the deal to close. Movie theater chains support it, with agreements guaranteeing them a minimum number of big theatrical releases per year. So basically everyone favors this deal except a state AG with some political ambitions.

We think once you get past the election, there’ll be negotiations and potentially a settlement this year. Worst case, you collect a ticking fee through March and get a settlement before trial, or if it goes the distance, any expert would say the merits favor the companies — there’s almost no precedent for a court ruling in the state’s favor. The only wildcard is that this particular judge’s rulings so far have leaned a bit biased toward the state. On pricing: depending on spread/timing and where you think it breaks, call it 60–65% implied probability, worth $3–4 of upside depending on timing/ticking fee.

Quickly on more of a GARP idea — we like Spotify. High-quality business, renegotiated all three major label deals last year, giving them the ability to unbundle, take price, and participate in margin. They had an investor day recently giving a multi-year aspiration toward 40% gross margins — you can pencil to $50+ of free cash flow per share; pick your multiple, and you can compound in the high teens-plus over the next few years. Near-term, there’s some excitement around product launches, including an AI-related ‘remix’ feature — though honestly this isn’t really an AI stock, we’re not trying to force that narrative.”

6. Stellantis (STLA) — Short

Squarepoint Capital

• Business: European/US multi-brand automaker (Jeep, RAM, Chrysler in the US; ~15 brands in Europe).

• Thesis: Structural share loser; Q2 was likely peak earnings and already missed by ~27%. North America/Europe margins are near breakeven-to-negative once adjusted for accounting changes (R&D capitalization ratio raised from 47% to 55%, flattering margins). The one genuinely profitable region, Latin America (~15% margins), is facing increasing Chinese competition.

• Balance sheet: Superficially fine, but net debt is understated via heavy receivables factoring (a short-term fix); inventory sits at ~180 days vs. peers’ 35–40 days, and the company is reportedly paying fleet/rental customers to hold cars longer to avoid worsening the inventory optics.

• Expectation: ~$5bn/year cash burn; likely dividend cut and/or rights issue within ~6 months.

• Hedge suggestion: Pair the short with a long in Volvo or Renault (better structural businesses) to isolate stock-specific risk from sector-wide risk (e.g., possible EU tariffs on Chinese EVs); Stellantis short interest is already ~2x peers.

• Risk: EU tariff action against Chinese imports could take pressure off the whole sector; China could also retaliate against Europe if such tariffs were imposed.

Transcript:

6. Stellantis — Squarepoint Capital

“I’m pitching a short — I think this stock goes to zero. It’s Stellantis (STLA). The auto industry being under pressure isn’t news, but I think this is a structural share loser. They over-committed for a long time; I think Q2 was peak earnings, and it already missed by 27%. Market share in North America and Europe is under pressure; margins there are barely positive on paper, and actually negative once you adjust for accounting changes. The one region that’s still genuinely profitable is Latin America, at about 15% margins — but Chinese competitors are coming in aggressively there too, and we expect those margins to shrink.

Net-net, they’ll generate about $5bn of cash burn a year, we think they’ll need to cut the dividend within about six months, and probably need a rights issue. The balance sheet looks okay at first glance but net debt is understated. They’ve changed accounting — capitalizing more R&D (from 47% to 55%), which flatters margins. Inventory is running at about 180 days versus 35–40 days for other players. We did dealer checks and found they’ve started paying fleet/rental companies to hold cars longer, because they don’t want the inventory coming back — they can’t sell it. They’ve guided second half higher than first half, which we think the market doesn’t fully appreciate the pressure behind.

On brands: in the US they make RAM, Jeep, Wagoneer; in Europe they have about 15 brands from years of acquisitions. They’ve done a technical joint venture with a third-tier Chinese company to use their plant to avoid tariffs, but that’s almost a poison pill — it lets a competitor take share while using your own capacity.

The risk to the short is Europe imposing tariffs on Chinese cars, which is possible — we’d hedge that by pairing the short with a long in Volvo or Renault, since their underlying businesses are structurally better, and Stellantis’s short interest is already about double peers’. On the balance sheet: they’re doing a lot of receivables factoring, which makes net debt look lower than it is — a short-term fix, since those receivables eventually come due.”

Q&A: Why has this persisted so long: European consumers may have more purchasing power to absorb pricier cars vs. Chinese alternatives than assumed; EU policy toward Chinese autos is fragmented across countries with different brand ownership and interests, so any coordinated tariff response takes time — and China has retaliatory leverage of its own.

7. DraftKings (DKNG) — Long

Frank, Longaeva Capital — prediction markets theme

• Setup: DKNG/FLUT sold off on fear that prediction markets (Kalshi, Polymarket) fragment sports betting from a duopoly into a 6-player market.

• Thesis: Prediction markets are actually a major tailwind — they effectively achieve nationwide legalization of sports betting overnight by sidestepping state-by-state licensing (roughly half the country is currently a legal sportsbook state; prediction markets open the other half). DraftKings already runs a “one app” strategy live in all states and is about to market its own prediction product hard starting with NFL season; no one is modeling this upside yet (treated as a 2026 headline risk rather than a 2027 opportunity).

• Math: Sees ~50%+ EBITDA upside in 2027 from prediction markets alone; stock trades ~12x 2027 EBITDA excluding that upside — a double is achievable on the combination of higher numbers and a re-rated multiple.

• Share-loss pushback: Believes reported share loss to Kalshi is mostly “sharp” (professional, negative-EV) bettors leaving, not core recreational users — DKNG’s own engagement data shows only ~1–2% wallet-share shift, with growth still accelerating.

• Why DKNG structurally wins: DKNG acts as a bookmaker (~15% hold) vs. Kalshi/Polymarket acting as an exchange (~4% take) — the exchange model is inherently less profitable at scale; also no state taxes apply to prediction-market gross profit, improving DKNG’s margin as it scales its own product.

• Related longs: Sportradar (SRAD) and Genius Sports (GENI) — correlated to DKNG handle, sold off similarly, still have room to recover; Robinhood (HOOD) now earns more from prediction/event markets than equity trading — a partial hedge/read-through.

• Risk: Supreme Court could rule against the prediction-market sports-betting structure (base case ~2027, viewed as a coin flip) — but even a ban is seen as bullish for DKNG since it removes the “competitive threat” narrative entirely (even though the upside also wouldn’t be priced in yet).

Transcript:

7. DraftKings — Frank, Longaeva Capital

“My theme is prediction markets. Everyone’s seen the Kalshi ads — they’ve raised a ton of money at big valuations and are using the proceeds to spend aggressively on customer acquisition. My favorite way to play prediction markets is actually through the online sportsbooks — DraftKings specifically, which got crushed alongside the traditional operators on fear these entrants shrink the market from a duopoly to a six-player market and everyone loses.

If you told me two years ago that sports betting would effectively be legalized nationwide, the stock would be at $80. We’ve effectively just done that. DraftKings has built a ‘one app’ strategy — log in from New York to California, it looks the same, it’s just routed as a prediction market in states without traditional sports betting. Heading into NFL season they’re going to spend real marketing money behind it. No one has prediction-market upside in their models yet — if anything it’s treated as a 2026 headline risk, when it should be a 2027 tailwind.

My math: prediction markets could add roughly 50%+ to 2027 EBITDA. The stock trades around 12x 2027 EBITDA excluding that. If this flips from headwind to tailwind narrative, you get a combination of higher numbers and multiple re-rating that gets you to a double.

Adjacent plays: Sportradar and Genius Sports — sports-data/media names correlated to DraftKings handle, also crushed, with room to recover. And interestingly, Robinhood now makes more money from prediction markets than equity trading — an interesting hedge.”

Q&A: “People think prediction markets are a headwind, but DraftKings is going to launch its own prediction product — they’ve barely started marketing it (a bit during the World Cup). On share loss — the data we’ve done, and what the company will tell you, is they’re not really losing meaningful share; what share is moving to Kalshi looks like ‘sharp’ (professional, negative-EV) bettors, not core recreational users. DraftKings’ own users are actually growing, with growth accelerating this quarter (some comp-driven, but directionally real) — wallet-share analysis suggests maybe 1–2% shift to Kalshi, essentially flat/steady otherwise. On a Supreme Court ban risk — our base case is a 2027 ruling, call it a coin toss — but ironically, a ban is bullish for these stocks since it removes the competitive threat narrative entirely (even though it also means the prediction-market upside never gets priced in). On the size of the opportunity — decriminalization/legalization matters less than simply doubling the addressable market by opening up the roughly half the country that’s currently illegal for sports betting; prediction markets achieve that without technically decriminalizing sports betting, since they’re run as a different product on top. On profitability — Kalshi and Polymarket both lose money because they run an exchange model (roughly a 4% take), whereas DraftKings makes markets and holds roughly 15% — a structurally more profitable model; also no state taxes apply to prediction-market gross profit, so margins there are actually better than the traditional sportsbook.”

• Thesis: Renegotiated all three major label deals last year, enabling unbundling, price increases, and margin participation. 13b. Manufactured Housing (Skyline Champion / Cavco) — Long

Vikash, Duquesne Family Office

• Setup: Recent federal housing legislation plus new state-level zoning reform in Texas, Florida, and Virginia (effective within ~6 months) mandating zoning allowances for manufactured housing. These three states alone represent ~35–40% of US manufactured housing sales.

• Thesis: Manufactured home quality has improved dramatically over 20 years — often visually indistinguishable from site-built homes — and zoning, not demand or quality, has been the binding constraint. Manufactured housing was once ~25% of all US homes vs. a small fraction today; volumes (~100K homes/year currently, an oligopoly industry) could double or triple over the next 5 years as zoning reform takes hold.

• How to play it: Skyline Champion (SKY) and Cavco (CVCO) — author owns both rather than picking a favorite.

Transcript:

13. Crown Castle / Manufactured Housing — Vikash, Duquesne Family Office

Crown Castle: “There’s a concern that SpaceX will build out a satellite network that competes with ground-based cell networks. The entire telecom sector has been quiet about this — the assumption is SpaceX builds ground-based cellular using their own satellites/dishes, which we think is physically not really possible at real scale. So they’ll need to rely on existing cell towers to build a ground network — either by pursuing an MVNO deal (there were rumors around Charter, which currently has an MVNO with Verizon) or by building out their own infrastructure.

On the MVNO route: even though 85% of Charter’s mobile usage happens on their own hotspots, the remaining 15% that runs over Verizon’s network is important — and that traffic wouldn’t transfer if Charter ever did an MVNO deal with SpaceX instead. Other carriers (AT&T, T-Mobile, owned by Deutsche Telekom) — you can run through the scenarios, but you consistently land on SpaceX needing to build at least part of a ground network. The biggest beneficiaries of that would be the existing cell tower players.

In the scenario where SpaceX has to build out like the other carriers, it’s almost like adding a fourth major tenant, increasing revenue for tower companies by as much as ~30-40%. Crown Castle, American Tower (AMT), and SBA are the three main players; Crown Castle is almost entirely US, while AMT and SBA have meaningful non-US exposure, so Crown Castle is the most levered pure-play. Crown Castle also has a quirk: because they bought many of their towers from AT&T and Verizon years ago, those leases had only a 2% annual escalator versus the typical 3% — so their current rents are below market, giving extra re-lease upside. In the extreme scenario where SpaceX fully builds out, we think Crown Castle’s revenue could rise roughly 40%, with about 90% of that flowing through to EBITDA. Even in the more modest scenario — SpaceX offering mobile mainly in areas without existing coverage (e.g., rural/national park areas) — existing towers still benefit over time as SpaceX’s ambitions expand.”

Q&A: “Why isn’t SpaceX talking about this? Probably because the fastest path for them is signing an MVNO with a major carrier, but it’s a prisoner’s dilemma — whoever signs first gets wholesale revenue but also helps build a future competitor, so no one wants to go first. Even with an MVNO, the economics likely wouldn’t be great for SpaceX, based on the Charter/Verizon precedent — 85% of Charter’s traffic still runs over its own hotspots, meaning SpaceX likely isn’t making real money purely from an MVNO relationship; it’s more about eventually monetizing their own network. The real offsetting risk: if SpaceX takes real share, carriers may cut back their own network capex — but tower rent is only about 4% of a typical carrier’s opex, so I don’t think this is a place carriers can meaningfully cut to offset SpaceX-related pressure; real damage to towers would require industry consolidation to fewer carriers, not just some share shift to SpaceX.”

Manufactured Housing: “Separate theme — there’s been federal housing legislation that doesn’t do much directly for traditional single-family housing, but does a lot for manufactured housing. In addition, Texas, Florida, and Virginia have all recently passed zoning reform bills specifically enabling manufactured housing — effective within the next six months. Those three states alone account for roughly 35-40% of US manufactured housing sales (Texas alone ~20-25%).

You genuinely can’t tell a manufactured home from a site-built home visually anymore — quality has improved enormously over the past 20 years. People still picture a trailer park, but these homes assembled on-site today are comparable to traditional construction. The reason manufactured housing isn’t bigger is mostly zoning, which is now partially being addressed. The industry currently produces around 100,000 homes a year — an oligopoly — and I think volumes could double or triple over the next five years as zoning restrictions ease. It used to be as much as 25% of all US homes historically, versus a small fraction today, so there’s a long runway back toward historical norms.

The two names to play this are Skyline Champion and Cavco — both trade at somewhat higher multiples already, but we own both rather than picking a favorite.”

8. APR Corp (Korea: 278470) — Long

Grace Li — K-beauty theme

• Theme: K-beauty is the fastest-growing category in global beauty; Korean beauty exports up ~30% in 1H26 and accelerating. Social media (TikTok, Instagram, Amazon) has eroded the distribution/ad-spend moat that let incumbents (L’Oréal, Estée Lauder) dominate, letting Korean brands go viral and scale direct without big ad budgets.

• APR specifics: Korea’s largest K-beauty platform, best known for Medicube (home beauty devices, now expanding into full skincare/cosmetics); triple-digit growth for 8 consecutive quarters, guided 50–80% growth for the rest of the year; industry-leading customer retention/repeat-purchase rates. Currently expanding into US offline retail (Walmart, Costco, Target, Nordstrom, CVS) plus Europe, Latin America, and the Middle East.

• Valuation framework: ~$2.5bn revenue today; benchmarked against established global dermatology/cosmetics brands (e.g., L’Oréal’s dermal brands, worth $6–8bn), author expects APR to reach that scale within 18–24 months, potentially becoming the #2 global beauty platform by ~2028. Trades ~18x on ~250% current growth (normalizing toward a still-strong 20–30%+).

• Pair idea: Long APR against a basket of legacy incumbents (L’Oréal, Estée Lauder, select Chinese brands) that lack TikTok/Amazon-native marketing sophistication.

• Risk raised in Q&A: A “Botox is the last chapter” argument — consumer preference shifting toward less invasive, ingredient-innovation skincare/boosters — plus a Korean licensing competitor possibly entering similar categories next year.

Transcript:

8. APR Corp (Korea, 278470) — Grace Li

“K-beauty is currently the fastest-growing category in global beauty markets — high-teens to twenties growth. Korea’s export data for the first half of 2026 shows about 30% growth, and it’s continuing to accelerate into the back half. Korean brands have a powerful internal ecosystem — ODM/OEM manufacturing, ingredient innovation, and social-media-savvy marketing. Historically, incumbents like L’Oréal and Estée Lauder built brands on massive distribution and advertising budgets that were a huge barrier to entry. TikTok, Instagram, Amazon, and direct-to-consumer channels have significantly weakened those barriers — a Korean brand can identify a standout ingredient or product, launch through its own distribution, and go viral globally without needing a traditional distribution network.

My favorite way to play this is APR (278470 KS), the largest K-beauty brand/platform right now, growing triple-digit for eight consecutive quarters, guided to continue 50–80% revenue growth through the rest of the year. The reason it keeps compounding is that it’s transitioning from a single viral product — the Medicube home beauty device — into a full global beauty brand and platform, adding cosmetics and skincare lines that drive customer acquisition and repeat purchase; they have the highest retention/repeat-purchase rate we’ve tracked among beauty brands, and are now expanding distribution offline into the US (Walmart, Costco, Target, Nordstrom, CVS) plus Europe, Latin America, and the Middle East.

They’re currently doing a bit under $2.5bn of revenue — already the largest Korean beauty company pursuing this export strategy. Benchmarked against successful incumbent dermatology/skincare/cosmetics brands (like some of the dermal brands under L’Oréal), which are worth $6–8bn, I think it takes APR about 18–24 months to get there, potentially becoming the second-largest global beauty platform around 2028. The reason for the success is execution — product innovation, ingredient innovation, and offering the most effective products at attractive prices relative to incumbents, reflected in the highest customer retention and increasing wallet share taken from incumbents.

On the short side of the theme — the incumbents, because of their lack of innovation and less sophisticated use of TikTok/Instagram/Amazon, are going to keep losing this race. APR alone is a meaningful driver of growth in Amazon’s beauty category, which is now accelerating to about 25%.”

Q&A: “Currently growing about 250%, trading around 18x. On the sustainability of growth — even normalizing to something like 20–30%, that’s still fast for the multiple, especially since we’ve been waiting for the ‘next fad brand wipes them out’ bear case to play out for eight quarters, and it hasn’t — they’re a very disciplined, intentional company about where they spend marketing and R&D dollars, and have consistently executed above consensus.” On the “Botox is the last chapter” comment — a personal view that consumer preference is shifting toward less invasive, ingredient-innovation-led skincare boosters over injectables like Botox, and that a Korean licensing player may launch a competing product next year — flagged as something to watch, not a reason to avoid the position.

10. Newell Brands (NWL) — Long

Cooper Creek

• Business: Consumer products conglomerate (Sharpie, Rubbermaid, home/kitchen and learning-and-development brands); ~$6 stock.

• Thesis: Turnaround delayed last year by tariffs and a weak consumer, now back on track under CEO Chris Peterson (former CFO). SKU rationalization (from 100+ down to ~50–60 manageable SKUs) plus a “SharkNinja-style” playbook — low-cost innovation and social-media-driven marketing — is reigniting broad-based top-line growth.

• Numbers: Street models Q3 about right, but Q4 (~1% top-line Street vs. author’s 2–3%) and next year (~2% Street vs. author’s 4%) look too low; operating margin next year likely ~10.5–11% vs. Street’s ~9.5%, driving EPS toward $0.88–0.90 vs. Street’s ~$0.60.

• Valuation: Historically traded 12–15x+; peers (Church & Dwight, Colgate) support a mid-teens multiple. Sees the stock roughly doubling ($6 to $12–16) over 9–18 months as the turnaround becomes visible in Q3/Q4 results.

Transcript:

10. Newell Brands — Cooper Creek

“A $6 stock I think is worth $12–16 over the next nine months to a year and a half. The turnaround story got interrupted last year — now getting back into stride. Upside to Q3/Q4 numbers — Street is too low on the top line. I think you actually have a pretty good management team that got camouflaged by last year’s issues, which were effectively tariffs and a very unsettled consumer. The turnaround is breathing again, and you saw it start in the Q2 numbers — growth for the first time in a while.

What’s great is it’s broad-based across all their consumer brands. The company has done a good job simplifying — historically it had something like a hundred-plus SKUs and a mess of categories; the CEO, Chris Peterson, the former CFO, has taken a very disciplined approach: cut SKUs down to about 50–60 well-managed core products, and layered in a page from the SharkNinja playbook — basic, low-cost innovation plus a real social-media presence. That story is now taking hold, turning a boring, unloved US consumer name into something with a bit of innovation buzz.

Numbers: Q2 was a step in the right direction. Q3 the Street’s modeling is roughly right, but Q4 the Street only has about 1% top-line growth — I think they do 2–3%. Next year the Street has about 2% top-line growth — I think it ends up being about 4%. The bigger point is the Street isn’t modeling next year’s operating margin correctly — instead of ~9.5%, I think they do 10.5–11%, and instead of about $0.60 of EPS, I think they do $0.88–0.90.

Historically this stock traded at a 12–15x-plus multiple. It’s currently much lower. If you look at comparable consumer names people feel comfortable owning — Church & Dwight, Colgate — a mid-teens multiple is justifiable. Combine EPS upside with a multiple re-rating and this could be a double from here. This story was very exciting a year and a half ago before last year’s tariff/consumer issues derailed it — the market is willing to pay up for this name again if it’s executing, especially with the SharkNinja-style playbook showing what’s possible when you put a little life into fairly boring household products.”

4. Natera (NTRA) — Long

Henry, Castle Hook

• Business: Blood-based test (MRD/liquid biopsy) that detects cancer recurrence roughly a year before it would show up on imaging.

• Thesis: Early-innings S-curve penetration story, growing ~50%; pharma is beginning to use the test as a clinical trial endpoint rather than waiting on imaging. 12. Mosaic — Castle Hook Partners

“My theme is commodity markets becoming less reliable — a lot of very boring, overlooked commodities are becoming genuinely hard to source, tied to broader mass destruction/demand-deferral dynamics. I think demand deferral creates opportunity because eventually demand has to come back, into a world with more supply of the underlying input cost. Mosaic is probably the most interesting of the fertilizer names — the second-largest fertilizer producer globally, with two main products: one fairly standard, and a second whose input cost is essentially a waste byproduct that historically has been very cheap.

Second, because the input cost is now roughly 4x higher, that’s incentivizing more supply of the byproduct itself (from changes in refining behavior), which should eventually bring that input cost back down. 7. DraftKings (DKNG) — Long

• Setup: DKNG/FLUT sold off on fear that prediction markets (Kalshi, Polymarket) fragment sports betting from a duopoly into a 6-player market.

• Thesis: Prediction markets are actually a major tailwind — they effectively achieve nationwide legalization of sports betting overnight by sidestepping state-by-state licensing (roughly half the country is currently a legal sportsbook state; prediction markets open the other half). • Share-loss pushback: Believes reported share loss to Kalshi is mostly “sharp” (professional, negative-EV) bettors leaving, not core recreational users — DKNG’s own engagement data shows only ~1–2% wallet-share shift, with growth still accelerating.

• Why DKNG structurally wins: DKNG acts as a bookmaker (~15% hold) vs. Kalshi/Polymarket acting as an exchange (~4% take) — the exchange model is inherently less profitable at scale; also no state taxes apply to prediction-market gross profit, improving DKNG’s margin as it scales its own product.

• Related longs: Sportradar (SRAD) and Genius Sports (GENI) — correlated to DKNG handle, sold off similarly, still have room to recover; Robinhood (HOOD) now earns more from prediction/event markets than equity trading — a partial hedge/read-through.

• Risk: Supreme Court could rule against the prediction-market sports-betting structure (base case ~2027, viewed as a coin flip) — but even a ban is seen as bullish for DKNG since it removes the “competitive threat” narrative entirely (even though the upside also wouldn’t be priced in yet).

7. DraftKings — Frank, Longaeva Capital

“My theme is prediction markets. Everyone’s seen the Kalshi ads — they’ve raised a ton of money at big valuations and are using the proceeds to spend aggressively on customer acquisition. My math: prediction markets could add roughly 50%+ to 2027 EBITDA. The stock trades around 12x 2027 EBITDA excluding that. If this flips from headwind to tailwind narrative, you get a combination of higher numbers and multiple re-rating that gets you to a double.

Adjacent plays: Sportradar and Genius Sports — sports-data/media names correlated to DraftKings handle, also crushed, with room to recover. And interestingly, Robinhood now makes more money from prediction markets than equity trading — an interesting hedge.”

Q&A: “People think prediction markets are a headwind, but DraftKings is going to launch its own prediction product — they’ve barely started marketing it (a bit during the World Cup). On share loss — the data we’ve done, and what the company will tell you, is they’re not really losing meaningful share; what share is moving to Kalshi looks like ‘sharp’ (professional, negative-EV) bettors, not core recreational users. DraftKings’ own users are actually growing, with growth accelerating this quarter (some comp-driven, but directionally real) — wallet-share analysis suggests maybe 1–2% shift to Kalshi, essentially flat/steady otherwise. On a Supreme Court ban risk — our base case is a 2027 ruling, call it a coin toss — but ironically, a ban is bullish for these stocks since it removes the competitive threat narrative entirely (even though it also means the prediction-market upside never gets priced in). On the size of the opportunity — decriminalization/legalization matters less than simply doubling the addressable market by opening up the roughly half the country that’s currently illegal for sports betting; prediction markets achieve that without technically decriminalizing sports betting, since they’re run as a different product on top. On profitability — Kalshi and Polymarket both lose money because they run an exchange model (roughly a 4% take), whereas DraftKings makes markets and holds roughly 15% — a structurally more profitable model; also no state taxes apply to prediction-market gross profit, so margins there are actually better than the traditional sportsbook.”

If someone pushed them to re-lever and buy back stock, they could retire something like 30% of the business within a year.
