My favorite way to play this is APR (278470 KS), the largest K-beauty brand/platform right now, growing triple-digit for eight consecutive quarters, guided to continue 50–80% revenue growth through the rest of the year. The reason it keeps compounding is that it’s transitioning from a single viral product — the Medicube home beauty device — into a full global beauty brand and platform, adding cosmetics and skincare lines that drive customer acquisition and repeat purchase; they have the highest retention/repeat-purchase rate we’ve tracked among beauty brands, and are now expanding distribution offline into the US (Walmart, Costco, Target, Nordstrom, CVS) plus Europe, Latin America, and the Middle East.

They’re currently doing a bit under $2.5bn of revenue — already the largest Korean beauty company pursuing this export strategy. Benchmarked against successful incumbent dermatology/skincare/cosmetics brands (like some of the dermal brands under L’Oréal), which are worth $6–8bn, I think it takes APR about 18–24 months to get there, potentially becoming the second-largest global beauty platform around 2028. The reason for the success is execution — product innovation, ingredient innovation, and offering the most effective products at attractive prices relative to incumbents, reflected in the highest customer retention and increasing wallet share taken from incumbents.

On the short side of the theme — the incumbents, because of their lack of innovation and less sophisticated use of TikTok/Instagram/Amazon, are going to keep losing this race. APR alone is a meaningful driver of growth in Amazon’s beauty category, which is now accelerating to about 25%.”

Q&A: “Currently growing about 250%, trading around 18x. On the sustainability of growth — even normalizing to something like 20–30%, that’s still fast for the multiple, especially since we’ve been waiting for the ‘next fad brand wipes them out’ bear case to play out for eight quarters, and it hasn’t — they’re a very disciplined, intentional company about where they spend marketing and R&D dollars, and have consistently executed above consensus.” On the “Botox is the last chapter” comment — a personal view that consumer preference is shifting toward less invasive, ingredient-innovation-led skincare boosters over injectables like Botox, and that a Korean licensing player may launch a competing product next year — flagged as something to watch, not a reason to avoid the position.
ideas.2026-08-14-myst-miko-tam-myst-tmt-idea-f:
Uber (Long) / DoorDash (SHORT) — pair — Mike Kosdan, Hudson Bay

• Long Uber: the AV narrative is turning positive. They lost Waymo in Phoenix but still have them elsewhere and appear to be at an impasse on terms rather than done. More important, near-term proof points are coming from non-Waymo AVs on the platform: Nuro with a driver in the Bay Area, Zoox driver-out in Las Vegas and the Bay Area next year. Mid-to-high-single-digit EPS upside next year.

• Short DoorDash: ~35x GAAP P/E on Street 2027, with mid-single-digit or worse risk to the number. The bull case assumes this year’s tech replatforming spend laps into a margin inflection, but there is a hidden negative margin mix shift from international growth where they have been buying companies and buying growth, while the US slows and is increasingly driven by AOV. Management also reinvests any upside.

• The core call is the valuation gap between the two has gotten way too wide — historically that converges if you are patient. 25%+ IRR over three to six months.

• Miko noted a lot of the group is positioned the other way: long DASH, short UBER.

Full pitch detail:

Uber (Long) / DoorDash (SHORT) — Mike Kosdan, Hudson Bay

I’m going to pitch a pair: long Uber, short DoorDash.

On Uber, I think the AV narrative is in the process of changing more to the positive. They lost Waymo in Phoenix but still have them in other cities, and I get the sense they’re just at an impasse on terms, so that could still come back. The market has now recalibrated on that. And even if it doesn’t happen in the next few months, they’re going to be launching with a driver in vehicles with Nuro in the Bay Area, and driver-out in Las Vegas with Zoox, and the Bay Area next year. All these AV partnerships Uber has done finally start producing near-term proof points where you have actual non-Waymo AVs being dispatched on the app.

The valuation difference between Uber and DoorDash — we’ve seen this before, and when it gets this wide it really is an opportunity, and you do tend to see convergence if you’re patient. DoorDash is trading at like 35 times GAAP P/E on Street 2027, and we think there could be mid-single-digit or more risk to that number. Uber is much cheaper on the same basis, and half of Uber’s business is food anyway. We also think there’s mid-to-high-single-digit upside at Uber next year. Pick your multiple between the two — we think the IRR on this trade over the next three to six months is at least 25% and potentially more.

On DoorDash specifically, there’s still an idea that the investments they’ve been making this year on tech replatforming get lapped next year and lead to a margin inflection, which is in both buy-side and sell-side numbers. But the more you dig into it, the clearer it is that they have a negative margin mix shift from international growth, where they’ve been buying companies and buying growth, while the US has been slowing on orders and is more driven by average order value and is just more mature. So they have a hidden margin headwind that prevents that inflection. And it’s a management team that invests whatever upside they have back into the business. But the main call is simply that the valuation gap has gotten way too wide.

Miko: a lot of guys are positioned the other way — long DoorDash, short Uber.

TTM Technologies (TTMI) — Long — Brett Lisle, Atalan Capital

• Re-pitch from May. Went from ~150–155 to 225, then gave back the entire year in the drawdown. Since then reported Q4 EPS 55% ahead of Street.

• One of the few companies that can make ultra-high-density PCBs that every AI chip sits on. Two major programs: NVIDIA switch trays (plus growing rack content) and Google TPU, where they are a primary PCB supplier.

• The underappreciated part is content, not units. PCB value per rack is rising exponentially on layers, complexity and materials — management says ASP growth is outpacing volume growth.

• Running ~$2 of EPS at Q4 run-rate versus Street at ~$7 for 2027. Stock is below 10x their 2028 number for what should be a 20–25x business. Onshoring kicker as they fill US capacity with AI customers. Over 100% upside.

• Miko flagged Golden Dome and munitions as further upside Brett did not even get to.

Full pitch detail:

TTM Technologies (TTMI) — Long — Brett Lisle, Atalan Capital

My pitch is TTMI again, and this will be brief. Last time in May it was on its way to working very well — pitched around 150 to 155, went to 225, then gave up all the gains on the year in the drawdown. I couldn’t believe how low it went. But since then they had an unbelievable quarter, with Q4 EPS 55% ahead of the Street. The numbers are explosive. I think this is a really underappreciated name and a key bottleneck in the AI infrastructure buildout.

The high level: they’re one of the few companies that can make ultra-high-density PCBs, the printed circuit boards that every AI chip needs to sit on top of. Their two major programs are NVIDIA — they provide the switch trays for the NVIDIA switches, and they’re gaining content within the rack — and the TPU, where they’re one of the primary PCB suppliers. Volume is going up dramatically in both programs.

But the really interesting thing is pricing and content growth. The value of a PCB is going up exponentially within the rack because of increasing layers, increasing complexity and more expensive materials. We’ve followed TTMI management a long time, and post-quarter they sounded the most bullish I’ve ever heard them. They’re saying ASP is going up by more than volume growth — which is pretty incredible when you think about how much TPU volume there could be.

They’re at roughly $2 of EPS on a Q4 run-rate basis. The Street is asleep at the wheel at about $7 for 2027, and we think volume and pricing grow a lot incrementally in 2027 versus Q4. There’s a great setup for these guys to annihilate numbers over the next six, twelve, eighteen months. The stock is well below 10x our 2028 EPS number, and we think this should be a 20 to 25 times business. Lastly there’s an onshoring kicker — they’re likely to fill out their US facility with AI customers and become an AI semiconductor onshoring beneficiary. Over 100% upside, hopefully in a reasonably short amount of time.

Miko: "Brett, you didn’t even get to Golden Dome and munitions. There’s just so much more left of the story."

Seagate (STX) — Long, update — Brett Lisle, Atalan Capital

• Never been more bullish on HDDs. The pricing inflection is happening sooner and to a larger degree than expected, and aggregate HDD demand keeps tracking to the upside.

• The key insight is the dollar spread, not ASP per gigabyte. With NAND up ~20x, a 32TB HDD versus a 32TB SSD has gone from a <$2,000 gap to $15,000–17,000 — a far wider pricing umbrella than previously contemplated.

• Stock is barely up over the past year despite guiding ~25% ahead of Street for the coming quarter. Earnings power described as "insane" when run out.

• HDDs are the more durable, earlier-cycle way to express the memory theme; expects rotation out of memory into HDDs. Still a memory bull, still owns Hynix.

Full pitch detail:

Seagate (STX) — Long, update — Brett Lisle, Atalan Capital

I was asked to give a quick update on Seagate before my pitch. I don’t think we’ve ever been more bullish on Seagate and on hard drives than we are right now, in the two years we’ve been following the space. Two things are really interesting.

First, the pricing inflection is happening to a larger degree and sooner than expected. Seagate is basically barely up over the past year despite guiding something like 25% ahead of the Street for this upcoming quarter, with pricing inflecting more quickly. Second, aggregate HDD demand continues to track to the upside — and with NAND potentially viewed as more stable over the long term, that gives them a broader pricing umbrella.

People typically focus on pricing on an ASP-per-gigabyte basis. I’d focus on the dollar spread gap. If a customer is buying a 32-terabyte hard drive versus a 32-terabyte SSD, and NAND prices have gone up 20x, that spread goes from historically less than $2,000 of difference to well over $15,000 to $17,000. SSD just becomes much more expensive. That gives hard drives far more of a pricing umbrella than we had been contemplating.

So pricing is going much higher than people think, and their earnings power is just insane when you run it out. Memory in general has healthy questions and skepticism around it; hard drives are a much more durable and easier way to get behind the theme, and much earlier in the pricing inflection. I’ve been expecting whoever got less bullish on memory to rotate into hard drives. For what it’s worth, I’m still a memory bull and we still own Hynix as well.

Spotify (SPOT) — Long — Joe Flaum, Newbrook

• Was going to pitch MongoDB but it ran too much — "I don’t like pitching the book report." Leading pure-play audio platform: 300mm premium subs, close to 800mm MAUs, two-thirds of all global premium music subscribers. Negative working capital, FCF above net income.

• Investor day was a few months ago; stock popped, faded quickly, then a squishy print. The medium-term thesis is intact: 2030 algorithm of mid-teens revenue growth and gross margins from the high-20s/low-30s to 40%+.

• The structural change: the old model paid out ~70% of revenue in royalties. They have recut all three majors — UMG in January ’25, Warner shortly after, Sony in 2H25 — around per-subscriber minimums. Fixed wholesale price per sub, and Spotify keeps the benefit above that floor. That is the key unlock to 40%.

• New premium vectors beyond price: reserved concert tickets, audiobooks, personalized podcasts, and AI Remix.

• Advertising is massively under-monetized: 9% of revenue at 19% gross margin, $4 of revenue per free user versus $13 at Snap, $18 at YouTube and $48 at Meta. Ads inflecting to double-digit growth in 2H.

• North of $23 of EPS in 2028; at 25–30x FCF that is more than a double.

• Corroborated by Ani Sailesh (SummitTX) and Vrajesh Shah (Scopus): AI Remix looks close to launch — Merlin and Cobalt deals signed in the last week, Sony publishing rights being worked, Warner receptive because it is ARPU-accretive. Both view it as a major product catalyst not in numbers.

Full pitch detail:

Spotify (SPOT) — Long — Joe Flaum, Newbrook

I was going to pitch a software name, MongoDB, but it’s run a lot in the last week or so, and I don’t like pitching the book report — I’d rather pitch something we think is still interesting or asymmetric from here. So I’m going to pitch Spotify long.

The business we all know: leading pure-play audio platform in the world, 300 million premium subscribers, close to 800 million MAUs. Two-thirds of all premium music subscribers globally are on Spotify. Great business — negative working capital, free cash flow runs above net income, all that good stuff.

Why it’s interesting now: they had their investor day a few months ago and the stock was initially up on it, then faded really quickly and had a squishy print subsequently. But the medium-term thesis is very much intact. They came out with a 2030 algorithm calling for mid-teens revenue growth and gross margins moving up toward 40%-plus from the high 20s / low 30s the business historically operated in, with continued compounding of free cash flow behind that. Run the numbers on that multi-year guidance and the stock is more than a double from here at 25 to 30 times free cash flow.

What’s really changed: in the old model they paid out royalties of about 70% of revenue. They’ve now recut all of the deals with the three major labels — UMG in January 2025, Warner a little after that, and Sony in the back half of 2025 — and they’re built around per-subscriber minimums. There’s a fixed wholesale price per sub and Spotify gets the benefit above that on pricing. That’s a huge part of what unlocks getting toward 40% gross margins.

The second piece is a set of new features they can charge a premium for beyond just raising price: the new reserved concert ticket concept, audiobooks doing well, personalized podcasts, and this AI Remix product coming where you can create your own.

The third leg of the stool — and numerically the most striking to us — is that advertising is massively under-monetized. Ads are 9% of revenue at a 19% gross margin, which translates to $4 of revenue per free user versus something like $13 at Snapchat, $18 at YouTube and $48 at Meta. There’s a lot of upside in monetizing those free users, and they’ve talked about ads finally inflecting to double-digit growth in the back half of this year.

Those three points pencil to a double over the next few years. We’re shooting for north of $23 of EPS in 2028 — put your favorite multiple on that and there’s decent upside from here.

Ani Sailesh (SummitTX) added: you don’t need to underwrite the full case to get a double over the next few years. Top of funnel is a product story with all these features. From what I can gather from the labels, the Remix feature launches pretty soon — they’re working with Sony to get the publishing rights, then they can launch. Warner Music on their earnings call also seemed receptive and like they want to do a deal, because it’s ARPU-accretive and they get more money. The ecosystem is for it. You’ll see top-of-funnel re-acceleration and, most importantly, quarter-over-quarter margin growth — which is historically when the stock has worked.

Vrajesh Shah (Scopus) added: on AI Remix, they struck deals with a bunch of the smaller independent labels just in the last week, including Merlin, and another one today with Cobalt. Warner is probably next. There was an article this week suggesting Warner was going to back Suno and help them launch a DSP, but to me that seems more like negotiating in public — Warner has historically been receptive to getting into a deal with Spotify. You have a big product catalyst that’s not in the numbers. That’s the biggest angle from my perspective.

Semtech (SMTC) — Long — Blake Friedman, Squarepoint

• Diversified analog and mixed-signal: ~35% Signal Integrity (high-growth fiber and copper connectivity), ~35% protection, sensing and wireless, ~30% IoT.

• The upside is Signal Integrity. On the fiber side they supply TIAs, drivers and other transceiver components into a transceiver cycle where volumes are growing nearly exponentially: from an 80–90mm base of 800G units this year to 160–180mm of 800G plus 1.6T next year — roughly a doubling.

• Additional optionality in gain chips and CW lasers as CPO and MPO ramp.

• The linear equalizer business (active copper cables) has a major design win ramping with Google over the next several quarters, with NVIDIA as future upside. Google plus some NVIDIA gets to hundreds of millions of copper revenue.

• They finally announced the divestiture of the Sierra Wireless cellular module business (a 20% gross margin drag) — worth 200+bps to gross margin, putting the model at mid-60s gross margin and ~40% operating margin in CY28.

• Nearly double the Street on Signal Integrity growth; sees roughly 2–3x upside in the stock.

Full pitch detail:

Semtech (SMTC) — Long — Blake Friedman, Squarepoint

I saw this one pitched last time, but I think it’s still a pretty attractive opportunity. Semtech, ticker SMTC — a diversified supplier of analog and mixed-signal components. About 35% of the business is Signal Integrity, which houses their high-growth fiber and copper connectivity assets. Another 35% is protection, sensing and wireless, and the remaining 30% is a wide array of IoT assets — though that has changed slightly, which I’ll get to.

The significant upside is in Signal Integrity. On the fiber side they make a variety of components that go into transceivers — primarily TIAs, but also drivers and others — and they should benefit materially from the upcoming transceiver cycle. First on volumes: high-speed transceivers are growing nearly exponentially. This year we come from a base of 80 to 90 million 800-gig transceiver units. Next year, combining 800-gig and 1.6T, you go to 160 to 180 million units. So the overall high-speed transceiver volume base roughly doubles. There are also opportunities from gain chips and the ability to produce CW lasers, which fits well into the portfolio as CPO and MPO opportunities ramp.

Also within Signal Integrity they have a linear equalizer business that people associate with active copper cables. What you need to know is that they have a major design win coming that ramps with Google over the next several quarters. NVIDIA in future designs represents upside, but even the Google business plus some NVIDIA gets them to hundreds of millions in overall copper revenue.

Outside Signal Integrity, they recently finally announced the divestiture of the Sierra Wireless cellular module business, which was a 20% gross margin business. With it removed, that’s 200-plus basis points to overall gross margins, which changes the operating model to approaching mid-60s gross margin and 40% operating margin in calendar 2028.

So when I put the high growth from Signal Integrity — where I’m nearly double the Street — together with the modified portfolio, I get to roughly two to three times where the stock is today.

SiriusXM (SIRI) — Long — Nick Aluru, Verition

• ~$10bn market cap, ~$20bn EV, 30mm+ subscribers, plus Pandora. A shrinking asset that has been a low-single-digit decliner.

• Pricing and packaging changes to the core have stabilized subscriber and revenue trends.

• The under-the-radar piece is the YouTube deal, announced in the spring and not yet quantified to the Street. When YouTube determines you are consuming a video in audio mode — smart speaker, phone in pocket, video podcast in the background — SiriusXM has exclusive rights to resell that audio ad inventory and takes a rate on it. Nick estimates 3–5% upside to next year’s EBITDA and more in 2028, and reads it as a proof point that the Sirius ad tech stack has real long-term value.

• Net: a decliner turning into visible low-single-digit EBITDA and FCF growth. North of $5 of FCF per share next year, capital intensity falling as satellite launches roll off; 7–8x FCF is 30–50% upside. ~4% dividend yield and capacity for a ~$1bn buyback, 10% of the market cap.

• Spectrum optionality on top, which he is not underwriting. Cregg Watner: spectrum could be worth ~$5bn, and a Bloomberg-reported iHeart combination — YouTube plus Sirius plus iHeart inventory — could generate $1bn+ of EBITDA from a fallow asset and double the stock into the 60s or 70s.

• Joe Flaum added the detail: 25 MHz of core spectrum, half potentially repurposable over the next couple of years, plus 10 MHz of guard bands purchased a few years ago that are available now and in negotiation. Potential SpaceX partnership (with the Tesla/autos-internet angle) could be a catalyst in three to six months; an in-car use case would not require additional FCC authority. He thinks an iHeart deal is less likely now given the YouTube partnership.

Full pitch detail:

SiriusXM (SIRI) — Long — Nick Aluru, Verition

I’ll be pitching SiriusXM, ticker SIRI. About a $10 billion market cap and almost a $20 billion enterprise value. The radio-in-the-car business is shockingly big — still over 30 million subscribers. They also own Pandora, which has traditionally been a shrinking asset.

This has been a low-single-digit declining business. They’ve made changes to the core around pricing and packaging that have actually stabilized subscriber and revenue trends. Then you layer on the deal they did with YouTube, which has been a little under the radar — announced in the spring and not yet quantified to the Street. It sounds like it ramps more into next year and 2028.

It’s an advertising reselling deal. If you’re consuming a YouTube video in what YouTube deems an audio-only capacity — connected to a smart speaker, phone in your pocket, a video podcast running in the background on your desktop — YouTube has the technology to identify that as audio mode, and they’re giving SiriusXM the exclusive rights to resell that audio ad inventory, with Sirius taking a small rate on it. It’s been hard to quantify and we’ve been doing the work, but we think it’s at least three to five percent upside to EBITDA estimates next year and probably more in 2028. If anything, it’s also an encouraging proof point that the ad tech stack at Sirius has longer-term value and is more sophisticated and built for the podcast world than Sirius used to be.

Net-net, it’s pretty simple: this has been a decliner and now you’re going to have visibility into low-single-digit EBITDA and free cash flow growth for the next couple of years. Couple that with a leverage target that has come down, and this is a business that traditionally wants to hit the gas on buybacks. Between the YouTube upside and the buybacks we think they could be doing north of $5 of free cash flow per share next year. With capital intensity coming down as satellite launches roll off, and cash flow actually growing, we think this could be a seven-to-eight-times free cash flow multiple, which gets you 30 to 50% upside. Dividend yield is about 4%, and we think they’d have capacity for about a billion dollars of buyback next year — 10% of the market cap.

I didn’t touch much on spectrum optionality. There are some assets bulls point to; I’ve heard people in the two-to-three-billion-dollar range on fallow spectrum they could sell. We’re not underwriting it much in our valuation, and don’t need it to make the stock work.

Cregg Watner added: I love this stock and agree with everything. On the spectrum, I think it’s more like $5 billion. There was a Bloomberg article that they’d been talking to iHeart — if you combine YouTube, Sirius and iHeart, that inventory makes a giant. If they took $5 billion from a spectrum sale and bought iHeart, you generate a billion-plus of EBITDA from a fallow asset and the stock doubles. That’s on top of everything else — you get a stock in the 60s or 70s.

Joe Flaum (Newbrook) added: we like it as well. I’m not close to the potential for an iHeart deal — from our conversations a deal seems less likely now given the YouTube partnership. On spectrum there are two parts. They have 25 megahertz of core spectrum, half of which could potentially be available over the next couple of years to repurpose as they migrate subscribers onto the upper part of the band. Separately they have guard bands they purchased a few years ago — 10 megahertz in total — that are available now and they are in negotiations on them. We think that could be a meaningful catalyst over the next three to six months if they partner with someone like SpaceX, who is looking to get spectrum, and SpaceX may combine with Tesla, so there’s an autos-internet angle. This particular spectrum would not require additional use granted from the FCC for an in-car application. We think they’ll get whatever approvals they need, but it’s even easier if it happens to be internet to automobiles.

Silicon Motion (SIMO) — Long — Ravi Patna, Hawk Ridge

• Transforming from a saturated, low-growth SSD and mobile controller supplier into a diversified ASIC and NAND module supplier.

• Step one is the data center: boot drives for NVIDIA Bluefield 3 and Bluefield 4 DPUs, the same coming for TPU, and they disclosed on Monday’s convert call that they won a CPU maker — a really big opportunity. Small capacity drives, but ASPs are in the hundreds of dollars given flash prices, at good margins. Also won Ericsson base stations.

• Their edge is a DRAM-less controller — the flash incumbents either exited these small-capacity markets or do not have one.

• The core business (PC SSD, mobile, eMMC, UFS) is growing nicely despite end markets down YoY, because the flash makers have diverted ASIC resources to HBM. Ravi thinks this is durable and insulated from flash price declines: SIMO consolidates spend at each successive node, and re-entry is a two-to-three-year qualification process.

• The big catalyst is MonTitan, the enterprise SSD controller. A historically conservative CEO is publicly targeting 20% share of the enterprise SSD controller market, at a 70% gross margin revenue line, north of $300mm in 2027, with the impact starting in Q4.

• 100% above Street EPS for 2027. Trades like a memory proxy but is insulated from flash prices — a couple of good quarters should force the divergence.

Full pitch detail:

Silicon Motion (SIMO) — Long — Ravi Patna, Hawk Ridge

I’m pitching Silicon Motion. This company is transforming from a supplier of SSD and mobile controllers into saturated, low-growth end markets, into a diversified ASIC and NAND module supplier.

The first step of that diversification is the data center. We’ve seen a bit of it year to date with their success in boot drives for the NVIDIA Bluefield 3 DPU, and later this year Bluefield 4. They’re going to do the same for TPU. And they disclosed on their convert call on Monday that they won a CPU maker as well — that’s a really big opportunity. These are small-capacity drives, but ASPs are still in the hundreds of dollars given where flash prices are, and they make good margins. They raised the convert to support that growth, and they’ve also won Ericsson base stations.

The opportunity there is that they have a DRAM-less controller, whereas the competition — historically the flash guys — either exited the market because the capacities are so small, or don’t have DRAM-less controllers. Silicon Motion is moving into that market by virtue of its controller lead.

In the core business — PC SSDs, mobile, eMMC and UFS controllers — the flash guys have diverted all their ASIC resources to HBM-based dies and stepped out of this market, opening an aperture for Silicon Motion to take a bunch of share. I think this is durable and insulated from flash price declines. If flash prices go down, do the flash guys get back into the controller business? I think the answer is no, because what Silicon Motion is doing is consolidating spend at each successive node, so there are economies of scale — and once these things are outsourced, it’s a two-to-three-year qualification process to get back in. Their SSD and mobile controller business is growing very nicely despite those end markets being down year over year, and you’re getting some ASP increase from PCIe 5 adoption in PCs.

The big win in the next six months is MonTitan. The CEO has historically been a really conservative guy, and he’s out there saying they’re going to get 20% share of the enterprise SSD controller market. That’s a function of wins with the flash makers, CSPs, and data storage providers like Pure Storage and Weka. It’s a 70% gross margin revenue line. I think they do north of $300 million in 2027, and you start to see the impact in Q4.

Put it all together and we’re 100% above Street EPS estimates for 2027. This trades like a memory proxy but it’s really insulated from flash prices. A couple of good quarters with the MonTitan business coming through and you’ll start to see the divergence. There’s a ton of upside in this stock.

SharonAI (SHAZ) — Long — Doug Wurtz, 10b (relayed by host)

• Doug could not join; Miko relayed. GPU-as-a-service, ~$3bn market cap, ~$50mm/day, not widely followed. One of the "situational awareness" names that got puked.

• Has a sweetheart NVIDIA deal that Doug thinks can produce ~$2bn of EBITDA per year if fully contracted — against a $3bn market cap.

• An Australia IPO in the fall has kept the company from guiding, which is part of why it is mispriced.

• At 5–6x EBITDA it is a three-bagger; $200 price target.

Full pitch detail:

SharonAI (SHAZ) — Long — Doug Wurtz, 10b (relayed by Miko)

Miko: Doug Wurtz from 10b was unable to join, but he wanted me to mention Sharon AI quickly — S-H-A-Z is the ticker. I’d never heard of it. This was one of the "situational awareness" names that got puked.

For those who don’t know it: it’s a GPU-as-a-service company, about a $3 billion market cap, trades about $50 million a day, not widely followed. The company is going to do an IPO in Australia in the fall, so they’ve been unable to provide any guidance.

What Doug thinks is that they have a sweetheart deal with NVIDIA where they can earn around $2 billion of EBITDA per year — against a $3 billion market cap. If they fully contract it out and use all the capacity, assuming five to six times EBITDA, it’s a three-bagger. He thinks it’s worth $200.

Sea Limited (SE) — Long — Darrion Mohan, Nishkama

• Dominant Southeast Asian e-commerce platform (~50% of regional GMV) and a fast-growing top-three player in Brazil. One-liner: a 20–30% GMV grower just exiting a heavy investment cycle.

• Margins are inflecting. Q2 e-commerce margins expanded sequentially for the first time in several quarters; messaging shifted from growth-at-all-costs to high growth plus profitability.

• Guidance is for 2H margins to at least match 1H, but callbacks make clear that is conservative, and their on-the-ground checks show profitability per order already improving in 3Q versus 2Q.

• Competition easing: TikTok Shop is pulling back regional marketing spend as ByteDance redirects capital to AI. Fewer subsidy wars makes the margin expansion more durable.

• E-commerce EBITDA is only 60bps of GMV today against a 2–3% long-term target. Just getting back to 1% — which they have done before — is ~$7 of EPS next year; 25x gets you $175, ~50–60% upside.

• Still likes VeriSign from the May pitch; flat since, happy to discuss offline.

Full pitch detail:

Sea Limited (SE) — Long — Darrion Mohan, Nishkama

Last event I pitched VeriSign; the stock is pretty much flat since. We still like it and I’m happy to chat offline. Today I’m pitching Sea. It’s one of my colleagues’ names so I’m more high level on it, but we like the risk/reward here the most right now.

Sea is the dominant e-commerce platform in Southeast Asia, about 50% share of regional GMV, and they’re also a top-three player in Brazil where they’re growing quite rapidly. The one-liner thesis is that this is a 20 to 30% GMV grower just about exiting a heavy investment cycle. Margins are inflecting, competition is getting better, and it’s much cheaper than peers like MercadoLibre and Coupang. We think it’s worth about $175 per share, 50 to 60% upside.

For context: Shopee was in a heavy investment cycle building out logistics and fulfillment to deepen the moat. It worked — GMV accelerated — but margins went the wrong way and that weighed on the stock. This most recent quarter they told you they’re past peak investment and unit economics are getting better, and there was a big change in messaging from growth-at-all-costs to high growth with a big focus on expanding profitability.

In 2Q, e-commerce margins expanded sequentially for the first time in several quarters. Guidance is for second-half margins to at least equal the first half, but when you talk to them on callbacks it’s clear that’s very conservative and margins should expand in the back half. Our checks on the ground show profitability per order has already started to improve in 3Q relative to 2Q, which corroborates what management is telling us.

The second leg is that competition is improving and take rates are going up. The big competitor in Southeast Asia is TikTok Shop, and they’ve been pulling back marketing spend in the region — mainly because ByteDance is focusing most of its capital on AI. Just getting back to 1% of GMV — which they’ve done before — gets you to about $7 of EPS next year. Full pitch detail:

Pattern Group (PTRN) — SHORT — Rich McCallum, Ararat

I’m going to pitch a short also: Pattern, ticker PTRN. It’s about a $22 stock, a $4 billion market cap. It went public about a year ago at $14.

What the company does is help companies sell products online, specifically on marketplaces and specifically on Amazon. In industry parlance this is called an e-commerce accelerator. Effectively they buy inventory from the brands themselves, take the inventory risk, and sell it as the exclusive third-party reseller.

A good way to think about the economics: they have roughly 50% gross margins. They pay Amazon 15% commissions, and fulfillment — the Amazon FBA fees plus getting product to an Amazon warehouse — is another 15 points of revenue. So the brand is giving up basically 20 points of margin. What do they get for that? They don’t have to hire a team to manage the e-commerce presence, they don’t need an ad agency, and they probably save on fulfillment because instead of sending less-than-truckload, Pattern can more efficiently send a full truckload from their warehouse to an Amazon distribution center.

So this business really only works when they’re selling product that is inherently very high margin and easy to ship. You see that in the mix: roughly 60 to 70% of their sales are in vitamins, minerals and supplements — low weight, easy to ship, very high margin.

It’s basically a distribution business. It’s inherently not what it’s sold to the marketplace as, which is an AI company doing all this proprietary stuff placing ads on Amazon. It’s not that, and it trades at a big multiple — 35 times free cash flow.

What makes it interesting now is customer concentration. P&G is the largest customer, and I think P&G is probably the worst possible customer for Pattern to have, because P&G famously in-housed their media buying a couple of years ago. They think they are the best at building brands — and they probably are. Basically everything Pattern does for a brand is the ethos of P&G and how they build a business. So I think there’s real potential that when this transaction closes, P&G sends them notice that they’re not going to renew. It may not happen this year, but I think it probably will eventually happen regardless.

Impinj (PI) — Long — Paul Oppenheim, Ardsley

Calling in from the car, on the way to the dentist — "that’s my punishment for pitching Lindy to you guys last month." Hinge Health (HNGE) — Long — Jeff Keller, Capelight

I’m going to pitch a non-AI business: Hinge Health as a long, ticker HNGE. It’s a recent IPO, came out about a year ago, with decent short interest. It’s a telehealth business — basically a digital physical therapy business, that’s the core product.

They’ve got about 3,000 clients right now. The model is simple — there are contracted lives, which is how many people have this as a benefit, and then there are members, which is the yield, plus how many bells and whistles are being used. Contracted lives are about 25 million right now, and most of the clients are self-insured employers who buy it because they see the ROI.

The catalyst is that they’re about to start moving into getting this paid for inside health insurance plans — having the health insurer pay Hinge Health and absorb the economic benefit. I think that’s a big unlock. Their current self-insured market is about 100 million lives, of which 22 million is currently theirs. The fully-insured, health-plan-paid market is about another 100 million lives, of which only 3 million is penetrated.

On the math: about a $7.5 billion EV, round numbers about a billion of revenue, $250 million of EBITDA, top line growing 45%, incremental margins year over year about 50%. So very high incremental margins on a billion of revenue today, entering a market as big as the one they’re already growing nearly 50% in. The core market is growing near 50%, the new market is basically greenfield. The bull case is whether they can two-to-three-x the number of covered lives.

Full pitch detail:

Disney (DIS) — Long — Ben Kaminsky, Dendur

I’m going to pitch a household $200 billion market cap name that is literally flat over the last ten years. Over the last two years the company has seen EPS revised higher by 20% across 2026, 2027 and 2028, it has a double-digit earnings growth algo, and yet the stock is up 10% over that period and has seen its multiple collapse by 30%. The company is Disney, and I’m going to tell you why there’s at least 40% upside and why the House of Mouse is back.

Over the last year the multiple has collapsed from call it high-teens / 20 times P/E to just 14 times — the lowest relative multiple it has ever traded at versus the S&P and the cheapest it has traded since 2018. The stock has been fighting ghosts, a rolling wave of bear cases that one by one have been torn down.

First they were bucketed as an AI loser, on the idea that AI would democratize content creation and nobody would watch Frozen or Moana again. In reality OpenAI shut down Sora — evidently there are better uses for compute — and the box office is putting up a record year with premium IP playing a big role.

Next it was that Disney had over-monetized the parks and killed the golden goose by raising price too much. The truth is they were dealing with two very real headwinds: Epic Universe opening in Orlando and foreign tourism down 20% on Trump’s rhetoric. This past quarter they grew domestic parks attendance 3% and per caps 4%, which resoundingly put that narrative to bed.

The last bear case is streaming — the durability of growth and the long-term margin profile. This year they’ve grown streaming top line double digits and expanded margins to well over 10%. Going forward, what they really emphasized this past quarter is that they’re going to cut a lot of cost and plow much of it back into content to drive engagement, lower churn, and grow the service internationally where they’re severely underpenetrated versus Netflix.

Stepping back, this company is exactly where you want to be in the AI era. Live experiences are the anti-AI trade, and people forget the experiences segment is 60% of operating income and is in year three of a massive ten-year growth capex cycle, with cruise ships being added and new lands going into the parks. That drives high-single-digit OI growth for the next half decade. And nobody has more premium IP than Disney, which is precisely what you want to cut through all the AI slop — look at how Toy Story and Spider-Man performed in recent weeks.

On the CEO change, it’s pretty clear there are no sacred cows under DeMauro. Does that mean they do something dramatic? Probably not, but he’s open to doing anything and everything to get the stock higher. The organization was essentially frozen in the latter innings of the Iger era, with Bob’s focus turning to other things like buying an NBA franchise.

The real problem in recent years has been the multiple, not the earnings, which speaks to a lack of confidence in the growth outlook. Ben Swinburne from Morgan Stanley took over IR and has been a godsend, giving both buy side and sell side far more access to management. This has been a funding short for years, more because it worked than because fundamentals cracked. When these large caps turn, they turn hard, and long-only buyers always live higher and don’t want to miss out. I think we’re at the precipice of one of those moments.

To put numbers on it: the Street is modeling call it $8.20 of EPS in fiscal 2028. I think they do closer to $8.50, and at a high-teens multiple that’s a $150 stock, up 40% from here.

Full pitch detail:

Uber (Long) / DoorDash (SHORT) — Mike Kosdan, Hudson Bay

I’m going to pitch a pair: long Uber, short DoorDash.

On Uber, I think the AV narrative is in the process of changing more to the positive. They lost Waymo in Phoenix but still have them in other cities, and I get the sense they’re just at an impasse on terms, so that could still come back. The market has now recalibrated on that. And even if it doesn’t happen in the next few months, they’re going to be launching with a driver in vehicles with Nuro in the Bay Area, and driver-out in Las Vegas with Zoox, and the Bay Area next year. All these AV partnerships Uber has done finally start producing near-term proof points where you have actual non-Waymo AVs being dispatched on the app.

The valuation difference between Uber and DoorDash — we’ve seen this before, and when it gets this wide it really is an opportunity, and you do tend to see convergence if you’re patient. DoorDash is trading at like 35 times GAAP P/E on Street 2027, and we think there could be mid-single-digit or more risk to that number. Uber is much cheaper on the same basis, and half of Uber’s business is food anyway. We also think there’s mid-to-high-single-digit upside at Uber next year. Pick your multiple between the two — we think the IRR on this trade over the next three to six months is at least 25% and potentially more.

On DoorDash specifically, there’s still an idea that the investments they’ve been making this year on tech replatforming get lapped next year and lead to a margin inflection, which is in both buy-side and sell-side numbers. But the more you dig into it, the clearer it is that they have a negative margin mix shift from international growth, where they’ve been buying companies and buying growth, while the US has been slowing on orders and is more driven by average order value and is just more mature. So they have a hidden margin headwind that prevents that inflection. And it’s a management team that invests whatever upside they have back into the business. But the main call is simply that the valuation gap has gotten way too wide.

Miko: a lot of guys are positioned the other way — long DoorDash, short Uber.

Alibaba (BABA) — Long — Chris Bonanni, Arvin

• At an inflection from a declining earnings story to ~20% compounded EPS growth.

• Core commerce is the least exciting part but growth is bottoming. Headline CMR looks weak on accounting changes; stripping that out it is low-to-mid single digit, slightly ahead of expectations. The bigger deal is that commerce losses are narrowing faster than expected and should roughly halve versus last year — the company has always found new loss-making businesses to absorb growth elsewhere, and that is ending.

• Cloud is the real story: 45% growth this quarter, up from 38%, with margins moving from 9% to 11–12% and management believing 20% over time. Unlike the US infrastructure names, this is accelerating revenue and expanding margin.

• AI compute is growing ~150% and goes to 40% of cloud mix exiting the year — roughly 40 points of cloud top-line growth from AI compute alone. Cloud is 20% of the company growing 50%, so 10 points of consolidated revenue growth from cloud alone.

• Unpriced optionality: the new Qwen frontier model (cheap, fast, Apple is using it — a validation) and their stake in Kimi, whose model is genuinely competitive with US frontier labs. Neither is in numbers.

• Street ~30% too low for next year; a high-teens multiple gets to $160–170 in about six months.

• Peer corroboration: the setup rhymes with how the Street re-rated Google when cloud re-acceleration became apparent. And this ends a five-year negative earnings revision cycle — that flip is powerful.

Full pitch detail:

Alibaba (BABA) — Long — Chris Bonanni, Arvin

I’m pitching BABA, which I think is at an inflection point right now, moving from a declining earnings story to one that puts out 20% compounded growth over the next couple of years.

Start with core commerce, the least exciting part, but growth is bottoming out there. Online retail sales ticked up slightly in June from May, and property prices are finally stabilizing, which could lead to a better consumption story in China — though I’ll put that aside because it’s not really worth calling. Headline CMR, their advertising growth, will look a little weak this quarter due to accounting changes, but stripping that out it’s still growing low to mid single digits, a little ahead of where people think.

The bigger deal is that margins are bottoming. Commerce losses, which have been a big overhang, are narrowing faster than expected and will probably halve versus last year. That’s what really kicks off a positive earnings revision story. The company has always found new loss-making businesses to absorb growth in other parts, and I think that’s ending — which should be an inflection for consolidated EBIT growth.

The exciting part is cloud, which is accelerating and should stay at a high growth level for years. We were at 45% this quarter, up from 38% last quarter, and margins are moving from 9% to 11 or 12%. Management believes it could be 20% over time. Unlike the domestic infrastructure story, where you have accelerating revenue on flat margins, here you have an EBIT story.

What’s particularly interesting is they’ve given loose disclosures on how AI compute is driving the business. I think it should be growing about 150%, and they’ve stated that mix goes to 40% exiting the year. So you should be getting something like 40 percentage points of cloud top-line growth from AI compute alone. Core CPU should also have a halo around it as inference takes off. You can see how this generates 40 to 50% growth for years. Cloud is 20% of overall top line growing 50%, so that’s 10 points of revenue growth from cloud alone.

The last piece, an option nobody is pricing including me, is the AI models. Qwen just dropped a new frontier model — cheap, fast, and Apple is using it, which I think is a validation. They also own a chunk of Kimi, which put out a model genuinely competitive with some of the US frontier labs. Neither the direct monetization of Qwen nor the value of the Kimi stake is in numbers today.

Put it together — stabilizing commerce and inflecting margins, cloud compounding, and AI monetization optionality — and I think Street numbers are 30% too low for next year. Put a high-teens multiple on that and you get a $160 to $170 stock in about six months.

A peer added: we saw how the Street treated Google when it became apparent cloud growth was re-accelerating and they had the full stack. It’s a different game in China, but when perception changes it can provide a meaningful catalyst — similar to Google a year, year and a half ago. Chris closed: the important thing is this has been in a five-year negative earnings revision cycle, and that’s going to go positive in a big way. That’s very powerful.

ASML — Long — Pete Grondin, Pennant

• Variant view is TerraFab. Elon Musk’s stated ambition of one terawatt of AI compute is barely imputed into the stock, and last week’s blog post was effectively the shovel in the ground.

• The math: one terawatt implies roughly 75 additional EUV tools and 150–170 additional DUV tools. ASML’s stated best-case 2028 capacity is only 110 EUV and 130–140 DUV in total.

• Even half of Musk’s ambition means ASML prices on supply/demand rather than value-to-customer for the first time in years.

• Sets up three to four years of massive beat-and-raise and backlog prints far beyond what is modeled. Arguably a more critical AI enabler than TSMC.

Full pitch detail:

ASML — Long — Pete Grondin, Pennant

The name is going to be familiar to most everybody on this call, so I’m not going into the dirty details — everyone knows what ASML does and how important it is to the whole semi ecosystem. The variant view, to my mind, is what’s happening with TerraFab.

You’re starting to get conversations around TerraFab and people trying to figure out exactly what Elon Musk is doing, but I still think it’s on the periphery of the discussion around ASML. When I was with the CFO of ASML back in April or May, I asked him how he was thinking about TerraFab. He said, in effect, "We’ll adjust our numbers and our thought process when I see said customer put a shovel in the ground." Last week, with their blog post, they effectively put a shovel in the ground — and they’re talking about one terawatt of AI compute capacity, which is just massive.

The bottom line is that if you give Elon any chance of success, I don’t think much of TerraFab is imputed into ASML. On very rough math — and I’m sure guys on this call could have different views, but directionally — a terawatt of AI compute means another 75 EUV tools and another 150 to 170 DUV tools. For those who don’t know, ASML currently says that if things go really well in 2028, they’ll have capacity for 110 EUV tools in total and about 130 to 140 DUV tools in total.

So think about what happens if even half of what Musk wants to bring online comes true. You get not only massive volume demand, but for the first time in a long, long time ASML prices on supply/demand dynamics rather than value to the customer. My view is you’re setting up for a string of three or four years of massive beats and raises, and backlog numbers far beyond what people can imagine. And this company, more than any other — arguably even more than TSMC, depending on what happens with fabs in the US over the next few years — is the one that drives the engine of AI growth. I’d encourage everybody to think about it in the context of TerraFab and what that truly means in terms of incremental demand.

Astera Labs (ALAB) — SHORT — Jay Joshi, North Rock Capital

• "A spicy short." Buy-side numbers are $20+ of EPS from everyone he speaks to, and he sees no revision story to support it.

• Aries retimers (~37% of revenue): challenged, because networks have evolved and signal integrity matters less as CPU and GPU move closer together on the board. Already visible at NVIDIA, the architecture leader.

• Taurus and CXL (~20% combined): small, competitive with Credo and Marvell, and Samsung is pushing CXL out because it is hard and is more of a band-aid for the memory wall than a solution.

• Scorpio (scale-up switching) is the juicy part — the piece everyone is excited about, set to become the largest part of the business exiting this year. It is indexed to Amazon and AMD on the PCIe and UAL protocols, and neither customer is committed to those protocols. Real risk they diversify or switch to Ethernet or NVLink.

• If protocol risk materializes, buy-side $20+ drops to ~$12 and the multiple de-rates: ~24% downside base case, more if you de-rate further.

• Timing: clarity on protocol direction in 1H 2027; the numbers impact lands in 2028 — which is where the material buy-side step-up sits.

Full pitch detail:

Astera Labs (ALAB) — SHORT — Jay Joshi, North Rock Capital

I’ve got a spicy short for the group — Astera as a short. Astera is a networking company providing a variety of products indexed to AI. Those include retimers through their Aries products, around 37% of revenues, which provide signal integrity; ADC modules through Taurus, which competes with Credo; CXL for memory, which is Leo; and finally Scorpio, which is scale-up switching for specific protocols, namely PCIe and UAL, primarily indexed to Amazon and AMD.

So what’s the view on this name that’s certainly gone bonkers? The short view is that there really isn’t much of a revision story here. Buy-side numbers from the variety of people I speak to are all massively at 20 bucks plus. There are several issues that put the risk/reward more toward the downside.

First, on the Aries retimer products: that business is challenged because networks have evolved. The need for that signal integrity becomes less important as the CPU and GPU on the board get closer together. We’ve already seen this with NVIDIA, and NVIDIA is the leader when it comes to network architecture. I see no reason why that wouldn’t continue as networks evolve going forward.

Second, Taurus and CXL. They’re very small, together about 20% of revenues. There’s been a lot of speculation. There’s a competitive element from both Credo and Marvell, but also a lot of that technology on the memory side is being pushed out — Samsung is pushing out CXL because it’s really hard to do and it’s more of a band-aid solution to the memory wall problem. So we don’t see it being a huge contributor.

But the juicy part of the short is Scorpio, which everyone is very excited about. The view is this product line becomes the largest part of the business as we exit this year. It’s very indexed to Amazon, AMD and those protocols. The bigger problem is that both those companies are not themselves indexed to those protocols. There’s a real possibility and risk that Amazon and AMD either diversify away or switch away from them. For context, there’s the Ethernet protocol as an alternative, and of course NVIDIA with NVLink.

If that happens, then the buy side’s 20-plus EPS drops materially — we’re getting something like $12 — and you get a multiple de-rate on top. For us that’s around 24% downside base case, and if you de-rate the multiple further, more than that.

On timing, in Q&A: we get clarity on protocol changes in the first half of 2027, when it becomes more apparent. Most people looking at this are really looking at it as a 2028 story, because that’s where the really material step-up in buy-side numbers sits. So the main impact is felt in 2028 numbers. If I’m right on protocol risk and on how management speaks to the exit run-rate on revenues, I don’t think that sets the name up well.
