The presenter thinks where the program could get more interesting is if it gets extended to purchase, because that is where all the economics are. The government is very focused on th is part of the market contributing to the housing affordability issue, and the presenter thinks this program is the linchpin of how they are trying to push pricing down.

In terms of the setup, the presenter believes it is AI meets regulation. Ten years ago, you could not create a program like this. Now you have businesses that can offer the service virtually for free. The presenter thinks that is interesting.

In terms of the numbers, the presenter runs various scenarios on how much discounting they think you will need to do. The blended fee is approximately $3,000 on purchases. So every $100 of discount is 5% of EPS, and every 5% of escrow revenue they lose is 15% of EPS. The presenter could see price coming down by a lot more than $100. They could see escrow eroding as well, and if you add those together, you have 20%+ EPS downside. Again, the presenter does not think the multiples reflect any AI risk. At a constant multiple, the presenter believes FNF is worth $40 versus $48 currently. If they get perceived as AI losers, pick your favorite P/E and it could be a lot lower, call it sub - $40.

Two final points the presenter would like to mention. First, there are interesting things happening in the real estate industry. Rocket is consolidating the mortgage side, and Compass is consolidating the broker side. They are internalizing a lot of these functions. The presenter thinks they are just going to peel away share from the title insurers. And then the other wrinkle is, in two states, the rates are actually set at the state level (in Texas and Florida). That is 15% of home volumes. They took down rates last year. The presenter thinks they are just going to continue to take rate. Those are just two states, but they are huge states.

The presenter thinks the free market is going to push down rate, and they think the states are going to push down the rate as well.

The presenter would like to discuss Darden Restaurants as a short.

The presenter acknowledges this has been a painful short year-to-date, but they think the setup is interesting here. They also think it is tactically interesting. They report this coming Thursday (6/25) for both Q4 and full year. The presenter believes there will obviously be a lot of pressure on that guide, and the presenter thinks a lot of investors will potentially be taking profit. The stock is up 15% year-to-date and it is trading near 52-week highs.

In terms of the business, they own 2,200 restaurants. It is a portfolio of casual dining including Olive Garden (the largest brand in the portfolio), Longhorn Steakhouse, Ruth’s Chris, as well as some fine dining (The Capital Grille, Eddie V’s Prime Seafood), and other.

The presenter thinks Olive Garden traffic is slowing, so at these elevated multiples, to be a bull, you effectively need to think that a lot of the menu innovation, portion downsizing, and new initiatives they are trying, are going to work longer term. The presenter does not buy any of that.

The presenter acknowledges it is a decent business that is well run but they do not think it should trade two turns from Texas Roadhouse. The presenter thinks it is just a better steakhouse. If you do work on how much price they have taken, the presenter believes consumers are now dramatically overpaying for the food quality.

In terms of importance, the bet is on Olive Garden, since that is what drives the multiple. To their credit, the presenter thinks they have managed the business quite well. They have done some portion changes. They have revamped the definition of “Never Ending Pasta Bowl.”

That worked well. But the presenter thinks that is effectively a tactical opportunity.

Over the last three quarters, you are starting to see traffic deteriorating. The company has given investors additional data points (such as weather comp sand catering comps), but the presenter believes giving those data points makes it far harder to see the truth, which is that traffic is deteriorating.

The presenter thinks if you take a step back, they have given us some very useful insights.

They have quite literally gone to a lighter-portions menu. The presenter believes th at is the downfall of high-end restaurants long term, especially when people are consuming less wine and alcohol. The company is essentially saying people are drinking less so they’re going to tell them they can have a quarter the size of pasta for $8 instead of $20 and management thinks that's going to work. To the presenter, that is just discounting at a QSR or at an entertainment facility. That is a negative long term, not a positive. The presenter thinks that people have hid in plain sight in what is quantified as a B-minus business model, and it has worked year-to-date, but it should not longer term. The presenter thinks the other big item to call out is that average check size is decreasing.

The company is showing us that. There are fewer discretionary add-ons. They are telling us that. They are admitting that consumers are buying less alcohol. That should be a bad thing, not a good thing. They still own a significant amount of fine dining restaurants that make up a huge percentage of their restaurant portfolio and operating mix.

In terms of why the print is interesting, even for investors who have done very limited work on it, if you just back out the Texas math, this has really nowhere to run. If they print perfectly on Thursday and they sound great about the World Cup, that sets up a nearly impossible 2027 lapping schedule of comps. The presenter does not think any investor thinks that they are going to lap well next Q4 or Q1 2028, because of the World Cup. They do not think that they are going to lap the Never Ending Pasta Bowl evolution well in Q1 and Q2.

So how is 2027 going to work? The presenter thinks they are basically going to guide to a very conservative, + 1.5% to + 3.5% in terms of same-store sales. They are going to give very limited detail around their cost-base right-sizing. They are going to sound just okay on the cost side. So what do you get for 13.5x forward EBITDA at a 20x PE of a business, where traffic is C to C-plus? The presenter just does not know how you can justify owning it here.

The presenter is blended for 2027. They are at + 2% in terms of same-store sales, with consensus closer to + 3%. For Olive Garden specifically, the presenter is only at + 1.5%, and almost all of it comes from price. They think traffic is about to inflect, and they do not know how this can work through the fiscal year if that is true.

The presenter actually thinks Longhorn Steakhouse is a great business. The presenter does not think it is as good as Texas Roadhouse, but they would quantify themself as in line there.

But the presenter does not think that you can get hurt at Longhorn, at this valuation. The presenter thinks investors know it well. Revenue-wise, the presenter is $200 million lighter than the Street, and they are light on EBITDA margins. The presenter thinks longer term, this deserves closer to a 10 to 12x multiple. That equates to 35% to 50% downside, depending on how aggressive investors want to be.

Is that going to happen in the next month? No. But if you stick to what works longer term in casual dining (on the short side), it is deteriorating traffic, over-promos, and discounting as the management tries to massage the actual health of the business. The presenter thinks Cheesecake Factory is facing similar challenges.

The presenter would like to discuss Ahold as a short.

A hold has a $30 billion market cap, levered approximately 1.7x including leases. It is trading at ~12x next year's earnings, which is a premium to Kroger, with a similar earnings algorithm.

In terms of the business, 60% of pre-corporate EBIT is in the U.S., primarily banners along the East Coast, the Mid-Atlantic and Southeast. In the U.S., they have 2,000 stores including Food Lion, Stop & Shop, Giant, and Hannaford. Europe represents 40% of pre-corporate EBIT with 7,500 stores (50% of European sales are in the Netherlands).

The thesis is that conventional grocers are in a difficult position. Volumes have been declining for the better part of five years. They are losing share to mass, to club, and to discounters, and online is taking away volume from in-store. Online grocery penetration is increasing, and Amazon and Walmart have been relentless competitors. Amazon piloted same-day perishables in 2024. It is now in 2,300 cities. Late last year they piloted 30-minute delivery, and rolled it out to more cities as of May. Walmart rolled out same-day delivery to 80% of the population in 2023. They have reached 95% of the population in under three hours as of today. The presenter heard at an industry conference last week, that Walmart is saying they are going to get $3 billion in refunds from tariffs, and they are going to be investing that in food and consumables.

So Amazon and Walmart continue to gain share. They do it first-party. They own the customer data. And players like Ahold and others are using Instac art, Door Dash, and Uber, where they are beholden to a third party and they do not receive any of the customer data.

On the other side, you have the discounters that continue to also take share. Aldi and Lidl continue to gain share and grow their footprint. Aldi is predominantly east of the Mississippi, and Lidl is growing on the East Coast and Mid-Atlantic, right in the backyard of Ahold's banners. There was an article last week about Aldi investing $9 billion in the next several years to ramp their store growth. Important to note, 50% of Ahold's footprint is within 10 minutes of an Aldi, and 20% of their footprint is within a 10-minute drive of a Lidl.

Comp tailwinds from pharmacy, like GLP-1s, are going to turn into a headwind because of the GLP-1 price compression and generics. And then changes from the Inflation Reduction Act are actually going to drive drug prices lower, and that is going to be a comp headwind.

And then the change in SNAP benefits is also going to be a headwind this year, although the company do es not quantify that. The presenter believes the way that they have been running the business is really geared for the short term, to the detriment of the long term. They are beholden to hitting a 4.0% EBIT margin target across the business. So they are, in effect, making a short-term decision to hit that. As the presenter discussed previously, their underlying volumes are negative. From an accounting perspective, vendor allowances were approximately 80 basis points of sales from 2018 to 2023. In 2024, it stepped up to 92 basis points. It stepped up in 2025 to 95 basis points.

So what was once, call it, 15% of EBIT is now closer to 25% of EBIT. Using those numbers allowed them to hit that 4.0% margin target exactly in 2024 and 2025. They are also extending the duration of the depreciation schedule.

It is also worth noting, the CEO announced that he is leaving in April of 2027. They are bringing in an outsider. The CEO of the US business also departed and they recently appointed someone from Amazon Fresh. The CEO of Europe recently left, and a lot of the leaders of the banners have also left. If you think about it from a stock standpoint, there is this management overhang in terms of what are they going to do when a new CEO comes in? Do you see a pricing reset in order for them to get more competitive?

Kroger has said that they need to invest in price. When they reported quarterly earnings last week, they did not quantify what that is. They said that they would give more information at their Analyst Day in October. They cited that the cost savings are significant, and it will allow them to fund price investments (so you can think the cost savings and price investments as also significant).

In terms of the bull case, EU investors like this stock. It is defensive and 100% of free cash flow is used for buybacks and dividends. But any uncertainty around the CEO transition should keep a lid on the multiple. What Kroger does (from a competitive standpoint) should also keep a lid on the multiple. And then there is this downside scenario, where a new CEO comes in and acknowledges that they are becoming uncompetitive in the US, and has to reset margins from 4.5% to something lower. The stock is trading at 12x, and the presenter can get to €2.50 earnings. Using a 10x multiple, that would equate to a €25 target price versus €34 today.

[2026-06-12] Investor Thesis: Marvell is positioned at the nexus of the AI and networking scale-up. The company is leveraging strong ASIC and networking segments to address the infrastructure needs of cloud service providers (CSPs) like Google and Amazon. Marvell is viewed as a vital independent partner that allows CSPs to avoid total reliance on Nvidia.

[2026-06-12] Catalysts: Potential $7 billion LPU (Linear Pluggable Optics) opportunity by 2029 to address memory constraints in inferencing. Expects them to win GOOGL’s LPU business and potentially TPU as well given the amount of demand that GOOGL has, which should increase dramatically going into 2028. SerDes technology is critical for 400G+ scale-ups. Marvell’s ability to bundle DSPs (Digital Signal Processors) with other technologies provides significant pricing power.

[2026-06-12] Valuation vs. Street: Revenue projections for CY2028 (FY29) are around $23B and the investor estimates that it could be closer to $27–$29 billion, with significant growth extending into 2029 as the LPU opportunity layers on top. This equates to $14 to $15 of EPS in 2028.

[2026-06-12] Risks and Other Key Details: Historical concerns regarding management credibility and execution issues. CSPs face "career risk" when switching ASIC providers. There is also reliance on TSMC allocation, though Marvell’s independent status is viewed as a hedge against being locked in by Nvidia. MRVL should be able to help with the TSMC allocation issue, which could give it an advantage in winning GOOGL’s business as it works to increase allocation. The recent acquisitions of Celestial AI (Dec 2025) and Polariton (April 2026) were interpreted by some as management moves to bolster market sentiment rather than sound strategic additions to the core business. There is skepticism regarding whether adding these optics businesses creates a truly more compelling investment.

[2026-06-12] Commentary: What is the view of MRVL vs AVGO? Marvell is seen as more attractive to CSPs because it offers an independent path (e.g., CPO/NPO) that avoids Nvidia lock-in. While there are lingering concerns about past management execution, the group felt the current industry demand environment makes the bear thesis difficult to maintain. The consensus suggests Google is likely to strengthen the partnership with Marvell.

[2026-06-12] Investor Thesis: Galaxy Digital is presented as a mispriced opportunity within the AI power infrastructure sector. However, the thesis posits that the core value lies in the company's high-value, front-of-the-meter power assets in West Texas (the Helios site). The market is failing to appropriately value these contracted megawatts, which offer a cleaner path to power than traditional utilities.

[2026-06-12] Catalysts: The company holds 1,500 acres at the Helios site, which is already contracted for an 800MW, 15-year deal with CoreWeave (Phase 1–3). Galaxy recently received ERCOT approval for an additional 800MW of power. The management is looking to contract this new capacity over the back half of the year, which serves as a significant near-term catalyst.

[2026-06-12] Valuation vs. Street: The crypto business (inclusive of cash, stablecoins, and Bitcoin on balance sheet) is valued at approximately $15–$16/share. Subtracting net debt of nearly $5/share results in a base valuation of ~$10–$11/share. The existing 800MW CoreWeave contract is valued at $15–$20/share, depending on terminal value and discount rate assumptions. The pending 800MW pipeline adds another $15–$20/share of value. With successful execution through the end of the year, the stock has a trajectory toward $40–$50/share.

[2026-06-12] Risks and other Key Details: The necessity to build out transmission facilities for the second 800MW phase and the complexities of negotiating with hyperscalers. High sensitivity to Bitcoin price volatility, though the group noted technical support at $60k.

[2026-06-12] Commentary: The group discussed why Galaxy has been a "catch-up" trade relative to peers like Hut 8. Participants debated whether to bet on individual management teams or buy a sector basket (e.g., WGMI). The consensus is that while peers like Hut 8 have performed well due to proven execution with hyperscalers, Galaxy remains a compelling value play due to the unique site assets and pending approvals.

The presenter would like to discuss Yesway as a long.

Yesway operates convenient stores / gas stations that recently IPO’d in April of this year. It is a convenience store roll-up that was founded in 2015. They made two dozen acquisitions over the past decade, but the transformative deal came in 2019 when they acquired Allsup’s.

The business predominantly operates in West Texas and Oklahoma (in very rural areas).

More than half of the locations are in towns that have less than 20,000 people in population, which means that there is generally very little competition in those markets.

The company came public in April at $20. It traded up to $28, and it has since then traded down to $22. On the first earnings call, they came out with guidance that was roughly in line with the Street and it looked fairly conservative, from a comp perspective and also on fuel margins, but there are a few items that they are improving on that the presenter thinks can help it re-rate up to where peers are currently trading.

For context, Casey’s is the peer that is considered best-in-class. It trades at 20x. Murphy's trades at approximately 12x, and Yesway trades approximately 9.5x. It trades at a discount to other peers despite being a substantial unit grower. In terms of unit growth, there are 450 units today. They are targeting 550 by 2030, equating to mid-single-digit unit growth over the next four years. Not only are they growing units, the unit economics have improved significantly as they redesigned the stores. In the new store format that they are rolling out, they do approximately 3x the annual fuel sales. They do double the inside sales, and the store contribution is about 3x. As the mix of new units comes in, the margins should improve.

And on top of that, because they operate in rural areas, their diesel mix is much higher than some of their peers, which on a cent-per-gallon basis has, on average, been higher. And cents-per-gallon in the most recent quarter was $0.49. The presenter thinks that if wholesale fuel costs start to come down, you have a bit of a tailwind in the near term, which they do not think is baked into the consensus numbers. Roughly a one cent movement in terms of fuel margin equates to ~$6 to $7 million in EBITDA, so there is good leverage there.

Lastly, as it relates to inside sales, there is a lot of room for them to grow in that regard. If you look at Casey’s, for example, inside sales account for ~30% of their sales, while Yesway is in the mid-teens. Private label is only 5% versus Casey’s at 10%. At the same time, their labor model is a lot lean er. They do not have a full kitchen. Instead, they have fryers. They sell 24 million fried burritos every year, and they have 2.6 average employees versus Casey’s 8 to 10. It is trading at 9.5x today. If you equate it to Murphy's, which is at 12x, it is worth ~$32 on next year's EBITDA versus $22 today.

The presenter would like to discuss U.S. Foods as a long.

U.S. Foods has a $19 billion market cap, and grows EBITDA 10% and earnings 20%. The crux of the thesis is the continuation of a compounding story. In the beginning of 2023, David Flitman stepped in to the role as CEO. Since then, they have grown EBITDA over 60%, earnings over 120%, while reducing leverage from 3.5x to 2.5x, and they are halfway through their three-year plan right now. At some point next year, the presenter believes they will lay out a new plan for 2028 to 2030, and the presenter believes that plan will bridge investors to EPS of $9.00 to $9.50 in 2030, up from $4.00 in 2025.

Like the presenter said, it is a continuation of that compounding story. There is a lot of room left in terms of some of the P&L work they are doing. They are tapping into new market share opportunities with smaller scale deliveries.

With the leverage where it is, the presenter believes they can buy back 3% to 5% of the company every year. The presenter is underwriting EPS of $9.00 to $9.50 at 15x, which would equate to no multiple expansion from here, and if you discount it back, it is $110. The stock is currently trading at $86.

The presenter believes you will get some multiple expansion based on the catalyst path which will lead to even further upside. The presenter thinks the company will get an investment grade credit rating at some point in the near future (since management has started talking about it), and the company could also get index inclusion.

The presenter would like to discuss Sphere Entertainment Co. as a long.

The stock is currently trading at $137.50 per share with a $4.9 billion market cap.

They have one Sphere in Las Vegas — that is the only one currently operating — and they have one in Abu Dhabi, which is under construction. They have one that was announced in Maryland, in National Harbor, and then there are rumors of at least two to four more venues.

There have been rumors regarding Nashville, Orlando, as well as in Japan, Singapore, Macau, etc.

It is a structurally differentiated asset in live entertainment that has been attracting consumers and social media buzz since it was created. The company puts on live entertainment and live events, including concert shows. Their shows are both owned IP plus third-party IP, but they also do corporate events. The Sphere segment is the segment investors care about, but they also own MSG Networks, which the presenter acknowledges is a dying asset.

For context, approximately 88% of their revenue is event-related. The majority of that comes from their Sphere experience, which consists of Wizard of Oz currently but also consists of Postcard from Earth, which was their first show which was viewed initially as a flop. And then they have some in the pipeline, which are Wizard of Oz 2.0, and then this live action entertainment show that is called From the Edge.

The other third of their business is focused on concert residencies (think Phish, Kenny Chesney, No Doubt, DJ Illenium, Backstreet Boys, etc.). The commentary has been very positive int ra-quarter. They consistently beat quarter after quarter.

Important to note, the company slightly changed their commentary on financing additional Spheres, originally stating that they are going to be asset light moving forward, and that they would get franchise & royalty fees in return. They switched some of their language, leaving open the possibility of doing strategic investments, sale leasebacks, etc. The stock was hit after those remarks, and then it was also wrapped up in this consumer unwind.

The presenter thinks it is a $170 stock, which is 25% upside from current levels. That assumes 20% growth in sponsorships (and the presenter believes you could argue even higher than that). In the presenter’s model, they obviously include Las Vegas, as well as Abu Dhabi, and National Harbor. As it relates to National Harbor, they are still waiting for that project to receive financing. Abu Dhabi is signed, sealed, and construction has started, and they get royalty fees starting from the moment shovels hit the ground. You get pre-construction, you get design royalty fees, and then once it is operating, you just clip a fee like a McDonald's would from a franchise e.

In terms of the current Sphere in Las Vegas, the presenter believes they can continue to increase the utilization factor. They started out doing two shows per day, and now they are doing between three and five a day. They are continuing to figure out how to layer in more residencies as well. Essentially, they are trying to optimize the one venue they currently have in operation.

The presenter’s price target of $170 assumes $260 million in Sphere AOI. The presenter is excluding the MSG networks. That is using a 17x EBITDA multiple.

The presenter would like to discuss Rocket as a long.

The stock is currently trading at $12.50. They are going to generate $0.70 per share of earnings in a soft housing environment, with mortgage rates at 6%. In terms of the setup, it is a combination of the origination business which is likely at trough (there is a base level of demand, but not much else), as well as a recurring servicing business.

In the presenter’s view, you are paying 18x trough earnings while gaining share. They are optimizing the business after the mergers with Mr. Cooper and Redfin, so there is potential upside to that $0.70 in the static environment we are in. In terms of interest rates, if they go down, you have a call option. They could generate $2 to $3 of earnings at some point. Let’s be clear, the presenter does not think that point is this year. What is going on in AI, the amount of IG issuance, persistent inflation with regards to Iran, the best that they could hope for is the 10-year gets back to 4% at some point this year. The presenter would not count on it.

The presenter’s point is that if the Strait of Hormuz opens up and rates hold here (or you get a little relief on the ten-year), you might see the stock trade back to the high teens. But the presenter acknowledges that it is very hard to find longs in the consumer sector.

The presenter would like to discuss Kering as a short.

Kering is a luxury goods business. The ir main brand is Gucci. They also have brands such as YSL and Bottega, but Gucci is the primary sentiment driver.

The bulls would argue that Gucci can get back to the $9+ billion in sales they generated in 2019 through COVID. The presenter thinks structurally there are a lot of reasons why that will not happen. First, to be successful in this industry, you need to catch the latest fashion trend. Gucci historically has been a “loud” luxury brand, and the presenter thinks by all accounts, they are still in a very quiet luxury market. The product does not really resonate with what consumers are looking for right now in terms of logos, brand, and color. The presenter believes that worked in the Alessandro Michele (the former creative director of Gucci) era, but now what is resonating with luxury consumers is brands like Loro Piana. The fashion cycle is not in their favor.

Then, the initial feedback from the first fashion show was not overly positive. The social media feedback was quite negative. That needs to work for them to have a ny chance of getting back to that level of sales.

And then structurally, the presenter thinks if you look at luxury through the COVID period, it was primarily driven by the aspirational consumer in the US and in Chin a. The presenter thinks the aspirational consumer in the US is simply not in the same place it used to be. In China, there is some slow improvement in terms of the Chinese consumer, but the presenter thinks there is a lot of dispersion by brand. By all accounts, Gucci is not resonating in China, which needs to happen for the brand turnaround to take place. Back in 2019, the presenter believes they were also heavily dependent on selling into the wholesale gray market in China, and they have now rationalized those practices. From a Gucci top line perspective, the presenter is quite skeptical on their ability to get back to that historical level of sales.

And then on the margin front, the bulls would argue that they can get to high 20%s / low 30% EBIT margins at Gucci. The presenter thinks that will be difficult, given all the investment needed back into the brand. Then, the CEO has said during buy-side callbacks that you are a luxury goods company if you have over 20% margins, which made the presenter believe that they are not likely getting back to high 20%s anytime soon, and that they are likely going to be reinvesting. That makes the presenter more skeptical on the margin front.

From a valuation perspective, Kering is currently trading at 25x 2027 EPS. Historically, this business traded in the mid-teens to 21x. Even during its heyday, it traded at 21x (on average). The presenter is putting 20x on their 2027 EPS assumption, and they are getting to a $210 price target.

The presenter would like to discuss Hilton Grand Vacations as a long.

The stock is currently trading at $48.50, with a $4 billion market cap, and a $9 billion TEV.

In terms of the business, they are a timeshare company: they sell, finance, and manage Hilton-branded timeshare resorts. It trades at 6.6x 2027 EBITDA. The core of the thesis is, it trades at a 20% forward free cash flow yield, which the presenter thinks grows to a 25% free cash flow yield in 2028.

After the Caesars take-private, there are not many companies in their coverage universe that trade at a 20% free cash flow yield. It currently trades at a material discount to both Travel + Leisure (TNL) and Marriott Vacation Worldwide (VAC), and there is 25% to 30% upside if it were to trade in line with those peers. The presenter thinks it should trade at a premium, because 10% to 20% of VAC and T&L's business comes from an exchange business, which they think is in secular decline (essentially into perpetuity). The industry backdrop is healthy, and all three companies are seeing fairly strong sales in real time.

The presenter thinks the stock is cheap because of an overhang from Apollo. Apollo took 25% of the equity in this company when they merged it with Diamond Resorts in 2021. They started selling their stake in 2024, selling one block in late 2024, one block in mid-2025, and one block just last week. They have taken their ownership stake of ~30 million shares down by 60%. They currently own 16% of the shares outstanding.

The only thing that keeps bringing their ownership up is the fact that HGV is very aggressively repurchasing stock. They repurchased 15% of the shares outstanding last year, and the presenter believes they are going to do an additional 15% this year; they have repurchased over 35% since they started a few years ago. The presenter thinks that will continue.

Now with Apollo's ownership down to a reasonable level, the presenter thinks it is less of an overhang. They think they should be fully out within the next year-and-a-half. If a 25% free cash flow yield in 2028 goes to a 15% free cash flow yield (which is in line with peers but the presenter would argue is too high), there is 70% upside over a year and a half, which the presenter believes is a compelling return opportunity.

The presenter would like to discuss Groupon as a long.

Groupon currently has a $600 million market cap and it trades approximately $24 million per day.

The presenter thinks Groupon is a misunderstood turnaround story which is currently inflecting and is positioning itself to be an AI beneficiary.

In terms of valuation, it is trading at ~4x the presenter’s 2027 EBITDA assumption and at a 22% free cash flow yield. Under CEO Dušan Šenkypl (who se investment firm owns 30% of the company), they have completely turned around the company. The company has returned to billings growth and is aggressively buying back stock now.

In terms of the macro backdrop, the presenter thinks it fits very well with a weakening consumer environment, where many consumers could be looking for deals.

For background, the pandemic obviously decimated the services economy, where Groupon was facing steep declines in sales, and there was a going concern during this period. Then, in 2022, the Czech Internet billionaire Dušan Šenkypl and his investment firm took over the operations of the company. They have completely turned around the business since then.

They have completely rebuilt the entire tech stack. They are now positioning the company to be a real AI beneficiary.

The stock was trading well last year and hit a high of $40, but it has now retraced a significant portion of that move. This was due to a gross billing slowdown in late 2025. This slowdown was due to two issues, one being weakness within their enterprise merchants’ segment, and two, weak managed & organic Internet traffic. The presenter thinks both those issues are now de-risked, and management has taken out improvement completely from the guide.

In terms of why enterprise is de-risked, they insourced their enterprise merchant acquisition.

They have recently launched a McDonald's deal, so the presenter thinks that is trending positively. They are also launching new products to help boost traffic, one being their customer data platform and their new app. This allows them to actually offer targeted marketing, which would seem like a very basic thing for a modern Internet company to be able to do, but this is something previously impossible for them. These are two factors that they think are helping the story right now.

In terms of the AI angle, Groupon recently announced a new initiative called Project Foundry. They announced a headcount reduction, which is resulting in $25 million of annualized cost savings. They are also positioning themselves to be an AI-first company, with many initiatives. Additionally, they think the financial model has a lot of operating leverage, and they also have significant free cash flow generation potential with a growing marketplace. They have a negative working capital cycle, so they have over 100% free cash flow conversion when they are growing gross billings.

In terms of the presenter’s estimates, they think 2026 EBITDA could be $88 million. In the presenter’s opinion, this will grow 50% in 2027 simply based on these cost savings and modest gross billings growth. They think free cash flow can reach just under $150 million in 2027, which would equate to a 22% free cash flow yield.

In terms of repurchases, just last quarter they repurchased 7% of shares outstanding.

Additionally, they hold a stake in a non-core asset, a European fintech company called SumUp. Just based on Financial Times articles regarding valuation, this could be worth in the range of $4.75+ per share. This would be monetized, when they have an opportunity, with an IPO.

Also, the short interest is extremely high. If you look at Bloomberg, it is quoted at 59% of the float. The presenter thinks it is materially higher than this when you take out passive ownership, as well as long-term holders.

In terms of valuation, at the current price of $16 per share, it is trading at ~4x the presenter’s 2027 EBITDA assumptions or at a 22% of the cash flow yield. The presenter thinks 10x on 2027 EBITDA and discounting this back would support a target price of $39 per share, or 120% upside from current levels. This would be approximately a 10% free-cash flow yield, which they think is more appropriate.

The presenter would like to discuss Dick’s Sporting Goods as a long.

The presenter acknowledges that there are a lot of investors on either side of this trade. It traded down after the Q1 results although the presenter believes the results were actually pretty good. Dick's comped +6%. The Foot Locker business was what caught the presenter’s attention in the quarter. It comped + 60 basis points positive for Foot Locker and had an operating margin a round 1%.

The stock trading down was more due to investors ’ focus on Dick's Sporting Goods. They had a great comp, but very little of it flowed through. They had higher costs. They were actually in-line in terms of operating margins, even though they had strong top line trends, which caused a lot of questions about investment spending.

The short thesis on this is very focused on the second-half margin inflection. What management has said is, they have some investments that are flowing through, some of it related to the World Cup, but most of it more related to integration, technology, etc., that is flowing through in the first half. That is going to roll off, and then in the second-half you are going to see some margin inflection. The short focus is betting against that margin inflection.

The presenter thinks the nice thing when you are talking about this and underwriting it is, you are not talking about revenue inflecting in the second-half and growth inflecting in the second-half. All you need is for their costs to normalize. In fact, the ir guidance says that comps are going to be weaker in the second half of the year than the first half of the year. For reference, this company is a notoriously conservative guider. The presenter thinks it will be easy for them to find 50 to 60 basis points of operating margin between the second half and the first half of the year, and that is really all you need to hit their numbers.

Longer term, what the presenter thinks is not being appreciated is the Foot Locker dynamic.

When Dick’s first acquired Foot Locker, it traded all the way down to 12x on a pro forma PE basis (that was down from 18x). It is now trading at 14x consensus earnings.

If you look into how the Street is modeling these businesses, the issue is that the Street does not break out the two businesses. So, in the presenter’s opinion, they get to numbers (on an operating margin basis) that imply very little improvement, and not enough improvement in the Foot Locker segment. If you go back to 2019, Foot Locker had 32.5% gross margin and a 9% operating margin. They have a 28% gross margin today. They are at a 1% operating margin. They do not need to do a whole lot on the top line. They basically need to just stabilize it, which they have already effectively done. They have comped positive in the most recent quarter. The presenter believes that you gain $0.75 of earnings for every 100 basis points of operating margin. The Street’s implied assumption for 2027 operating margin is a little more than 3%. The presenter thinks it is likely going to be more than 5%. You can get outperformance anywhere from $1.40 to $1.60 simply based off of modeling the margin improvement better than what is currently anticipated. Most of the Street is not doing that on purpose. They are just modeling a consolidated operating margin, and they are not breaking out what the implied dynamic is for either business.

The Street is assuming $16.40 of EPS in 2027. The presenter thinks there is a clear path for it to be above $18. Using a conservative multiple, you can get to $285 - $290 per share. That is before you start thinking about 2028, where if they can get Foot Locker to a 6% operating margin, and you can get a 50 basis point contribution over that period from core Dick's, this company could earn $20 per share. Again, the Street is expecting $14 of EPS in 2026, trading at 14x that number. It is trading 11x $20 EPS in 2028.

In summary, this is mostly a mis-modeled situation. You do not need any Herculean effort from Dick's Sporting Goods while Foot Locker is making significant progress. Again, it is mostly margin progress, which is a lot easier. They have had a lot of markdowns. Inventory is in a much better position now. The presenter thinks you can get 400 to 500 basis points out of gross margin between this year and next year, just by selling goods at full price. The presenter thinks there is a relatively easy, underwrite-able path. It is not a triple, it is not a double, but from $213 today, it could trade up to $260 to $270 over the course of this year.

The presenter would like to discuss Coca-Cola Consolidated as a short.

It is a $10 billion market cap, a $12.5 billion TEV, and the stock is currently trading at $180.

It is the largest US Coca-Cola bottler. They buy the concentrate from Coca-Cola, then package and distribute it across 14 different states and DC, covering a consumer population of approximately 60 million.

The presenter likes it short for four reasons. One, you have the SNAP benefit regulations from the MAHA movement, which is a near-term headwind to volumes. Seven out of the ir twelve primary states have soda bans. Two of them are already active — Indiana and West Virginia — and five will be implemented in the next year. That is a high single-digit percent of their total population, and likely higher percentage of their actual customers, since SNAP users tend to buy more soda. If you do channel checks with distributors or C-store operators in the states where they have already implemented these changes, you will see there is already a material volume impact in terms of the SNAP accounts.

Number two, pricing has outpaced normal “food-at-home” inflation by over 20% since 2019.

This has enabled Coke to expand gross margins by 600 bps. On top of that, you have GLP-1 pressure, and Pepsi talked about cutting prices on some of the ir snack food offerings.

Number three, the ir cost stack is hurting them again this year. Aluminum, PET resin, and diesel account for ~12% of total COGS and selling, distribution, and administration expenses are all up ~50%.

Finally, they will have a harder time pushing price through, because Coca-Cola Company sold their stake (they had a 25% stake but sold it in November), so the presenter does not think they are going to have as favorable terms on the concentrate.

Using the presenter’s numbers, Coca-Cola Consolidated is trading at 30x this year's EPS. The presenter thinks it should probably trade at 20x. Coca-Cola trades at 24x and that is obviously a much better business, with less capital intensity, and they own the brands. That gets the presenter to 35% downside from here.

The presenter would like to discuss Cineplex as a long.

Cineplex is a movie theater monopoly in Canada with approximately 75% market share. This business came under a lot of duress coming out of COVID. As you can imagine, it takes quite some time to produce movies. Just as people started to get excited that movies were coming back again, they were hit with a writer and actor strike, which further exacerbated those issues.

These businesses traded at 14x EBITDA prior to peak streaming fears. The presenter’s view is that this is the best macro backdrop for movie theaters that they have seen since 2017, given the fact they have seen a lot of these digital-first entrants (Netflix, Amazon Prime, and Apple TV), decide to go into theatrical and actually embrace theatrical. Amazon, the presenter thinks, is going to put up to 18 movies in theaters next year.

The presenter thinks that Generation Z is really embracing movies. You have seen that recently with Backrooms and Obsession. There is tremendous operating and financial leverage in the model. This is a 20%+ free cash flow-yielding business with leverage th at is coming down materially. On the presenter’s math, they have leverage coming down a turn each quarter over the next three quarters. The accretion to equity at a fixed multiple is a 75% premium to the equity, and that is with the stock trading at ~7x EBITDA. It was 4.5x last quarter, and the presenter thinks it will be 3.5x when they report this quarter, 2.5x when they report Q3, and 1.7x when they report Q4.

Why this is interesting now is that the business is at a fundamental inflection, but from an event perspective, the setup is as good as it gets. This management team sold the company to what is now Cineworld, which was Regal Cinemas, in 2019 for $34 per share. The stock is currently trading at $11. The presenter thinks EBITDAL, which is EBITDA after lease expense, will be in line to slightly higher than where it was in 2019 with a healthier / better backdrop. The CEO announced that he is retiring nine months ago with no successor. He gets $20+ million under a change of control provision. The presenter is highly confident that they want to sell the business. There have been some press articles that they are talking to Cinemark (and potentially Cineworld) to do a deal. If you run the math on Cinemark, in the presenter’s opinion, they can do a 50/50 equity cash deal and still be sub-3x levered, get 20% accretion, and still buy this company in the $20s.

If that does not happen — which the presenter thinks is a very high probability — they are very confident that management is going to either buy back stock and/or issue a dividend. If you study how their restrictive payments work, they are in a situation now based on their leverage that they could start buying back stock post-June. Their covenants are based on cumulative EBITDA L over cumulative interest expense. The presenter thinks that kicks in, where they will have over $100 million of buyback powder over the rest of the year — which would be 15% of the company — into the back half of the year.

In addition, the presenter thinks that the company will likely issue a dividend. The presenter is not a big dividend fan, but thinks Canadians investors love dividends. So, investors are looking at a company that previously had a dividend that subsequently got pulled, and is now very likely to initiate a dividend once leverage goes below 3x.

This is a completely mismodeled business. The presenter believes that it will be very evident when they report this quarter that leverage will be 3.5x on the way to 2.5x. Investors will likely “skate to the puck” and realize the dividend is coming in the out quarters.

In summary, you have the potential dividend, buyback, asset sales, and a massive inflection in terms of the movie slate. The presenter believes that June is now tracking up 30% year-over-year and in line to slightly higher than in 2019. They believe that July and August will be in line to higher than 2019. This will be the first time they have seen the box office in line to higher than 2019 for a sustained period of time.

The presenter thinks the timing for the catalyst is now as the inflection is happening. In the presenter’s opinion, a buyback at a minimum is going to happen by August, a dividend is likely going to happen within the next few months, and they think the odds this company is sold within the next three months is extremely high.

The presenter would like to discuss Richemont as a long.

Richemont currently has a ~€100 billion market cap (it is net cash).

In a tough consumer environment, the presenter is looking for companies that reported strong earnings, sounded optimistic on the key drivers of the business, and that would objectively go up 10% if the Strait of Hormuz reopened. In the presenter’s view, Richemont checks those boxes. More than 60% of the business is exposed to APAC, Europe, and the Middle East, creating headline pressure in the current environment, while the growth story at Cartier and Van Cleef continues to unfold. Against a backdrop where broader luxury data is beginning to stabilize, the presenter sees an attractive tactical entry point over the next few weeks if oil remains elevated. When the market is no longer forced to discount that geopolitical risk, the stock could re-rate sharply higher.

In terms of the business, it is a luxury holding company. They own a lot of different brands, but the major driver of the stock is Cartier as well as Van Cleef.

Historically, it was known as a best in class operator. In the presenter’s view, management has had a hard time recently communicating some of their cost pressures (in particular gold), which has created a more challenging setup for investors focused on near-term margin progression. But if you have longer duration, the truth is that they have taken materially less price when compared to their peers plus the fashion trends are in their favor if you wanted to build the qualitative argument, particularly for Cartier.

The stock is currently trading at 11x to 12x 2028 estimates and 12x to 13.5x 2027 estimates, depending on whether you are using consensus or the presenter’s numbers, and you have a lot of time until the next major catalyst / earnings print (since they recently released FY 26 on May 22nd).

The presenter thinks they also have meaningful pricing power. The resilience of the high-end consumers in what has increasingly become a K-shaped economy supports that view. China remains the largest area of uncertainty, given the limited visibility into the pace and durability of any recovery. Japan and North America in particular continue to accelerate.

The presenter acknowledges that after the runup in the shares, it is less interesting for some at these levels. But the presenter thinks with time and its net cash profile, it is a 14x to 15x EBITDA story.

The presenter gets to €211 per share as an exit price target, which would equate to ~30% upside from here. The presenter thinks that Cartier and Van Cleef (as brands) are a safe place to hide within consumer in the short term. They will put RCL in that bucket, too, where if you get a ceasefire announcement, it is going up 10% rather quickly. On the other hand, the presenter does not necessarily think it trades down materially if the war continues.

The presenter would like to discuss Cava as a short.

The presenter has to give credit to the company for Cava's outperformance against the industry, the main reason why it trades at a premium multiple relative to other unit growth peers like Shake Shack and Wingstop. Both of those stocks have seen a significant multiple de-rating as a result of deteriorating comp growth. Cava is now trading at 40x NTM consensus EBITD A — essentially the same multiple as Shopify, and at a significant premium versus Wingstop and Shake Shack (after Shake Shack’s recent miss), despite similar unit growth. So, the only difference is basically the comp.

They are also operating in a hyper-competitive restaurant industry that is not only getting pressured by value wars (among the participants) as well as unit oversaturation (across the board), but also from grocery share gains by Walmart and Costco, stemming from years of exorbitant restaurant pricing.

In terms of the setup, the presenter believes that restaurants have little pricing power at the moment. That is not ideal, when wage inflation continues to trend around low-single digits to mid-single digits. Food inflation is likely going to accelerate because of the Iran War. For example, you had Cambell’s come out today and state that further food inflation is likely coming. You also have a strong El Niño weather pattern that is likely going to result in even more food inflation. All those factors are going to affect the restaurant supply chain, and without pricing power, that is going to hurt these businesses. That is partly why restaurant chains like Texas Roadhouse and Darden are struggling right now.

Cava is not immune to this because they did a + 10% comp in Q1 but they did not expand their restaurant level margins at all. There is no leverage because the presenter thinks they are basically investing in their price to drive that comp. At 40x EBITDA, to make the valuation work, you need to drive leverage in this business. Without that, it does not work.

That is only one part of the thesis, but additionally comp growth was already guided to accelerate. In the presenter’s opinion, investors do not believe that, because on a year-over-year comparison basis, compares do look like they are going to ease. Bulls are playing for material upside in the upcoming quarters in terms of the comp.

In the presenter’s opinion, the appropriate way to look at comparisons in the restaurant sector currently is on a three-year basis, because you need to lap the strength seen in 2024.

Cava had a very popular steak product in Q2 of 2024 that they need to lap. The presenter thinks investors who are expecting them to meaningfully beat these numbers are going to be disappointed, because the data is already showing a significant deceleration on a two-year basis, particularly within the last several weeks. The three-year data seems to be more stable to slightly decelerating. If you extrapolate the three-year data for the rest of the year, you are likely not going to get much upside. You are likely going to see deceleration in the comp as well. The comp is basically the only metric that is driving the premium for this company against the other restaurant unit growers.

The presenter thinks with positioning skewed long here, this seems pretty safe, particularly with the lack of restaurant demand currently on the long side. On the last print, they beat buy-side expectations on comps by two to three points, but the stock only had a 3% reaction to that print, despite coming in above the bar, and it was already going into the print pretty depressed. The presenter feels like positioning is also on your side here. Is Shack worth 8x EBITDA? The presenter does not think so, but if Cava comps negative — the presenter does not know if it will, but if it ever comps negative, it is going straight to Wingstop and Shake Shack levels (in terms of the multiple).
