ideas.2026-04-20-monness-crespi-mch-industrial:
The presenter would like to discuss Thyssenkrupp as a long.

The company has a €6 billion market cap. In terms of the business, it is a European steel and industrial conglomerate.

The presenter thinks there are two angles to the thesis. The first is that it is a restructuring / sum of the parts story, but the more interesting angle to the thesis is the changing regulatory environment in Europe. That has huge upside optionality as it relates to the actual profitability and cash flow of their steel business.

On the restructuring piece of the story, they are going through the ir entire industrial portfolio and simply spinning off or separating out assets. For example, last year they spun out half of their naval shipbuilding business as a public company. Next, they are going to spin off what is called Material Services, which is a steel / metals trading & distribution business. So that will be listed, and you will get half of the value of that in shares as a shareholder later this year.

There is also the IPO of Thyssenkrupp Elevators, or a potential merger with Kone. They own 16% of Thyssen, so you will get value realization there. In 2027, they will likely spin off or separate the automotive business, which is worth approximately $2 billion. Then they are going to likely separate out the steel business, which is the “legacy” company. They could sell this segment but the presenter thinks they may simply wait and spin it.

If you do the sum of the parts math using reasonable valuations, the presenter gets to €15 (before any discount), and putting a 25% discount on it, maybe that is €11. The stock is at €9.

The presenter thinks there is upside just on the restructuring piece alone, with additional catalysts throughout the year.

But the huge upside case is really based on tariffs and protectionism in Europe that could cause steel prices to go up materially. Just to give numbers around that opportunity: in that sum of the parts math, the presenter values the steel business at zero equity value. That gets you to €11. They are doing a restructuring of th is steel segment, which will add €500 million of EBITDA. €500 million of EBITDA at 5x is an incremental €2 to €2.5 billion. That alone would get you to €15 per share. These restructuring initiatives are actually happening. The CEO is superb ulled up about it. It is going to take place over the next few years. Again, that takes you from €11 to €15.

And then the blue-sky case, which the presenter thinks is going to happen, is regulatory EBITDA uplift. So, Europe has decided they want local steel capabilities and production.

They do not want to rely on China. Obviously, Europe wants to also protect themselves in terms of defense. They also want to be able to make steel domestically to have an industrial ecosystem. The tariffs they are putting in place are really significant. Currently, there is a 25% tariff on any imported steel into Europe above 38 million tons per year (so no tariff on the first 38 million, and 25% above that). They are doubling that tariff (likely starting in July), so it is going to be 50% tariff above 38 million tons.

More interesting, the quota is actually going to be cut by 47%. The quota used to be 38, and now it is getting cut by 47%. Not only do you have twice as high of a fee on those incremental tons, it is also going to start affecting more tons. Using simple math, if you just took a 25% price increase on steel (steel is ~€600 per ton, so 25% of that is €150). Let us haircut that and assume €100 per ton of incremental EBITDA, they have 8.5 million tons of production, so that would equate to another €850 million euros of EBITDA. Again, at 5x, that is another €4 billion of value. That would take you to €22 per share.

The EBITDA uplift from that could actually be higher because you are doubling the quota, but it is on so many more tons. It is really hard to know exactly how this plays out because the world is dynamic. Tons will shift around to avoid tariffs. But there is huge optionality and they are just starting to see prices on steel in Europe go up a materially, and this company is highly leveraged to that.

The presenter would like to discuss Rolls-Royce as a long.

The presenter has been involved in the stock previously, but they have gained increased confidence in the story after meeting with their relatively new CEO Tufan Erginbilgic (who has been in position since 2023). Tufan is very aggressive, especially when it comes to cutting costs.

In terms of the business, Rolls-Royce has three segments. Civil aero is ~50% of revenue. The presenter thinks top line is going to be 9% or 10% growth for the next three or four years, with upside longer term with new partnerships on narrow body. The presenter does not know if that happens this year or next, but it obviously a topic of discussion. The presenter feels like there is a decision that needs to be made in the next 12 to 24 months, so it is hard to know, but the presenter thinks that is upside optionality.

The incrementals on the sell-side for civil aero seem conservative, and maybe with what is going on in the world, that means less downside. But they have done 40% to 45% incrementals. The presenter feels like the Street is in between 25% and 35% on civil aero.

The seconds egment is power generation. The power segment that is experiencing very strong growth and is sold out for the next two years. Given the CEO's credibility in his execution and listening to him talk, even beyond that two-year mark sounds very compelling. Then there are other growth drivers within the power segment which is approximately 25% of sales.

Then the final 25% is defense. Clearly with what is going on with Israel, Iran, NATO, Europe, Trump, and the rest of the European leaders, the UK and Europe should be a driver of defense revenue for Rolls-Royce. Consensus is 5% to 7% revenue growth, which does not seem very heroic.

If you combine the three segments, they should be growing 10% or more over the next three years while showing margin improvement. On top of that, the company has a buyback. They have a £5 billion free cash flow target in 2028. The presenter thinks £6 billion is easy, based on various upsides from three segments. Using a 25x multiple, would lead to a target price of £1,800 which equates to 45% upside over the next 18 months.

The presenter would like to discuss Renault as a long.

Renault is an OEM in Europe. For context, the company had a terrible first half in 2025. They had hiccups in deliveries and subsequently ousted the CEO.

It is a sum of the parts story. On a sum of the parts basis, the presenter gets to ~€55 in terms of assets that they own, and you are getting the auto business — which is a profitable business — for free.

The company currently has a €9.4 billion market cap trading at €31 per share. They own a 36% stake in Nissan, worth €2.2 billion, which is €7 per share. They have a highly profitable financial services business, which at 6x P/E is worth another €4.4 billion, or €15 per share.

Th is business has been generating €700 million to €1 billion euros of annual net income for the past seven years. They have a stake in a powertrain JV with Geely and Aramco, worth €2.2 billion, or €8 per share. They are basing that off the valuation that Aramco transacted in 2023 and putting on a 25% discount.

And then they have their real automotive business that we all know, which trades at 4x normalized EBIT, worth another €6 billion or €20 per share. They do not have any financial debt. They have a few euros per share in terms of pension underfunding.

In summary, the presenter believes you are getting €55 in terms of sum of the parts value for a stock that is currently trading at €30. The presenter noted that the vol. is very cheap and the story is underfollowed. The presenter thinks it has torque to the upside with al ot of optionality regarding divestitures and further monetization. PE has a ton of money now that private credit is having issues, and Renault has some interesting assets that they can potentially divest such as the Nissan stake. The presenter thinks it is only upside from here.

The presenter would like to discuss QXO as a long.

If you have known Brad Jacobs or you have followed anything in the industrial sector, he is known as a serial entrepreneur. The presenter thinks he has been waiting to do something with the Apollo backstop. First, it was with Rex el which primarily specializes in the distribution of electrical equipment, and then it was housing with Beacon. Today, he announced a deal with TopBuild (ticker: BLD) that caught the presenter a little off guard.

Taking a step back, QXO was simply a sheet of paper with a balance sheet from a really good entrepreneur over 12 months ago. He bought Beacon last year, which is the largest distribution provider of residential roofing at the trough of the cycle. Brad Jacobs has stated publicly that he thinks we are at a trough in terms of housing but admits we might not be.

He wants to apply technology and cut costs in order to dominate an industry, in order to have optionality for when their end markets recover.

In terms of today’s news, they announced the acquisition of TopBuild. TopBuild is the largest installer of insulation. They recently got into commercial roofing. Beacon and TopBuild have a combined commercial roofing business in terms of distribution, and TopBuild had transitioned some of their business into commercial installation (i. e. data centers).

So you now have what will be the second largest building products company. The synergy assumptions a few years out translate to $300 million of synergies. At a range of 12x (at the low end) and 17x or 18x (at the high end), you get $20x $30. But the presenter thinks knowing Brad Jacobs and having dealt with XPO for a long period of time, he is a serial entrepreneur. This company, at the end of 18 months from now, will have 1.5x turns of leverage. Whatever metric you put on this business, in terms of what you think the value is, this just became the “platform.” The presenter believes Brad Jacobs would argue he now has a platform, so he is going to either execute with the cycle turning, or he is going to cut costs aggressively.

His suppliers are OC and Carlisle, on insulation and commercial roofing, and his customers are data centers and residences. He competes with IBP and a whole bunch of other distribution providers, and he is either going to win by growing volume or win by cutting costs. He has given you $300 million of synergies which the presenter believes are understated.

The presenter thinks this is now the platform, and 12 or 18 months from now will have a different leverage profile (it is ~3x now, but he is going to be ~1x in 18 months if he remotely executes). This is going to be XPO all over again, where there is the next deal, then the next deal.

The presenter feels like this is a good entrepreneur making a good bet at the bottom of a cycle where he is going to create some ways to win.

The presenter would like to discuss MasTec as a long.

The presenter admits it is a well-known story at this stage. A significant portion of the business looks like Qanta Services, but arguably slightly lower quality. On the execution front, part of the business looks like Dycom. The presenter thinks the most hated or previously ignored part of the business is their pipeline end market, which is approximately 1/3 of the EBITDA. It is a specialty contractor. They have the number one share in terms of building new gas pipelines in the United States.

The presenter thinks a majority of the move investors have seen over the last six months has been entirely on the multiple. It tracks PWR at a 5x to 10x discount on PE (in that range), but you have yet to see any big revisions, and that is where the excitement in the story comes in to play. The presenter thinks that is driven mostly by the pipeline business, and the Street is backwards looking (in a way) on that segment.

The presenter thinks there are a lot of reasons to believe that there will be a lot more pipeline being built over the course of the next decade. In the US, LNG is obviously a big demand driver. One demand driver that the presenter thinks is a bit more overlooked — which you can back test historically — is that gas turbine deliveries actually have a high correlation with midstream CAPEX dollars in past cycles. So if invest o rs believe GEV (when they report in a couple of days) is going to have 100 gigawatts of backlog, and the majority of that is in the US, as well as other OEMs sending gas turbines to the U.S. over the course of the next five years, the presenter believes you will clearly need a lot more takeaway capacity. That takeaway capacity needs to connect to turbines that are now in more disparate areas with inferior gas interconnect ors and MasTec builds all of that.

Historically, investors would look at that business and index it to its share of midstream CAPEX. The presenter thinks the issue is the Street, when it forecasts midstream CAPEX, does not account for any projects that the companies have not told investors they have already FID'd. And so obviously, every time a new project is FID'd, if you look at EEB on Bloomberg for CAPEX for Kinder Morgan or Williams, it always ticks up — sometimes 100% to 200% — from the one or two years prior. So if you take your favorite top-down demand model from turbines, LNG, etc., you are clearly going to need a lot more gas capacity for takeaway. In the US, that is the most exciting part of the business.

The presenter believes this segment was previously hated because it is a boom-or-bust business. The presenter thinks you are entering a decade-long pipeline super cycle, because of gas generation and LNG, and the presenter thinks they should be able to push price or margin in that business to approximately the 25% - ish range (a historical peak which they have said they can achieve). The presenter gets to approximately 50% above the Street by 2029 on EPS. The presenter acknowledges that the multiple is rich today, at 40x, but the presenter thinks there is no reason why that cannot hold for some time if you believe GEV should trade at north of 60x.

The presenter would like to discuss MTSI as a long.

They produce high-performance RF and microwave solutions. They operate three business segments, including industrial & defense, data center, and telecommunications. It currently trades at $280 per share, which equates to 41x consensus earnings of $6.79 in 2028 (which the presenter knows is very steep but can be justified). The presenter sees a path to over $400 in the next 18 months, off EPS approaching and surpassing $10, which equates to 40% plus upside.

Before jumping into the segments, the presenter wants to talk about the gallium nitride opportunity that they have, compared to the majority of the rest of the field. It is a pretty scarce asset, and it is critical for anything within space or hardened semiconductor environments. Essentially, in the presenter’s opinion, they have communicated to investors that there are only 10 or so companies that are fully integrated and can work with the material, and the majority, almost 95% of them, are not North American-centric. So, they are one of the only players here, if you want to work within the North American supply chain.

They have the majority of the fabs operational here.

Essentially, if anyone wanted to enter into this market; first, they would have to get a fab up and running, and MACOM already has fabs that have great yields and availability. Second, since they are the only domestic producer, they already have DoD approval, which gives them another layer of security. And then they also have a very strong R&D presence. So, it would take a lot of money and time for a new entrant to come in to this market.

Starting with their industrials & defense business, this originally was a more industrial-focused business, but lately they have been seeing 20%+ growth within the defense segment, which the presenter thinks will easily continue with the shifting landscape and the continuation onto more electronics within defense weaponry. They also have DoD satellite contracts within th is segment, as well as additional tailwinds coming from drones and missiles.

Then, if you get any cyclical uplift within the industrial segment, that would be the cherry on top within that segment. That is simply coming from commentary getting better from ADI and TXN. Within data center, they do a few things, mostly TIA drivers, PVs, and linear equalizers, as well as CW lasers. They essentially guided to 37.5% growth this year, which the presenter thinks is extremely light, based on most of the components are going to get transceiver modules and them gaining a lot of share. Just based off that, with the PVs alone, the presenter thinks you could probably get 40% to 50% growth. Anything else on top of that is more upside. The bear case has been that they lost some linear equalizers to Semtech, with Google not ramping them immediately, but the presenter believes that is coming online later this year. It is not baked into their guide, so the presenter believes that you have minimal risk there.

Lastly, within their telecommunication segment, that is where their satellite exposure sits right now. They are noncommi t tal about how large the exposure is, but you can use various methods of going through the transcripts and earnings call to figure out where it sits and the presenter thinks it is approximately $40 to $50 million of the last year's revenue. The presenter thinks that is going to show exponential growth based off their existing customer, SpaceX. In the presenter’s opinion, they have already talked about another contract coming, anywhere between $55 and $85 million, and another five or six other customers that are already in the pipeline for 2027 and 2028. Based off that, the presenter believes they can generate between $400 to $500 million in revenue in that segment alone, which is a massive 50% CAGR as well.

Finally, the presenter acknowledges that the valuation is expensive — but they are defending it. First, the moat that they have and that there are no other competitors that provides this type of technology or has the speed to do it. Second, the massive growth that the company is playing in right now. There are not many companies that have meaningful exposure to the three best end markets at the moment. Third, the potential take-out case of ADI coming in and buying them. They overlap headquarters. Most of the employees know each other. If MACOM gets cheap enough, the presenter believes a takeout would be very complementary to ADI’s portfolio.

The presenter would like to discuss Harley-Davidson as a long.

It has a $2.5 billion market cap and is very liquid ($75 million of ADV).

The company recently went through a CEO transition. The new CEO was previously the CEO of Topgolf and Pizza Hut.

So why is it on sale and how did it get here? They moved really aggressively to the big touring bikes, the 1,200cc bikes with a price of $40,000 to $50,000 MSRPs, and they really alienated the entry-level bike cohort. This new CEO understands this concept, that they need to bring back the $15,000 bikes that have mass appeal. They announced a FinCo. transaction with KKR and PIMCO; so, they are selling $6 billion of loans to these entities and there is a forward flow agreement.

The new CEO is also changing some of the operations of the motor business. You are transitioning to this capital-light transformation, where two-thirds of your forward flow is going to go to KKR and PIMCO. Important to note, the presenter believes this will unlock $1 billion plus for buyback activity. They have already shrunk the share count by 30% in the past four years and reduced it by 10.5% in 2025. The presenter thinks the re is a lot more to go. They have cut net debt by $450 million. The servicing fees from the loans that they have now sold into KKR and PIMCO are going to be recognized as non-lending income, so it is going to make the story cleaner for investors. On top of that, the motor co. is actually going to show some growth.

In terms of the catalyst path, the presenter believes you have six or seven catalysts. The balance sheet on Cap IQ is not accurate because of the F in Co. (it is a net cash balance sheet at this point). The motorcycle business, you are getting for 3x EBIT. That is on $450 million of trailing EBIT. The presenter thinks motorcycle EBIT goes to $730 million in the next 18 months. For reference, they generated $855 million of EBIT in 2023, $850 million in 2022, and $920 million in 2021.

If you want to look at the whole business, including the FinCo., you are buying it for approximately sub-7x EV/EBITDA, ~8x PE, and a 16% free cash flow yield, which the presenter thinks actually improves. The technicals look really good. You have sliced through the 50-day. You actually just got through the 200-day moving average today. MACD looks really good as well.

The company is really focused on the $15,000 entry bikes. There was a sell-side report that focused on dealer inventory checks, and it was the most positive dealer inventory check in three years. The presenter thinks a lot of that is based on the green space for these $15,000 to $20,000 entry level bikes. The dealers are just clamoring for it. In the presenter’s opinion, the CEO fully understands this now and he is going to subsequently ramp up capacity utilization. That is going to drive down your COGS. He is going to sell right into that channel, so you are going to get a nice short-term pop in the next couple of quarters that the motor company is not dead, and the stock should re-rate from 3x EBIT.

Important to note, they have an analyst day that they have committed to for May or June. It is the first one in three years. Last week, on the 16th of April, they had a call regarding HDFS (the F in Co.): what that is going to look like going forward, what the net income is going to look like, and how it contributes to the motor company. They are trying to get the story out there especially to the industrial analyst community that do es not fully understand the F in Co. element to the story.

The real albatross here has been their stake in Livewire (ticker: LYWR). Harley-Davidson owns 88% of the shares outstanding of Livewire which is focused on producing EV motorcycles. It is a $400 million market cap. It is down ~90% since the IPO in 2022. They have been consolidating that into their financials and it has created a negative $130 million headwind to EBIT. That is going away. Harley-Davidson’s CEO has publicly stated there will be no more funding for this EV motorcycle business. They had tried pivoting during the pandemic, but it has been an absolute disaster. When th is gets off their consolidated income statement eventually, that will make the Harley-Davidson story much cleaner.

The two-year thesis is that they are leaning more into aftermarket parts, accessories, services, as well as servicing the used bike fleet. Customization, which was de-emphasized under the previous CEO, but is really high margin, is going to be a focus under the new CEO. It is a good offset, since new motorcycle sales are still flat, but there is this whole universe, probably 3x the new bike universe, from servicing the used bike fleet.

The company has a new focus on capital returns. CAPEX is coming down significantly. All the growth CAPEX is going to come off, and it is just going to be maintenance CAPEX. Some of the R&D spending that they have been incurring is for an automatic transmission motorcycle. The presenter does not know when or if that will hit, but if that does hit, that could represent a massive share gain. The presenter can speak for their demographic that does not want to drive a manual transmission motorcycle and believes that would be a game changer.

Finally, this is a tariff beneficiary in the presenter’s opinion. Whether you get USMCA figured out in terms of what they are paying, or maybe they get a little bit of tariff inflow from a rebate. Also, the short interest is 17%.

The presenter would like to discuss FMC as a short.

FMC has a $2.2 billion market cap with $4 billion of net debt. As it relates to the Strait of Hormuz, investors think FMC is advantaged. It is not. Estimates are assuming $700 million of EBITDA. The presenter is below that. Interesting and important to the short thesis, the presenter thinks the first quarter is only expected to generate $45 million; so, the company is expecting to see a back half ramp. The stock is up from $13 to $17 because about a month ago at a sell-side conference — and the presenter encourages investors to listen to it, not just read the transcript — an analyst asked the CEO (since the company is exploring all sorts of alternatives) if they would you sell for $30.

The CEO gave an answer that some investors have bought in the teens and they would be happy with $30, and other investors are longer term, and they would not be happy with $30, and as a shareholder, the CEO personally would not be happy for $30. Then he also said, importantly, that they have had interest from five to ten strategic industry players. So the industry news publications put that all together and ran with the story that there was a $30 bid for the company that the management had turned down, and that took the stock up 4 or 5 points.

If you read or listen to the transcript, the presenter concludes that there was definitely not a $30 bid. The analyst simply threw out a number and asked if they would sell it for $30. But that is not what all the headlines wrote. That is not what some of the other analysts who were not present at that moment put out.

FMC has a lot of problems. They are pretty well documented. Its largest product went off patent last year; that accounted for almost $1 billion of EBITDA. It has been cut in half, and it is not returning. They have a serious balance sheet / debt issue. They have $500 million due in October. They have put up their India subsidiary for sale. They have said their expectation is to generate $450 million of proceeds for their Indian subsidiary. The question is, who buys it? The presenter thinks the re is only one logical buyer, which is UPL. But the presenter believes that UPL is not in the best shape financially at the moment to buy it.

If they do offload India, they have already said they will keep the manufacturing and will just sell the distribution. They are doing everything they can to get this asset off their balance sheet and bring in cash to pay down debt. Also worth noting, they filed a 10-K in February; if you look at the 10-K, they made some really interesting comments about their payables. In the presenter’s opinion, they essentially admitted that they extended their payables to make net working capital look better and, of course, get in line with their banking ratios. So, they admitted that, to the tune of ~$300 or $400 million. The presenter thinks there have been a lot of issues. The reason why they mentioned first quarter EBITDA as being so light is the way this business works, they have to build inventory to sell the following quarter. They are really cash-starved, and the presenter thinks that the stock is up on miscommunication.

In terms of risk/reward, the stock is currently trading at $17. The presenter thinks the downside, if they sold the company miraculously, they could potentially sell it for $20. The presenter thinks that is your biggest risk. The presenter thinks you are playing for $10 on the downside.

The presenter would like to discuss Element Solutions as a long.

Element Solutions is a specialty chemical company which the presenter describes as an upstream provider to the semiconductor supply chain. The presenter believes that data center PCB and chip packaging end markets could constitute 40% of the business in a few years.

The presenter believes that if you pick your favorite AI supply/demand model, and if you run that through the numbers, you can get to Street growth or higher and everything else, such as an industrials acceleration exiting the year, which also provides upside to estimates this year. Semis could also provide more than current Street growth next year.

The company has 35% incrementals, which is what the company has guided to cross-cycle and what they have hit previously. They should generate approximately $850 million in EBITDA in 2027. The presenter thinks that is 15% to 20% above Street estimates. Using a 15x to 20x multiple on that would equate to 50% upside. If investors want to get more aggressive, there is a layer count thesis, which is effectively higher content on the PCB circuit boards and growing complexity in chip packaging. If investors get that, plus some benefit on pricing, you are easily underwriting $950 million (in that range) of EBITDA in 2027, which is approximately $2.50 to $2.60 in EPS. If investors put a multiple on that closer to where faster growing specialty chemical companies that ESI's growth algorithm can converge towards, yields 90% upside on the stock. The presenter believes it is classified as a chemicals/ industrials company, and the presenter thinks it is less trafficked by technology investors.

The presenter would like to discuss Ducommun as a long.

The company has a $2.5 billion market cap and is an aerospace & defense supplier.

The presenter thinks it is an underfollowed story that investors are just beginning to notice since it is entering the exit velocity phase, where daily volume is starting to pick up. It used to trade $5, $10, or $15 million per day, but now it is $25 to $50 million. There are only four analysts that currently cover it, and it is entering this major discovery phase where the multiple can go materially higher. For reference, it is currently trading at ~13x 2027 EBITDA.

The presenter thinks a 15x to 17x multiple is reasonable for the ir end market exposures.

The business has high-teens EBITDA margins, generating close to $1 billion in revenue. It is 60% defense and 40% commercial aerospace. Within the defense business, 25% to 30% is missiles. In Q4, they did a 4x book-to-bill in their missiles business, of which $80 million of that was awards for electronic wire harnesses and other electronic products for interceptors for the Iron Dome. That occurred in Q4, even before the war started. For reference, their missile business grew 20% last year. The presenter believes that they are the outsourced electronics assembly and production for RTX and Lockheed, as well as a small portion with Northrop. They have content on a majority of programs that are going to 4x to 6x over the next five years.

In terms of the setup, the presenter believes that the guidance set for this year is very reasonable. Of the commercial aerospace business (~40% of EBITDA), it is almost all OE, and a lot of it is Boeing and Airbus. And they are overweight the Max. They overproduced the Max last year, so they are still in a bit of a destocking phase, so the aerospace segment is not expected to grow materially until the second half of the year.

But the presenter believes once you get past this year and into next year, they will have the Max and the A320neo ramping, and the missiles segment should grow materially. This company should grow double digits over the next three to five years. At some point, the presenter believes they are going to book a missile award. For reference, their backlog is currently over $1 billion; so, the missile award alone could represent their entire backlog in a single order.

What is interesting is that they have consistently outsourced work from RTX and Lockheed, and the presenter thinks if Lockheed and RTX are going to be able to hit these 4x to 6x targets, they are likely going to outsource even more to Ducommun. For background, there was a takeout offer long ago at $65 per share. The stock is currently trading at $140 per share. Although the stock has traded well, the presenter thinks the discovery value for investors who are just waking up to the story now is pretty significant.

They are having an Investor Day in September where the presenter thinks they are going to give new five-year targets. Their previous targets were to get from 13% EBITDA margins to 18%. Next year, they are going to be at 18%. The presenter can get to $190 million of EBITDA next year. The Street is at $170 million, and the presenter does not think they are making aggressive assumptions.

In terms of the management team, the CEO is really good. He owns $60 million worth of the stock (with minimal stock sales), so he is clearly incentivized.

In summary, the presenter believes that you are getting missiles and commercial OEM exposure at a discount to most peers in the space.

The bears would argue there is some bill-to-print exposure, it is a lower quality business, and the margins are lower than peers. But the presenter believes based on where we are in both the defense and commercial aerospace build cycles, you want to own the companies that are going to benefit from more volume. And the presenter thinks that is what this is. In terms of a target price, the presenter believes it is worth $200 without making crazy assumptions. The stock is currently trading at $140 per share.

The presenter would like to discuss Celanese as a long.

The company generates $10 billion in revenue and $2 billion of EBITDA. It has $11.5 billion of net debt.

In terms of the setup, the presenter would describe it as a left-for-dead chemical stock, as the sector has been a significant underperformer for the last three years.

Half of their business is selling acetic acid. The other half is selling compounded polymers, which they call “engineered materials.”

The simple pitch is that for a long time China was adding acetic acid capacity and 50% of the raw material input is methanol. They are buying methanol at approximately a 20% discount to the global index. They are buying at $250 to $280 per ton (70% of their imports are from Iran). They import somewhere between 15% and 20% of their methanol needs. They also have internal capabilities in terms of coal to gas, etc.

Ultimately, the presenter thinks that even if this is resolved, that discount goes away. Then the marginal cost of methanol into China will be at the appropriate cost curve. That alone, in the presenter's opinion, gets you another $100 per ton spread on the acetic side. They have 4.5 million tons of acetic acid and another 1.5 to 1.6 million tons of VAM. The presenter thinks in that half of the business, EBITDA goes from $800 million to $1 billion to $1.5 billion mid-cycle. Near term, the presenter thinks it is higher than that, but we will see how high spreads stay for how long.

And then on the other side of the business, engineering materials, it is compounded monomers that they turn into polymers. When the upstream gets tight, the pricing power moves to the compounders (where it is now). They took a 5% price increase in the first week of March and then they took another price increase last week (that varied depending on the grades). But ultimately, they are more than covering their cost inflation, so the presenter thinks you get another 200 to 400 basis points of margin expansion for that business.

Ultimately, the presenter thinks mid-cycle goes from low $2 billion of EBITDA to mid to high - $2 billion of EBITDA. Recently it has been trading with a high single digit multiple, but historically it traded at 15x, because they have a technology differential versus their peers.

Ultimately, the presenter thinks the stock goes from $60 to $90 to $150 over time as this all plays out, and investors get comfort that it is not just a short-term bump.

The presenter would like to discuss Chemours as a long.

While the outcome regarding the Strait of Hormuz is still to be determined, the presenter thinks Chemours is a winner either way.

Given Chemours' history, most investors still think that this is a TiO2 business. It is not. They will generate between $800 to $900 million of EBITDA this year. That is approximately $1 billion pre-corporate. Seventy per cent of that is in their refrigerants business. The refrigerants business is a phenomenal business. There is change occurring where legacy refrigerants, which are fairly commoditized, get stepped down over time. That is being transitioned into the new generation of refrigerants, which is a duopoly between them and Solstice, which was spun off from Honeywell. That business is expected to grow. Most of it is going to aftermarket, with some going to HVAC as well as data centers.

The data center business is fine. It is not a big part of the business (approximately 5%). There is a call option in a couple of years — they have patents on immersion cooling (which the presenter acknowledges is many years away). If that happens, it is going to be multiples of the volume that are consumed. Right now, later this year, they are launching direct-to-chip cooling, which is going to be a tailwind to growth.

In the meantime, recent current checks show that they are sold out of their refrigerants, and that is with housing being depressed. If they get pricing and volumes slightly pick up, they can see a tight market there.

The TiO2 business is where the presenter thinks the stock has gotten a little mojo, but they think that is the tail wagging the dog. Eighty-five percent of Chinese capacity is based off the sulfate process, which depends on sulfur. In 2025, prior to the Iran conflict, the industry was operating at 70% capacity in China. It exited in the 60%s. Sulfur is a huge cost, and half of Chinese sulfur supply is imported and half of that comes from the Gulf; so, 25% of Chinese capacity is coming from the Gulf. Seventy percent of Chinese demand is for fertilizers.

Beyond that, you have su l fur demand drivers coming from EV and grid batteries for cobalt and for copper smelting, all of which come ahead in the line of TiO2. There has been a structural increase to sulfur pricing ahead of the Iran conflict, and now you have Iran, which is likely going to be offline for some time.

LNG was a big source of sulfur coming out of Qatar. One of the first things that was hit was the Ras Laffan plant, where 2 of the 20 trains are offline. The supply chain there is 3+ years for brazed aluminum heat exchangers, which is what got damaged; so, that alone is going to be at least a year or two, even if they are successful in pulling the supply chain forward. The remainder comes from the rest of the Gulf Coast countries. Iran is going to take a while.

Sulfur is going to be higher for longer.

When you had an industry that was a ta sub-70% capacity utilization now having their biggest cost increase coming through, the presenter thinks a lot of capacity may shut down permanently. When that happens — if that happens — what they have already seen, China TiO2 pricing is up over 20% year to date. It is approximately $400 per ton, before you deal with shipping and anti-dumping tariffs in some countries.

So what was guided to be ~$150 million of EBITDA this year (vs. peak th a t was north of a billion), the presenter thinks $500 million is more likely mid-cycle. You do not put a big multiple on that, but every turn is ~$3 per share, for a stock that is currently trading at $23.

Finally, as it relates to the PFAS liability, the presenter thinks it is a lot lower than what the Street expects, and you should get more clarity regarding that later this year. The last time they resolved a part of their PFAS liability, the stock was up 30% the next day. The presenter thinks the stock could double or triple from current levels.

The presenter would like to discuss Belden as a long.

The stock is currently trading at ~$130 per share and trades over $30 million per day. It has a $5 billion market cap and a $6 billion EV. The company generated just over $450 million of EBITDA last year on $2.7 billion of sales.

The company makes cables, connectivity, and networking products, such as copper cables, datacom cables, connectors, racks, enclosures, & switches. Historically, they had other business segments that they have since sold. Now the company has two reporting divisions that they are going to be merging into one.

Two thirds of EBITDA comes from Automation Solutions, which includes discrete automation, process automation, and mass transit. It is higher margin than their other division, which is called Smart Infrastructure, which consists of building automation, campus work, and telecom work.

The thesis is that the valuation is compelling. It is trading 16x this year’s consensus earnings estimates, and 15x next year, with less than 2x leverage. Discrete automation is recovering now following two years of a downturn. This is also a direct play on physical AI. If you want to put humanoids into your factory, if you want to merge IT and OT in your factory, or if you want to automate your buildings, you really need to redo the wiring / infrastructure inside the building, which is where Belden plays.

Also worth noting, historically Belden never really sold to the hyperscalers or the large data centers. But they recently won their first contract last year, and now the presenter believes they have other contracts pending; so, the presenter believes none of those potential wins are factored into Street numbers.

The presenter thinks they can grow organically high single digits over the next several years with ~25% to 30% incremental margins. The presenter is underwriting approximately $10.00 of earnings for next year, while the stock is trading at $130 per share. Also, they are combining their two reporting segments into one starting next quarter. The presenter thinks this might be a precursor to them selling off their small telco business. If they were to do that, the presenter thinks this would be a very attractive buyout target for somebody like a TE Connectivity or other potential suitors.

The presenter would like to discuss Autoliv as a short.

It is of similar ilk from a theme perspective. The presenter thinks what the Street is largely completely complacent on is not the shortage of oil, because the marginal demand for oil is no longer gasoline. The presenter thinks the marginal demand is plastics, and if you look at what has been restricted, it is approximately 10% to 20% of the oil. But the naphtha and downstream (on the petrochem side) and sulfur have been massively restricted, especially into Asia, which is a net importer, on the order of 40% of their total supply.

As an example, the ships were flowing normally, but that stopped in mid-March. Then, on March 31st, INVISTA’s nylon plant, which is one of the largest in the world (and politically connected, in the presenter’s opinion), declared force majeure. It is a massive nylon exporter (one of dozens), which is causing a massive supply dislocation.

Then on the sulfur side, it is a similar type of magnitude. Butadiene goes into nylon 66, sulfur goes into nylon 6, which is more for apparel, but both go into auto parts. This shortage, the presenter believes, is going to last at least 6 to 12 months, and it is not going to be a case where customer can just pay up and get it; the presenter believes customers will not be able to get it. The presenter thinks this is going to reverberate through the auto supply chain.

Autos are 35% of nylon demand, and even within acetic acid, there is downstream, where it is even more acute of a shortage.

So, the reason the presenter is picking Autoliv is because it is trading within its historical range, assuming global auto SA AR is flat. For reference, 37% of their volumes are in Asia.

They make seat belts and airbags, a.k.a. nylon and polyester (while polyethylene has a similar problem as well).

The company just reported. They buy $1 billion dollars of plastics. There is a lag, because it takes time for their suppliers to get it and then pass it on, and then a little bit more of a lag to get it through the income statement. But the company claimed it is a $90 million headwind on $1 billion of plastics. Spot prices would suggest it is substantially more than that.

The presenter admits they will have pricing power since it is a duopoly. They have 40% share, and they will pass it through. You are not buying a BMW because you did not buy the airbag. They will pass it through with a lag, but that is a headwind on the short. But the real question is, are there enough before they need to idle production themselves? And the presenter thinks in Asia, there is a high probability that something will go wrong there. The stock is essentially pricing in a good set of circumstances; the company only cited a $90 million headwind and did not talk about supply chain problems. There are a lot of different ways to play the disruption, and the presenter thinks Autoliv is an interesting way to short this theme.
