ideas.2026-03-10-monness-crespi-mch-consumer-i:
The presenter would like to discuss Wynn Resorts as a long.

The stock has sold off recently because the ir major growth asset is in the UAE.

The presenter believes it is a high-quality asset, and they think the current dislocation will go away. The presenter thinks there is a lot of upside based on the way investors are modeling Dubai. It is a play on luxury, believing that the K-shaped economy gets accentuated in an AI-focused world, where there will be a lot of growth in wealth at the high end.

It is a smaller collection of assets when compared to MGM, but the asset base is a little bit more high-end focused. The biggest asset is in Macau. Again, you can value it separately.

The presenter tends not to anchor to the public valuation, since they do not think they are ever going to sell or spin it off, so the presenter simply thinks you own it.

Wynn currently has a ~$10 billion market cap. There is $9 billion of debt. Consensus estimates for EBITDA this year and next year are $2.1 billion and $2.2 billion respectively.

Free cash, adding back the CAPEX they are spending on Dubai, is approximately $1.1 billion or $1.2 billion, so you are getting paid about 10% a year to wait. You can argue whether or not that is the right multiple in the standalone business, although the presenter thinks that it is.

Of the EBITDA and the free cash, approximately 55% to 60% of it comes from Macau, approximately 35% to 40% of it comes from Vegas, and then they have a small asset in Boston which deserves a discounted multiple. If you put a discounted multiple on it, it is not going to swing the math much, it is approximately 10% of EBITDA.

The presenter agrees with everything the other presenter said about Vegas. As it relates to Wynn, it is a luxury asset that has been growing modestly. If investors think Vegas picks up, it should pick up a bit more because it has the right customer base and brand. It is also well managed. You are more exposed to China with Wynn than you are in a lot of other stocks.

That is a market that has seen a much-anticipated recovery that has yet to occur, and so that is the big risk factor to the story, in the presenter's opinion. But their China business has been fairly stable, the cash flow has been stable, and they have a good collection of assets there.

As it relates to the UAE asset, the presenter has done similar math that the other presenter was talking about in relation to Japan. If you look at Singapore and reason back, they have guided explicitly to cash flow with and without the management fee in Dubai. They have a low-case, a mid-case, and a high-case. Most of the sell side has the mid-case as an anchor.

The mid-case backs off to approximately $3.25 in free cash flow when it is stabilized. Approximately half comes from the management fee, and approximately half comes from their 40% interest in the hotel and casino.

It is a low-rate jurisdiction. You can talk about travel time, but the idea is a lot of people are going to come from Dubai, so you need to believe that Dubai is a growth asset.

There are three assets licensed. The math that they are doing is they are looking at the GGR (Gross Gaming Revenue) in Macau. And in the mid-case, they are assuming that is what the GGR looks like in the market, and then they are divided by three. If you look at Singapore, at the high case, the math they are doing gets you about halfway between where Macau is and Singapore is. So the presenter does not think you are going to get to Singapore, and neither does anyone else. In the high case, rather than $3.25, it is $5 per share in free cash.

When the presenter looks at the stock, they believe you are getting paid 10% a year to wait for a high-quality / stable collection of assets that have a lot of upside on the valuation of a luxury asset. If you think that you can get somewhere between the mid and the high case, there is approximately 60% up side in the stock, and investors are getting paid 10% a year to wait.

As it relates to the war, the presenter does not know what is going to happen better than anybody else. The presenter believes yesterday was a pretty big tell, ultimately, as to what happens. But in the throes of Liberation Day, the stock was trading in the mid - $70s. It has generated $6 per share of cash on the balance sheet ex-the dividend since then (so low $80s).

For reference, the current stock price is ~$102. So in terms of the risk/reward, the presenter looks at it as $20 down (in a disaster downside case). You can sensitize the cash flow hit.

Reasoning against periods of dislocation-including 2022 or going back to previous recessions – investors can put a 10% free cash flow yield on the business. For something that is well-capitalized and well-run, the presenter thinks that is reasonable. It implies approximately the same kind of math. The presenter thinks you are risking ~20%.

The presenter thinks that this is a business that has not generated any free cash, because they have been investing aggressively in this asset. They will generate meaningful free cash flow starting in 2027 and 2028. They have allocated capital really well. The sum of the parts value (in their base case), is up 40% to 50%, and in the high case, add another 20% or so to that.

The presenter would like to discuss Williams-Sonoma as a short.

The stock is currently trading at $188 per share or 22x 2026 EPS.

There are a few points to the short thesis. One, the presenter thinks they have pushed pricing too far. Pricing has driven over 100% of their comp growth for the past several years. Units are still declining. You can see this in their merchandise margin gains. Merchandise margins are up 1,000 bps since 2019.

Even since 2022, their merchandise margins are up 250 bps, and that is with revenues down 10% over that period; so, a peak margin business. They do not actually disclose units versus price versus mix, but ex their B2B business, the presenter thinks organically units are only up mid-single digits in total since 2019 while revenues are up + 31%. In the presenter’s view, there is ample evidence to illustrate what we know to be true, that they have taken a lot of price.

The presenter thinks there is some risk of that going backwards, rather than pricing continuing to move higher. You are seeing RH aggressively clear inventory right now. A lot of investors are bullish on lower tariffs for Sonoma – which the presenter cannot really deny-but the presenter thinks with a muted housing backdrop, that is likely to result in more price competition from competitors and potentially industry deflation.

The presenter also thinks there is unpriced tail risk to their core customer from AI. Their main customer is $150,000 household income / white collar professional. The presenter is not here to give you the doomsday pitch, but the presenter simply thinks rising anxiety among st that cohort at a minimum results in some deferral of spend (ie you can hold off on that $5,000 couch). The presenter covers luxury stocks, too. The presenter is already hearing this a little bit anecdotally from some luxury management teams that are talking about; the really rich are spending obviously, but the head of a legal department at corporate is kind of pulling back on some of the bigger ticket or more discretionary purchases. In the presenter’s view, this is right in the crosshairs of that.

The valuation also leaves no margin of safety. It is trading at 22x 2026 EPS and 21x 2027 EPS.

The presenter thinks this is a normalized mid-single digit EPS grower. They do not grow stores. It is expensive versus its own history. It is expensive relative to the growth algo. It is expensive for specialty retail. It is priced like a quality compounder on peak pricing driven margins, and the presenter believes it needs everything to go right from here.

The “why now” is, the earnings print is on March 1 8th. The presenter thinks 4Q data has been mixed. The laterals from other furniture or home furnishings companies that have reported already (RH has not reported) have not been great, whether that is the A rhaus exit rates or Somni Group-formerly Tempur-Pedic-also not great. Ethan Allen, which is a much smaller player, was also not great. This is very different than what we saw with the 3Q prints, where all the home furnishing companies beat and had accelerating trends.

The presenter also thinks there is guidance risk to 2026. Tariffs, just given the delayed impact, are still going to be a headwind in the first half on gross margins. The presenter does not think that management is going to bake in aggressive relief in the back half, even though India relief has been a positive. The presenter thinks they would probably guide EBIT margins flattish to down 20 bps in 2026. The presenter do es not think that is enough at this current multiple. On the comp guide, the presenter thinks it is a low single-digit comp guide.

The Street is at 3% for 2026. That is a “meet” at best.

Obviously, the big caveat here is, what sort of housing recovery we experience. The presenter thinks if you are bullish housing, there are higher torque, better ways to play that recovery. You can play it on the long side, and short this against it.

The presenter believes they generate $9 in EPS in 2027. The Street is at $10. The presenter is assuming low single digits, closer to flat to 2% comp growth over the next two years, and then giving up 100 to 150 basis points of merchandise margins. The presenter thinks it should trade at 16x to 17x which is 20% to 25% downside in a base case.

In a more bearish but not recession case, the presenter thinks they can do $8 EPS in 2027, and that is if they give back 200 to 250 basis points of that merchandise margin. Again, that is 20% to 25% of the merch margin gains since 2019, where units are still not really growing.

And at 14x to 15x, a real specialty retail multiple, that equates to almost 40% downside.

The presenter would like to discuss SmartRent as a long.

The market cap is only $350 to $360 million, with a cash balance of $105 million, for an enterprise value around $250 million. It is a VC-backed, prop tech failed startup that is down 85% to 90% since the stock’s 2022 highs. It checks all the boxes in terms of a turnaround thesis, with an improving execution roadmap and M&A buoyancy. It has gotten caught up in this SaaS multiple compression, when it really has very little to do with it.

For background, they effectively sell to multifamily developers. They are currently partnered with 15 of the top 20 developers. They have 890,000 deployed units. They just released what they are internally calling “Vision 28,” but effectively it is a guide to 1 million units in the next four to five quarters, growing to 1.2 million by the end of 2028.

For reference, the reason why the stock sold off – and rightfully so-is that the previous management team effectively could not hit guidance, were known for having a choppy deployed unit cadence, and were also known for what the presenter would describe as “giving away their software stack for compressed ARPU,” because a t the time, there were a ton of competitors in the space (almost 8 different competitors) who had recently raised money and were well capitalized.

Now, it has effectively been left for dead. Nobody covers it. They had a really good print last Wednesday (no one really took notice). It caught the presenter's eye in August, based on incessant insider buying. The presenter has been impressed with the CEO who took the job last February. In the presenter’s opinion, he should be at a better company. The presenter thinks the insider buying level up to $2.08 (the stock is currently trading at $1.80) creates a little bit of a floor. As you look out into 2026, the presenter thinks that you are going to get somewhere in the range of 25K units per quarter, and each print the booked unit number keeps moving higher. So, the blended SaaS ARPU is $5.50. Current bookings are just north of $8. That gap continues to grow.

They are basically going through an ARPU refresh cycle at an EV/ARR multiple that is shockingly small. The presenter thinks a very reasonable outcome for the company is that they sell themselves to one of the top five multifamily developers. Why would they pay $8 per unit to then have to sell to their tenant for $40 bucks per month when they can buy the whole company for $500 million and then deploy it overnight into every unit they own.

The presenter thinks the major question is, is there ARPU compression because of all the AI noise, or is there some multiple risk? But that was not the story. The story has been historically, the asset was horrifically run. In the presenter’s opinion, they are now soft-guiding to a break-even full-year EBITDA number. The presenter has it at 15x in 2026, all the way down to 5x in 2027 (extremely cheap).

The presenter thinks there is a high likelihood that there is a takeout prior to that. The presenter thinks it is interesting, and the presenter also thinks it is really dis-correlated from a lot of the other noise, a pretty safe place to be with all the insider buying.

The presenter would like to discuss Royal Caribbean as a long.

The stock has pulled back 20% since the company reported earnings at the end of January.

There is some consternation around yield guidance for the year, where investors are concerned that yields in Q1 are going to grow more than Q2, and then recover in the second half.

In the presenter’s opinion, the company is sort of pushing back, and the CFO is suggesting that yields will grow year-over-year in Q2 versus Q1. The presenter does not have a strong view. Whatever the case may be, the presenter believes that investors will want to own the stock very soon after they report earnings.

The presenter thinks that many investors are missing the bigger picture, which is they have new ships coming on this year and next year. They have two islands coming on this year and two islands coming on next year. They have one in the Bahamas this year as well as in Greece, and then next year, they have “Perfect Day in Mexico,” and they have one in the South Pacific. And the one in Mexico next year, the presenter thinks, is a huge driver. Each of these islands can add a few hundred basis points to year-over-year yields, as can the ship hardware.

The Street is assuming approximately 2% yield growth, and next year something similar, but the presenter thinks the ability for them to do more than that is in place. In terms of the Street assumptions, they are assuming earnings of $18 this year and $20 next year. The presenter thinks the number is going to be higher than that this year, and next year closer to $22 of EPS.

In terms of the technical setup, the stock tends to hold the $250 level pretty well. The stock is currently trading at $285; so, let us assume approximately 10% downside. If they hit $22 and they get an 18x multiple, it would equate to a $400 stock price, or roughly 40% upside.

The simple math is 10% down and 40% up. Obviously, in the 40% upside scenario, you need oil to trade back towards $70. They are 60% hedged on oil, so it is not an immediate impact.

It could cost them $0.25 to $0.50 cents of earnings this year on an $18 basis. It is not the end of the world. If it is 1% to 2%, they could offset that with yield.

Then the other concern, obviously, would be unemployment. If you think that the payrolls data from Friday is going to be the trend going forward, then there is probably some exposure here. The other part of the bull case is that this is a more affordable vacation than your typical land-based vacations. Their labor is non-US, so they have the ability to deliver cheaper vacations, and the value proposition is quite good. In summary, the risk/reward is good and the setup is good. The stock has sold off ~20%, creating an attractive entry point while the management team is pushing back on some of the bear thesis, and it is not a crowded position. If anything, the presenter believes that sentiment likely skews negatively.

The presenter would like to discuss Primo Brands as a long.

It is a pretty simple story. You are getting the chance to own a lean company in an attractive category.

Primo is the largest pure play water company in the world. It operates in roughly two segments. One is retail, which is the case pack water business. And then the home and office delivery business. That is where the debate on the stock is right now. In that segment, it is a virtual monopoly, with 65% to 70% share, with likely mid-single-digit (and possibly more) pricing power, competing against a long tail of regional mom & pops.

The opportunity exists because this company is a post-merger equity. The thesis around the merger was based on a bunch of cost outs through route optimization, closing depots, and some revenue synergies based on cross-selling brands through the respective distribution networks of each company. The presenter thinks that thesis is still in play. What happened was, they essentially pulled those levers too hard last year and rationalized everything virtually all at once. From what the presenter can tell, they are happy with the plan, but it was the speed of implementing the plan that was problematic, because it required perfect execution on the other side, and that is not what you got.

And now we are at a point where the old CEO is out. There is a new CEO and, in the presenter’s opinion, he sandbagged the guidance coming out of the Q3 call. The stock subsequently gapped down 40%. And now with the benefit of hindsight from Q4, and second derivatives improving in terms of the home and office delivery business, the stock trades in line with all of the KPIs that investors care about. The stock is trading at 13.5x earnings. The original merger math or synergy math was, at announcement, $300 million.

Investors were excited that that number could be materially higher than that. Now if you pencil $200 million and assume pretty reasonable re-investment, you still get a couple hundred basis points of margin expansion. The algo here through 2028 is 4% top-line growth, mid-teens TSR, and at 17x earnings, that would equate to 50% upside.

The presenter would like to discuss Performance Food Group as a long.

Performance Food Group currently has a $13.7 billion market cap, a $19 billion EV, with a June fiscal year. But on a calendar basis, it is trading at 13.5x 2027 earnings, 8x EBITDA, with a 8% free cash flow yield. It is trading at a 20% to 25% discount to Sysco and US Foods on an EV/ EBITDA basis, and that gap has actually widened year-to-date.

In terms of the business, approximately 60% of pre-corporate EBITDA is food service (very much like US Foods and the core of Sysco), while 20% to 25% of pre-corporate EBITDA is convenience stores, and 15% to 20% of pre-corporate EBITDA is distributing to specialty.

From an industry perspective (approximately a $400 billion industry in the US), Sysco is number one with 22% share, US Foods has 10% share, and PFGC has 8% share. Regional competitors have 10% share, and the long tail of independents have 50%.

The stock has been weak as of late, and actually weaker than Sysco and US Foods. They reported in February, which came in at the low end of guidance. PFGC generally beats and raises. The old CEO, who investors love, was not on the call, and the presenter guesses investors would have liked to see him allay some concerns. Two headwinds pressuring PFGC in Q 2 were deflation in dairy and expenses related to a new DC for Cheney Brothers.

These are guided to continue into Q 3 but the presenter views these as transitory.

More recently, there are concerns over diesel prices. They note in the 10 K that a 10% move in diesel prices is roughly 1% to EBITDA. In prior calls, they have said that fuel surcharges covered two-thirds of the pressure, and one-third of the pressure by collar hedges. The presenter guesses there is maybe some concern of high oil prices, and what it means to the consumer and C-stores and restaurants, but that is obviously TBD.

So the thesis is, PFGC is the fastest growing of the “Big Three,” and they are very much a super-regional player. They are dominant east of the Mississippi, so they have a lot of white space in the West. There are some M&A opportunities in the West and the Southwest, and PFGC is proficient at acquiring businesses, running them, harvesting synergies, and accelerating growth.

Sysco and US Foods had strong quarters. Both those stocks were up low double digits. PFGC missed and the stock was down high-single digits. Their algorithm is low to mid-single-digit revenue growth and low double-digit EBITDA growth, and that flows through to approximately 20% EPS growth before any capital allocation. What is also nice about the story is that there is no AI risk. The industry is highly fragmented and ripe for consolidation.

The “Big Three” have roughly 40% share. That is up to 600 basis points versus 2019. Sysco and US Foods have been out recently saying that they believe that the “Big Three” will continue to gain share. Scale is super important here, as it is not a high-margin business.

Also, the typical independent food service customer (which is more profitable than servicing a Chili's or Outback Steakhouse) may use six to ten distributors, so there is a real opportunity to gain share from existing business.

Areas of potential upside to estimates versus the stated valuation on calendar 2027 include: integration of recent M&A, harvesting of synergies, upside to cost-savings program, additional M&A (now that leverage will be at their target by June), as well as any improvement to the industry backdrop. Last year, industry traffic was down ~2% in restaurants, and C-store traffic was down low to mid-single digits in the categories that they service.

PFGC announced their first cost savings program in May at their Analyst Day ($125 million over three years). For context, that is 5% of 2026 EBITDA. US Foods drove $115 million in cost savings in 2025 alone. PFGC's cost savings is roughly 45 basis points of their food service COGS, or 22 basis points of their entire company COGS. US Foods' program was 80 basis points and 100 basis points of their base-year COGS. The presenter believes there is room for upside here in what is a 3% EBITDA margin business.

In terms of capital allocation, the presenter would argue that leverage is within their targets.

They do a deal almost every two to three years; if something aligns, that would line up in the next 12 months or so. And they announced a $500 million authorization for buybacks, which is new to the story, but obviously well-received at US Foods. Again, it is trading at an unwarranted 20% to 25% discount to Sysco and US Foods, with a better growth outlook. If you pull it up on Bloomberg, they are growing faster and have been growing faster.

Looking at calendar 2027, the presenter believes you can underwrite 50% to 60% upside if they trade at the same multiple as Sysco and US Foods, and then the stock should continue to compound from there. The presenter thinks a realistic upside case is a combination of better growth, more cost savings, and M&A, which would lead to even greater upside.

The presenter would like to discuss MGM Resorts as a long.

This is a stock that the presenter has disliked for the past few years because they thought estimates were way too high coming out of the pandemic. The Street mis-modeled operating leverage on the downside. Costs, post-union contracts, were elevated. The union contracts were signed right after the pandemic, when the unions had all the negotiating leverage. Most of that occurred in year one, a nd a small portion in year two. You are now in year three, where the year-over-year change in cost has now moderated to the low-single digits.

The Street has come to a place where they are expecting no growth ever again in Las Vegas.

The presenter thinks you have seen weakness in the mid-scale to lower-scale properties-primarily off-strip, and Luxor, Excalibur, Circus Circus (the low end). The luxury properties have held up rather well.

From here on out, the presenter thinks you have likely taken all of the hit to EBITDA. You have very easy comps going forward. As long as you get to a place where EBITDA and free cash flow are roughly stable, the presenter believes the story is not going to be about Las Vegas for much longer. You just need to have a base of free cash flow that you can count on, and beyond that, the rest is all free call options. If you assume the Street is roughly accurate, +/ - 5% for free cash flow in 2027 – which assumes essentially zero growth in Las Vegas-you get to approximately $3.20 per share in free cash flow for Las Vegas.

In terms of the balance sheet, there is no traditional debt on the company. It is all lease debt.

That is why it trades at a very cheap free cash flow yield. Say it is a 15% yield, because they do not own their real estate. That equates to $21 per share for Las Vegas as a whole. Investors could debate plus or minus, but the presenter does not think it is going to matter at the end of the pitch, if it is +10% or-10%, because that $50 to $60 million in free cash at 7x is $350 million. You are talking about a dollar or two to the share price in either direction. So either it grows 3%, or does not grow 3%, it is $1. So it is $21 per share for that business.

Then you have a publicly traded entity in MGM China. The public value of that stake is currently $14 per share to MGM; so, using the presenter’s math it is $21 + $14 = $35. That is where the stock is today. You can easily argue that there is a branding fee that goes along with MGM China that is separate from the value of MGM China. It is likely worth $4 to $5 per share but the presenter believes it is simply option value.

Then they own BetMGM. The presenter dislikes OSB (Online Sports Betting), so they give it a low multiple of 8x EBITDA. EBITDA for Bet MGM is expected to be $500 million. A t 8x EBITDA, that equates to $7 per share. Using the presenter’s math, it is $21 + $14 + $7 = $41 per share. You can debate the $5 per share for the stake in the licensing fee. So what is MGM going to be in three years from now? They have two huge projects. One is in Japan, and the other is in Dubai.

Let us start with Japan. Singapore generates $5.5 billion of gross gaming revenue. It has a 50% margin in th at market because the tax rate is lower than Japan. So Singapore generates approximately $2.5 billion to $3 billion of EBITDA. The population of Singapore is 6 million, the population of Malaysia is 34 million, and it is a five to six hour flight from Beijing and Shanghai. Assuming Japan, with a population of 122 million and 7,000 slot parlors, generates approximately USD $35 billion in gaming revenues currently, and only being two-and-a-half to five hours from China-and with a tax rate that is only slightly higher-should yield them roughly similar gross gaming revenue, if not higher, than Singapore (there is only one asset in the country). The presenter thinks it will ultimately be greater than $6 billion, but not many investors seem to care because it is too far out.

The margin on that is likely going to be ~45% instead of 53%, like Singapore. It is ~$2.5 billion of EBITDA, which is similar to Singapore but for only one asset, versus two assets in Singapore. MGM owns 43% of that. They also get a 3% management fee. So, in the presenter’s opinion, investors are looking at ~$1.2 billion of value for it to MGM. The presenter thinks it is likely the most stable market in gaming other than Singapore. It has a 25-year license, and the tax rate is set. They funded this at ~2% (they pre-funded it), and they hedged the yen when the yen was very weak. This asset is likely going to generate $4 of cash flow per share.

The presenter thinks it is worth 15x to 20x. The presenter thinks Singapore would be worth 20x if it were to be sold. So that is $60 per share. The presenter believes it is appropriate to put a heavy discount rate on this, because it is in the future and there is execution risk. If you want to discount it back at 15% to 20% over three years to today, it equals $32 per share. So $32 + $41 is a number that is materially higher than the current stock price.

Investors are clearly worried about the demise of Las Vegas. The presenter does not think that is going to be the case. The presenter believes Adam Silver (NBA Commissioner) will announce that an NBA team is coming to Las Vegas this summer, and then you have the Oakland A's baseball franchise coming. That is an extra 1 20 nights per year of programming.

The Sphere has proven to be way more impactful than anybody thought. Then, you have the NCAA Football National Championship next year as well as two WrestleMania s. The presenter believes more and more events are coming to Las Vegas, since it is the easiest place to host large events.

The presenter does not believe that Vegas is dead. The presenter simply believes it had its COVID hangover, and it is now poised to start growing low single digits. The presenter does not think we are talking about 10% growth, but the presenter thinks low to mid-single digit growth, as they have proven to have their cost structure under control, and hopefully AI can help them more on the cost structure as well as with marketing.

In terms of risk/reward, the presenter thinks you have a stock that has $2 to $3 in terms of downside, and if you hold the stock for a few years, you have approximately $50 of upside, and possibly more, depending on how well Japan does. Also worth noting, IAC bought a million shares in December. The presenter has heard he could be doing a roadshow with MGM management in April. They have bought back half of their stock over the past three years. There is no reason they cannot buy more. Every single share they buy is just buying more of Japan. The presenter would not think about it as buying back stock of MGM, the presenter views it as they want to own more of Japan.

The presenter would describe Duolingo as a consensus consumer software short that still has 30% downside. It is a $3.7 billion EV with a billion dollars net cash and no debt. It is at $95 today and trades $350 million a day. It has a 20% short interest. It is the world's most popular language learning app. It has 53 million daily active users and 12 million paid subscribers.

They generated $1 billion of revenue last year and $300 million of EBITDA.

The presenter likes the short here for a few reasons. Obviously, there is a lot of uncertainty right now with in the software and internet sectors, debating over which companies will be disintermediated by agentic AI. The presenter believes Duolingo is a company that is clearly on the losing side. While there are valid debates around gig economy names like DoorDash or Uber that rely on the tangible delivery of products, Duolingo does not offer any tangible products. It simply gives you a daily streak that you can artificially edit with good branding.

Within the last six months, we have seen a step change in the productivity of AI, as it has shifted from people using it more as chatbots, to this agentic AI, on its way to AGI. While the adoption is still slow-paced, it is pretty clear that for language learning or any other learning, you will likely use your AI agent that knows your work style, your interests, and your projects, to build out any sort of curriculum for you.

The presenter used their Claude Code agent to scrape 20,000 Reddit posts across ten different language learning forums over the last five years, and saw that over the last six months, the frequency of posts relating to AI substitution for Duolingo has increased 90% over the three-year period from when ChatGPT was first released. There is obviously interest in this.

Growth has already decelerated at Duolingo, and they have guided to spending 500 bps of margin this year on R&D, sales and marketing, and giving away premium features for free.

While next year they might be able to cut back on R&D or sales and marketing, the presenter thinks it would be hard to convince any upselling to premium now, unless their product innovation can differentiate against the LLM alternatives.

Right now, the valuation is essentially in no man's land. The presenter does not think it is an effective language learning tool. In the presenter’s opinion, people have year-plus long streaks, and they still cannot hold a basic conversation. It is also not a real gaming company.

You do not have a full content library or owned IP, and you have single product risk. The presenter thinks it deserves a slight premium to the ed tech companies, which have been left for dead at 3x to 6x EBITDA, because it has a slightly better engagement model. But it definitely does not deserve the multiple of these gaming companies in the mid to high-teens.

When the consumer is weak and people are losing jobs, the presenter thinks it would be one of the first subscriptions people canceled. In terms of valuation, it is currently trading at 12x 2026 Street EBITDA and 9.5x 2027 EBITDA, which The Street is baking in that nearly all the margin comes back and that top line grows at 15%. The presenter thinks that as consumer adoption of these agentic AI solutions increases (not simply using ChatGPT or Claude Chat), once more people adopt those tools (for anyone that has used Claude Code, you truly realize the power of it), the presenter thinks Duolingo's subscribers and pricing start to decline next year, or as early as Q4. The presenter is underwriting EBITDA of $280 million for 2027, putting an 8x multiple on it, and getting to a $70 target price.

The presenter would like to discuss Dollar General as a short.

The presenter thinks it is timely given the print on Thursday. For background, this stock has had a wild ride, from when it was loved during the pandemic (2020-2022), to when it collapsed in 2023, and then it had a bit of a resurgence more recently in 2024 and 2025. It now trades at ~20x earnings.

The presenter does not think the stock is overly loved, but they believe that investors think it is a “safe” place to hide at the moment. The presenter believes most investors over the long term would not want to own the stock, given the perception that it is a market share loser to bigger players, particularly Walmart. The reason why it is likely trading at 20x EPS currently, despite unit growth having come down significantly, is because the credit card data looks good. That, in the presenter’s opinion, has been the demise of many fast money investors in the space. They are likely going to comp + 5% to + 6% in Q4. That is against The Street at + 3%.

They are likely going to crush gross margin again, and they are likely going to beat EPS by another 20% to 30% this quarter.

The problem is that they like to guide conservatively. So if they are looking out to next year, and want to build a cushion for themselves, it will be tough to do so, particularly given the amount that they have built in for this year (given that a lot of the gross margin wins are gone / behind them). The presenter thinks that has been the main driver as to why investors have been excited to own the stock as well as costs stabilizing.

As it relates to gross margins, a lot of it was getting back shrink losses, and now it is in-line with what they are targeting. They say there is more opportunity, particularly from damages within inventory, but if you look at their inventory turns and the way they are managing it currently (credit to Todd Vasos who has done a great job fixing the business), the presenter simply does not see much more opportunity. Looking at this most recent quarter, you saw the sequential sales essentially act right in line with what the historical seasonality has been.

Going forward, it leads the presenter to believe that gross margins could expand by 10 to 20 basis points per year, versus the hundreds of basis points that they have recovered recently.

The Street is more like 30 basis points.

If you look at sales, they are beating Q4, but the presenter believes you are seeing right now within February that the 6% comp has basically gone to a 1% comp, and the two-year has significantly decelerated. You have been seeing this with a lot of discretionary names recently. The presenter would say this is a function of the holiday season simply being very strong. DG is basically a grocer, so it has no business in the other parts of the year benefiting from that discretionary strength. So you have the comp trend slowing significantly. You do not have much margin upside anymore. They are going to beat this quarter, but they will likely guide below the Street or at the midpoint. You are left with a low single-digit comp grower, with limited margin expansion, 1% to 2% unit growth going forward, trading at 20x PE, which does not seem that exciting versus off-price names.

Not only that, you also have other headwinds as well. For example, SNAP (Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program) Dollars are down 10% YTD. The presenter believes the company has a mid-single-digit exposure to SNAP spending, so that is going to be headwind to comps. Grocery deflation /disinflation is also hitting right now. That is also going to be headwind to comps. Their average income cohort is $30K. That is not going to benefit from stimulus. If oil stays elevated, th at will likely cause additional pressures as well. And then the company lapping some initiatives from 2025, like the DoorDash launch. The presenter does not know why Dollar Store is using that partnership, but it actually did benefit the company slightly.

The presenter thinks investors are scared to short it right now because we are heading into a Q4 beat-and frankly the presenter is as well, because it is going to be pretty big-but the presenter does not know what investors are playing for after that. And what we have seen this quarter so far is that stocks where investors do not really have long-term conviction in the story (like a Victoria's Secret, an American Eagle, or a Gap), you can beat and guide above, but if it is below expectations, your stock is going to decline significantly. The presenter thinks there could be an element of that this quarter, but the presenter thinks there is going to be an element of that coming soon.

The presenter would like to discuss Booking Holdings as a long.

The presenter is going to go against the short software to zero agentic theme. The presenter thinks booking.com is an attractive long here.

The presenter specifically does not think Booking.com as an OTA can be disintermediated, given the way the niche travel segment works in Europe. The presenter thinks if it is going to happen, it can happen a lot easier here in the US, which would expose something like an Expedia a lot more. But just given the mom & pop branding in Europe, those types of travel destinations, those types of room nights, that type of inventory as a whole-the same way China has its own unique dynamics-for the presenter, that historically has been what Booking.com has dominated. It has been what everyone has always paid a massive premium multiple for, and the presenter does not think it is going away.

Right now, The Street has Booking.com earning $315 in EPS for 2027 and $360 in EPS in 2028, so 10x to 12x PE. And they are growing earnings and revenue, high single to low double digits. You are dealing with the most conservative management in all of travel that has historically beat and raised (obviously outside of COVID when the world shut down). Other than the pandemic period sell-off, it is now the cheapest that the stock has ever been. It is trading at a below-market multiple. Even in a K-shaped economy where the world is saving right now, the presenter still believes in this “experience” thesis.

The bear case is that AI is coming, and obviously you do not need any type of travel planning. The presenter thinks you can short something like American Express, or Travel & Leisure or something where you are actually planning a trip. The presenter thinks if you want to go on Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT, whatever you want, and ask it to plan a 10-day trip to Europe, it will create the itinerary, but you still need to go on line and actually book your room nights. Google has been an overarching threat to Booking.com and their travel engine for many years now, but they have never been able to crack the code. It has never worked. If you are buying Google because of Gemini's growth, and Gemini is the better engine — the presenter thinks there is a reason why Google has not gone after the OTAs yet, given that they have their own OTA.

From a free cash flow standpoint, you are at a double-digit free cash flow yield right now, you are at single-digit EBITDA multiple, and you are at low-teens EPS on double-digit growth, purely because of an irrefutable macro thesis that the presenter cannot defend. The presenter thinks that is the opportunity longer-term, and the presenter thinks there are plenty of other real AI threat baskets that you can short against something like this. If you need to hedge your travel aspect because you are worried about unemployment, investors could short a Marriott or Hilton, which trade at north of 25x because of the REIT algo that never goes down. Booking.com’s algo never goes down like them, and they always had a premium multiple.

This macro threat reminds the presenter a lot of when you were able to buy TJ Maxx during the onset of the pandemic (when you had massive supply chain disruption, and you could not get any inventory), when you were able to buy TJ Maxx at 12x to 15x. The presenter thinks Booking.com for so long has been the name to own. It has been a consistent / stable business, a beat and raise story that most investors wanted to own, and the presenter thinks it is simply getting caught up in the macro uncertainty and basket trading. When they reported earnings, they beat once again, and they guided up again.

The stock has bounced about 8% to 10% off the lows since that earnings report, but if you get back to any type of historic multiple, you are talking 40% upside from here. The presenter believes they are not going to miss numbers, so it is really a question of whether or not you believe that an AI engine can find a way to “steal” room nights from hotel operators. The presenter does not believe that occurs.

The presenter would like to discuss ADP as a short.

A DP is a provider of software that helps companies pay their employees, and they have various other HR modules and things like that. The company has approximately 20% share of US payrolls, and 90% of revenues and profits are derived in the US.

There are a couple of reasons to be short, both macro and micro. First, on the more micro industry-specific side, this has historically been a growth industry that has benefited from the back offices of SMBs and mid-market getting increasingly digitized, and that accelerated coming out of the pandemic. Now, the presenter thinks that penetration-if you stack up the public disclosures from ADP and their peers – gets you to approximately 80% penetration.

The balance is mostly regional payroll providers. Regional software providers were a larger percentage of the pie historically, and for the public vendors a source of jump balls in the industry. As they get smaller, they spit off fewer new business opportunities / the public peers have higher retention which means new business is harder every rolling year.

Historically, in FY 23 and FY 24, new business grew 20% to 30%. The presenter thinks this year it is on track to grow 10%, and over the next couple of years, the presenter thinks it is hard to believe that it will accelerate further, given the competitive dynamic is increasing.

On the macro side, the presenter thinks same-store payrolls, or what they call PPC, is likely asymmetric to the downside. The presenter thinks we are likely close to full employment. If you look at where unemployment is, it is less than a point off the lows. The presenter thinks there are a couple of discrete factors that are not well understood to the downside. The presenter thinks you can stack to one to two points of headwinds from both net migration coming down in the next couple of years, and also from an aging workforce. From 2010 to approximately 2015, we had two to two-and-a-half million people retiring. The presenter thinks going forward, it is something closer to four million, and then net migrations were a one-to-two-point tailwind in the last couple of years. This year, it is likely only 80 bps. That, depending on who you ask, could even go negative into the future. So you get a couple of extra points issued to PPC on that side.

And then last, the presenter thinks you also have the x-factor of AI getting materially better.

And if you listen to the way the frontier model companies are talking about the capabilities of this, as more of these systems get properly stitched together at the enterprise, the presenter thinks you have the additional risk that you see more cuts. The presenter does not think that we are going to have 40% - style cuts like Block, but the presenter does think it is more possible that you have some sort of a slow drip. If you just look at employment data by industry, the presenter stacks to approximately 30% of total employees that are in categories that they would deem “at risk.” Those include roles in management, legal, office & admin, devs, programming, and data science. Obviously very broad, but a 2.5% cut to that would be another one point, and you can sensitize that.

To wrap up all three of these points, the presenter thinks PPC is already pretty muted. The Street has that going to + 1% next year and + 3% the following year. The presenter thinks it is closer to flat to-1% or-2%. Combine that with what we were talking about in terms of new business getting more and more difficult, and maybe it grows high single digits to 10%, you can get to a company that grows revenues 3% versus The Street at 6% or 7%. And you can get to a company with margins that, as you have to work harder to acquire a new customer, you obviously have lower margins on that customer. If you say margins are flat to down versus the Street’s flat to up, you can get to a company that grows EPS in the low single digit range versus the Street at 9%. It is currently trading 19x fiscal 2027. If that de-rates to 15x, it would equate to a $160 share price. For reference, the stock is currently trading around $220 per share.

The presenter thinks the biggest risk to the call is, in the immediate term, if you get more war news, this is a defensive stock and it is going to go up. The presenter thinks over the medium term, if we see additional large RIFs (Reduction in Force) - which is not in the presenter's base case-but if you think there are more headlines like Block’s RIF, then this is going to be a material worse algorithm for sure, but it will be one of the more certain algorithms in the economy, and the presenter thinks you will pay up for that.

Investor's Thesis: Trimble is a highly "un-AI-able" software business focused on real-world data and industrial workflows (surveying, architectural equipment, construction sites). Its core business has durable network effects between architects, engineers, and contractors. The recurring portion of the business is growing mid-to-high teens, and the stock is undervalued, trading at a material discount to comps like Autodesk, PTC, and Procore.

Catalysts: Recent divestiture of the low-margin, slow-growing traditional telematics business accelerates the growth of its Logistics and Transportation segment (from single digits to a projected 9%). Street estimates are not yet updated for this divestiture and he expects it to lead to an EPS of $4.50-$4.60 in 2027, well above the Street's $4.00 estimate. Expectation of an uplift in the valuation multiple from 17-18x to over 20x earnings, which is more in line with higher-quality industrial software peers.

Valuation vs. The Street: It currently trades at 17-18x NTM earnings and he sees a path to a $90+ stock, based on a 20x+ multiple on the expected $4.50-$4.60 EPS.

Risks and Key Details: The CEO performs a "dumb deal" or a "transformative M&A," reverting to its historical reputation as a "Frankenstein" company built on questionable acquisitions. The tie-in with hardware (for measuring and validating construction) is considered a new, durable moat, similar to the AXON thesis. The cyclicality of the construction business is actually desired to catch the eventual "AI data center uplift." This would be an issue looking further out as we move through the cycle.

Investor's Thesis: Oracle's core business (ERP and database) is durable and sticky, providing a strong valuation floor with an estimated $7-$10 in EPS over the next couple of years. The stock is currently priced to essentially zero for the upside call option on its massive OCI (Oracle Cloud Infrastructure) build-out, including the "Stargate" project to serve OpenAI.

Catalysts: Any sign of traction or progress with the OCI build-out and the OpenAI partnership could cause a significant "sentiment shift" and re-rate the stock. Ongoing moves to issue equity and the buying of its debt by credit investors de-risk the balance sheet and support an investment-grade view.

Valuation vs. The Street: Management projected $21 EPS in FY30 (Calendar 2029), which the investor sees as $11 coming from OCI/AI and $10 from the core business. Whereas it seems the street values the entire OCI build-out at only $1 earnings power per share. The reality is somewhere between the two extremes (e.g., $8-9 from core + $5-6 from OCI, resulting in mid-teens EPS over the next three years). The core business alone covers a $120-$135 bear-case price floor and $180+ is viewed as reasonable upon a sentiment shift around OCI.

Risks and Key Details: Management's $21 EPS guide is likely too high given the execution risk on the massive capex build-out, including constraints on power and memory. The theoretical risk of OpenAI defaulting on its non-cancelable contract, leaving Oracle on the hook for significant leases. Management may be too focused on OCI and neglecting the core database/legacy software business.

It has direct AI revenue exposure (Azure) and high-quality recurring revenue with a best-in-class margin profile (~50% operating margins). The stock has been temporarily "thrown out" and is down 25% from its highs, presenting a buying opportunity.

Catalysts: Continued acceleration in Azure growth, potentially reaching the mid-40s, driven by high AI-related capex. Three simultaneous drivers with regard to Microsoft 365: 1) Continuation of the E3-to-E5 upgrade cycle. 2) Upcoming like-for-like pricing increases across different SKUs starting in the next fiscal year (summer). 3) Accelerating Copilot adoption ($30/seat/month, $5B ARR business), which is already adding about 5 points of growth. Operating margins are expected to grind up toward 50% due to disciplined cash OPEX/COGS management, even with the massive D&A ramp from the AI build-out.

Valuation vs. The Street: Trades around 22-23x consensus GAAP earnings, and under 20 times on buy side numbers, viewed as a discount caught up in negative market sentiment.

Risks and Key Details: Long-term multiple compression, especially if it's viewed more as a high-capex hyperscaler business rather than a pure software business. Risk to free cash flow from massive capex intensity. The power of Copilot is in the "bundling," ensuring adoption even if individual users don't immediately utilize the product. For the stock to work in the next six months, Azure growth likely needs to hit above 40%. Near-term catalysts include the Open AI fundraising details and the FY27 capex guide in July.

Investor's Thesis: EPAM is currently misclassified in the "AI short bucket" despite being a high-quality software engineering, architecture, and consulting firm. The investor argues that EPAM's core expertise is in complex software architecture, engineering, and enabling enterprise AI (e.g., helping clients with data silos and partnering with Databricks), not in low-level coding easily commoditized by AI. Their top customer list, which includes Google, SAP, and Oracle, supports the focus on high-end engineering. The business is fundamentally strong but its valuation is suffering due to the general negative AI narrative around the services sector.

Catalysts: The new CEO, a company veteran of 20 years, has set conservative guidance for the current year. This is a pattern that led to beats last year and suggests they are poised to exceed expectations again. Their native AI-related revenue is seeing rapid growth, with the expectation of doubling from $300 million to $600 million ARR in 2026, which helps to counter the negative market perception. Bookings remain strong, and both consultant utilization and pricing are improving, with price increases moving into the low-to-mid single-digit range. Potential for positive tailwinds if geopolitical stability increases, allowing more of their historically large base of engineers in the region to fully return to work.

Valuation vs. The Street: The stock is currently trading at approximately 11x earnings. The investor believes a fair valuation for a company of this quality should be in the range of 15x to 25x earnings. With an expected 2026 EPS of around $12.00, the stock is viewed as significantly undervalued, with a price target expected to be well north of $200 after a couple of strong quarters.

Risks and Key Details: The biggest risk is the pervasive uncertainty around AI causing enterprises to indefinitely halt all non-essential tech spending, a scenario where people "tap the brakes" for a year or more. The stock has been hit by the general "AI story" applied to services firms, leading to a steep sell-off as the "baby with the bathwater" narrative takes hold. A recent acquisition in Latin America (Norris) experienced minor financial noise due to tariffs impacting a contractual minimum payment, which contributed to a small miss in the latest quarter. The founder/CEO recently retired but remains the effective chairman, maintaining engagement with the company.

Commentary: How does EPAM deal with the potential commoditization of labor (FTE component) in a services business? Their work is high-level software architecture and engineering, which is less susceptible to immediate AI automation than simple code typing. Furthermore, their consultant utilization is currently rising, and pricing is improving across the business. How does EPAM break the "AI loser" narrative in the market? They were already successfully breaking the narrative until the latest quarter's conservative guidance. Their AI projects are categorized as native AI revenues, representing genuine AI enablement for clients, which distinguishes them from competitors who merely reclassify old work.

Investor's Thesis: Commvault is the "poster child" of high-quality software companies that have been unfairly "annihilated" by the market due to the broad-based AI narrative. It is described as the "Switzerland of data protection," operating in a sticky, growing market with a security overlay on top. The business is fundamentally strong and difficult to "rip out" (similar to an Oracle database), yet the stock is trading at a depressed multiple, making it an ideal long opportunity and an attractive target for Private Equity (PE) or other mid-sized software companies.

Catalysts: The stock has high upside convexity. If the market's fears about the AI-driven destruction of the business prove to be false the stock has the potential to double from its current level of approximately $80. The depressed valuation (3x trailing revenue) combined with the potential to significantly expand margins makes it a prime acquisition target. Acquirers can unlock value by taking the company private, cutting costs (especially by leveraging AI in the engineering function or moving engineers), and pushing currently near-zero GAAP margins to a more robust 20-30% range. Other mid-sized software companies may see the opportunity to acquire a billion-dollar sales company for 2.5x to 3x sales.

Valuation vs. The Street: Trading at approximately 3x trailing revenue. The investor prefers buying the stock at this valuation over the credit because the upside is so significant (a double, or over 100% return) if the market is incorrect about the severity of the AI risk.

Risks and Key Details: The stock was "annihilated" and investors "lost their minds" after missing a quarter by only a "whisper," indicating high volatility and overreaction to minor news. The company is attractive due to having no debt on its balance sheet. The primary thesis is predicated on the ability to realize massive cost savings, as the vast majority of its operating expenditure is engineering headcount, which could be reduced to unlock significant free cash flow.

Commentary: Why is this considered a better trade than buying distressed software company loans? The stock offers superior "convexity." A loan trading at 75 cents on the dollar, even with a two-to-three-year term, offers an equity-like yield but limited upside. Buying a stock like Commvault, which could double from its current price if the bear case is wrong, is a much higher-upside way to play the trade that "everyone's freaking out for no reason." How feasible is it to "rip out" the Commvault business? A conversation with a CIO suggested that ripping out Commvault would be a similar, difficult, and expensive proposition to trying to rip out an Oracle database, confirming the business's high level of stickiness. How would a private acquirer unlock cash flow? Private equity could throw out up to 80% of the headcount, especially engineers, without facing the negative public headlines that a publicly traded company would. This drastic cost-cutting could lead to free cash flow twice what people currently anticipate, even with slower revenue declines.

Investor's Thesis: ADP is a "melting ice cube" payroll provider. Its 20% market share is largely capped, and it faces intensifying competition from a mature market, including over six competitors with $1 billion-plus revenue (like Paylocity, PAYCOM, Ceridian, UKG) and cloud-native startups (like Rippling and Gusto). The business is highly exposed to white-collar employment, which is under pressure from full employment flatlining and the rise of AI.

Catalysts: Intensifying competitor pricing pressure (e.g., Rippling is as low as $8 per seat/month versus ADP's typical $60). Inability to meet their growth guidance due to high customer churn and price pushback. Risk to float income if interest rates decline. Disruption from an AI-related startup that offers a superior or cheaper service.

Valuation vs. The Street: Trades at approximately 20x earnings, based on management’s medium-term guide of 6-7% long-term revenue growth and 9-11% earnings growth. The 6% growth rate is questionable, as an 8% annual churn rate requires 14% growth in new business/upsells/pricing to achieve 6% total growth. If growth is closer to 3-4%, or near zero due to "AI Armageddon," the stock should trade much lower with a downside target of around $165 (15x earnings) and the potential for it to drop to 10-12x earnings if growth stalls.

Risks and Key Details: The primary risk is that management successfully hits its guided growth and earnings numbers, causing the stock to trade back up to 22x earnings. The PEO (Professional Employer Organization) segment, which handles payroll for small businesses, is concentrated in financial and broader services and is considered at high risk from AI's impact on white-collar jobs. The balance sheet is relatively clean, with no meaningful leverage. The company's margins are high-20s, but there are few operational levers left to overcome revenue pressure.
