The presenter would like to discuss Take-Two Interactive as a long.

Take-Two has a $36 billion market cap. The stock is currently trading at $195 per share with essentially no debt.

Take-Two is one of the last publicly traded video game publishers. They operate three distinct studios. Zynga focuses on mobile gaming, while their 2K Studios focuses on sports franchises, and their crown jewel is their Rockstar studio.

In terms of the setup, the stock is down 25% year to date. A portion of that sell-off is from the software slump that affected most of the premium software stocks. But more interestingly and unique to the AI threat to the gaming industry, Google’s Genie was a tool that was released on January 30th, and it took down most of the gaming sector. This is a tool that if you give it a prompt, it builds you an interactive world, in some sense. The immediate reaction from the Street, but mainly consumers, has been, wow, can this really just disrupt the gaming sector in general? You can build your own game in a week with just a simple prompt.

Under the hood, this is extremely unlikely to have any impact on video game creation itself.

If anything, the presenter believes it is benefiting the creative aspect of building a game.

Speaking with gaming companies in general, the presenter believes the impact will be minimal, especially if Google can create one these tools that pale in comparison to what actual engines are required to build in terms of a consumer-facing game and something that resonates with the consumer. That overhang has primarily been the biggest drag year to date.

But the biggest catalyst for Take-Two, which is going to flip the financials upside down, is their release of Grand Theft Auto 6 (which is slated for November). It has been in development for almost ten years, has been delayed twice, but is now finally set for November 19th. Analyst estimates for this seem bullish in comparison to historicals, but the presenter believes they completely disregard the potential for this game, and what they have built over the past two years silently. They are projected to “print” 40 million copies the first year, or roughly $2 billion of revenue. But frankly, their predecessor, GTA 5, printed 250 million copies over the last ten years.

On top of that, and something that has been misunderstood, is they made an acquisition in 2023. They bought a team of third-party “integrators”, which essentially flipped the on switch for every single one of their titles. Last year, for example, a 13-year-old game made half a billion dollars effectively running online services for a very small player base. Analysts are currently projecting a $1.5 billion run rate for these live service revenues. The presenter thinks it is just grossly low to be projecting that type, with the fact that they are essentially doubling their first fiscal year sales for GTA 6.

The presenter thinks with the Google Genie threat really taking this stock down, and a lot of investors, positioning-wise, kicking this name to the curb given the two delays, there is opportunity given game publishers trade a t approximately 20x earnings when they are operating at full speed. With GTA coming online, analysts right now have $9 for 2028 and $11 for 2029. Once the marketing of the game kicks off — which is going to be sometime in August — the presenter believes the stock has some room to run well into the $300s.

The presenter acknowledges it is a bit of a long-term play, with not too many near-term catalysts, but the fact that you had a 25% drawdown caused by some tool that has no impact to their IP whatsoever is pretty exciting.

The presenter would like to discuss Tip tree as a long.

In terms of the setup, the company owned 70% of a specialty and E&S insurer called Fortegra that they recently sold in the fall. The deal is going to close in the next two months. The proceeds from that sale, plus the liquidation of the rest of their business, is going to leave the company with approximately $950 million to $1 billion in cash, which equates to approximately ~$24.50 per share versus a current stock price of ~$16.60.

The company will not have any operations; they will just have cash, no debt. They will not have any tax benefits, but they will have the cash. The clock will be ticking over the next 12 months after this deal closes for them to be able to find an asset to buy. The presenter does not think they are simply going to waste their cash. Their CEO, Michael Barnes, was credited with the Fortegra investment which had a 22% compounded annual return over approximately eight years; so, he clearly has experience buying financial assets.

Looking forward, the presenter believes the re are plenty of distressed financial assets that are going to be out there and available over the next six months. Important to note, he owns 27% of the company, his old partner owns another 9%, and then the co-CEO owns another 2% or 3%. Basically, there are three senior executives who own ~40% of the company. They do not need the money, so they are not going to be sitting there just clipping a paycheck. Of that almost billion dollars, Michael has about $250 million at risk. The presenter thinks he is going to make a decent trade, and if he cannot, he will just dividend the cash back to shareholders in a very tax-efficient manner.

As previously mentioned, the deal will likely close in March, April, or May, and then investors will see what they do. The presenter does not have a hard catalyst, but the stock would need to be up almost 50% from here to get to cash value.

The presenter would like to discuss Stellantis as a long.

The company has made identifiable, largely self-inflicted strategic errors, and that was through over committing to EVs, while also abandoning / neglecting to pay enough attention to the ir most profitable US vehicle segments. A t the beginning of February, they announced their second-half of 202 6 earnings. In the presenter’s view, they took a €22.2 billion “kitchen sink” charge. Most of that, approximately €15 billion of that, was essentially just balance sheet. The balance (~€6bil+) is going to be actual cash payments out over the next four years. This is intended to clean the earnings base, and they are now executing a product-led recovery targeting exactly the segments they previously ceded. There are early indications of strength here. The early data out of North America is strong. In terms of the current valuation, the stock trades at 4x to 4.5x FY 27 EPS versus peers at 6x to 7x EPS.

The presenter thinks there are three reasons why this is cheap with respect to the potential turnaround. Number one, the “kitchen sink” is done. Of the €22 billion in charges, only €6.5 billion is cash spread over those four years, or approximately €1.6 billion per year. That is manageable against €46 billion in gross liquidity. The cancelled EV programs have been written off, platform impairments booked, and warranty provisions topped up, and the earnings base that the market will eventually value this company on is now clean.

Management has confirmed no equity raise (they specifically mentioned on the call no rights offering). The board has authorized €5 billion of hybrid bonds to protect the ir investment grade rating.

Second, the North American recovery already has observable traction. Shipments grew 39% year over year in the second-half of 2025. Stellantis achieved those gains while cutting incentive spending by 20% year-over-year in January and growing share. They were able to do so while spending less on incentives, which is the strongest signal that new products are creating demand on their own merits, not through discounting.

Third, the earnings downgrade cycle is ending. Estimates have been rebased. FY 26 revenue converge s around €160 billion, with approximately €4 billion in EBIT, with quarterly reporting starting in FY26 to give the market regular repricing catalysts. The presenter thinks that is an important part of this narrative here, in that investors are going to be looking for real indications that the U.S. turnaround is occurring, and that will lead to more opportunities for the stock to re-price further.

In terms of downside risk, they have a capital markets day in May. That could be the next positive catalyst, but also the next major “risk” event, because they are going to give an update on that charge and the implications of it. If it reveals that the “kitchen sink” was not complete, or if there are additional European charges, or if management revises medium-term targets lower, the presenter acknowledges that the stock would reprice lower. The presenter’s downside scenario has the stock at €5, versus the 52-week low of €5.73 on February 5th, which occurred right after the earnings came out. €5 would equate to FY 27 EPS getting cut from €1.77 to approximately €1.10, and the market applying the same multiple, which is already effectively a distressed multiple.

In terms of outside indicators or catalysts, monthly U.S. sales data starting in March will start to show whether the new launches are translating into volume. The first quarterly earnings report will tell us whether operating leverage is materializing. Ultimately, the presenter thinks it is a “show me” story, but the market has ultimately priced in failure, while the company has begun to put in place the initiatives to materialize a turnaround. The presenter’s price target is €10.

The presenter would like to discuss EchoStar as a long.

The reason the presenter is pitching it is because they think this is a great way to play the IPO of SpaceX. As many investors know, EchoStar sold $11 billion worth of spectrum to SpaceX when SpaceX had a $400 billion valuation.

In terms of the setup, EchoStar has $24 billion of cash, which comes from selling spectrum to, the presenter believes, both Verizon and AT&T. They have debt of $13.4 billion, so they have $10.7 billion of net cash, which equates to approximately $31 per share. They had owned 2.75% of SpaceX, but after the xAI merger they now own 2.2% of SpaceX. At the valuation of $1.25 trillion, SpaceX was valued at $1 trillion and xAI was valued at $250 billion, that is equal to $27.5 billion, which equates to $80 per share.

There has been a lot of press that they are trying to take it public at a $1.5 trillion valuation, and that was before the xAI merger; so, it could even be $1.75 trillion, which would be the $250 billion for xAI plus the $1.5 trillion for SpaceX. But let us assume it is still $1.5 trillion.

So 2.2% of $1.5 trillion, equates to $96 per share. That is likely worth between $80 to $96 per share. They also have $9 billion of spectrum left that Verizon or SpaceX could be interested in, as well as a $9 to $10 billion retail and wireless asset (if you value that segment at approximately 3x EBITDA).

If you add all of this up, you get to $185 per share, and if you apply a 20% HoldCo discount, because investors might not want to own this at the same level once SpaceX is publicly trading, that would equate to $150 per share (for reference, the stock is currently trading at ~$107 per share).

The press is speculating that the SpaceX IPO could be as early as mid-June, which means an S-1 filing for SpaceX likely comes out in a month or so. The presenter thinks it is a good event-driven / special situation trade for the next couple of months, and obviously if retail investors are very excited about this IPO, they will be playing this ahead of it. The presenter does not think you will need to own this by the day of the IPO, if it really works.

The presenter would like to discuss Enviri as a long.

In terms of the setup, Enviri is selling their Clean Earth division for $3 billion to Ve ol ia, and there is no indication that it is going to get a second review (although that is the risk in terms of the timing of the trade). But if this goes through, they have restructured the business so that Enviri is going to have another HoldCo business. So the plan is to sell this division, collect $3 billion, and then shareholders are going to receive approximately a $16.50 dividend in a tax-friendly manner.

They are going to leave approximately $300 million of net debt on the balance sheet, and they will have approximately $150 million of cash. The company told investors that there will be no tax leakage. The presenter thinks that is why they are creating this other / new entity, and they will have a very sizable NOL as well.

The RemainCo will have two divisions. One of the divisions is likely worth $6.50 to $7.50 per share, which consists of a steel remediation business. If you think about how Nippon Steel is putting over a billion dollars of CAPEX into US Steel, domestically that is a good sign for Enviri.

And then they have a business division which manufactures tamping equipment for railroads. The thing to know about this is, it is a long-dated contract when they manufacture for railroads. The tamping equipment is like an engine with machinery that basically tamps down the rails, which is a very high CAPEX business. They locked in a bunch of contracts, which they called EOTs, at loss-making numbers because the Euro moved against them. That made th is business effectively unsellable. In the presenter’s opinion, they say the business will get rid of all of those negative contracts by the end of next year, and most of them by the end of this year. T hereafter, you have line of sight to that business being fairly profitable.

Once that happens, that business could be worth $3 to $4 per share.

Once this transaction goes through — the $3 billion sale of Clean Earth — the CEO resigns, and the new CEO is the company’s current general counsel, and he becomes the CEO. It is all pretty much laid out that for $19 today, you are going to get $16.50 a share, and then in all likelihood between $7 and $10, but the presenter thinks maybe closer to $10.

The presenter would like to discuss Liberty Global as a long.

At a high level, this is an old Malone entity of European telco assets plus cash. It has traded at a massive discount for a long time, but the presenter thinks Malone wants to get his affairs in order as he ages; as a result, they are trying to crystallize value. The presenter believes that over the next 16 months, there will be two meaningful changes to the business structure.

First, they are combining their Belgium and Netherlands assets, and they are going to spin that off into a new company called the Ziggo Group. The presenter thinks that will likely occur in early 2027. There is no real financing risk associated with it; it simply needs to happen. They are basically buying out Vodafone’s stake in the Netherlands, then they are combining it with their Belgium asset (they have already separated Belgium’s telco business into a NetCo and a ServCo), and they have raised debt at the NetCo (this deal with Belgium and the Netherlands was announced last week which likely caused the pop on earnings).

It is a complicated structure, but what is going to likely happen is that it is going to end up with a new company that the presenter thinks will likely, in a couple of years, have approximately 4.5 turns of leverage. For context, Belgium is a very attractive market while the Netherlands is only okay. Telco peers trade anywhere from 6x to 8x EBITDA. The presenter thinks this business will trade at 6.75x EBITDA, which is a 7% free cash flow yield.

That alone is worth ~$15 per share. For reference, the current stock price is ~$13.

The second deal involves a telco business that they own in the UK called VMO2. They just announced that they are selling the NetCo that they already owned in the UK to a new company called Next Fiber, which is going to be half owned by them and half owned by a large private equity firm in the UK called InfraVia Capital, who is putting approximately $1 billion of capital into the deal.

This new entity will essentially be the number two fiber owner in the UK (number one is Openreach, who has enjoyed a monopoly for a long time). As it relates to this new entity, Liberty will own approximately a 25% stake, and they will also be getting cash flows from the ir ServCo VMO2 business that they already own.

There is a wide range of outcomes, but the presenter’s base case is that their UK assets are likely worth ~$5 per share, which will become clear when they start receiving dividends every year, and potentially new capital comes into the newly created Next Fiber business. So the presenter values the UK business at ~$5 per share and the Belgium business at ~$15 per share.

What is remaining is what they call the “re-growth”, which is a collection of assets that are on their balance sheet consisting of old cable or data center assets. If you add all these up, based on their marks, the presenter believes there is little risk on the marks since there is very little software or services in terms of mix. But if you take a 20% discount to the marks, the presenter thinks that is approximately ~$7 of value.

In terms of the corporate structure, they used to have a few hundred people to manage all of this. But what is interesting about the historical structure is that LBTYA was simply a HoldCo, which had no debt and all of these investments. And then all the debt was at the O p C os, which are now spinning off. So the HoldCo consists mostly of the CEO, CFO, & IR, and in the presenter’s opinion, they do not do that much. There have been some corporate expenses, but they have been coming down. For instance, one example is that Mike Fries, the CEO, used to have access to two private jets, and he only has access to one. But there was literally $150 million of corporate expenses at this HoldCo, which has already come down to approximately a $100 million run rate, but the presenter thinks there is more to go.

All of these transaction structures will collapse the SO TP discount, because in a year and a half, if you own LBTYA, all you will own at that entity is the investments in some of these private cable businesses, and you will be getting dividends from the UK. The other countries will be a separate ticker. The business historically has been very levered at the OpCo level, and the presenter believes sell side analysts were always skeptical due to the leverage and failed to appreciate the equity value. The structure has been the re despite $13 or $14 of cash investments at the HoldCo, and then they have been getting dividends from the O p C os.

That is all going to change in the next year and a half. The presenter thinks if you add up all the different buckets of value, there is likely $25 of value, using what they think are fairly conservative assumptions.

The presenter would like to discuss International Paper as a short.

IP has a $23 billion market cap and a $35 billion EV. It trades a t 9x 2026 EBITDA and 25x EPS. In late January, IP decided to spin off its European packaging business, creating two distinct packaging companies focused in North America and EMEA. This looks more like an asset disposal masked as value creation, and it is a pretty complex deal. They need to execute this separation on top of a massive cost-out program, while they are still integrating assets from a pretty large deal they did in 2025. All the while, having to track towards almost doubling EBITDA in 2027, from $3 billion in 2025 to $5 billion in 2027.

When you look at the market / industry, containerboard demand does not grow. It has been flat to down since pre-pandemic. E-commerce is really the only driver that offsets lower industrial demand. But now you are seeing a continuation of e-commerce giants offsetting some of this containerboard demand with lightweight plastic bags, and you are starting to see a lot weaker pricing in the U.S.

IP was expecting March pricing around $70 per ton, but it came in at $50 per ton, which was a surprise to the over all industry and caused the group to trade down. The U.S. is a pretty concentrated industry. There are three or four players, all of which are cutting supply to match the waning demand. This has propped up prices for quite a few years, but you are starting to see some interlopers who are converting other paper grades into containerboard, and they are running these facilities flat out. You are starting to see these industry leaders lose share. These capacity cuts have not been enough to capture any price increase. Europe is seeing the weakness in price here and is sending in more supply.

The presenter believes that the only way to see the price increase that they are guiding to would be caused by a massive surge in industrial activity, which would come from a strong rebound in housing. That is what is happening in the U.S., which is 80% to 90% of the value of this business.

Then when you look at Europe, it is an absolute mess. It is a very fragmented industry, with a few national champions (owned by wealthy families that are subsidized by local governments). So, in the presenter’s view, they are not going away. Capacity utilization is at ~85%, and you need mid-90%s to get any real pricing. The asset that they are spinning, IP Europe, is free cash flow-negative, and needs a few billion dollars to move lower on the cost curve. The presenter thinks the CEO knows this, understands that it is a drag to shareholder value.

Important to note, their European business is third on the cost curve compared to other European containerboard peers. An asset of this quality likely trades at 5x EBITDA, versus the company average at 9x currently. This would imply IP's US assets trade at a premium to PKG, the undisputed industry leader from an execution perspective. In the presenter’s opinion, IP North America should undoubtedly trade at a discount to PKG.

Using a sum of the parts: You give a slight discount to IP North America, which would equate to 8x or 9x, and then you assign 5x to the SpinCo, you are looking at a $30 stock price versus $44 today. If you want to value the entire business at a slight discount to PKG, you are looking at only 20% risk to the upside.

The presenter would like to discuss ICON as a long.

The event / catalyst is the release of their audited financial statements and some restating of recent financials.

For background, ICON is one of the largest CROs (Contract Research Organizations).

Basically, they help large pharma and biotech companies run clinical trials. This is a company that for a long time was a darling. All these CROs had great tailwinds through COVID. When pharma and biotech companies were investing a lot in R&D, they were increasingly outsourcing their R&D to companies like ICON, and pharma spend kept growing. Then after the pandemic, there was a consolidation and Big Pharma started cutting their budgets. You saw Pfizer cutting their budgets on R&D. And then the biotech sector sold off dramatically, so a lot of those companies had to cut the number of trials they were running.

What happened was from 2023 through 2025, under the prior management team, it appears revenue was overstated for those years under their watch, in order to continue hitting numbers so they could get paid. Then, in the presenter’s opinion, they subsequently sold a large portion of their stock and quit.

That takes us to earlier this year, when the company came out and said that their revenue was overstated. Their revenue was overstated by less than 2%. Candidly, the presenter followed this space for a long time. The presenter believes it is now too cheap on a cash flow basis. The presenter thinks the cash flow is real. The company has confirmed that cash is cash. This is a revenue and EBITDA impact, but not a free cash flow impact. Important to note, the company has had excellent free cash flow throughout this entire period.

The stock is currently trading at approximately 10x free cash flow. The presenter thinks that free cash flow is going to grow. You have to pick your free cash multiple, but us ing a 13x free cash flow multiple would equate to approximately 30% upside from current levels. The presenter thinks you could get that move reasonably soon, once the company comes out with their restated financials, where the presenter expects lower revenue, lower EBITDA, and cash flow to be unchanged. Then the business can get back to a low single-digit growth trajectory, which the presenter thinks can support a low double-digit free cash flow multiple.

The presenter would like to discuss Anterix as a long.

It is a unique spectrum owner that has been starting to get some business momentum. The stock is up lately, but it is only back to where it was trading approximately a year ago.

Unlike EchoStar or other spectrum monetization s, they have an operating business. It is the largest sole owner of 900 megahertz low-band spectrum in the US. They sell to utilities on long-term leases. The goal is for utilities to convert from analog networks to broadband.

Important to note, these are private networks. Utilities are not going to Verizon or AT&T, because they need guaranteed uptime. This grid needs modernization, especially with everything that is going on right now. Use cases are, as an example, sensors, wildfire mitigation, and cybersecurity. While the company is behind schedule to monetize its customers, at this point, they have the majority of Texas through multiple different customers. For reference, they have 8 utility customers now which they had built up over the past few years, and a $3 billion sales pipeline, which is obviously multiples of today’s market cap of approximately $700 million.

When these utilities then enter into long-term leases, utilities capitalize them, so they get paid in the first few years. By the end of this current March quarter, the company expects to have net cash of 15% of their current market cap without any debt. The main issue here is that ever since they got FCC approval, they have been very slow, but now they are trying to hit critical mass. They are up to 8 utilities. The presenter thinks they are at an inflection. They have a refreshed management team, and two large shareholders also have board seats. They are very well aligned.

Last week, the FCC held a vote to expand their spectrum from 6 megahertz to 10 megahertz, which enables more capacity and use cases. We do not know exactly what that translates to in terms of use cases, but, in the presenter’s opinion, the company is going to be communicating those benefits to investors in the near future.

In terms of the numbers, based on the contracts they have signed to date, they averaged approximately $1.50 MHz-POP. If you look at their current spectrum and where the stock trades currently, it is trading around $0.20 (obviously a big disconnect). Obviously $0.20 is extremely too cheap, and there are many precedent transactions — not only their own deals with utility customers, but a lot of different spectrum transactions over the past few years at similar or higher valuations.

There is obviously robust spectrum activity and the presenter believes it is truly a scarce asset. Assuming a few of these contracts close this year, the presenter thinks the stock has potential to double. The company mentioned on the November earnings call, that they are selected as a finalist with a large utility, though they have yet to be named there. The new CEO started an accelerator program to discount the first 5 00 million contracts to come in the building, to move things along more quickly. The presenter thinks, with the new spectrum capacity they have, and with utilities finally focusing on modernization, that some of this $3 billion pipeline converts, which will create a lot of upside for Anterix.

As far as direct risk, there is a telecom focused private equity firm that bought competing / similar spectrum from T-Mobile. That deal has yet to close, but they paid a lot for it, and Anterix already has a very large ecosystem, and they already have significant customer momentum; so, the presenter thinks they have a great head start. While they may not win every contract, the presenter thinks they are likely to be in the lead.

Also worth noting, this company has significant NOLs. They also have a share buyback authorization which equates to one third of the company. The presenter thinks it is going to be interesting to see what they say over the coming weeks and months about this increased capacity and the traction they are getting in the marketplace.

They have other monetization streams that they are talking about. For example, they did a tower deal with Crown Castle. There are additional services and ecosystem partners they want to monetize.

The presenter acknowledges that it has taken a long time to get here. The company is definitely behind plan. But with the current management team and the inflection point they are currently at, the stock seems like it has minimal downside in a very complex market. It seems like the valuation support is there now, and there is a lot of momentum behind them.

The presenter would like to discuss Vistra as a long.

The presenter became interested weeks ago on this PJM announcement.

In terms of the business, Vistra is an IPP. In terms of the setup, you have a company that has a $50 billion equity cap that the presenter thinks is going to generate between $6.5 to $7 billion per year in free cash flow. It is a $53 billion equity market cap, pro forma for the Meta transaction and the transaction that they announced late last year on one of their Texas assets.

They are locking in, slowly but surely, free cash flow and free cash flow visibility. Right now, if you decompose the $6 billion of free cash flow, about $2 billion is locked in and $4 billion is effectively from the current spot market of power, which has not gone parabolic. The presenter acknowledges that a lot of smart people think that because of AI demand, power demand is going to expand rapidly, but the presenter does not have a strong view.

The way the presenter is looking at Vistra is, they are basically putting a 5% to 7% free cash flow yield on the $2 billion of locked in free cash flow, and they are sensitizing the remaining $4 billion and saying, if the market is unwilling to pay because they do not believe that, they will put a 15% or so free cash flow yield, which would equate to downside in the mid $140s.

If they start to tackle locking in more and more of that free cash flow into long-term PPAs, there is a massive opportunity for a market re-rate for the present value of those free cash flows.

Some background as to why the stock has been so volatile: Investors came into last year thinking that IPPs were the only source of incremental power. All of last year you had incremental news on Cat, Cummins, Bloom Energy, etc. coming out with incremental power production. There is this perception that these high-cost power providers are going to flood the market with power.

The news that came out two weeks ago was an about-face from the government, where they, in the presenter’s opinion, basically said, “Time out. We have all these shiny new toys, we have nuclear that is 10 + years away, and we have an existing grid that is operating at a rate that is not fully utilized.” The average utilization rate in this country of the power grid is probably 50% (on the gas side). So, the presenter thinks the regulators, and the agenda behind the regulators, was to basically utilize the current base of assets more than they are currently being used.

They are doing that by providing incentives for the existing IPPs. So if you ramp up the utilization on your existing assets, you can fast track the regulatory hurdles to providing that incremental power to a data center. The agenda is this affordability concept. What can we do immediately that ramps up power, so that the onus is not on the consumer?

IPPs have existing assets, have existing power, and they are underutilized. The presenter believes the reason why they were not ramping capacity is because the power prices have not gone up enough right here, right now, and the IPPs were afraid that if they increased production, they would flood the market, and power prices would to actually go down. That was not what they wanted. So, the presenter thinks the government is providing an incentive in terms of fast-tracking the regulatory process and allowing them to sign deals with the hyperscalers.

The presenter thinks investors have simply been fatigued and the stock action is terrible. The company generates so much free cash flow that they are going to be able to create demand for their stock over time. So, in terms of risk/reward, the presenter believes it is $10 down and $40 up. From the presenter’s best guess, from what has been in the press, Constellation has a deal. Talen is talking about doing more deals. You have been in purgatory, but you are kind of slowly coming out of that now.

The presenter would like to discuss Tutor Perini as a long.

The stock is currently trading at $77 per share with 50 million shares outstanding (a $4 billion market cap with $200 million in net cash).

In terms of the business, Tutor Perini is an E&C firm (it is mostly non-AI related). Their backlog has gone from $7 billion to $21 billion. Margins are going from-3% to 10% on an EBITDA basis. They are generating, both through cash flow from operations and collections, somewhere between $400 and $500 million per year for the next three years at a minimum.

For reference, non-AI peers, companies like Granite Construction, etc., trade at a 2x to 3x premium to Tutor. The presenter thinks there are a few contributing factors that have led to this discount. The former founder / CEO / majority stockholder, Ron Tutor, is now off the management team and coming off the board at the end of this year. Not necessarily a new group, but, in the presenter’s opinion, an elevated group of internal employees has taken over. They have started buying back stock. The presenter expects them to initiate and increase dividends over time.

Operationally, the reason the business is doing well is that very few firms are competing for their projects, because the ir peers are chasing a lot of new demand work such as data centers, etc. This has enabled Tutor to take a lot of price.

In terms of the setup, the presenter thinks it is a clean story trading at 7.5x next year’s EBITDA, versus others trading at 15x+. Tutor has a clean balance sheet that is generating a lot of cash, and the presenter believes that a capital return is on the way.

The presenter thinks Tutor will generate, without a lot of aggressive assumptions, $350 million of EBITDA going to $700 million, or $4 in earnings going to $6. The presenter thinks the stock is $100. If you do the math where you include all the cash that they are going to generate over the next two years and put a peer multiple on that $700 million of EBITDA, you actually get to $160 per share, and then you can discount that back at whatever rate you want. The presenter thinks it is a $75 stock going to $100 and then longer-term to $160.

The presenter would like to discuss Smurfit WestRock as a long.

In terms of the setup, the presenter thinks there is 100% upside, and that there is an imminent inflection in US pricing. It is a $23 billion market cap and $36 billion TEV. It is investment grade, and the stock trades ~$200 million per day. In terms of the segments, 85% of their business is containerboard and 15% is box board. Geographically, approximately 50% of the business is US, 35% Europe, and 15% LATAM.

In the US, 75% plus of the capacity is controlled by an oligopoly, made up of PKG, IP, and WestRock. PKG is a super efficient and effective capital allocator. They are truly incredible operators, with 20% EBITDA margins through thick and thin, and that has always traded at a big premium (10x to 12x EBITDA). IP has been viewed as inferior to PKG with slightly better assets than WestRock, but it has not been optimized. It has lower EBITDA margins than WestRock in total. It trades at 9.5x EBITDA due to a new CEO who investors are excited about, but the presenter thinks there is a limit to how much he can really do. It is a commodity industry, ultimately, so despite inferior margins it trades at a premium, with a similar portfolio because they have a lot of Europe an exposure as well. In the presenter’s opinion, WestRock has better EBITDA margins, higher free cash flow conversion, a better new management team, and trades at 6.5x EBITDA.

Just to quickly run through Europe, it is a little bit more fragmented. It is in a very deep trough. Their European business is first quartile and then some, based off the Smurfit management team, which is like the PKG of Europe. That business is doing a 15% EBITDA margin in the fourth quarter on trough-like conditions, with industry players cutting capacity because they are literally losing money. It is a classic economic trough there. Brazil and LATAM are global low-cost curve producers, and they also have low costs there, with 20% EBITDA margins that are pretty stable.

On the assets, WestRock was a roll up of decent assets. In the presenter’s opinion, the old management team did not optimize the roll up, but instead starved the assets a little bit for capital. They did not spring forward in terms of the cost curve, and did not do the right things in terms of optimizing it as well. That was lacklusterly received, mostly because of the management team.

Smurfit, on the other hand, was basically the PKG of Europe. It had the best management team. They took these assets via acquisition, via efficient allocation of capital, and portfolio optimization, and as the presenter mentioned, it turned this asset base into generating cash when the average commodity producer is deeply EBITDA-negative. So why does the presenter like it here? The presenter thinks Europe cannot get much worse.

In fact, there has been capacity rationalization, such that there is a chance it gets better. Brazil is very stable. Here is the real kicker. The oligopoly pulled 10% of net capacity out. The presenter believes they overdid it because they were reading destocking demand as sort of the run rate on demand, and overdid it. This is occurring just as the presenter thinks they are seeing PMI and the ISM improving. So the presenter believes we could be entering a period where existing home sales move up, industrial activity improves from the second half of last year, and the industry goes from a destocking to a restocking environment after having pulled out way too much capacity.

There was an expectation that they would raise prices in April. PKG announced one on Friday. IP followed today ($70 a ton). If the presenter’s math is correct, the market is already very tight due to these capacity reductions. Any type of economic improvement, and the industry is going to be sold out. So EBITDA expectations of $5.3 billion could turn into $6.5 billion to $7 billion. EPS moves from $3.00 to $7.00. On the low end of that upside, the presenter has 6x to 7x EBITDA. At 7x EBITDA, it is still a big discount to where IP trades today. If it trades at 15x PE, you will double your money. If Europe improves off the trough, the upside is even greater.

PKG reports tomorrow, and the presenter thinks the fourth quarter is not going to be great. If they accurately describe why they think they can raise price, the presenter thinks the whole group will be up. If they do not do a great job defending it, the stock will be down. The presenter thinks investors should keep doing the work, because the presenter thinks there is a real inflection here.

The presenter would like to discuss StandardAero as a long.

It has an $11 billion market cap with roughly $100 million of ADV. It is a $33 stock.

StandardAero is a newer IPO (October 2024). They are the largest pure play engine aftermarket service provider. Roughly 90% of revenues are generated from engine repairs (what the presenter would categorize as high value engine repairs), while 10% - 11% are component repairs, which are a much smaller part of the mix, but roughly twice the margins when compared to the engine repair business. So it is very accretive as they grow that segment.

The majority of the business is very sticky. It is through long-term agreements with major engine OEMs that StandarAero has number one or number two market share positions on 40 different platforms. Importantly, two of those platforms happen to be the LEAP and the C FM 56, which are at an interesting inflection point for them.

From a strategic asset value perspective, they operate 55 test cells for certifying engines.

These are a significant barriers to entry for engine MRO work. They cost $40 to $60 million dollars to build, and realistically they take three to five years to build and require regulatory approval. They have 55 of these test cell sites, which the presenter would argue is approximately a $3 billion irreplaceable asset base that the company has.

Their mix from an end market perspective is approximately 60% commercial, 20% military, and 20% business jet. Why it is interesting to look at now is the LEAP engine program on the commercial side. It is less than $100 million of revenue today, but it has the trajectory to get to $1 billion of revenue by 2030, as shop visits increase over the next few years. It is a structural market dynamic that is at play. 2026 marks years nine and ten for the 536 LEAP engines that were delivered in 2016 and 2017, and the overhauls are required after seven to ten years. The number of LEAP engines delivered from 2018 to 2019 jumps to 2,800, or up 5x and deliveries continued at an elevated rate through 2025. The expected LEAP contribution is structural, it is required, and there is only a finite amount of time that airlines could push that out.

It is important to note that in the early part of the inflection, you do a lot of “light” maintenance, and as you move towards more full performance restoration shop visits, those are much more labor-intensive. For this company, that means much more margin-rich. The mid-cycle and later-cycle LEAP program contribution to the margin profile will be more significant. As mentioned, the margins on the component repair business are 2x that of the core repair business. That business is growing faster than the company overall. So, you are mixing up in that business from 11% of revenues to possibly 15% plus in 2027 and 2028 which is accretive to the margin line as well. If you put together the LEAP ramp and the mix of component repair, you could probably get 200 to 300 basis points of margin expansion at the EBITDA line over the next couple of years, and it is meaningful to the earnings story.

Lastly, you are tied to aero aftermarket, and you are tied to the highly regulated engine MRO work, which should grow faster than the rest of the industry on a go-forward basis over the next number of years.

From a stock perspective, it is compelling here. They are expected to generate ~$1.20 of earnings in 202 6 (essentially a starting point the presenter would argue). The presenter thinks the earnings power looking out to fiscal year 2028 is ~$2.00. From an EBITDA perspective, it trades just under 1 5x on FY26 expectations. The presenter thinks two years out, the stock could have 50% upside from $33 to $50 (which would equate to 15x 2028 EBITDA or 25x the earnings power number).

The presenter would like to discuss Roper Technologies as a short.

Roper has a $44 billion market cap that is now considered a software stock but up until three or four years ago was considered more of an industrial conglomerate. Over the last 20 years, they have transformed from ~90% industrial in 2010 to ~80% software today (through a number of bolt-on software acquisitions). They were considered the software compounder that was not really a software stock.

They grow in the mid-single digit range through the cycle while software names typically grow in more of the high single digit to mid-teens organically. Because there is this dynamic for software investors, that is really the KPI. Given the fact that this name does not grow, the presenter believes most software investors are apathetic to it — or they are just outright short.

The fact that they are deemed a software compounder, the presenter believes the story has really played itself out. They have 40% EBITDA margins, and now that is making it tougher to do margin accretive deals. The math gets harder at that margin level, because most of the software businesses that they look to acquire actually have much lower margin profiles than that, but much higher growth.

Taking a step back, software names in general are viewed as AI losers. The presenter does not think that is idiosyncratic to Roper, but the fact that they are 80% software just adds an incremental headwind from a software perspective. Approximately 10% of their end markets are tied to truckload transport markets. Investors can debate as to whether that is really getting better, but the presenter thinks their business is certainly not, and they have been very vocal about that. Then finally, approximately 25% of their business is tied to areas where the government is cutting funding, mainly in education and healthcare.

The presenter acknowledges that the stock has de-rated. It is trading at ~19x 2026 EPS on the presenter’s numbers. If you look at Adobe, which the presenter thinks is likely their closest software peer, it is trading at ~13x. The presenter thinks Adobe has, frankly, a better business than they do. If you put Adobe’s multiple on the presenter’s Roper EPS, it implies almost 30% downside from current levels. A gain, that is not going to happen overnight, but the presenter thinks that this is more of a structural short.

The presenter would like to discuss NRG as a long.

NRG is an IPP. The presenter is pitching the stock now because of the move lower in the stock price. For reference, the stock is almost at its August ‘25 lows post-Q2. The re are a few reasons why the presenter is pitching NRG. One is valuation. It trades at a 16% free cash flow yield off 2027. Yes, Talen, Vistra, and Constellation are a lot tighter. NRG sold their nuclear plant two years ago, so they do not have nuclear capability, but they are the best gas developer.

The presenter thinks they are best positioned to build new gas plants in PJM and in Texas because they have 5.4 gigawatts of GE Vernova turbines. The presenter believes there are 1.3 or 1.4 gigawatts a year that they need to decide on. One of those is coming up this year. The presenter thinks by mid-year you are going to see them announce a large deal with NRG on a gas plant. In the presenter’s opinion, that is going to be over a gigawatt in Texas, back to that $80 to $90 per megawatt hour (that would be pretty lucrative for them).

In the near term, the catalyst path is rich. The presenter thinks LS Power is going to close sometime in February; they are telling you it is happening imminently. When that happens, the presenter believes they are going to come out with a presentation that day, and they are going to basically just update you on the numbers. The numbers they originally gave were too low, $1.6 billion. If you run the model, it is like $1.75 or $1.8 billion.

What investors are not focused on is the 600mw or so in Ohio and Pennsylvania which can be uprated to a CCGT plant for around $1,500 per kw. These are LS Power plants. This could add an additional $400 to $500 million of EBITDA, which could add a present value of mid teens to the equity. There are also going to be other potential uprating opportunities to existing LS Power plants. The presenter thinks we will hear more about this post closure of LS Power and thinks these are two potential events which are clearly not in the stock price.

Then they said they are also going to give a five-year plan. The presenter does not know if that is going to happen that day or it is going to happen around earnings, but they will give an up dated pro forma five-year plan.

If you push them on synergies, the presenter believes they will suggest zero for LS Power, but the read-through is, they beat synergies in every deal they did over the last 10 years. The presenter thinks you are probably going to see these synergies as well.

On a valuation perspective, while Vistra has a lot of cash flow locked in — which totally makes sense — the presenter would argue NRG’s retail business (they have 40% of retail in Texas and ERCOT), is in a great position there with Vistra. A lot of that cash flow is locked in every 18 months, and that gets restruck higher as power prices go higher. They are pretty stable on retail. If you asked ten years ago, maybe the retail business was worth lower, but the presenter thinks that retail business has become a lot more valuable over time.

The presenter also believes that the Vivint acquisition has actually been a very good acquisition. They are doing these virtual power plants in Texas. Their goal was a gigawatt by 2035, and they are already at 150 megawatts. The presenter thinks they will tell you a gig is worth a couple hundred million dollars of EBITDA. That is where they are in your home through the thermostat. It is in-home demand response, and they are going to cross-sell other things through that over time.

On a valuation perspective, if Vistra and Talen and the nuclear power players are trading in the mid-single digits, the presenter would argue NRG should not trade that far behind. But if you want to say NRG should trade 10% to 12%, there is 30% to 60% upside from here. That does not include the LS Power deal the presenter previously discussed. That could be another $15, or another 10% of upside, a nd that does not include the data center upside.

When the presenter runs the data center upside, they run a range of four to six gigawatts, discount it back, and at $90, the presenter gets to $43 to $65 of additional upside.

In summary, the catalyst / event path is good. The stock is cheap. The new CEO is really good. The presenter thinks for the first time, you have someone running the business who actually really understands the assets, which the presenter thinks is going to be very helpful.

The presenter would like to discuss Johnson Controls as a long.

They are the leader in commercial HVAC and building controls. They have pruned the portfolio and have gotten rid of some of the lower quality businesses, including residential HVAC, and now their HVAC exposure is purely on the commercial applied markets, which are the highest quality portion within HVAC. And given the installed base, it is a razor / razor blade model with 35% exposure and they are the leaders alongside Trane.

What makes it interesting is that this is a business with a solid core foundation, but it has been mismanaged for a decade now. Now it is on the verge of its “dare to be great moment” under a new CEO. His name is Joa kim Weidemanis. He joined from Danaher approximately nine months ago. He led Danaher’s largest business segment and took it from a 20% margin business to a 30% margin business.

Starting off on the revenue side, it has a solid foundation and strong exposure to secularly growing end markets. The 12% exposure to data centers is well understood in terms of tailwinds there. But what is underappreciated is, they are also a beneficiary of nearshoring and advanced manufacturing and life sciences, which represents about 25% of the exposure, and that will benefit from pharma nearshoring. All the pharma CAPEX announcements that the presenter has seen over the last year should start flowing into orders and start flowing into revenue eventually. Broadly, a private non-res recovery or CAPEX acceleration will also be a positive. That is on the top line. It should do mid-single digit-plus growth.

Where things get exciting is on the bottom line, specifically on the margin front. The presenter thinks it under-earns its potential by 500 basis points. They can close the gap to its peer, Trane, and they can get to a 20% margin by 2028 or 2029. The presenter believes that 500 basis points of the gap is simply bloated SG&A. Their gross margins are generally similar. So the ir CEO is bringing in the “Danaher business systems”. He is really taking the Danaher playbook. The presenter thinks checks on him have been quite positive, and the presenter thinks he will show some nice incrementals over the next couple of years. This year he will likely go to the market in an attempt to size the opportunity and the potential.

If you put it all together, you can get to more than $7.00 of EPS by 2028. Consensus is at $6.00. If you just hold the multiple constant, which is a 10% discount to Trane at 25x NTM earnings, it is a $175 stock or 58% upside in less than two years.

Important to note, the stock traded down 8% a few weeks ago on Jensen Huang’s comments regarding the potential for next generation data centers to eliminate chillers. The presenter thinks this provides a good entry point. The presenter has done quite a bit of work on this.

The presenter thinks there is no material change in the next few years for JCI’s content in terms of chillers within data centers, and again, that is 12% of the business. The presenter thinks the data center decision maker or developer, who is focused on 99.999% uptime are too risk averse to spec a data center without chillers, and chillers are only ~2% of the cost of a data center.

The presenter would like to discuss IMI as a long.

IMI has a £7 billion market cap. By year end, leverage should be just over 1x. The presenter thinks IMI is an under-the-radar story, but soon to be considered a UK compounder, with takeout optionality.

IMI has five key subdivisions or end markets it talks about, and it reports in two major divisions. It does process automation. The common theme is that they do valves, actuators, and control systems. In the case of process automation, they are in power generation, some oil & gas — including LNG — and some nuclear. For reference, their main competitor is Emerson.

It has a nice aftermarket mix of over 60%. They have an industrial automation business.

Their main competitor in that segment is SMC Corp. This is just more general industry. Like most other peers, industrial automation has been weak for a while. They do climate control and smart temperature control systems, mostly in Europe (85% of the business). Competitors would be Belimo. It is 75% retrofit.

They have a life sciences and fluid control business. Again, flow control detection systems for things like analytical instruments, diagnostics, medtech, and life sciences. Like a lot of other multis have seen, it has been pretty weak. Competitors there would be IDEX, Parker, or Emerson. Finally, they have a small transport business which supports the commercial vehicle OE market that they are in the process of fixing.

The presenter believes it is important to note that they have a good management team. The CEO has been in place since 2019. He previously ran the process automation group, which was called Critical Engineering. He took margins from 13% to 20%, while mixing up the business from 50% aftermarket to 60% aftermarket, and the business has done better than double-digit revenue growth. The company has essentially hit the algorithm they laid out a few years ago, which was mid-single-digit organic growth and 20% EBIT margins. The presenter likes that the company has been on point in terms of hitting their targets, and thinks they are actually pretty conservative in how they think about incremental margins.

The presenter thinks the portfolio is generally underrated and under-earning. The presenter would argue that the process is doing well in general between oil & gas and LNG, but they also like the fact that they have a lot of power exposure. Flowserve talks a lot about it, but, in the presenter’s opinion, IMI has 30% to 35% of the process business in natural gas and nuclear. If you take the portfolio in totality, approximately 40% of the business is not doing great in terms of industrial automation and life sciences. But when those businesses rebound, incremental margins should be strong. So how does the presenter view the business differently than others? The presenter just mentioned the incremental margins potentially being stronger than 30%, which the presenter believes the company has essentially messaged. Gross margins happen to be 47%, so they are not quite sure why incremental should only be 30%, especially if these facilities are under-absorbed. In terms of capital allocation, the company is committed to being above 1x levered.

They just sold a business for 15x EBIT, and they are going to be generating over £350 million of free cash a year. The presenter thinks over the next two years they could buy £800 million worth of stock, which will flow through to the ir valuation. Free cash flow is going to inflect, as they are recovering from a cyber incident, so no more cash out from that, and working capital becomes more of a tailwind or less of a headwind.

Finally, th is transport business that is 8% of revenue which the presenter believes they are either going to sell it, turn it around or do both.

In terms of valuation, the comp set is not great given the mix of end markets, but if you were to compare it to the likes of Smith Group, Spirax, Rotork, or Weir, you could likely see a free cash flow yield in 2027 just south of 5x. Using that free cash flow yield, and reducing the share count to reflect that level of buyback, you get a £34 price target or about 24% upside.

Just given the size of the company and given its attractive exposure to the power sector, it could be a takeout target for the likes of a Parker Hannifin. The company’s stock price likely got a lift this past year because of Spectris getting taken out by KKR. If you move the free cash flow yield to 4% or use 25x earnings, you are getting closer to £41 pounds or 50% upside.

The presenter would like to discuss Honeywell as a long.

The stock has done pretty well this year, but the presenter thinks you are at the inflection point of a lot of different catalysts that are occurring. This past week, the business leaders and CFO were announced for the new aerospace segment. Late last year, Honeywell announced that the current aerospace president was going to run the aerospace spin out. You are five to six months away from an aero spin out that is going to be tens of billions of dollars of market cap, which is going to be open to an investor base that the presenter thinks is largely not looking at the stock. The presenter is sure there are some dedicated Aerospace & Defense investors that own the stock, but the presenter thinks the aero asset is going to be a very attractive asset for investors.

There has been a lot of debate around this business. It has a decent percentage of business jet exposure, and it has a decent percentage of defense. It is 40% defense, which the presenter thinks is good right now. It is 20% or 25% commercial OE, and the rest is commercial aftermarket. Around half the commercial business is business jet, which the presenter thinks people have thought was a negative, but would argue the business jet market has held in much better than people would have thought post-COVID.

The presenter thinks the aero business will likely get a multiple in line with a Raytheon or, even if you look at companies like Woodward or Crane, there are a lot of these SMID cap A&D companies that are trading 20x plus EBITDA. If you use a low 20s EBITDA multiple for Honeywell, and you put peer multiples on the rest of the business, it would equate to a $300 stock price versus $220 today.

As many investors are aware, an activist investor essentially spearheaded this breakup.

There have been some fits and starts along the way, but generally numbers have been okay, and organic growth is actually amongst the best of US multi-industrials. This year will be mid-single digits. Next year, the presenter thinks they guide to something like 4% to 6% or 5% to 7%. The presenter thinks the number ends up being at least 6% and possibly 7%.

You are on the precipice of a very large conglomerate that has undergone so many different re-segment ing. For example, they just spun off Solstice. They did Resideo and Garrett a few years ago. There has just been this massive portfolio transition that is basically going to be done in six months. Granted, the RemainCo. is a mixed collection of assets. Two thirds of it is a building automation business, that is basically fire and security and building controls. It has actually had very strong growth. It is growing 7% this year, which is amongst the best of companies that are exposed to non-residential construction. As mentioned, the RemainCo. is going to be a bit convoluted, with this building automation business and industrial automation business. That includes some process end markets, and two warehouse automation-related businesses that the presenter thinks they are trying to sell. The presenter thinks there are other non-core asset sales that occur when that business spins on its own.

The presenter thinks there has been a lot of debate around the upcoming 2026 guide.

Numbers are generally in the right place. The presenter thinks they guide in line-ish, maybe a touch below consensus, and that acts as a clearing event for investors that have been looking to get involved in this name.

In aerospace, what is most underappreciated is their commercial OE business which has gotten zero pricing since the pandemic. They have essentially repriced none of their contracts with Boeing and Airbus. Their commercial OE business, which is 25% of aerospace, half of that is Boeing and Airbus. In the presenter’s opinion, they have started to hint that they are potentially going to get a 50% repricing, because they have not taken price since 2020 and inflation is up meaningfully since then. The presenter thinks that is a meaningful margin tailwind for the aerospace business in 2027 and beyond.

A lot of the consternation around the stock last summer was when they went to the Paris A ir S how and basically said margins are going to be flat for the next three years, because OE is going to be an increasing percentage of the mix, and it is a headwind. Clearly, they have realized that they can reprice a lot of these agreements, and the presenter thinks that narrative is definitely dead. So the presenter thinks they have a big margin opportunity in aerospace that can definitely help them offset a lot of the stranded costs, which are in people’s sum of the parts.

To conclude, the presenter believes you have good upside on a sum of the parts basis plus numbers have been reset. The presenter thinks it is thematically the right end markets and the type of stock that investors want to own currently.

The presenter would like to discuss Huntington Ingalls as a long.

Huntington Ingalls is effectively the only shipbuilder and submarine manufacturer for the US government. As a result of the reinvestment in the Navy and the war games with China, they are going to be a huge beneficiary from the US defense budget over the next couple of years. There is also a very good margin opportunity. Together, this makes the setup very attractive, and the re is clearly scarcity value in being the only Navy supplier.

First, the presenter would like to address the margin opportunity. Most of the ir contracts are fixed price contracts, so they were unable to raise wages because of the fixed price nature of their contract. And as a result of the pandemic, a lot of the ir employment base left to go work for Amazon, Target, and Walmart because those jobs were paying a lot more on an hourly basis as opposed to building a ship. That is easier work for the same money, so that had a negative impact on margins and caused higher workforce churn.

To combat this problem, the government gave them a few billion dollars last year to pay their workforce more in an effort to reduce churn. The government started to basically retroactively “fix” some of the contracts which lowered the churn of the workforce.

Second, the company is in the process of moving from 70% pre-COVID contracts today to 50% in two years. In other words, the mix shift of contracts that have a better margin structure is going up from 30% to 50%, in addition to the workforce churn coming down.

That has the impact of helping margins.

Third, they have four years of backlog, which is essentially $50 billion on annual revenues of ~$12 billion. That backlog and book-to-bill is increasing, a nd that is before the impact of 1BBB, which the presenter believes is going to have significant allocation towards the shipbuilding industry.

So you have a company that is going from mid-single-digit margins to high-single-digit margins, with the top line currently growing 4%, but likely accelerating from here. It is a company that has the potential to earn somewhere between $20 and $30 per share in the next few years. Given the scarcity value, the company should be a big beneficiary of the increase in Navy spending.

This company has had some fits and starts in improving the margin profile, so the presenter believes there has been some skepticism from the long-only community. But if the company can execute, the stock will work. The first step is going to be when they give guidance in a few weeks. They said that the guidance will show ~4% revenue growth, and the presenter believes they should surpass that and beat on margins as well. If you use a 25x multiple on $25 of earnings mid-term, you have a stock that could double from where it is today.

The presenter would like to discuss CH Robinson as a long.

The stock is up significantly over the last 6 months, but the presenter thinks there is still meaningful upside. The presenter sees this stock on 2027 numbers trading at $300 per share (almost a 2x from current levels).

In terms of the business, CH Robinson is a freight broker. They sit between shippers, that is the truckers, and then customers trying to ship goods, like a Walmart or smaller mom and pops that need to move things. They are asset light. They have 15,000 employees.

It is basically a call center in disguise. That has been the thesis, and what most of the debate is around, is how real AI OPEX improvement is at CHRW. To talk about the AI angle, basically what they have said is over the last two years, they have improved shipments per employee per day; how many shipments people in the call center can process per day, by over 30%. They think they can continue to do that. The argument on the Street is really how much of this is AI, how much of this is a new CEO cutting fat at the company, and what the potential go-forward looks like.

From a number of calls the presenter has done, the presenter thinks they can continue to run this level of AI productivity through the business. From a headcount perspective, they have taken out 30% of headcount from the peak, or approximately 5,000 employees. Granted, that has been on a trough volume market. That is the part the presenter likes. The presenter thinks they are not going to do a great job underwriting when a trucking cycle inflects, but even if the presenter runs their model at 0% transportation volume growth, continued penetration of brokerage, and then a little bit of share gain from CHRW, and then adds in some more AI OPEX productivity improvement, they get some pretty great EBIT margin expansion. The presenter gets to almost $10 of EPS in 2027, without any real market volume inflection. If you get market volume inflection on top of that, which it seems like they are starting the year with some hints of in the trucking market, you get a whole lot more than $10 of EPS.

The presenter would like to discuss Chemours as a long.

Chemours currently has a $6 billion TEV, a $2.5 billion dollar market cap, with $3.5 billion of net debt. It is a chemical company that trades $50 million per day. The presenter thinks it is a double from here, and that is based on using a 7.5x multiple on $1 billion of EBITDA. The presenter is applying a 3x multiple on their TIO2 business, and a 9x multiple (which is a two-turn discount), for their refrigerant business.

There are two core drivers of the business that the presenter will focus on. There is a refrigerants business and a TIO2 business. The company has historically traded with commodity TIO2 peers like Tronox, but the refrigerant business is now the real earnings driver, and it is approximately 60% of the EBITDA.

The thesis is threefold. First, there is upside to the refrigerants business for two reasons. First, governments globally are forcing adoption of next-gen refrigerants; they are called the HFOs.

That is going to drive market share gains for Chemours. They are one of only two players (the other is Solstice) to develop the next-gen patented HFOs. So the presenter describes it as a forced duopoly on the next-gen refrigerants. And importantly, they sell for 2x to 4x more than the old refrigerants, with 2x higher margins.

The second reason why the presenter likes the refrigerants business is, it is a call option on immersion cooling technology. They are testing with various hyperscalers. A Google executive also joined the board earlier this year. They announced that they qualified with Samsung for immersion cooling SSD. The presenter thinks there is a possibility that the cooling business could be worth the entire market cap today.

The second component of the thesis is the PFAS liability, which has been a significant overhang on the stock for awhile. It has been effectively unownable. The presenter thinks that is rapidly coming to a head. They settled in New Jersey on favorable terms. It is a 30-year settlement, but there is no cash out over the first five years. The presenter expects a positive outcome from the personal injury case, which will resolve a majority of the remaining settlement. The presenter thinks that this liability is coming in lower than the market appreciates, and thinks that the market boxing the liability is going to be a big catalyst. 3M doubled after it settled the majority. Also, the presenter thinks there is potential to separate the TIO2 business after PFAS is resolved.

The last component to the thesis is that TIO2 is at a trough and has the potential to improve.

TIO2 is a focus of China’s anti-involution campaign. China has overbuilt capacity there, just like every other upstream chemical. They are currently 60% of the world’s supply. But Chinese TIO2 production was down in the most recent data point for the first time in 20 years. China’s plan is hinting at further capacity rationalization. Prices have increased $100 per ton in recent months, so the presenter thinks there are signs of a potential inflection there. The presenter thinks they are getting that for free.

The company is asset rich. They sold some land in Taiwan recently that helped them delever half a turn. Nobody knew that was there. In the presenter’s opinion, that is worth $3 per share on a $15 stock. There is a whole host of other non-core assets as well.

The presenter would like to discuss Axalta as a long.

Axalta recently announced a merger with Akzo Nobel. Pro forma for the deal, it will have approximately $17 billion of revenue and a $16 billion market cap. The presenter thinks this merger will create a leading global coatings company with significant scale and diversification, that should lead to a re-rating and substantial margin improvement.

Historically, Axalta traded at a pretty significant discount to its peers. Given its smaller scale, it was only generating ~$5 billion of revenue versus PPG’s $16 billion, with a heavy automotive focus (75% of sales from refinish and automotive OEM paints) and higher financial leverage.

However, the presenter thinks the merger addresses those concerns. It will be a $17 billion business as previously discussed, a billion dollars more than PPG, with very broad exposure.

They will have the leading positions in general industrial coatings, European decorative paints, automotive refinish, marine coatings, and powder coatings. A nd important to note, auto drops for those two businesses to only ~31% of revenue. And the presenter would argue that it is a balanced business geographically.

In terms of synergies, the company is targeting $600 million of cost synergies, which would add more than 25% to the combined EBIT. The synergies are a combination of back office, procurement, and footprint optimization. The presenter has high confidence in the ir ability to achieve these synergies, as Axalta’s current CEO will be leading the execution of the synergy program. During his time as CEO of Axalta, he oversaw EBIT growth of 50% from 2022 to 2025, and improved EBITDA margins from 6.5% to 22%. While he obviously benefited from an improvement in the macro environment, a lot of the performance was driven by contract renegotiations, procurement savings, and efficiency improvements, the latter of which is expected to drive $125 million of savings through 2026.

The presenter also believes the combined companies’ end markets have the potential for a cyclical recovery over the next few years, as general construction activity, automotive production, and other key industrial end markets have seen weaker volumes in recent years.

Lastly, Axalta benefits from Akzo’s own cost savings program, which is expected to raise their margins by approximately 200 basis points to 16%. If investors put 15x on 2028 earnings, that would result in a doubling of Axalta’s share price over the next few years. That translates to around a 6% free cash flow yield.
