Katz TMT Ideas Call — September 23, 2026

Host: Anton   |   Date: Wednesday, September 23, 2026, 12:00 PM ET (Zoom)

Format: One long and one short per presenter, five minutes total.

Ideas Presented

Josh Resnick, Jericho — Long: FFIV — Short: European automakers (MBG, BMW, VOW, STLA)

Shane Sandoval, Atreides — Long: CBRS — Short: GDDY

Eric Bannasch, Cadian Capital — Long: AG1 GY — Short: SOUN

Emilio Lamar, Third Point — Long: QBR/B CN — Short: CHTR, TMUS (US telecom without the full home bundle)

Aaron Weitman, CastleKnight — Long: AKER NO, MOD, SIMO, CLS — Short: None

Tyler Fischer, TOMS Capital — Long: INTC — Short: PANW (cybersecurity broadly)

Ravee Mehta, Nishkama — Long: 700 HK (also owns META, TWLO, OKTA) — Short: SCHW

Spencer Waxman, Shannon River — Long: HNGE (plus IDCC update) — Short: HPQ

Casey Savage, Avala Global — Long: U — Short: DUOL

Brian Finn, Findell Capital — Long: BULL — Short: SCHW (traditional brokerages/custodians)

Charles Kornblith, Verition — Long: SIRI — Short: OMC

Noel Culhane, Artisan Partners — Long: MTSI — Short: TTWO

Greg Brenner, Oribel — Long: GOOGL — Short: EXPE

Joe Flaum, Newbrook Capital — Long: SPOT, MDB — Short: APP

Adir Ron, Sender Companies — Long: LASR — Short: None

Key Themes & Takeaways

• Agentic AI ("Muse") is the lens for almost everything. Nearly every pitch was framed by who wins or loses as consumer AI agents shop, compare and act on users' behalf. Businesses that monetize inertia or information gaps were the losers: SCHW (cash sweep), EXPE (hotel/B2B fees), GDDY (top-of-funnel referrals), telcos without a full bundle. The winners were the low-cost provider (QBR/B), AI security (FFIV), transactional databases (MDB) and agent-native platforms (BULL, Tencent).

• "AI loser" baskets are mispricing stocks both ways. Several longs were pitched as wrongly lumped in with AI losers: AG1 GY (quant-fund shorts), U, SIRI, SPOT and GOOGL. The shorts in the same basket (OMC, SOUN, EXPE, SCHW) were argued to be real losers. Charles described the market as at "peak Muse hysteria."

• AI infrastructure is still the favored long bucket. CBRS (SRAM inference, token speed), INTC (Granite Rapids pricing plus a foundry option), MTSI (1.6T optics, 60%+ growth), MOD, AKER NO (Nscale IPO), SIMO, CLS and the GOOGL TPU optionality. Aaron declined to short neoclouds: "too messy, life's too short."

• Cybersecurity split. Josh is long FFIV because its Layer 7 traffic visibility makes it the leader in agentic AI security. Tyler is short PANW and CRWD on valuation and on frontier labs (OpenAI, Anthropic) internalizing model security.

• Consensus short: SCHW and traditional brokerages. Ravee and Brian both shorted Schwab independently. Agents can sweep idle cash into money funds, and share is moving to Robinhood and Webull.

• Mobile ad-tech pair. Casey is long U on AI-driven Vector share gains; Joe is short APP on the other side of the same trend (peak margins, a slow e-commerce push, a shrinking gaming ad ecosystem).

• Structural and secular shorts: European autos (Chinese EVs, tariffs, likely dividend cuts), HPQ (PC pull-forward, print decline), TTWO (GTA VI "travel and arrive"), DUOL (users growing faster than monetization), OMC (a failing IPG integration and client defections).

• Defense and physical-world AI. LASR (directed-energy lasers against cheap drones, $627M DoW contract, 1MW demo at year-end) and MTSI's defense segment (radar, anti-drone, Iron Dome) point to strong defense budget exposure.

• Valuation anchors. Several longs trade at single-digit to high-teens multiples: SIRI 7x P/E, QBR/B 8x EBITDA, 700 HK 12x, AG1 GY ~18x, GOOGL ~20x, FFIV mid-teens. The high-flyers pitched as shorts sit on elevated multiples: APP, TTWO after a double, cybersecurity.

Full Readable Transcript

Anton (Host): Thanks for joining. Just a reminder, please, no MNPI. I will call on each of you, and we'll have a timer — five minutes total for both the long and the short. We lost one participant, Val, to a stomach bug that's going around; one advantage of Zoom is there's no contagion. Josh, why don't we start with you?

Josh Resnick (Jericho): The long I'm pitching is F5, ticker FFIV. We've been involved for about a year and a half. We got very involved when they were breached by the Chinese government last fall and the stock took a beating — we thought that was a great opportunity. As I've gotten to know the company, I've been more and more impressed. I think the CEO is exceptional.

The stock has had a big run and it's still extremely cheap, but what's most interesting is that they launched an agentic AI security product in June, and it's had a tremendous amount of traction in short order. I met with the CEO two weeks ago — he's not a promotional guy at all — and he said this product is exploding in popularity and that it has the potential to be larger than the entire company. And fast, he says.

At a mid-teens earnings and free cash flow multiple, with a tremendous amount of free cash flow and a buyback, I don't think there's a lot of downside despite the run. If the agentic AI product takes off, the stock can go up a lot. What's interesting about the product is that F5 sits at Layer 7 of the tech stack, where they see the packets of data going back and forth in the data center. So they're uniquely positioned to sell a security product based on what's happening with agents. Agents are exploding right now, F5 is the number one player in a very emerging space, and I think they're better positioned than anyone. Palo Alto, the number two player, really just has the firewall — they don't see all the traffic — and customers seem to understand that. Tremendous upside, not a lot of downside.

On the short side, it's thematic. We're short a number of the European automakers — Mercedes, BMW, Volkswagen, Stellantis. They made money in China, and that's gone. They made money in the US, and that's being challenged by tariffs and the requirement to build their own US factories. And in Europe they're increasingly pressured by Chinese EVs. That's the theme underlying the whole thesis: China now has electric vehicles that are better cars at half the price. You see the same chart in every country — Chinese share of the market going up and to the right.

Now the Chinese manufacturers are building their own factories in Europe, so they won't have to pay import duties. It could be a wrecking ball for this industry. In the last few weeks, Volkswagen imploded with a big profit warning. Stellantis, despite anemic sales, saw inventories go up 20% last quarter, so I think there's more to come on the outlook. They all have pretty large dividends, except Stellantis, and Volkswagen had to agree with the unions to cut 50,000 people. When push comes to shove, what matters are the employees, not the dividends, so I suspect all the dividends go away in the next year or two. I don't think there's support for any of these stocks or equity value longer term, and in the case of Stellantis it's probably going to zero in pretty short order.

Anton (Host): Thank you, Josh. Shane, why don't we go to you next?

Shane Sandoval (Atreides): Thanks again for having us, Anton. I'll pitch long Cerebras, CBRS. It's an accelerator company we've been invested in for many years. It recently came public and has been pretty anemic since day one. Cerebras takes a very different approach to solving AI's memory-bandwidth needs. There are a lot of accelerator companies outside of Nvidia — the custom ASICs and the whole startup ecosystem — and Cerebras has made a different trade-off than anyone: going wafer-scale, being all-SRAM, and doing it on lagging-edge nodes at TSMC. There's been a lot of controversy about the technical efficiency of the product for very large models and different MoE structures, and about their ability to scale the business many multiples.

I think there are three vectors of growth. First, they came public with an OpenAI deal, where the first tranche is 750 megawatts. Second, they recently signed AMD and AWS, which should go live at the beginning of next year. Third, enterprises and labs — the disaggregation of prefill and decode, and more specifically between attention and feed-forward networks, is going to drive multiplicative demand for Cerebras.

Over time, latency has proven to be one of the most important aspects of technology. They've published 750 tokens per second on leading OpenAI models, and over the next six to nine months I think we'll see a move to single-digit thousands of tokens per second — a dramatically different paradigm. You can price those tokens at many multiples of today's GPU spot pricing. The first and second quarters out of the gate weren't great, but I think they're more supply-constrained on power than the market gives them credit for. We think they'll expand the customer footprint beyond the three massive labs and silicon providers and can do north of $20 of earnings in 2028. So this should be closer to $500–550 over the next 24 to 36 months.

The simplest proxy is the gigawatt math everyone uses in cloud. There's line of sight to close to a gigawatt of power exiting 2027 into early 2028, which is only about 40% of their wafer supply, and they should monetize that at roughly $15 billion per gig with massively expanding incremental margins — because they use SRAM rather than HBM DRAM, and because lagging-edge TSMC nodes give them a structural lead-time advantage.

On the short side, I'll pitch short GoDaddy. There are a lot of structural pressures. First, the top of the funnel is changing because of AI. Whatever chatbot you use — ChatGPT, Gemini — GoDaddy's referral share for net new domains and SMBs is falling, and .com registrations are at a five-year low. At the same time, there are pricing and contractual headwinds — not so much Airo, their new product migration, but the fact that they signed the longest-duration deals at the highest prices. So while the top of funnel is pressured, those economics roll off and drive pricing degradation and a duration headwind, which hits operating cash flow and free cash flow. I think there's more than 25% downside from below-street EBITDA and free cash flow with some multiple compression — and that's before Muse, Grok and these agents really expand into the SMB space.

Anton (Host): Terrific, thank you, Shane. Eric, would you like to go next?

Eric Bannasch (Cadian Capital): Sorry for joining a little late. On the long side I'm going to talk about Auto1, a European auto retailer and buyer of cars. About 90% of their purchases are from consumers selling their used cars, and they sell them to dealers and merchants or to consumers. So you bifurcate it into merchant versus retail. They've been in the merchant business since inception, over 15 years, and entered retail about seven or eight years ago.

The merchant business is growing in the mid-teens — a bit higher recently, probably 12–16% over the next two to three years — and contributes about $300 million of EBITDA this year. It sells about 900,000 units, it's profitable and dominant in Europe, yet it's only 2–3% of used-car turnover. They're structurally the only player doing this and very entrenched: over a thousand intake sites and a massive consumer brand. It's almost the default Kelley Blue Book — something like 40–50% of consumers selling a car in Europe download the app and get a price check, even if they don't sell to Auto1. That's a great top-of-funnel tool.

That business represents over 100% of company profit. The company trades at about 18 times — actually a little less — street 2027 earnings. That's quite reasonable for 20%-plus profit growth, and we think the stock is undervalued on that business alone; it deserves a higher multiple. Then there's the retail business — the analogy isn't perfect, but think of it as the Carvana of Europe. It does about 135,000 units, is growing 20–40%, and is losing roughly $25–30 million of EBITDA. They're the second-largest dealer in continental Europe and will become by far the biggest as it scales, focused on Germany, France and Spain, with presence in Italy, the Netherlands, Portugal and Belgium. That business is being valued at zero to negative. Structurally it's super sound — you can't replicate their supply side. Put together, total company earnings growth is closer to 40%, at 18 times next year's earnings.

The biggest reason it's this cheap is that it's been grouped as an AI loser. In the first quarter, when AI caused the software sell-off, short interest in Auto1 jumped from maybe 3–4% to 17% in a quarter. European filings show roughly 10–14 quant funds and one fundamental long/short fund short. So I think a lot of it is a quant read of the business. I don't think they're an AI loser — they repair cars, they move 4,000-pound vehicles.

On the short side, SoundHound. I was going to talk about Bending Spoons — this is a mini version of the same idea, though not low float. The company buys secularly declining assets that are definitely exposed to AI disruption, on top of already declining before AI. It buys these cheap assets, calls itself an AI company and gets a huge premium to anything that looks like it. It's been a decent short over the last two years, and I think it keeps de-rating. It's still very expensive, it's burning cash, and given the scale of the core business and the size of the market cap, it's very difficult to keep buying assets to cover the declines. We think the assets decline 5–15% annually, its cost of capital has gone up, and it can't buy its way out.

One more thing — it's a slightly spiffy management team. We met with them a month ago, and the CEO said he's trying to sign more term licenses rather than recurring licenses to inflate reported revenue. He actually said he was anxious to sign a bunch of term deals as quickly as possible to cover the declines and report revenue that looks different from the fundamentals.

Anton (Host): Thank you, Eric. Emilio at Third Point.

Emilio Lamar (Third Point): My favorite way to play Muse right now is actually in telco. We really like the Canadian discount wireless company, Quebecor. The narrative in the US is that Muse is a race to the bottom — it bids your telco bill down to the lowest option. That's the case when pricing is close to parity. Canada is totally different: three incumbents sell at $58 and one new entrant sells a monthly wireless plan at $35. They're 12% of subs and did 33% of industry net adds over the last year. Typically it's slow going for a new entrant — you have to convince the market your network is good, advertise a lot, and grow slowly, which is what they're doing now.

This is the ultimate Muse winner. I see it with my Canadian friends: ask your phone for the most rational wireless bill and it points you to the $35 entrant riding on the Rogers network. You have one lower-marginal-cost provider that's 30% below the incumbents, and the incumbents are so levered they can't cut price quickly. It trades at eight times 2027 EBITDA, and I think EBITDA accelerates to high single digits. Sell-side coverage is weak and people don't look very far out. You paid 11–12 times for T-Mobile when it was growing similarly, and T-Mobile never faced competitors this far off on price or this levered. I can't find many true low-marginal-cost providers of a commodity that benefit from the consumer push from Muse, but this is the cleanest.

On the other side, I'm shorting anything in US telco that doesn't own the complete bundle. It's all about owning the home. If you look at how Muse interacts with your AT&T bill, it typically tries to cross-sell home internet onto a wireless plan at the lowest possible price to clear the sale — there's no marginal cost to add onto the bundle. I like pressing Charter here — I'm shorting the unsecureds as well — and I like shorting T-Mobile because they're wireless-only and don't have the same home internet bundle to compete on aggregate pricing.

Anton (Host): Terrific, thank you, Emilio. Aaron.

Aaron Weitman (CastleKnight): I'm still pretty positive on AI. A side comment first: it feels like a lot of people have been shorting neoclouds and AI companies, and that feels masochistic to me — too messy, and life's too short. Moving on, a couple of AI longs I still like. Aker in Norway, ticker AKER, is interesting as a public-market way to play the upcoming Nscale IPO. We'll see where that prices, but it could move Aker up 20–40% quickly, and longer term I view it, like most AI names, as a double.

Another with a catalyst in the next week or so is Modine. It's getting rid of its industrial business. There have been almost leaks of potential customer wins — people knew they had Google, and they may have won Amazon. I think earnings power can move materially above consensus over the next couple of years. They're finally separating the industrial business in the next week or so and changing the name of the company — you can view that as lipstick, but it makes it more interesting.

And as side mentions, Silicon Motion, SIMO, and Celestica — other ways to keep playing the AI theme, and names that could be doubles or more over the next year. I'll end it there.

Anton (Host): Thank you, Aaron. Tyler?

Tyler Fischer (TOMS Capital): Thanks, Anton. On the long side, Intel. Despite the run, I think it can still go up 70%. There's a mix shift: more of the CPU business is moving to data center AI, which carries 70% incremental margins. Granite Rapids is the product seeing significant hyperscaler demand. Intel has talked about adding over 100% capacity next year, with pricing up 20–30%. Granite Rapids is still less than 50% of DCAI, and it should be the majority, or a much larger share, next year and keep growing into 2028.

On a sum-of-the-parts basis, the products business can get to $8 in 2028. Pick your multiple — 20 times 2028 is reasonable — and that's well above the current price for products alone. Then there's the call option on foundry, where they're quickly ramping the ASIC business, plus advanced packaging, where they work with Google on TPUs and a number of other rumored products. I look at foundry through tangible book value, roughly $50 a share, and as they add capacity for both their CPU business and external foundry customers, that should grow over the next few years. That's how I get to over $200 a share.

On the short side, it's thematic: cybersecurity has high multiples, and you're starting to hear OpenAI and Anthropic talk more about internalizing those efforts and shifting engineers to focus on defending their models before fully deploying them. If the models keep improving at the same rate, it'll be hard for Palo Alto, CrowdStrike and the external cyber companies to stay at the leading edge. And from a valuation perspective there's not much support. So valuation plus potential competition.

Anton (Host): Terrific, thank you, Tyler. Ravee.

Ravee Mehta (Nishkama): I'll pitch Schwab short, SCHW. This is an agentic AI loser. Almost all of their earnings come from the fact that they don't pay much interest on cash balances. With Muse you can just ask it every day or every week to sweep your Schwab cash into money markets. If everybody does that, the $10 of 2028 earnings the bulls have goes to $2. It's also generally a market-share loser in brokerage — the average customer is 49, and weighted by AUM it's much higher — and they're clearly losing share to Robinhood and others. It's a short on any rally.

For the long, I'm surprised people haven't pitched things like Meta and Twilio that have been declared Muse winners — we own some of those, and Okta as well. But the name with interesting risk/reward is Tencent. It's 12 times earnings. The street is modeling a deceleration even though they just re-accelerated a bit. And Tencent could have the next Muse product — very likely will. It's a matter of getting enough compute capacity. It'll probably be even better than Muse because of the WeChat app ecosystem and all the companies they've invested in, which will likely integrate right away. I think the stock has probably bottomed; there's not much downside to the lows because people know the product is coming. I don't know what the upside is or exactly what the product is, but at 12 times earnings it's a pretty good risk/reward.

Anton (Host): Terrific, thank you, Ravee. Spencer.

Spencer Waxman (Shannon River): Thanks, Anton, for inviting me again. I'll go a little off-piste first: InterDigital, IDCC, which I've talked about before and owned for four years, has had major announcements. It's an IP company whose first leg was getting the cell phone market under license. Now they've won their first video streaming cases against Disney in court and signed Amazon. They literally have patents on video streaming and are in the early days of getting that market under license. That's a 45-second update.

My long today is Hinge Health, HNGE. We like platforms that deliver healthcare over the internet — administering a plan or delivering care — at a point where they have a tremendous number of covered lives but are early in usage uptake. Their main offering is MSK, musculoskeletal, where they administer regimens via app with visual assistance, and usage has been ticking up. They have a new FDA-approved migraine offering, still early, and a recent acquisition opened up GI care, with a coach answering questions and making sure the program is followed. There's a tailwind from GLP-1 usage, which causes a lot of GI issues.

All of these programs are early in uptake. Only a very low single-digit percentage of covered lives use it today, our checks say it's growing faster than the street, and our numbers for next year are well above consensus. It's also heavily shorted on the belief that usage won't tick up, so it's a bit turbocharged. A simple land-and-expand thesis — we've had a few of these in recent years — with a very asymmetric opportunity.

Our short is HPQ. AI demand has driven DRAM prices and PC prices up, and we think there was a first-half pull-forward of orders as a result, so 2027 numbers are too high. We don't believe the narrative that AI will drive greater PC demand, because most of it will happen in the cloud on servers rather than on laptops. They've been cutting costs for a couple of years to maintain cash flow, and that can't go on forever. Print is in secular decline; they got an uptick from moving ink to subscription, but that's going to anniversary. We've had this on for a while — it's a grinder that underperforms in a good tape and in a bad tape.

Anton (Host): Thank you, Spencer. Casey at Avala.

Casey Savage (Avala Global): Thanks for having us. My long is Unity and my short is Duolingo. Earlier this year we thought Unity was a good dislocated opportunity: the stock was viewed as an AI loser and there were questions about execution. The company has done a really good job changing the narrative — they're not an AI loser — and executing on the plan.

For background, Unity runs a mobile gaming ad network connecting games with advertisers, and the other part of the business is the game engine. The thesis is simple: mobile gaming is greatly under-monetized versus other ad businesses — pennies on the dollar versus Meta — and Unity is going through an AI-led product inflection. It has gone from one of the worst-performing networks to the second best. They're using AI models to bid more effectively in auctions and are now using gameplay data from the engine to inform bidding, and it's starting to work, with incrementals around 80%. The biggest thing at the end of Q2 was the beginning of the runtime data integration. Vector growth has been accelerating quarter over quarter in the low 20s, and we think it accelerates in Q3.

We're excited about the catalyst path for Q3 and Q4 earnings, but it's more than the next couple of quarters; the next couple of years look good. Our point of differentiation is a full market-share and impression-level build, and we believe the conversion-rate math isn't well understood. Checks have been pretty decent, and management has sounded constructive at recent conferences that the runtime integration is performing well — in my opinion maybe a little ahead. I think Unity can do over $1.3 billion of EBITDA; at 20 times that's a high-$50s price target — maybe 30% into year-end and 70% a year from now. The biggest risk is AppLovin, which is twice as big, and whether the runtime impact plateaus. The narrative has changed, they're executing, and the data points get us excited to be long.

On the short side, Duolingo, a gamified learning app focused on languages, with newer offerings in chess, math and music, monetized through paid subscriptions. The data trends have been quite good over the summer and into the fall — probably the biggest acceleration in a couple of years — but we think it's setting up for a big slowdown. The debate is whether they can monetize users, and we don't believe they can. Daily users don't necessarily translate into higher-value subscribers or earnings. Max conversions, renewals and user acquisition costs are all headwinds. Q2 dailies grew 23%, but total bookings grew only 8% and adjusted EBITDA margins fell 530 basis points. User data good, revenue and margin data not so great.

We anticipate the first growth slowdown is coming — we haven't seen it yet. We think it's an $80 stock over the next 12 months, using 25 times 2027 EPS of about $3.24. The biggest risk is that product improvements lead to sustained, better paid conversion; we're monitoring downloads, monthly DAUs by geography, paid conversion and renewal rates. Notably, YipitData recently flagged reduced confidence in its daily user tracking — not saying it's wrong, but it's interesting. On costs, there's likely some pressure: bonuses need to be paid out, maybe $10 million-plus. Not a lot, but calling it out made me think there could be margin issues in the back half. Management is controlling what it can, but monetization is a tremendous challenge, and it's an interesting chance to short into a deceleration in users with monetization we're very skeptical of.

Anton (Host): Perfect, thank you, Casey. Brian Finn from Findell.

Brian Finn (Findell Capital): Thank you, Anton. On the short side, we agree with Ravee on Schwab and the traditional brokerages, custodians and wealth managers — that's our thematic short. The corollary on the long side is Webull, ticker BULL, a newer online platform that competes with Robinhood and Interactive Brokers — a retail brokerage for very active traders. What makes them different is a very data-rich platform that's well integrated with AI: you can use AI agents to create trade reports and actually execute trades. Robinhood can't do that yet, and IBKR's agents are read-only and still being built out.

What makes it compelling today is the June catalyst: the SEC got rid of the rule from 2001 that prevented accounts under $25,000 from trading on margin. That matters a lot for Webull because their average account is about $5,000, so more than any other broker they benefit, and they already have. Management guided to roughly 20% transaction growth from the change, and we saw more than 70% — equity notional volume jumped 73% in the second quarter. August is still well ahead of last year and consensus.

Two risks get people's attention. First, China: the founder is a Chinese national with voting control and some employees are in China. The mitigants: it's a US broker-dealer, the board and management are US-based, the auditor is KPMG, and they deregistered their Chinese brokerage. If needed, they could move the Chinese employees to Singapore or hire higher-cost engineers — right now they're arbitraging cheaper Chinese engineering labor. We view it as headline risk that's more or less contained. Second, macro: the stock has traded off on last week's rate hike, and in the 2022 cycle Robinhood and IBKR saw big volume declines. But we don't think this cycle is analogous to 2022, when the Fed raised 375 basis points; it's more like 2023 — higher for longer, but an orderly tape.

Countering that is the data. They make money on trades. Trades per dollar of notional volume ran between 8 and 11 throughout 2025, hit 15 in August and keeps rising. Notional stock volume looks a little weak, but trade count drives revenue, and it's going the right way because of the rule change and people deploying little AI agents to trade. We get to 51 cents of 2027 earnings, above consensus. Robinhood trades at 49 times, IBKR at 34 times. At 25 times, you get about $13 a share, and we think the China risk is well reflected in the multiple. The stock is a little under $8, so we see maybe $2 of downside and $5–6 of upside near term.

Anton (Host): All right, thank you, Brian. Charles?

Charles Kornblith (Verition): Thanks, Anton. I'm going to pitch two AI losers, both trading at seven times earnings — one long, one short. My short is Omnicom, OMC, one of the three large agency holdcos. Their business is under pressure from AI on both the creative and media side. What's unique is that they recently merged with one of their largest competitors, Interpublic, and that integration, six to nine months along, is becoming a disaster. They fired a ton of people to get to the merger synergies, and it turns out they fired enough senior relationship managers that CMOs and clients are voting with their feet. Highly unusual: Pepsi fired them two weeks ago and went to Publicis without even doing a review. Our industry checks suggest more Pepsis are coming, and Omnicom hasn't been winning new business in bake-offs for the last year.

The street has organic growth at 4% this year and next. We think next year is closer to zero or even negative as these losses flow through. There's also a quality-of-earnings issue: the only reason they'll grow 4% this year is that they put their weakest businesses into discontinued operations, which flatters organic growth. There are also a lot of charges being added back, so I'm skeptical it's really seven times earnings. We have 5–10% lower revisions for 2027 and think the multiple can de-rate from seven times — 15–20% downside in our base case.

The long is Sirius XM, SIRI. I think it's a double in the next 12 months. It's in the AI-loser basket — it's one of the largest weightings in the Muse short baskets this week, and the stock is down 10%. Sirius has about 30 million satellite subs and has chopped around without growing for a long time. What's unique and changing is that it has the premier digital audio advertising business in the country, built over 10–15 years starting with Pandora, plus SoundCloud and others, and it now sells about 10% of all digital audio advertising.

What made me cover my short and flip long a couple of months ago is that Google decided to hand its YouTube audio inventory to Sirius to sell, because Sirius sells it better than Google can. We did a lot of work, and it's true: Sirius is better at selling audio-only advertising. That relationship is a game changer. From the filings, you can conclude both companies think it's worth $500–600 million of incremental revenue starting in 2027, and we think it goes to $2 billion over the next two to three years. That takes Sirius from no growth to mid-single-digit growth in 2027 and high single digits in 2028, versus the street at low single digits. Meaningful estimate revisions, and the seven times multiple re-rates to 10 times on our above-street 2027 numbers — that's a double.

On top of that there's spectrum. They have 35 megahertz of mid-band spectrum and only need 12.5 to run the business, so 22.5 megahertz will be sold at some point over the next couple of years. At a dollar per megahertz-pop, a rough comp, that's $8 billion gross — call it $5 billion after tax on a discounted basis — another 50% upside to the core. On the AI-loser point: we'll see, but I think we're in peak Muse hysteria. Muse could modestly grind down ARPU, but I'm skeptical of much churn, because the 30 million people who pay for Sirius are older and listen regularly in their cars. It's not a positive, but at seven times earnings and about to accelerate growth, I'm not too concerned.

Anton (Host): Thank you very much, Charles. Noel.

Noel Culhane (Artisan Partners): I'm going to pitch an AI winner long: Macom, MTSI. It's three businesses. About 40% is data center, exposed to AI, which is accelerating and can grow north of 90% next year. That alone takes total company growth north of 35%, which is where the street is for the year. They sell optical TIAs and drivers into optical transceivers. The transceiver market doubles next year, moving from 800G to 1.6T is at least a 50% like-for-like ASP increase, and they're ramping a 200G photodetector business with the best photodetector in the market. So we expect data center to accelerate further, driven more by socket wins in transceivers than total capex. For 2028, they're qualifying CW lasers for CPO and beyond and have a good chance at a lot of socket wins, especially at Amazon, so strong growth continues beyond 2027.

Another 40% is industrial and defense, roughly the same size as data center, which can grow north of 30% — another 12–13 points of top-line growth. They're exposed to Iron Dome and European and US defense budgets, selling to primes and new primes, typically radar and anti-drone systems that are taking a lot of share. They have manufacturing in Europe and the US to serve both markets and aren't at full utilization, so that can run materially. The last 20% is telecom, which doesn't really grow because it's base-station dependent and we're in a 5G lull; it'll re-accelerate with 6G. But they have a lot of low-earth-orbit satellite exposure, with programs at Starlink and the other large LEO providers like Kuiper, ramping in the back half of 2026. Their fiscal year ends in September, so telecom accelerates and can grow north of mid-teens next year — another three or four points of growth.

So the business can grow north of 60% versus the street at 37%. Gross margins should rise every quarter sequentially with better utilization, and opex grows slower, so EPS growth is very fast. They're probably the number one takeout target in analog, which is why it always trades at a premium. Probably the best management team — Steve Daly already sold his last business to ADI, and ADI is the natural acquirer. Long term, we have about $15 of earnings in 2028; at a mid-20s multiple that's 50% upside.

On the short side, Take-Two, TTWO. Grand Theft Auto, their big release that's been coming for 13 years, launches in a couple of months, and the stock has more than doubled over the last couple of years in anticipation. Buy-side unit expectations look high to me. Video game stocks typically don't do well around a launch — it's travel and arrive. Whether it's Nintendo six months after a hardware launch, Red Dead Redemption for Take-Two or Cyberpunk for CD Projekt, there's not much incremental information once your biggest, and probably only, hit comes out. The street models roughly $10 billion of free cash flow over the next four years, growing every year, which implies close to 200 million units of GTA over the cycle. I don't think there will be 200 million consoles to sell into, so the long-term estimates look wrong. The stock already reacted negatively after the trailer and is down about $50 in two months. It might pop into the retail launch, but it's a good spot to short. I think you'll see earnings above the street in 2027 and lower in the years after.

Anton (Host): Thank you, Noel. Greg?

Greg Brenner (Oribel): Thank you, Anton. I'll talk about two names in the crosshairs of Muse and the latest AI — one long, one short. Long Google. The stock has been under pressure for most of the last quarter. Initially it was because of senior departures in the AI business and models falling further behind OpenAI and Anthropic, and people took it as Google being dead at the frontier. We don't think so. The company's messaging has been clear that it won't give up at the frontier, and the turnover has actually helped increase focus and execution and made the team more product-focused.

The weakness over the last couple of weeks is more about Muse raising the question of why Google didn't do this first, given Gmail and how much more it knows about the consumer than Meta. But Google introduced a similar capability before Meta with Gemini Spark at I/O earlier this year — it just hasn't launched it as a standalone app or service. We think that's a matter of time, and they have big advantages in Gmail, what they know about you, and verticals like shopping and travel. On timing, Google tends to release models in Q4, so we think Gemini 4 — which sounds like a pretty large model that should help them catch up — comes in Q4 and shows improvement. Google is also well capitalized, whereas a lot of peers still seem to have a cash shortfall.

We see significant upside in the TPU business — through rental via GCP, selling chips outright, or incremental capacity for upcoming consumer offerings — and medium-term margin upside as they diversify their supply base away from Broadcom. The stock got as high as 28 times earnings earlier this year and is down to 20. We see re-rating potential as they position their products and models closer to the frontier, plus earnings upside mostly from TPUs.

On the negative side, Expedia. We think they're much more at risk from Muse and other agentic offerings, along with other dynamics in travel. They've done a good job accelerating growth relative to peers, partly through the B2B business, a part of the market people and competitors hadn't focused on. But Booking is now restructuring its B2B business, which should take some share from Expedia at the margin or at least keep fees in check. On the agentic side, Expedia over-indexes to B2B and has much more hotel exposure, which leads to fee compression once agentic traffic becomes material. The stock trades in a wide range depending on sentiment — around 8 to 15 times earnings — and it's in the middle at about 11. We think there's risk toward the low end as the agentic risk becomes clearer.

Anton (Host): Thank you, Greg. Two left. Joe?

Joe Flaum (Newbrook Capital): First I'll throw in my Muse pick, since that's what everyone's doing: MongoDB long. We liked it anyway, but we think Muse accelerates the uptake of transactional databases, which are basically the language of AI and what agents need to process all the work they'll be doing.

The long I'll defend, on the opposite side of the Muse headwind, is Spotify. It's the leading franchise in streaming audio. Over the last year they've reset their deals with the three major labels. They still pay a healthy percentage to artists for licensing content, but these deals unbundle Spotify's ability to up-tier and sell additional features — Audiobooks+, which carries a higher gross margin; superfan offerings for people who want concert tickets; and the key feature rolling out soon, the remix product everyone's been talking about. They were waiting on a couple of labels to sign, and they'll do an early rollout to work through usability and what consumers really like to do with it. That trial period likely starts later this year, and we expect a Warner Music deal potentially ahead of earnings, which is a nice catalyst.

That's exciting because Spotify could turn into more of a social, two-way, multiplayer platform. If people are creating their own songs and sharing them with friends, it creates a flywheel that drives engagement you can monetize in many ways, at more attractive gross margins. At their investor day in May they put out a nice medium-term algorithm. If they hit those numbers, free cash flow per share could be north of $40 in a few years; at a mid-20s multiple, that's a double. We think they can get to at least $25 of free cash flow per share next year, and at a reasonable multiple there's decent upside from where the stock has de-rated on the Muse attack on anything with a subscription.

On the short side, we'll take the other side of Casey's Unity long: we like AppLovin short, which fits nicely with his thesis that Unity is becoming a presence and taking share — we agree. AppLovin has been an incredible story, reaching a market cap of about a quarter of a trillion. They were the first mover in implementing the recommendation-engine technology AI has brought forth, like you see at Meta and Google, and they were effectively a monopoly — they locked up the supply side with a timely acquisition and had a good recommendation engine. Now Unity Vector has a competing product. In the overall ecosystem of ads in video games, inventory and engagement are actually down, so the industry isn't growing. They're at what we think are max margins, which can only go the other direction as they invest to roll out the new e-commerce business.

Historically they only showed video game ads inside games. The e-commerce initiative has gotten off to a slow start, and we think it stays difficult; experimental ad dollars today tend to go to chatbots like OpenAI and other exciting AI initiatives. Overall, we think the beat machine is broken. As growth slows and the stock de-rates, estimates come down, and at 10 times EBITDA you can see the stock de-rate toward the low to mid $200s.

Anton (Host): Thank you very much, Joe. And lastly, Adir.

Adir Ron (Sender Companies): English isn't my native language, and I'm changing the format a bit — I'll save you two and a half minutes because I only have a long. The idea is nLight, ticker LASR. Over the past couple of years, since the Russia–Ukraine war and especially the Israel–Iran–US conflict, the geopolitical situation has revealed a major issue in how Western militaries eliminate threats. A small drone costs $20,000–40,000, but taking it down requires an interceptor that costs $4 million. US stockpiles are down 60–70% from the right level. The military needs another solution to take down drones and, in the future, threats like cruise missiles.

That's where this company comes in. nLight used to be an industrial laser company and a few years ago identified the opportunity to move into aerospace and defense, developing technology that doesn't exist elsewhere for using laser beams to eliminate threats. They combine many laser beams and amplifiers so they can shoot down any threat — a drone or, in the future, a cruise missile. Competitors in the space are Lockheed Martin, AeroVironment and a few others getting small contracts to demonstrate capability. The whole industry is transitioning from demonstration to production. AeroVironment just got its first contract from the Department of War a month ago, for $500 million — the first real contract the DoW has awarded for this technology.

nLight is a supplier to every company in the industry, and it won a $627 million DoW contract two or three months ago. Since they have technology no one else has and supply everyone, I'd call it a one-of-one company that you can't really compare to others on valuation. Still, it trades at seven times this year's revenue. They're developing a one-megawatt laser, which will be by far the strongest laser weapon in the world. At the end of this year they'll demonstrate it to the DoW. A one-megawatt laser can take down cruise missiles and might eventually handle hypersonic missiles, so anything related to Golden Dome or other administration projects gives the company scarcity value.

One risk: on the last earnings call they were supposed to beat guidance by about 25%, but they had an issue with China. Like every other company, they source optics from China. After the $627 million DoW contract, the Chinese understood they were supplying a company that would put the strongest weapon in US hands, and the day after they stopped shipping optics. That's why, instead of beating guidance, they had to lower it. The stock is now 52% off its all-time high, and I think that's overdone. We know the Chinese are sending supply again, and in the meantime the company is qualifying other sources. Sorry for the extra 50 seconds.

Anton (Host): Thank you, Adir. Interesting. Thank you all — I appreciate it and I'm grateful for your support. We kept it as tight as possible. Thanks, all.

Sell-Side Sector Positioning Call: Financials, TMT and Energy/Industrials — Key Debates, Positioning and Top Ideas

Date: September 22, 2026

Firm: Morgan Stanley (not stated outright on the call; inferred from the MSXX thematic basket tickers and the research analysts referenced)

Moderator: Kate

Presenters: Wendy — Financials specialist sales; Skylar — TMT specialist sales; Mark — Energy specialist sales, also absorbing Industrials coverage from Mark Vanderplume in a few weeks

Research referenced: Steven Bird (head AI strategist), Mita Marshall (cybersecurity), Brian Nowak and Matt Koss (internet/OTAs), Mike Cypress (brokers), Martin Rats (oil), John Story (thematic baskets), Tom Wigg (TMT specialist sales) — names as transcribed

Key Topics and Takeaways

Cross-call summary

• Financials: after the broadening-out rotation, diversified banks, exchanges and life insurance are the most crowded; consumer finance, fintech payments and info services carry the highest squeeze risk. Four live debates — the rate cycle, the mortgage trough, where we sit in the capital markets cycle, and the durability of the retail trading frenzy.

• TMT: the AI safety / "frontier pacing" debate resolves bullish for compute; the agentic trade has violently re-awakened on Meta's Muse launch; software's rally has been overwhelmingly short covering, leaving room to run; the disrupted side is OTAs, gig economy and telco.

• Energy & Industrials: data center commentary out of the Laguna conference was excellent and disconnected from a volatile tape; shorter-cycle industrials are mixed-to-positive with fuel and labor costs biting; oil is now essentially a conflict play, with refining the most-asked-about pocket.

• The common thread across all three: positioning has washed out of several fundamentally intact trades — merchant power, engineering & construction, software shorts — while company-level commentary has stayed strong. The gap between sentiment and ground truth is where the presenters are pointing.

1. Financials (Wendy)

Positioning

• Most crowded subsectors: diversified banks, exchanges, life insurance.

• Highest short-squeeze risk: consumer finance, fintech payments, info services — positioning still relatively short, partly a function of higher-for-longer rates.

The four key debates

• Rate cycle. Is last week's 25bp Fed hike the start of a new hiking cycle or a mid-cycle adjustment? If it is a mid-cycle adjustment, hikes get priced out of the curve as oil comes down and the hike is cosmetic. If it is the start of a cycle, you want to be short most of financials — higher-for-longer slows the economy and does not help the multiple.

• Mortgage cycle. The only cycle within financials still at the trough — CRE, transaction activity, new home sales. With the 10-year heading toward 5%+, recovery is hard to see. The debate is not whether to short the mortgage names; it is the opportunity cost of getting long too early, since the 10-year could come down in three months or three years.

• Capital markets cycle. Big banks at last week's conference characterized it as early-to-mid innings. The question is how to position across big banks, M&A boutiques and alternatives.

• Retail trading and the Clarity Act. Retail volumes look structurally higher on agentic trading and the post-Clarity-Act crypto boom. The Clarity Act itself is dead, but the SEC and CFTC are following with their own legislation. How durable is the strength?

• AI (carried over). The simple long-AI-winners / short-AI-losers trade is now more nuanced — Muse AI's launch sold off the losers again, but from here it is about valuation interacting with the timing of disruption rather than a clean binary.

Wendy's trade ideas

• Long Robinhood (tactical). Pitched since $100, up ~20%, Mike Cypress upgraded to overweight. Near-term target $130–140, based on 30–40x ~$4 of 2028 EPS. Catalysts: a potential agentic trading announcement at the September 29–30 Active Trader Summit; incremental prediction-market and sports-betting volumes; and a return of mega IPOs — the SpaceX IPO in June drove roughly 3x retail volumes. Acknowledged risk: prediction-market regulation.

• Long AXP / short KRE (tactical). No positive catalyst between now and the October 14 CPI; one employment report in between that is bad for KRE either way. The house economist view is the market prices too little hiking in 2026 and too much in 2027. Long AXP is the hedge against a beta rally if oil falls.

• Longer horizon: alternatives as a group (sponsor recovery still early innings, stock has sold off); TradeWeb (beneficiary of higher rates volatility under a new Fed, plus misconceptions about the impact of ICE's MarketAxess acquisition); and Nasdaq.

2. TMT (Skylar)

AI safety / frontier pacing

• Last weekend's discourse from AI executives on frontier pacing — safety, measured deployment, lab hacks and rogue agents — raised the question of what it means for AI capex beneficiaries and the pace of the build-out.

• The house conclusion is net bullish for compute, on two grounds. Technically, taking more time to release models consumes more of the resources already being deployed to build safeguards. Narratively, a more paced, measured build-out quells the bubble concern and acts as a smoother on the expansion.

• NIMBY / local and state-level data center backlash is read the same way — a smoother rather than a stopper. With federal support under the current administration, the team does not expect an overarching restrictive framework, though midterms remain an overhang.

• Most tactical way to play it: cyber. Preference for the expensive scaled platforms — CrowdStrike, Palo Alto — with Okta the cheaper, smaller-scale option, plus the cyber basket (MSXXCYBR). The scaled platforms have the customer relationships and product breadth that give them the right to win.

The agentic resurgence

• The trade lay dormant for five or six months after the OpenClaw launch, on the expectation that a frontier lab or hyperscaler would ship a larger-scale version. Meta did exactly that with Muse — still number one in the App Store, with blistering adoption. Brian Nowak had flagged Meta as a top idea on exactly this product-launch setup, reading the teen-user ruling as an overhang removal akin to Google's 2H25 moment.

• Beneficiaries (MSXX claw basket, constituents available): Meta itself; the CPU names — Intel, AMD, Qualcomm — which have been on fire; Shopify as a critical enablement layer for agentic transactions, with the ShopPay partnership with Meta just expanded so saved payment and address details now carry into Muse; and Akamai for inference at the edge, a cheaper play than Cloudflare on greater agentic traffic, with a recent unnamed deal investors are speculating may be with Meta.

• Disrupted (agentic risk basket, MSXXARSK, released yesterday): OTAs, gig economy names, and telcos/cable — the latter already pressured by SpaceX disruption risk, and now by consumers using agents to negotiate bills down. Early agentic use cases skew heavily toward trip planning, booking rides and ordering food.

OTAs

• Matt Koss assumed lead coverage from Brian Nowak: kept Booking at overweight (mildly controversial to have any overweight in the space), assumed Airbnb at equal weight, and downgraded Expedia to underweight from Nowak's equal weight.

Software positioning — the key message

• The rallies and exposure changes in software, especially after the Salesforce print and its collaboration with a frontier lab on a new agentic product, have been materially driven by short covering rather than long adds. That is a constructive setup for building conviction.

• The 15–20% rally in those names is still meaningfully below the recent high, which has only just been matched within the last twelve months.

• Genuine long demand is showing up in infrastructure software, unsurprising as a conventional AI winner on observability demand.

• Cyber is also still mostly short covering, which Skylar found surprising given the fundamental case — likely hedge funds short on valuation, while long-only money has been positioned there for months, driving an intense rally.

• What still has to be proven: AI monetization under the more complementary model, where software becomes the enterprise context layer for agentic operations and has to retain economics while working with a third-party access layer.

Skylar's ideas

• Top long — Microsoft. The safe venue for enterprise AI deployment, a narrative Satya has been pitching for years; very long tail of enterprise relationships and contracts; positioned as the ultimate model router letting enterprises deploy AI safely and cost-efficiently; Copilot improving; still under-owned, and long-only investors need to track it given its benchmark weight.

• Top short — Expedia. Riskier exposure via airlines and C-corp hotels; Matt Koss assumed coverage at underweight.

The headcount bear case may be resolving — strength at Salesforce and Atlassian, GitLab improving, with AI-generated code arguing for more developer seats plus a broader TAM into IT, operations, finance and legal. Names liked: Atlassian in SaaS, Dynatrace in infrastructure software, Akamai on agentic AI.

3. Energy and Industrials (Mark) — Laguna conference feedback

Data centers: commentary excellent

• Sterling does site prep for data centers and is among the earliest parties on a project — a self-described canary in the coal mine. Texas is a big focus. No slowdown at all, and its $7bn backlog is a small fraction of the shadow backlog it sees (a 100MW project may carry visibility to a 100MW expansion that never enters backlog).

• GE Vernova gave one of the better presentations — the kind after which numbers go higher. Mark is sympathetic to the view that it has gotten expensive with various risks, but the numbers keep moving up.

• The broader observation: a real dissonance between how volatile the tape and investor sentiment have been versus what companies are actually saying. Investors are struggling to reconcile the two, and sentiment has flipped back to more positive.

Shorter-cycle industrials: mixed, leaning positive

• Freight companies spoke to an inflection in the cycle with rates coming back higher — the broader economy seems fine and the short-cycle inflection investors have hoped for looks intact.

• The nuance is cost: fuel and labor are starting to eat into margins. JB Hunt was the only company to call it out explicitly, but it was discussed broadly.

• On the consumer, AutoNation flagged pricing pressure and customers deferring vehicle servicing — two cracks, against an otherwise fine backdrop.

Traditional oil and gas

• Largely a play on the conflict at this point. Refining draws the most investor interest — refined product inventories are so low that the trade becomes very convex the longer this goes on.

• Risks to that: refiners are historically expensive, a potential export ban, higher Chinese runs, and de-escalation in Russia-Ukraine. But given where inventories sit, investors struggle to turn negative — a keep-it-on-a-short-leash sector.

• Increasing inbounds on upstream E&Ps, which should track refined product cracks more directionally than during the prior US-Iran episode. Then the system had buffers (Martin Rats has written this up); this time it does not, and inventories are depressed — in some areas at operational tank bottoms, including Cushing. Occidental Petroleum named as an example in the underinvested pocket.

• Near-term events flagged: the UN meeting, Trump meeting Zelensky at 1:30pm ET, and chatter — mixed reporting — that Trump could meet Iran's president.

Mark's ideas

• Top long — Talen Energy (TLN). Positioning is totally washed out: generalists who owned the merchant power AI-trade left when deals went to regulated utilities instead, and many rotated into crypto miners. • From Laguna — engineering and construction broadly, Sterling in particular. Same generalist exodus as in IPPs, with positioning back to the lowest in a couple of years. These are the companies that build the data centers and the gas plants, labor is extremely constrained, and this is as real a bottleneck as grid interconnection. It may be a clearing event or not; a blue wave would push investors to think about the presidential election and what that means for the data center trade. A related question is rotation back into renewables — First Solar (as transcribed) is drawing more investor traction into the election.

events.2026-09-16-revelere-revelere-idea-lunch:
Macro / room tone

• AI longs have outperformed by only a couple hundred bps - crowded, not lucrative. Nobody in the room owns a portfolio that made money on the July/Aug or Mon/Tue AI drawdowns. High confidence that this is the read; the room has no hedge.

• The one anti-consensus frame offered: software/consumer internet as the "inference keeps compounding after capex plateaus" trade. That is exactly the scenario your book is short (SaaS basket) and only MSFT covers. Worth noting, not acting on yet.

• Source-of-funds question for $200B+ lab raises went unanswered: what gets sold - hyperscalers, semis, software? This is the financing-constraint thesis stated as a dinner question. Nobody had a view. Moderate confidence the room's silence means it is not priced.

• Sub-themes across pitches: analog/power semis de-rated from 30x+ peaks back to cyclical-recovery multiples; memory cost pass-through is bifurcating winners (TXN raising across the board) from losers (TOST); electrician labor is the un-capitalizable bottleneck; 300mm wafer spot may have crossed contract.

Best three

• Talabat - highest confidence (moderate-high). Only pitch with a mechanical catalyst that does not need a debate to resolve: 35% of float retired in three quarters by a controller who has said it publicly, on a 10x business growing mid-teens, with conservative guidance and a strategic buyer already telling the world it wants the asset. Zero AI correlation, which your book needs. Liquidity is the real constraint.

• SWKS - moderate confidence. Hard event inside weeks, consolidation to a duopoly, dividend-to-buyback swap at 8-9x '28, content-per-device inflecting after years of Apple stripping RF. Risks are real (Apple concentration, iPhone units vs memory pricing, synergy delivery) but they are underwriteable and not correlated to capex sentiment.

• Sino-American Silicon - moderate-low confidence on timing, high on asymmetry. The math is the pitch: 1.8x the market cap in a listed stake, cash-flowing solar as the residual, and the solar leg is a genuine answer to the room's opening question about what pays when AI fails. Holdco discount can persist indefinitely; the spot-over-contract catalyst is what converts it. Runner-up is Renesas, which is the better fundamental story but adds to your capex-growth concentration rather than diversifying it.

FIX and DT are good businesses at fair prices with AI-sympathy risk in opposite directions. SNPS has the widest dispersion of outcomes in the room; 9/30 is the whole trade. TOST is a clean short thesis but 30x on 20% GP growth is not obviously wrong, and memory-cost shorts have a bad track record - the differentiator is whether the competitive set blocks pass-through, which is unproven.

Views From The Valley: Demand for Intelligence as Effectively Unbounded, Open vs Closed as a Go-to-Market Choice, and Where the Value Actually Accrues

Event: Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference — panel titled "Views From The Valley"

Date: September 10 2026

Panelists (from the session slide):

• Sarah Guo — Founder, Conviction Partners

• Jerry Chen — Partner, Greylock Partners

• Guru Chahal — Partner, Lightspeed Venture Partners

• Glenn Solomon — Managing Partner, Notable Capital

Moderator: Gabriela Borges, Goldman Sachs

Key Takeaways

The framing question: open versus closed

• Chahal (Lightspeed): His headline argument, and the sharpest thing on the panel: the question is wrong. What matters is the TAM, and the TAM is large enough to accommodate multiple go-to-market approaches simultaneously. Open weight versus closed weight is a go-to-market decision, not a winner-take-all technology contest. His analogies were Splunk versus Elastic, and Datadog versus Grafana — in any sufficiently large enterprise market there is room for enormous value creation across almost any go-to-market.

• Solomon (Notable): Reads the question as a symptom: public investors have real consternation about closed frontier versus open weights, and the question presupposes a bounded, zero-sum market. Thirty years in, he has never seen a curve as steep or as consistently misjudged as token demand. Nobody he talks to has gotten it right; everyone underestimates it. His conclusion is that this is about the size of the pie, not the slicing of it.

• Chen (Greylock): Accepts the pie is big and redirects to the harder question — where does the value sit? His conundrum: switching costs between models are very low while the value of a frontier model is very high, which produces enormous error bars. Same in software: vastly more software gets written, so the value of GOOD software and SECURE software goes up, not down. His answer on value: good models, trusted models, good and secure software.

The data points that matter most

• Guo (Conviction): Portfolio companies figured out how to make long-horizon tasks work in a new way over the last few months, and inference consumption went up 100x — in verticals that are NOT code. Gross margin went down in these companies at scale, but the reaction was "make it cheaper": use open source, post-train, work out where the frontier is genuinely needed. Large enterprises are already buying open-source inference for coding use cases.

• Solomon: A few years ago engineers' AI tooling spend was de minimis; then roughly $1,000 per person; this year roughly $10,000 per month per software engineer. [Figures partly garbled — verify — but the trajectory is the point.]

Cyber security — incumbents versus AI natives

• Solomon: Both schools are true. More software plus far more agents creates a genuine CISO problem. Where he is investing: application security, and agent-oriented security; identity and access for agents; using AI to defend AI.

• Chahal: One set of companies wins on technology and another wins on distribution; he explicitly did not write incumbents off.

The stack: where to own position

• Chen: Barbell framework — the top layer (front door: chat interface, devices) where distribution matters and the bottom (power, generation, chips) where scale matters; the middle "semantic layer" (agents, data, context, workflows, prompts) is contested.

World models

• Guo: Domain reasoning models (biology, longitudinal health, engineering, materials) are the interesting investor category; thousands of people now know how to train frontier pipelines and that talent is dispersing.

Lightning round: what the market has wrong

• Chen: The China versus US framing is overblown and headline-driven.

• Chahal: The jobs apocalypse is overplayed; AI-native companies still cannot find enough people.

• Guo: Agreed; customers are moving budget to AI and making it bigger rather than cutting headcount first.

[Note: non-idea sections lightly condensed from Joe Flaum's write-up.]

Readable Transcript

Host (pre-call, on airlines): You've got the airlines actually performing well in the face of trade wars and real wars. Nico: We have a really big group today. John is going to run a three-minute timer, so when you hear the Grammy Awards song please wrap up so we get you out of here on a Friday. BPRE — Long — Kent Escalera, Centiva

Kent Escalera: I definitely don't have anything as good as VCX, but staying with the theme of closed-end funds, I'm pitching Blue Rock Private Real Estate Fund, ticker BPRE. It's a $3.2 billion closed-end fund, originally an interval fund that did a direct listing back in December. This is a non-traded product that gets sold to dentists and the like, and eventually they had to have a liquidity event. It came public with a NAV of around $24 and quickly traded to $12.50.

Kent Escalera: This fund is unique in the world of closed-end funds in that it's a fund of funds holding LP stakes in institutional private real estate funds — Blackstone, Ares, Brookfield and so on. Right now it's trading at about a 42% discount to NAV.

Kent Escalera: There are three interesting points. First, it's novel — there are no similar closed-end funds listed in the US, so the price discovery process has been a little chaotic. Two, Saba has gotten involved in a pretty big way, and they've obviously had a lot of success coercing managers into actioning the discount. Three, while parts of the portfolio are stressed, over 40% of it is in funds with 45- or 90-day redemption terms, and they've been redeeming those stakes at a relatively accelerated pace.

Kent Escalera: The question is what they do with that cash. More recently they've been deploying it into directly originated investments, but I'd argue that's likely better placed in a third-party fund. Still, with Saba there you have a very big cushion, and they pay a relatively high distribution yield, which effectively returns your cash and should be discount-compressing. So this isn't something where you're going to make 100%, or probably not even 50% — but at a 12 handle or an 11 handle, the risk-reward is very attractive.

Nico: Super interesting, Kent. I had not heard of this one before, so I appreciate you going through it.

GPGI — Long — Wayne Wilkey, Diametric

Wayne Wilkey: I'm pitching GPGI Inc., ticker GPGI. This is a permanent capital vehicle created by Dave Coates and Tom Knott, Tom formerly of Goldman permanent capital. The strategy is to be a buyer of well-positioned but under-managed PE companies — not just stakes, entire companies. They've bought two so far.

Wayne Wilkey: The first was CompoSecure. If you have a metal credit card, chances are they made it. That business was under-managed — not a lot of great selling effort, really just taking orders — and it's been doing really well. Currently about 1% of the card market is metal, but about 12% of the card market is premium, meaning it carries an annual fee. The cost of a metal card is about $20 amortized over four years or so, a de minimis expense. So you have a 1% share of market and the TAM is a lot higher, and it's growing nicely. That segment could be a multibagger by itself.

Wayne Wilkey: The second acquisition is Husky, which makes injection molding equipment — a comp to what used to be Hillenbrand. They bought it right at the beginning of the year, right before the Iran war when oil prices spiked. Resin prices are obviously a big deal if you make plastics, and that caused some delays in their order book. But that's coming back now — the second quarter went well, and by the time we get into next year there will have been substantial de-levering. You're looking at about eight and a half, nine times EBITDA right now.

Wayne Wilkey: One thing to know: there's a sister company, Resolute Holdings, RHLD, which is basically the management company and gets 10% of EBITDA. On Bloomberg, the roughly $2 billion of debt that GPGI has shows up under Resolute — so watch that when you do the calculations.

Wayne Wilkey: The two partners themselves have a billion in personal capital in this. Dave Coates has a great reputation; I'm sure some of you have met him. This is a very high quality shareholder list, and I think you're getting something that has a wartime reason for trading where it does. Nico: What are you playing for? Do you have a price target, a multiple?

Wayne Wilkey: Bolt-on acquisitions from the PE firms that need to offload good businesses they've been milking.

6963 JT — Rohm — Long — Chris Bonanni, Arvin

Chris Bonanni: I know this was pitched before, but I'm pitching Rohm, a Japanese analog power semiconductor manufacturer. The thesis is that there's a hidden asset, a turnaround story, and really accretive M&A they can participate in.

Chris: On the core business, we think global analog and power semis are basically three months into an upcycle after a four-year downturn. Rohm has really low operating margins, in the low single digits, and this is the central restructuring opportunity right now. They have a new CEO and an American CFO who've targeted 500 billion yen in sales and 100 billion yen of EBIT by 2028 — and even half of that is basically just taking their loss-making silicon carbide business to breakeven, plus a little bit of cost cuts and pricing. Chris: On the special sits element, we think there's an opportunity to consolidate a portion of Toshiba's power semis business, and this could be announced as early as this September. Mitsubishi Electric has signaled interest in consolidation as well. We think Rohm is in talks to acquire the power analog unit from Toshiba, that it's fundable with cash and very cheap debt, that it's 40% accretive, and that it adds 130 yen of per-share value — roughly 2,000 yen of cumulative value to the company.

Chris: And lastly, and maybe most interestingly, they hold a 14% stake in now-private Toshiba. We think Toshiba is misunderstood: it owns a large stake in Kioxia and it's the third largest HDD business after Seagate and Western Digital. If you mark their current financials to market with the publicly traded peers and apply a heavy discount, we get an after-tax value for the Toshiba stake of 3,000 to 5,000 yen per share — and this is a stock that itself touched 4,000 at the recent lows. Chris: So putting the pieces together: the core business worth 4,200 to 5,000; the M&A, which is 40% accretive, gets you to a total of 7,200 to 10,000; and then the Toshiba stake worth 3,000 to 5,000.
