Nico: Right under the gun too, Chris. Interesting pitch — definitely had more angles than the last one I heard, and it's a good looking chart. I didn't know you did so much in Asia; you pitched Baba before.

Chris: Yeah, I don't like sleeping very much.

HUBG — Long — Bo Yang, J. Goldman

Bo Yang: I think this got pitched last time by a different gentleman — HUBG. It's the second largest player in intermodal trucking, which has structural tailwinds right now with oil, cost inflation, the driver shortage, a host of things. They're going to be the biggest beneficiary if this UNP–Norfolk merger goes through, because they're UNP's biggest partner.

Bo Yang: The stock has underperformed this year because they had some accounting irregularities due to accounts payable and purchased transportation, and they're reviewing the books. They haven't filed a 10-Q or a 10-K since last year. That investigation is supposed to wrap up by September 14th.

Bo Yang: I think the business isn't impaired. I've spoken to competitors, I've spoken to customers — no one has seen anything unusual going on with the company. They've come out and said there's no impact to free cash flow from these accounting issues. So they're supposed to start filing by September 14th. It might be the 14th, maybe it's a week or two after if they ask for an extension. But if they file and reiterate there's no free cash flow impact, I think people really want to own this thing and the stock could double — not double on the day, but they're in such a good spot fundamentally. You just need this accounting overhang to be done.

Nico: Simple pitch, and it makes sense. Are you pretty bullish on transports and truckers in general?

Bo Yang: I think there are some structural tailwinds that should be pretty powerful over the next two years. The macro spot is weakening a little, which is why these stocks fell back, but they should pick up after Labor Day just seasonally. If you see that, I think people will focus on the tailwinds again. So I'd be more bullish than bearish right now. Intermodal is one of the better places to be, because they deal with the cost inflation of higher insurance costs and higher driver wages and can just benefit from the tailwinds instead of absorbing the cost offset. It's a good neighborhood to be in.

Q: In terms of the timing of the resolution on the accounting issues?

Bo Yang: They have until September 14th to file or they'll get delisted from the Nasdaq, I believe. They can ask for an extension — I don't think there's anything preventing them — but they're all hands on deck trying to meet the date. So it could be very interesting over the next few weeks. It's obviously binary at this point, and I think the calls are really interesting, because this thing could really rip if it gets resolved. And I actually think the issue is in the non-core part of the business that no one really cares about — there's a chance the whole thing is contained to logistics and brokerage, which isn't what people own it for. If that's the case, I think it really rips. So I'd buy short-dated if you don't want to deal with a potentially binary situation. At the end of the day I don't think the business is impaired. It's a trucking company — you can't do that much funky math here.

AC — Air Canada — Long — Jason Pauley, Wolfhill

Jason Pauley: I'm pitching Air Canada, ticker AC. Just shy of an $8 billion Canadian market cap, one and a half times levered, trades at three and a half times next year's EBITDA — that's two turns cheap to US peers for no discernible reason. We think it's a multi-bagger over the next 24 months.

Jason Pauley: The company recently announced the sale of 25% of its loyalty program to Blackstone for $2.5 billion, which values the loyalty program at $10 billion — in excess of the current market cap. We actually think it's better than that, because the company effectively owns a call that allows them to buy back the stake, capping Blackstone's return at a 6.5% IRR. They're using the proceeds to buy back stock, tendering for 10%. Upon completion they'll have bought back 30% of their market cap since their December 2024 analyst day — hiding in plain sight. The last time they tendered for 10%, in May of 2025, after completing it in June the stock ripped 30% in a straight line.

Jason Pauley: A few other things about Air Canada. It was the best performing stock in the TSX — up over 50x in the decade preceding COVID and 4x in the five years preceding it. We think the conditions are in place fundamentally for another period of outperformance. If you like the US industry for its consolidation, this is far more consolidated: Air Canada commands 55% domestic market share, and number two WestJet has 30% share and is privately owned by Onex, who sold a 25% stake to a consortium of international airlines last year for over 6x.

Jason Pauley: It has a number of other underappreciated assets. It owns 80% of its fleet where US peers own 65%. Its order book is struck below where airplane values are right now, and US peers have been monetizing their order books through sale-leaseback transactions. Earnings understate free cash flow for the foreseeable future: they've got a $4 billion pension surplus, and that pension expense runs through the income statement but they don't have to contribute cash. They also have a $7.2 billion tax loss, so they won't be paying taxes for a long time. And the AeroPlan asset is obviously worth a fortune — they proved that — which also provides a huge working capital tailwind to free cash flow.

Jason Pauley: Earnings are depressed and there are structural tailwinds in Canada. The Canadian population grows faster than the US population. They've taken pricing in a steady way. And they have six-freedom traffic rights, which gives them a unique competitive advantage in the transborder and international markets. They're at a cyclical trough: Asian traffic hasn't recovered to pre-COVID levels because they can't fly over Russia, and they'll eventually get that back; transborder traffic is still 10% below 2024 levels due to trade wars, and that'll come back too.

Jason Pauley: On valuation — at its 2024 analyst day the company laid out a plan to grow EBITDA to $5 billion by 2028, and they haven't backed away from it. Putting a US peer multiple on that, you'd get a $100 stock. The stock's at $28. If you assume they just get back to where they were pre-trade wars and real wars at $4 billion, at a one-turn discount, which would be a 12% free cash flow yield, that's a $60 stock. Last thing: the last time the company spoke they said the fall booking environment was probably one of the stronger ones they've seen in their history.

Nico: I asked Jason to join because a TMT fund, surprisingly, asked us to do a call with him on United Airlines. He started saying, well, I like United, but I love this Air Canada. I heard the pitch and thought, that's a really good story.

Sagar Gupta: Two questions, Jason. Do you think the clampdown on immigration trends in Canada is weighing on fundamentals or sentiment? And there was a CEO change not too long ago — any thoughts on new management?

Jason Pauley: In order. No, I think the six-freedom traffic is structurally a huge tailwind, and the Canadian population still grows in excess of the US population despite the clampdown on immigration. Air traffic in Canada is still recovering at a faster pace than the US — they're still a bit behind, and you've got all the cyclically depressed dynamics. So maybe it's an impact on sentiment, but the company is buying back stock as fast as humanly possible, which says what they think about valuation and where this company is capable of going. On the CEO change: they announced this transaction after the CEO change, so I don't think there's any change in the board or the way they see value. As for the new CEO, I'd expect more of the same. It's like a monopoly — it kind of runs itself.

ROG — Rogers — Long — Dan Arecchio, Clearline Capital

Dan Arecchio: I want to pitch Rogers, ticker ROG. It's a $2.2 billion provider of PCB materials, substrates, and poly and silicone materials to semi and industrial companies — broadly, think of it as upstream from analog semi manufacturers. I actually pitched this name roughly a year ago. The stock has done well, but mostly on earnings growth; you haven't really seen much multiple expansion, unlike a lot of semi-related stuff. And I think the setup is better here than it was a year ago, as there's a better catalyst path.

Dan Arecchio: High level, after an extended downturn the core industrial and auto end markets have bottomed and are recovering. On a mid-cycle billion of revenue I think they do $200 million-plus of EBITDA. So the stock is at like 10 times EBITDA now, a little less, versus mid-teens pre-COVID. Just getting back there is $150 a share, about 25% upside. And I think they're going to beat numbers in 2027 without heroic macro assumptions — I have EPS 20% above the street, and beats in Q3 and Q4.

Dan Arecchio: The near-term catalyst is that the company is holding an investor day — this is a new management team — where they'll provide mid-term targets and incremental detail on multiple data center opportunities, which are not in the numbers. And frankly it reminds the market that this company still exists; it basically has no real sell-side coverage.

Dan Arecchio: On the data center options, there are two key ones. One, they're one of two or three providers of PTFE, which — if anyone has been following all the noise about the Rubin Ultra — historically was not used in data center applications. Current supply chain checks say NVIDIA wants to use it for a couple of layers in the switch tray. From there you could see a significant expansion of PTFE usage across data centers as spec requirements go up. And two, they're developing a microchannel cooling product; if anyone follows Coherent, it's similar to what Coherent has.

Dan Arecchio: So $150 of base value plus maybe $30 for the data center options, without assuming much multiple expansion, gets to 40% upside from here. Upside to numbers, a low historical multiple, and data center upside.

CC — Chemours — Long — Sam Elder, Irenic

Sam Elder: I was going to talk about Chemours. I know this has been sort of a perennial special sits name, but I think there are some interesting developments that make the upside really attractive from where we are now.

Sam Elder: For quick background, it's a combination of a refrigerants business, which is a duopoly, their titanium dioxide business, and a small specialty chemicals business. The main overhang for many years has been the PFAS liability. But post-Q2 there are some interesting developments that make the setup attractive.

Sam Elder: First, in Q2 they downgraded full-year guidance for the refrigerants business quite substantially on inventory destocking. People were very concerned, since Solstice didn't report similar dynamics, that this was a structural shift in the competitive structure and pricing for that market. We've done a lot of checks on that front and we don't think that's the case. We think it was largely driven by Solstice having operational issues last year that didn't allow them to participate in the sell-in — so they just didn't have the exposure to the destocking that Chemours did. The go-forward dynamic hasn't changed, and neither has the go-forward growth rate. So we think that business is intact and unimpaired.

Sam Elder: On the TiO2 side, there's been a lot of focus on Middle East-related sulfur pricing and the impact on China and exports. I think this business is slightly more disconnected than many people give it credit for. It's already run-rating in the second half based on price increases in tariff-protected markets, due to more independent supply and demand dynamics within those markets, at rates above consensus. And there's an unappreciated opportunity over the next few years: they have a large stock of historical ore they had to buy at elevated prices for a plant they've since shut down, which on a steady-state basis should provide a $100 million positive impact over the next few years, both on cash flow and eventually profitability as it flows through.

Nico: Why don't we wrap it up. Andres, you can connect with Nikhil if you like. Thanks everyone for joining, have a great weekend. Don't forget to vote — we'll send out the survey and we'll see who wins in a few months.

Readable Transcript

BHP — Short — Howard

Howard: The adjusted number is $2.60 against $2.00 — $2.60 is their adjustment and that's the forecast. Their whole business is resting on copper. Their other businesses are struggling: steel, met coal, nickel is on care and maintenance. If you look at their pre-tax margins as reported, for the current year they were 38%. They should teach Microsoft how to run the business, perhaps — or maybe there's a cyclical peak. If you take off the write-off I described, it's 44%. My case is that's not sustainable. We know some of their markets are soft, but the hot market of course is AI and maybe military, at roughly 40 or 50 times earnings. This sounds kind of crazy to me.

Q: How do you look at earnings versus EBITDA for a company like this? And how do you see the stock earning $5 — that's 20 times earnings.

Howard: There's something wrong with that number. They had the same forecast last year on public sources. I checked with the company, and the very helpful North American investor relations lady said, “I don't know where those numbers come from.” The forecast for the year ended was about two bucks, and the forecast for the current year is about $2.60 — which is the adjusted number they just reported. They report every six months; it's semi-annual. And I don't know where that public number comes from. Last year there was a similar deceptive number — the forecast was about $4.75 or $5 on public sources. The Bloomberg presentation shows $2.23 this year, which is 50 times earnings. So call it $2.60, roughly equal to the adjusted number, if copper doesn't fall apart.

Howard: The five-year record is pretty good, but if you go back ten years they were deeply in the red — and they were in the red even excluding the accident they and Vale had in Brazil. So it's highly cyclical.

John: Why short it now, Howard?

Howard: Fifty times earnings on the derivative of AI. It was the same as the derivative of the internet in 1999. The other pressure I believe is coming is that some of their earnings come from gold — whether you call it revenue or reduced costs, that would amount to 15, 20, 25, 30 cents a share. That would disappoint anybody at this multiple. I think it's a really interesting way to hedge against the AI craze, as I did against the internet craze at the end of '99.

Ed: They pay out all their earnings — they pay a dividend of about $2.50.

Howard: That was accidental; they overpaid last year because they had such a good year. They try to pay half their earnings. But even half the earnings doesn't give you a big yield, and three quarters doesn't either. The balance sheet's okay — debt is about 20% or 25% of equity, and book is $9. The whole thing is really the copper craze. One more thing: if you look at the inventories of copper among speculators on the COMEX, they have rocketed in the last two months. It's like a very steep hockey stick. So it looks to me like there are chances of a shortfall, and if things really slow down this stock has a lot of downside. That's my story.

SOC — Sable Offshore — Long — Ed Hajim, with John Levin

Ed Hajim: I'm going to pitch one really small, interesting company: SOC, Sable Oil. It is offshore Santa Barbara. It has a valuation that's about 10% of the value of the oil they have in the ground. You may remember this — it was owned by Union Oil and it had a spill that killed a few birds, and the president of the union said, “who worries about a few fucking birds?” And they closed the field for 15 years because of that.

Ed: The market cap is about $800 million at this point. They did two ugly financings: they sold 32 million shares of stock and then did a $300 million convertible, so it diluted the thing a bit. They've supposedly got 190 million barrels of oil, which calculates into about $10 to $12 billion worth of oil — so it's like 10% of the valuation. They're producing 40,000 barrels a day now.

Ed: The big negative was that they couldn't use the pipeline in California. They were suing for that, and the judge finally allowed them to use it. So instead of building a platform to send the stuff overseas, they can now send it through the pipeline. And California is in desperate need of oil — gasoline in California is two dollars a gallon greater than any place in the United States.

Ed: I thought it was going to take off once the court case was done and it didn't — it just sat there. I don't think there's a lot of risk; probably down to three bucks again. They did the offering at $3 for 32 million shares, and that's probably what's leaning on the stock now. If you look at the numbers it sells at about one and a half times cash flow — actually 1.8 times cash flow in 2027 and two and a half times EBITDA. So SOC is worth doing some work on.

Ed: Otherwise, I think gold and silver have both bottomed. I think you can put those away — you'll bounce around, but basically everybody in the world is buying gold except the US public, and the US public started about two weeks ago. And finally, uranium is starting to move: the spot price just moved from about $85, $86 to $90. That's all I've got.

John Levin: I'd like to pause on this for a second. SOC gave a presentation yesterday and we bought stock on that offering. The stock is going down because it's oil. People have completely ignored it — everything Ed is saying is correct. The enterprise value is $1.7 billion. I have slightly different numbers: I think you're paying $3 a barrel for proven oil in federal waters, where the judges have said you can do this production. So I thought the stock was going to trade at $8, $12 or $16. I thought immediately after that court case it would double, and it hasn't.

John: But there's an item coming. If you listen to the Roth presentation or get the transcript, they're saying the federal government is going to create a special petroleum reserve in California and buy a lot of this oil. If that is announced, the stock is going to open with a double or a triple. The price of the stock is wrong. The court things are over. And there's possible, probable, hopeful, really bombshell news coming — the Department of Energy head is a cabinet member, and I know the guy who runs it pretty well.

John: I've been in good touch with Jim Flores. I've known Jim for 20, 30, 40 years. I've lost money bets to him and won money bets from him. He's perceived as aggressive — and he is aggressive, but he's winning here. And somebody is going to buy this thing. You have all this oil in federal waters in the United States of America.

Q: Ed, did you say they have 600 million barrels of reserves?

John: They have 678 million barrels proven, but really it's going to be a billion barrels. You're paying nothing for it. Ed's right on the equity; the enterprise value is about a billion seven. So they have 678 on the PV-10 — you're paying three bucks for proven, and there's plenty more. There's a decline rate, and some of it's sulfur, but they have a lot that's non-sulfur. And if a Republican gets elected governor of California, the stock is probably 15.

Q: Could California stop these guys?

Ed / John: California sues every day in five different courts for seven different reasons. That's why it's here. But they're losing.

Q: You said one or one and a half times cash flow. What price is built into that assumption?

John: Frank Rango did a discount for us. He took their price deck, a 15% discount rate, and the reinvestment, and got a $12 present value.

HNGE — Long, and RMD — Short — Neil Gagnon

Neil Gagnon: I'm going to bore you all with a stock I've talked about, which is just about at its new high, and you probably think it's too high a price. The company is Hinge Health, symbol HNGE, currently a $7.5 billion market cap. I've been yakking about this since the stock was $74; it's currently $91 and a fraction. The reason I'd like you to pay attention is that I think this is going to be a great growth stock over the next five years or more.

Neil: It was started by two men, each of whom had a very serious accident and needed physical therapy. They're currently 39 and 40 years old. This is the leader in digital physical therapy. The way it works is you use your iPhone, it looks at you and tells you what you're doing, AI tells you what to do, and they also have a physical person looking at this. It's been accepted by 2,800 self-insured companies with 21 million employees, and it's paid for by each of the five major health plans — UnitedHealth and the rest.

Neil: Four years ago this company had revenues of $200 million. This year they'll be over $850 million. When they went public in 2025 they sold shares to pay the taxes on employees' stock options. It went public at $32 in May of '25.

Neil: What's really interesting is that digital physical therapy has a lot of growth in it. Today, with 25 million employees under their belt, only about 4% of them use the services. They think that can go to 9%, and it's been rising about half a percent per year. They add about 400 to 500 new clients every year. They just won Costco; they also have Walmart, Accenture and others.

Neil: It's much more than physical therapy. The company is going beyond PT — they've just added migraine, with very good numbers, and it's the beginning of that. Their biggest customers came to them and said, “you have to get involved in gastrointestinal issues, it's very important to us.” The three that pushed them were Walmart, Costco and Accenture. They didn't have that capability, so they went out and acquired a company for it. We've talked to them, and by the way we've talked to several large self-insured companies.

Neil: About 4.5% of employees are using it today. The price is fixed per employee — it averages about $850 per employee per year of the 4.5% using it, and it could max at $1,200. They don't want to raise the price; they just want more employees to use it. By adding migraine — I may not have a migraine problem, but maybe someone else does, and then they pay attention to it.

Neil: We think that 4.5% can be 9%, and the earnings growth is sensational. At the IPO they said they'd grow 18 to 20% a year. In June of this year, at their user group analyst day in Chicago, they raised it to 20 to 25% per year. Last year they grew at 50%, and in the first half of 2026 they've grown at 50%.

Neil: So the bottom line is a major growth story — the $850 million I'm thinking about for this year, which is the company's own estimate, can be many multiple billions. The street estimate for 2027 is $2.95. There's a new Morgan Stanley report out August 24 using $2.95, but they don't include the new GI work. So there's a great deal more here. We're thinking 2027 might be on the order of $4 a share, which makes the stock full but not still expensive. Do you go in and buy a new high today? I doubt it. But put it on your radar — we believe it's very exciting. And by the way, when we talk to major companies about it, they're using it themselves.

Neil: My short idea is the same one I've been talking about — ResMed, symbol RMD. It's bounced a bit because most things in med tech have gone up recently, but the story is the same: revenue growth is slowing. First of all, GLPs — when you lose weight the need for a breathing device goes down. Some aren't cured, but it does go down. More importantly, Philips, who had to get out of the US market and still makes masks but not machines, will likely be back in the market in 2027. Why do we think that? Because we've talked to a number of sleep specialist doctors and they said they're coming back in '27.

Neil: A company by the name of APMD went public recently, on July 30th, at $16. The stock is currently $28. Why is that important? They make a pill to help some people with sleep apnea. Some believe it's going to be very exciting. Do we know? No. So the company's rate of growth is slowing now. This used to be a 5% growth market and went up to 10% because Philips got out. It's starting to slow in and of itself, and when Philips comes back we think it'll be a major shock. The company is using its cash flow to make a bunch of silly acquisitions, overpaying for things that don't make any sense whatsoever. So we just like it as a short against our other areas.

Mark: I looked at Hinge and bought some stock. The numbers are unbelievable — the growth rate, gross margins of 87%, the retention rates, all the KPIs are through the roof. My question is that they have almost no competition and very few people are doing this. The one worry I have is that it's a very low barrier to entry. Anyone, especially with AI, can make one of these things. How do you get around that? Aren't there going to be a hundred new people who come in and do this?

Neil: Mark, we've looked at that question in every way we can. We're aware of the AI risk — and by the way, one of the reasons the stock tanked in the middle of '25 is “oh gee, this is a software company and AI will kill them.” First of all, they've got 25 million employees already signed up. They've got all that data, all that information. The video component is important, and the way they present it is important. But the payoff to the user is sensational: as the companies are telling us, they're saving two or three dollars for every dollar they spend. They don't want to go anywhere, and they like the additional services. We've talked to Sword and to companies that have used Sword — Sword just lost Costco to them. Sword came out saying their ARR is growing at 70%, but there are no numbers behind that. We don't see any real way that competition can come in and do this. And if you need a physical therapist, they have 5,000 on staff to back you up.

SBUX — Short, and BPRE — Long — Rick Reiss

Rick Reiss: The one short in the restaurant area that hasn't worked for me is Starbucks. I can't tell you there's any one thing I can put my finger on. I think it's pretty fully priced, like 36, 38 times earnings. But there are issues — there are issues with labor. I don't think they can conceivably grow at the rate they've done in the past. And primarily I think there's just going to be continued pressure on margins, and the analysts are kind of overestimating what they can deliver over the next couple of years. So I don't have a trigger, but it's the one that hasn't worked for me, and I'm sticking with it.

Rick: I don't have anything really new, but there's a stock I bought earlier in the year which is now doing poorly — BPRE. It's a closed-end fund that invests in other real estate funds and to some extent in some direct real estate. They bit the bullet at the end of last year: they were getting significant withdrawal requests because they had this opportunity to put in for withdrawals, and they had too many requests.

Rick: The stock had been trading around NAV, which is around $24 a share. They decided to stop withdrawals, convert to a closed-end fund, and pay out their cash distributions — which they did. The stock immediately collapsed to $13, $14. But the net asset value didn't collapse. The stock climbed back to $16, $17, and is now back under $12. I think this is market related.

Rick: They've actually raised their distribution every month since they made this announcement. The most recent distribution, for August, is 13.7 cents. So with the stock under $12 and a distribution on the order of a dollar fifty-five or sixty annualized, you're getting a very high cash-on-cash return, and you're buying this at what I'd call a 50% discount from stated NAV. I can't underwrite the NAV, but this isn't something they make up out of the blue — it's compiled on a regular basis and these are audited numbers. So take a 20% or 25% haircut and call the real NAV $18 to $20. That's a huge discount with a giant distribution. And for those who care, about 30 or 40 percent is tax sheltered, so the after-tax effective distribution, which they tell you every month, is higher than the current rate. I just think it's dropped back into the value range.

Rick: Saba has bought about 5% of it. Someone sooner or later is going to push them to do something to close the NAV gap. And I think they are in the process of selling some assets they're not crazy about going forward.

Q: Why are they paying dividends in four digits — 13.7 cents?

Rick: It's calculated. They have a certain number of shares and they decide how much they're going to pay out, and that's what it rounds to. If you look year to date, literally every month it's gone up by some small fractional amount. They feel pretty good about their portfolio.

John: I'm only looking at Bloomberg, but it's interesting — the Fidelity government portfolio is 20% of the assets. Then the rest are other funds, it looks like.

Rick: They are. It is a fund of funds, John. They invested in private real estate funds that the poor public like us could not get into — the Ares funds and some others — and passed through the distributions. People bought that until last fall, when everybody decided they wanted out at the same time. So they shut off the quarterly window and said we're converting to a closed-end fund, and everyone who wanted out pretty much got out the same day. You can see the stock going from twenty-something to twelve in one day. It doesn't show who the management is other than the two co-managers, Waterman and Ruddy — there is a management company with a board, you just have to go to their website.

WULF — Long — Craig Beresin

Craig Beresin: I've been buying shares in WULF, TeraWulf, a little bit below here. I think we know why the stock is down. It was in the high twenties, and then there's everything from profit taking to some worries about friction on data center building — mostly from Democrats; the Republicans are making some noise, I think mostly for political reasons. Bitcoin came down, which tends to affect the trading of WULF a little, even though it shouldn't anymore. And they raised a bunch of money. They did the right thing: April was about $900 million of equity, and May was a ton of debt.

Craig: The reason I like it is that this is a cash machine. They've got building to do over the next couple of years, but they are power experts and they're very well regarded. The key for me getting in was that Anthropic signed a 20-year deal with them — a $19 billion deal. Do I trust OpenAI? Kind of, maybe, or maybe not. I think Anthropic is probably the best player. They're going to come public probably soon, having raised $70, $80 billion, late September or early October. And I think the stock can do well into that, especially because it's depressed down here.

Craig: Once you get through the building over the next couple of years — which I think in the fifteens and sixteens you're not paying for at all — you're not paying for them completing all the current projects associated with the leases they've signed. And then you have good optionality on new leases, both domestically and globally. Very, very well-run company. So I think it's an opportunity sitting here almost down 50% from the highs, where the fluff's been taken out of it. So, long WULF.

CAT — Long — Wes Guylay

Wes Guylay: These AI development stocks — Caterpillar Tractor, Reliance — have all come down, and there's a lot of angst about putting these things near where anybody lives. But I think that's going to cure itself.

Wes: Caterpillar's down probably 250 points, and it sells at about 20 times what we think they're going to earn this year, and less than that next year. I think it's a little bit like fracking. There was a lot of angst about that as well, and that was in process. The states that don't use it, like New York State, just don't get ahead — they have to turn to gambling or something else to raise money. Or just raise taxes.

Wes: So I think the AI production stocks have sort of made a bottom here, and are certainly searching for a bottom. I think that's an interesting thing to take a look at, because the rebound, if it comes, could be pretty significant. The other things are working just fine — JP Morgan and Union Pacific just hit new highs, all those are going along fine. The real correction has been in things like Caterpillar Tractor.

Neil / John: Interesting thing I read over the weekend — Loudoun, Virginia, which is the biggest data center hub in the United States, takes 3% of the land for the data centers and pays 45% of the taxes. And 100% of the opposition.

TWST and QURE — Long — Adam Silverschotz

Adam Silverschotz: My area of interest right now is buying biotech, particularly as it intersects with AI — I think it's a huge theme. On this call several months ago I pitched a company called Twist Bioscience, TWST. They are the leading maker of synthetic DNA in the world. Think of them as a consumption business for all of the increasingly automated wet labs testing the new drug ideas coming out of these AI models. You have closed-loop robotic wet labs, and you need the raw materials to do that at increasing scale. They're the leading player producing synthetic DNA. It's already been a big stock, so it's better understood — I think it probably runs to $200 and takes a breather. But this theme more broadly, at an index level, I think it's very interesting to be long the biotech ETF against the Qs.

Adam: A single name that I really, really like is uniQure, ticker QURE. They are going to be coming out with a drug that is going to cure Huntington's disease, and it's going to be a gigantic stock. And the production model they have for this drug can be replicated across a bunch of other disease types. They came out with a very strong presentation the other day — there's a webinar on their website. There's still some short interest, and the market cap's like three and a half, four billion. I think, based on just the Huntington's drug, this could be a $20 billion market cap next year.

PAL — Long — Richard Shuster

Richard Shuster: The name I want to talk about, which I mentioned a couple of quarters back and which has done nothing — gone down a little, actually — is Proficient, PAL. It is tiny. They move cars on trucks; they have the trucks and the trailers that move the cars.

Richard: The reason I'm repeating it is that in the last month they went out and bought the number two competitor. The number three competitor, Jack Cooper, went bankrupt last year. So on a pro forma basis — this is a tiny one — the stock is $160 million of market cap, $200 million of debt, so an EV of $350 million. The combined EBITDA right now is $65 million, so it's trading at six times. Next year I think they'll do $100 million.

Richard: There are basically four or five things that have happened that make me want to do this right now. Number one, trucking has bottomed. The operating ratio has been 100, so the operating margin has been zero, and it's normally 94, 95 — which means a 5% or 6% operating margin. This has $900 million to a billion dollars of revenue right now. And you have a consolidating industry: a guy goes bankrupt, number two buys number three, industry capacity is tightening. You have a hard asset fleet, all of this leverage, and no one cares. The company went public two years ago at $15, is now $5, and it just doesn't matter. So I'd go out and buy PAL here. I think the downside is probably a buck and the upside is $10.

QXO — Long — Mark Megalli

Mark Megalli: John, I did a bunch of work on QXO and bought some stock. John knows this better than anybody. Brad Jacobs has an unbelievable track record — he started United Rentals, started XPO, each one a huge home run success. Now he's got QXO.

Mark: This is essentially a roll-up of roofing, insulation and building products companies. They bought Beacon and they bought TopBuild. Beacon was doing a billion of EBITDA, TopBuild adds a billion, so that gets you to $2 billion. He's saying they're going to get to $4 billion based on synergies, procurement, centralized buying — he's got a bunch of categories he thinks will be highly impactful to EBITDA. And if you add tuck-ins, he's saying $5.5 billion of EBITDA by the end of the decade. The enterprise value is like $15 billion. If he gets to these numbers, it is super cheap.

Mark: They're number one in insulation, number two in roofing, number one in waterproofing, and number one or two in lumber and building depending on the geography. John said to me the other day, it's a jockey bet — you're betting on the jockey. The TAMs are hundreds of billions of dollars. They're doing $14 billion in revenue; $20 billion is where the street is for next year; and they're saying $50 billion in revenue is their goal over time. The guy's had a lot of success with these kinds of roll-up strategies in the past.

John: You're betting with the best jockey ever.

ATRO — Long — Tyler Meotti

Tyler Meotti: I'm going to be pitching Astronics, ticker ATRO. From a high level, they basically provide all of the electrical power and lighting on an airplane. They also do the TV sets, so the in-flight connectivity. And their third business is test systems — a much smaller portion, probably $40 million on a billion in revenue.

Tyler: It was at a high of $95 and has come down to $75. The street has them doing $250 million in EBITDA, and the enterprise value is about $4 billion, so about 16 times 2027 numbers. I think a reasonable multiple on a high-quality company in aerospace would probably be 20, so you get to about $130 a share net of debt, versus $75 today.

Tyler: Two things on thesis. One, why is it down — the stock has had a big run up from $25. And it's probably important to mention there are only five analysts covering it: one from TD and four from boutique shops, so a higher level of inefficiency on the name.

Tyler: Two, where am I different. I think street estimates on sales are just too low given the ramp at Boeing and Airbus — Boeing going from 42 to 52 737s a month and Airbus going from 50 to 75 on the A320s. You also have an increasing tendency from airlines to do more retrofits on the electrical side. American just announced they're going to have in-flight connectivity on their premium side. And their test system business is actually going to double revenue next year based on a contract they just won — so that's reliable revenue growth in 2027 as well. That's pretty much my thesis.

ENS — Short — attributed to Adam Silverschotz

Speaker: John, I forgot to give a short — EnerSys, the ticker is ENS. They make lead-acid batteries. Overall, lead-acid is losing share to lithium-ion, and they don't have any real lithium-ion solution.

Speaker: The stock is up a ton because of all this data center build-out — the data centers are taking whatever they can get for backup power. But as the generations of the data centers improve, NVIDIA's next generation is 800 volt, and lead-acid doesn't work. So basically the market is mix-shifting from 100% lead-acid to 0% lead-acid, and the stock has re-rated. It's tech obsolescence that got a one-time earnings boost, but it's probably going to get cut in half in the next 18 months.

SPOT — Long — Joe Flaum, Newbrook Capital

Joe Flaum: I'm going to pitch a large cap long today — Spotify. Everyone knows this business. It's the leading pure-play audio platform in the world; two thirds of all premium music streams globally happen on Spotify. It's a great business — subscription, recurring revenues, real network effects, all that good stuff.

Joe: The reason we're interested now, and got involved over the last month or so, is that the business became a materially better quality business over the past year. I'd followed this company for a while, and one of my hesitations was always that they had a somewhat commoditized product — all the streamers that sell streaming audio have the same music catalogs, whether it's Apple or Google or Spotify or Amazon. So what's the way you really differentiate yourself, and how do you expand margins if you're paying 70% to the labels?

Joe: What's happened over the last year is that they negotiated new label deals that effectively bifurcate the music business and set a per-user floor for the cost they're paying, which escalates over time, and allow them to earn more if they start to make more money on the advertising piece for audio.

John: Great high quality company — the kind we should emphasize in this meeting.

NN — NextNav — Long — Harvey Eisen

Harvey Eisen: I have a highly, highly speculative idea. I'll preface this by saying that this year the source of this idea got me into a company called Anterix, symbol ATEX. Ariel: No — VCX is, in my opinion, a short. It trades at about a 50% premium at the moment. Last time we discussed it, it was about a 400, 500% premium. You can play it with puts still. WMB, PSX, BKR — Long; MOD — Watch — Evan Ratner, Levin Capital

Evan Ratner: I'll do a quick pitch. Evan: My pitch is that we like Williams, which is a pipeline company, and we also like Phillips 66, which owns a pipeline and a refinery. Refining capacity is incredibly tight and it's going to remain tight. Svetlana: And the street kind of doesn't believe them. They don't believe they're going to get to $4 exiting 2028, and they don't believe they can get to $6 in 2030. John Levin: I tried to run this thing with a one o'clock hard stop because everybody's very respectful, and I'm going to stick to that. I'll mention only one thing, in honor of Ed. Needham Investment Idea Sharing Session — 14 Stock Pitches

Host: Eric Ritter, Needham & Company

Date: August 25, 2026

Format: Buy-side idea-sharing Zoom — 14 pitches, roughly 3 to 3.5 minutes each, minimal Q&A by design

Pitch List

In the order presented. Tickers are as stated on the call; where a name was transcribed phonetically the likely ticker is flagged.

• SIRI (Sirius XM) — LONG — Steve Scherr, Shames Partners (a Millennium unit)  ($9.8B cap, 19% short interest)

• PURR (Hyperliquid Strategies) — LONG — Zach, TCS Capital Family Office  ($2.6B cap)

• SPOT (Spotify) — LONG — Joe Flaum, Newbrook Capital  ($115B cap)

• FELE (Franklin Electric) — LONG — Dennis Vishni, Ararat Capital  ($4.5B cap)

• For-profit education basket — SHORT — Jason Rubrick, firm not stated  (Grand Canyon, “Covista,” Strayer, Phoenix Education, “Prodocio” — caps $1B to $6B)

• ASTS (AST SpaceMobile) — SHORT — Paul, introduced by the host as Holwick  (~$25.5B EV)

• MAR (Marriott) — SHORT — Sam, firm not stated  ($93B cap, ~2% short interest)

• FTAI Aviation (spoken as “FTI Aviation”) — LONG — Ari Friedman, firm not stated  (~$20–30B EV, ~$200/share)

• LBTYA (Liberty Global) — LONG — Josh Learman, Wolf Hill  ($3.6B cap, ~$11/share)

• KBR (KBR Inc.) — LONG — Daniel, Kettle Hill  ($4.7B cap, ~$37/share)

• SNPS (Synopsys) — LONG — Shubhoya “Shubo” Shubhogoj, Opti Capital  ($77B cap, ~$405/share)

• AZUL (Azul) — LONG — Ben Ziff, Black Barn  ($1.4B cap)

• WULF (TeraWulf) — LONG — Brandon Lee, Venlite  ($8B cap, ~$16/share)

• COMP (Compass) — LONG — Mitch Shapiro, Clearline Capital  ($9.5B cap, ~$11.50/share)

Tally: 11 longs, 3 shorts (education basket, ASTS, MAR).

Cross-Cutting Observations

• SEO disintermediation was the one genuinely new theme. Jason Rubrick's education short is really a bet that LLM search kills a lead-generation channel — explicitly framed as applying to any company reliant on SEO for leads. Mitch Shapiro's Compass pitch is the mirror image: a name previously bucketed as an AI loser now re-rating as a winner.

• Three ways to play data center power without owning a hyperscaler. FELE (spec'd into CDUs), FTAI (end-of-life jet engines as turbine power), WULF (powered shells) — with WULF adding an explicit regulatory-geography screen against PJM and Texas.

• Two hard-catalyst holdco/spin stories. LBTYA (Ziggo spin, mid-2027) and KBR (November investor day, January spin), both pitched as sum-of-parts with the market discounting timing slippage.

• Only three shorts, all crowd-resistant. Rubrick noted that “usually at these venues, no one pitches a short.” Notably, MAR is at ~2% short interest and Scherr's SIRI long leans on 19% short interest — opposite sides of the same positioning logic.

Readable Transcript

Lightly edited for readability. Speaker names as identified on the call.

Eric Ritter, Needham — housekeeping

The reason we keep doing these is that we try to be as efficient as possible — you walk out with 15 to 17 ideas in a total of one hour. A couple of my colleagues are on, and one of them is taking notes; we're happy to share those with everyone here. Afterward, if any of you want to be connected with each other to go through an idea, we do that a lot — just through Bloomberg, it's easy. If you have questions, ask me or any of my Needham associates.

Some people asked about Q&A. Once in a while there's time — if someone has a quick question after a pitch, please. Otherwise let's take it offline so we can get through all the ideas. If anyone has a time constraint, hit me on IB. When each person speaks, to save time, please say the name of the stock, the ticker, the market cap, and whether it's a long or a short — roughly three to three and a half minutes. I'll let a timer go; if you hear it, wrap up in the next 10 to 15 seconds. And please state your name and the fund you're at, so everyone gets to know each other. I'll choose at random. Steve Scherr, would you like to kick us off?

SIRI — Long — Steve Scherr, Shames Partners (Millennium)

I'll go first. Steve Scherr, we're at Shames Partners, a unit within Millennium; we're long-short. I'll pitch a long today: Sirius Satellite. $9.8 billion market cap, 19% short interest, ticker SIRI.

Historically I've been a short seller for 20 years, and in the last few years we started taking over the long book. One of the classifications we look for in longs is businesses that are broken, because a category of names that would hurt us as consensus shorts were the ones with a potential change agent.

Quick bull case. Sirius has been a secular decliner for 20 years — subscriptions down to about 33 million from north of 50 million. But it has stabilized: churn has come in a bit, or at least it's getting matched by new adds. People are somewhat excited about the spectrum sale opportunity; I don't really care that much. I think it takes a long time to unlock and I don't think it's an immediately feasible catalyst.

What gets us excited is that Google has picked Sirius to manage its entire audio advertising platform, because of their expertise in the space. We think it fundamentally becomes a different business over the next two to three years. The street right now sees potential for $2 billion of revenue and $300 million of EBITDA from that business by 2028. We've done about 15 calls, including with the world's largest podcasting company and a bunch of others, and it seems like the story grows faster than that. It fundamentally changes the business model from a slowly decaying music delivery mechanism into an advertising platform where they have real domain expertise.

It currently trades at about 7x EBITDA. We think 10x on 2028 EBITDA of about $3 billion — or at least a $3 billion run rate by 2028 — is 100% upside if the growth manifests with Google the way we think. Bear case is 6x on flat to modestly negative growth persisting, which is probably 35% to 40% downside from here. So we really like the risk-reward.

The nice thing is the massive short interest. It feels right now like if we're wrong it's not a clearing event, and if we're right everybody figures it out at the same time. One other thing, if anyone wants to reach out offline: there's commentary about whether they'd buy iHeartRadio, which is taking leverage and putting more leverage on top of it. I think the iHeart deal is unlikely, even though there are some compelling reasons an acquisition would work. They've been doing bolt-on acquisitions, which suggests to me they're leaving that aside. I'll leave it there — fast, short, sweet.

PURR — Long — Zach, TCS Capital Family Office

Thanks. I'm with TCS Capital Family Office in New York City. I like the idea of going long PURR, which is Hyperliquid Strategies. They're a digital asset treasury — those have been out of favor for a while, but this one seems more interesting than the others.

The token is HYPE, the native token of the Hyperliquid exchange. Right now the exchange is mostly offshore, but there was a recent article that the Trump administration is trying to bring this crypto exchange to the US. It's been a huge movement in crypto. The token might be one of the only ones in the crypto market at all-time highs.

Last year, in 2025, they did $3 trillion of trading volume. The platform offers tokenized equities, including private companies, and other crypto offerings. They generated a billion dollars of fees, all of which is used to buy back the token and burn total supply — an interesting tactic.

It's a $2.6 billion market cap right now. They hold $30 million of these HYPE tokens, valued at roughly the same as their market cap. Clean balance sheet, no debt, $100 million of cash. I think this is a big trend in the industry and market, and more unique than just your typical Bitcoin or Ethereum vehicle.

SPOT — Long — Joe Flaum, Newbrook

Sorry about the mute. I'll be quick. I'll pitch SPOT long — a $115 billion market cap company. We all know it: great business, leader in streaming audio. A few things got us involved over the last month or so.

Number one, deals were struck with the labels last year which allow for a bifurcation and an unlock of gross margin. Historically it had really just been a pass-through to the labels on the music side, but now there's an ability to unbundle and price differently and get disproportionate upside — both inside music, with their marketplace business scaling, which is effectively artists paying for advertising and distribution, and advertising in music generally; and outside music with books, podcasts and some premium features coming in, some of which have already been released. So the label deals have been very helpful going forward.

That led to management coming out with a pretty robust multi-year algorithm through 2030 at their investor day a few months ago: basically mid-teens revenue, 35 to 40% gross margins, and 20%-plus EBIT margins. You can pencil to $50 of free cash flow per share toward the upper end of that range.

Third, there was a bunch of questions on AI — was it a loser, was it a winner, was it generally outside the AI trade. We've seen the fears around Spotify dissipate a bit, and frankly it's been helpful not to be in that bucket recently. There are a bunch of new features where they're benefiting from AI. They're pushing more products today than I've seen in years, and you have the AI Remix feature coming soon that a lot of people are excited about.

Fourth, it's a relatively attractive valuation for a high-quality GARP story, with this revenue CAGR, margin improvement and free cash flow inflecting — while a lot of other internet names are seeing free cash flow go the other way. So we can pencil it to more than a double over the next few years.

Near term, we like the setup. Q4 should see users inflect; that's implied in their guidance, and in our conversations it seems largely intact. Ads should also inflect in the second half. They've replatformed the advertising business and the programmatic side is now closer to half of the entire ads business than the legacy high-touch business, so you have a mix shift. There are a lot more advertisers coming to the platform, and more supply as engagement improves.

On the cost side, there's been elevated OpEx this year for investments around their AI and product roadmap, but they've talked about seeing leverage into 2027. So the setup from here into Q4 and 2027 looks good, and you have announcements on the product side, including AI Remix, that could be attractive. They recently upped their buyback, which signals a free cash flow inflection to us. And stepping back, industry competition seems to be in a more benign place — Apple raising price recently is good for everyone.

So to sum up: overall high-quality asset, numbers upside near term, great medium-term story, an AI winner or at least outside the crosshairs, decent product roadmap and good valuation. I'll leave it there.

FELE — Long — Dennis Vishni, Ararat Capital

My name is Dennis Vishni, chairman analyst at Ararat Capital. The stock I'm pitching long is Franklin Electric, ticker FELE, $4.5 billion market cap.

Franklin is a bit of an old-world industrial business, best known for water pumps that go into residential groundwater systems — think a well in your backyard. The company was run by an older, conservative CEO for two decades, but he was replaced at the end of 2024 by the president of nVent's enclosures business. That guy, Joe, has come in and changed up a lot within the business.

The thesis has three parts. First, given Joe's background in the enclosures business, which is focused on cooling distribution units, he came to Franklin to leverage their experience in pumping systems — pumps, motors and drives — to sell into the data center, specifically to get designed into hyperscalers' next-generation CDU models and into OEMs. I've done a bunch of work, spoke to the CFO several times, spoke to people in the industry including somebody currently at nVent. Franklin started working with those OEMs in Q4 of 2025 to get spec'd into their next generation. The company is pretty certain they'll get orders by the end of this year. The opportunity is significant if you're familiar with the CDU market, and I don't think it's reflected in sell-side estimates or priced into the stock at all.

The second piece is the company's energy systems business — pumping systems for the forecourt of a gas station, everything under the pump that pumps into your car. About 30% of that segment is software. The largest competitor is Vontier, and they're currently forcing a replacement cycle based on the end of life of their monitoring product. Franklin is going to that installed base with a full monitoring software and hardware system at the same price as the module replacement Vontier is pushing, to gain market share and win more software revenue — cheaper price to get the recurring revenue. Another opportunity not really reflected in street numbers, and the company has only started to talk about it.

The third is a significant margin opportunity from unintegrated acquisitions and, as I said, the previous sleepy old management team. They're having an investor day in March 2027 to outline all of this. I think there are several hundred basis points of margin opportunity in every segment. The data center opportunity is about a dollar of EPS in 2028 above the street, energy systems is something like 50 cents, and the margin opportunity plays into some of that $1.50 of upside as well. That's the idea in a nutshell.

For-Profit Education — Short — Jason Rubrick

I'm actually going to pitch a short idea. Usually at these venues no one pitches a short, so I'll raise my hand — especially if Steve isn't going to do it. Our idea is to be short a for-profit education company. I'll give you some tickers. Market caps run anywhere from five or six billion down to a billion dollars: Grand Canyon, a company called Covista, another called Strayer, a company called Phoenix Education, and depending on how far down-cap you can go, Prodocio.

The thesis is pretty simple. These stocks trade with the vagaries of political change and views on how favorable the regulatory environment is, but the North Star for these businesses is enrollment and enrollment growth. We think there's a significant change going on right now, as more and more prospective students, instead of using SEO to get to these sites, are doing those searches natively in LLMs.

When you search for what school you should go to, whether on ChatGPT or Gemini, they keep you inside their own walled garden rather than clicking off to these schools. About 50% of these schools' leads come directly from SEO traffic — these companies are masters at generating traffic through SEO and their marketing agencies. That channel is starting to get shut off. So they're paying more for leads as fewer people do these searches through SEO.

And importantly, the LLMs are optimizing for cost, for reputation, and for proximity — none of which online schools have. So we think there's a significant cliff coming in enrollment growth for all of these schools, whether undergraduate or graduate programs. They're all going to face the same fate. It's starting already — one or two companies have warned on it. But we're focused very broadly on this theme of SEO traffic disintermediation: companies that rely on it to drive leads or starts, we think, are very exposed in the years ahead.

ASTS — Short — Paul (Holwick)

My apologies, I'm a little disorganized today. We had a couple of those education companies, Universal Technical Institute and Lincoln, that both blew up recently, so it seems like a fertile area.

I was going to pitch AST SpaceMobile short. This company has run up quite a bit over the last couple of years on hype in the space sector. They're trying to put in place a constellation of satellites — I think they need 65 — to enable cell-phone-to-satellite connectivity for voice communications.

They've had all sorts of obstacles getting the constellation into space. These are really large satellites, and the cost of each seems to be over $100 million — because they had one that had an accident, which they had to write off because it was deposited at the wrong altitude in space. They ended up taking over a $100 million loss on that satellite, I think about six months ago.

More recently they've had further obstacles with Blue Origin having that catastrophic explosion at their launch pad. Blue Origin is their key partner for getting satellites into space, and with Blue Origin sidelined for the next year or so, they're really kind of stuck. They've been able to get a number of additional satellites up on SpaceX, but I think once you go past October they won't have additional launch slots on SpaceX for quite a long time. So they're not going to get this constellation up and running and ready to deliver service until probably mid-calendar 2028 at the earliest.

In the meantime the company is spending a ton of money building satellites. Quarterly cash burn is over $500 million. The enterprise value is around $25.5 billion. There's been a fair amount of insider selling.

And at the end of the day, even if they get the constellation up and running, it's not clear to us anyone is really going to use it to any meaningful degree, simply because most people are already well served with terrestrial cell phone service. The large wireless carriers have set-it-and-forget-it customers; most people are not in dead cell zones for long periods. And there are other limitations to direct-to-satellite service: a latency issue, a signal strength problem, and you can't be indoors — you have to be outside.

So bottom line: huge financial obstacles to get the constellation running, and once they get there, no guarantee they'll ever have meaningful revenues to support the business. It's one of our favorite short ideas. The industry has had quite a few bankruptcies over the years — I remember Iridium quite well in the early 2000s. I think this is Iridium Part 2.

MAR — Short — Sam

Pitching Marriott short, ticker MAR. About $93 billion market cap, average daily volume somewhere around $600 million.

The issue for Marriott, which is trading at just about peak multiples, is that their franchisees are in something of a revolt over how much Marriott is making off the credit card business while filling their rooms with very well-paying customers. Marriott did make some concessions, revealed on their last earnings call, but franchisees we've spoken with have described that as making them angrier, not sated.

Any more concessions Marriott makes drop directly to the bottom line. If you slap a more average multiple on this and take 2027 or 2028 earnings with some more concessions to the franchisees — either via the royalty rate or by giving them a cut of the credit card money — you can get to 30% or 40% downside here. It's got a very low short interest as well, a couple percent. That's it.

FTAI Aviation — Long — Ari Friedman

I'm going to pitch FTI Aviation as a long. It's about 200 bucks right now — probably the most volatile stock in my portfolio — with maybe a $20, $30, $40 billion enterprise value. These guys have three businesses and the company has been in transition. We've owned this thing since it was around 17 bucks a share and we keep trading it, but I think the setup here is probably the best it's ever been.

The core business is remanufacturing jet engines. They're the lead on the CFM56. They're now global and are going to be the lowest-cost provider, because they have private label parts that are the only ones FAA approved — so they can do this cheaper. Big airlines have started noticing. They have about 14% share of remanufacturing right now, with an interim target of about 25% of the global market, and I think it could go well higher over time. That business does around $2 billion of EBITDA next year, hopefully with a pathway to doubling or tripling.

The second part is turbine power — and who isn't getting into turbine power? Why do they have a leg up? They can take old engines after their useful lives on airplanes, rebuild them, and use them for data center power. This is a new business. They have their first major contract, which I believe is somewhere between 15 and 60 turbines, rumored to be with SpaceX, and I believe they'll announce a couple more in this segment over the next year or so. They've guided to $450 million of EBITDA in that segment next year, just assuming the contracts they have in the bank. If they do 100 turbines, which was their original target, it could be upwards of $750 million of EBITDA — and that's the starting point. These aren't stopgap solutions; they're 10-year contracts with a service tail. So a lot of growth in front of it.

The third segment is the old aviation leasing business. They're moving it off balance sheet to create what they call an asset management business. Who knows if it actually gets an asset management multiple, but they're putting in a little firm equity, raising third-party equity, and putting it into SPVs. They did $6 billion in the first one, they'll do $6 billion again this year, and next year we'll see how much they can do. You could have an $18 to $20 billion asset management business they're taking fees off. And when they take fees, it's not just a management fee on the equity like a hedge fund — they take a management fee on the whole kit and caboodle, equity and debt. So it ends up being a pretty juicy fee stream.

The company just blew up because they got everybody too excited. There was some chop on the call, but everything seems totally fine and the fundamentals seem totally intact. At 200 bucks I can see the stock doubling. That's the pitch in a nutshell. People don't like it because of the Fortress history, but I think they've done everything they said they would and the accounting has proven out to be very clean.

LBTYA — Long — Josh Learman, Wolf Hill

Today I'm going to pitch Liberty Global, long, ticker LBTYA. This is a $3.6 billion market cap holdco of European telecom assets. It's currently just shy of 11 bucks and trades $25 million a day. At today's price you're paying roughly for the current cash and minority investments on the balance sheet alone, before giving any credit to any of the opcos, including VMO2 or Ziggo Group. So the setup is a solid margin of safety plus a real catalyst in the next year from the Ziggo Group spinoff.

This is John Malone's holdco. He's slowly been liquidating the portfolio to get his estate in order. Part of the reason it's cheap is the capital structure — over $8 billion of non-recourse debt at the opcos — and some distrust in the management team to successfully liquidate the portfolio. However, management has spent this year preparing for a big event scheduled for mid-2027 that I think could roughly double the stock.

They already ran a similar event back in the fall of 2024, when they spun off the Swiss broadband and mobile asset Sunrise. That brought about $12 per share of value to Liberty shareholders at the time and trades between a 10% and 14% free cash flow yield on the Swiss exchange.

This time they're preparing to spin Ziggo Group. They bought out Vodafone's 50% stake in VodafoneZiggo and separated the Belgian fiber network into its own netco, and they intend to spin the servco mid-2027. They have a target of €500 million of levered free cash flow in 2028. Put a conservative mid-teens yield on that — call it 15% — and account for Liberty owning 90% of the business, and that adds an extra $10 per share of value. That plus the cash and minority investments gets you close to a double, and that's accounting for VMO2 as zero. That's the idea.

KBR — Long — Daniel, Kettle Hill

Daniel from Kettle Hill. I'm pitching KBR long. KBR is an engineering, technology and government services business doing around $8 billion of sales. It has two different businesses, STS and MTS, and they both do around $500 million of EBITDA. It's about a $4.7 billion cap, $6.7 billion EV, shares around $37, $65 million ADV — around 7x EBITDA, 9x earnings, double-digit free cash flow yield.

I got interested because there were four insider buys, the first time since 2023. The business is having an investor day in November, and the two businesses will split effective the beginning of next year. At $37 today I think it's worth $60 in my base case — over 50% upside with pretty limited downside.

A few quick points. There's a potential sale of either business at any time. An activist said they should sell the whole company before the spin to create value, in the $50 to $55 range. Personally I think the spin makes each business more attractive to potential strategics. On sum-of-parts you get to $60 pretty easily.

Fundamentally, a couple of specific opportunities are interesting, mostly in STS, which is the RemainCo. They have a lot of exposure to food security and energy security, which I think are very durable global themes. They have half the global ammonia patent or licensed technology, and they announced two or three of those recently. They do a lot of specialty jet fuel and LNG builds, so there's a lot of opportunity there.

They gave guidance two years ago in a long-term plan with next-year EBITDA of $1.15 billion. Right now the street's a little below $1 billion — $150 million below the guidance — and management keeps saying they think they can get near or close to their guidance. So you have a built-in beat, plus food and energy security optionality, plus hard catalysts in November and January.

The stock really fell two quarters ago because they moved the timing of the spin back three or four months, which took it out of the time horizon of a lot of folks who need to make money this year. So the stock got really cheap, and I think people start coming back to the story pretty shortly. It also traded low-to-mid $40s pre-war, so this war dying down is a nice little benefit. Quickly on comps: MTS is more of a Leidos, SAIC, Booz business; STS, the RemainCo, is more like a Jacobs or Tetra Tech — a little higher multiple, higher growth. That's the quick pitch.

SNPS — Long — Shubo, Opti Capital

Thanks for having me on, Eric — it's been a while, good to reconnect. I'm going to pitch a long: Synopsys, ticker SNPS. This is Shubhoya Shubhogoj from Opti Capital. $77 billion market cap, $85 billion EV, revenue run rate about $9.5 to $9.7 billion now.

Why do I like Synopsys? It's one of those names that happens to be a software company exposed entirely to the semi supply chain. Think of them as the software that enables hardware manufacturing — the glue that binds the entire process together, supplying fabs and manufacturers with the software they use to actually make the chips. So you're getting exposure to both the semi supply chain and software.

We all know what's been happening to software — the bear case with OpenAI and so on, leading to a bit of this disintermediation, AI-loser kind of play. So the stock's been caught up in that noise, number one. Number two, it's been caught up in the fact that they're doing an acquisition which is apparently going to be accretive in the end, but people aren't very happy with the deal and aren't seeing the synergies yet.

Net-net, think of it as a stock trading at $600 a year ago and $400 now — a software company that supplies into the semi supply chain, and importantly a company in a duopoly. This kind of software is very hard-coded into the manufacturing process, and only two companies supply it: Cadence and Synopsys. So you're running a duopoly software business supplying most semiconductor manufacturers out there, down from $600 to $400 on a deal and on software weakness. That's the setup.

Analysts are a little shocked overall on the sell side. On price targets — not that they're a leading indicator — the highest is JP Morgan at $650, the lowest is Wells Fargo at $450, and it's trading at $405 right now. So it's well below the lowest price target on the street.

On valuation, this company is trading at five-year lows on P/E — 25 times. Back in 2021 it traded at 48 times. What's changed in five years? They've become more profitable: EBITDA margins were 31%, next year they'll be 48%. Gross margins were 79%, now 83%. Revenues were $5 billion, now $10 billion on acquisitions plus organic growth. So a company that traded at 48 times five years ago now trades at 25 times, and is a duopoly software company supplying most of the semiconductor companies out there. That's what makes it compelling.

Last but not least, you've got Elliott, who got intrigued by this. They're an activist not in it to force a sale necessarily — they're in it to force even better margin appreciation. If you get that, there's a lot of upside. So: a 10 to 15% organic grower, tack in another $3 billion from the ANSYS deal with no synergies taken into account at this point. The street expects about $17.50 of 2028 EPS. There's a lot of upside from $17.50 — at a 35 multiple you're looking at a $600 stock. I'll stop there.

AZUL — Long — Ben Ziff, Black Barn

I'll be pitching Azul equity, A-Z-U-L, one of three commercial passenger airlines in Brazil. To orient folks: historically a low-double-digit grower doing $1.5 billion US of EBITDA at a 34% margin. That's against a $1.4 billion market cap, trading at 4x P/E and about 3x 2027 EBITDA on consensus.

Who on planet earth is crazy enough to pitch a recently restructured Brazilian airline equity in 2026? Two answers. Number one, me — I'm that crazy, and I forgot to take my antipsychotics today, so you're stuck with this one. Number two, more importantly, it's decently interesting and more nuanced.

The short and sweet of it: unlike US airlines, where relentless competition drives economic profits to zero, Brazil is a very different setup. We think this is a very moated business with a fresh balance sheet in an underpenetrated market. They have the strongest per-liter unit profitability across all of the Americas. Despite that, they trade at a 25% levered free cash flow yield and a greater than 50% discount to all the relevant peers, GOL and LATAM.

Prior to the 2025 restructuring they were a premium name. Our view is that today's discount is driven by a tough post-reorg technical and a complex story — Hormuz, the Brazilian election coming up, and so on in this exact moment. But fundamentally we think there's really nothing wrong with the business, and there's a lot of convexity and upside levers to be pulled as those headwinds roll off.

On the moat: Azul is a regional provider in Brazil, one of three carriers. There simply isn't enough demand to serve those markets with giant Airbus and Boeing planes. Over the last decade they developed a frankly bizarre mixed fleet, carrying planes as small as seven-seaters all the way up to A330s with 300-plus seats. As a result, the other two competitors really cannot fly the routes Azul flies profitably at the density Azul has. So we've seen a rational market: today 82% of Azul's routes are a monopoly, and they're the leading provider by market share on over 90%.

They restructured in 2025 and emerged recently, in Q1 2026, with the youngest fleet across the Americas and renegotiated below-market lease deals — a great outcome fundamentally. On the technical side: they lost sell-side coverage when they filed, so it's been under-followed. The first half of 2026 was frankly very strong but very noisy with non-recurring and restructuring one-offs. And they lost part of their fleet, which I think the market misunderstood as a demand issue — but it was planned, and they get those planes back in the back half of the year, when Latin American airlines really generate all their cash flow anyway.

So: the business is exceptionally cheap and it's a great business. Over the months ahead we think there's quarterly index inclusion and analyst initiations. I think the company will pursue discounted stock and bond buybacks, running the LATAM Airlines post-reorg playbook from 2023. And at some point this Hormuz headwind turns into a tailwind, as you sell at higher prices and then face the market cost of fuel months later.

WULF — Long — Brandon Lee, Venlite

Brandon Lee from Venlite. I'm going to pitch TeraWulf long, ticker WULF, an $8 billion market cap company. Basically they have transitioned from a Bitcoin miner to a powered-shell provider for these hyperscalers. They have a number of deals under their belt with Google backstopping the payments.

Right now the stock's trading at $16 and I think the value of the signed contracts is about $20. So it's a value play with a huge margin of safety.

There are a lot of headwinds to signing data center deals in the space right now. You want to avoid PJM, which includes Pennsylvania and Maryland, and also Texas recently — Governor Abbott came out with an executive order to do audits on data center deals. Wolf's next site is in Kentucky. It's a one-gigawatt site, and if they sign the whole gigawatt the stock should be worth $30. So this is a great way to play it: a stock trading below the value of its contracts, with a catalyst that could essentially double it.

COMP — Long — Mitch Shapiro, Clearline Capital

Mitch here from Clearline Capital, pitching Compass long, ticker COMP. About $11.50 today, $9.5 billion market cap and about $12 billion EV. Most of you know Compass, so I don't need much detail — it's the largest residential real estate brokerage. They merged with Anywhere in January and now have about 80,000 agents on the platform.

The obvious case is that it's a great way to play the existing-home recovery, with great torque to the housing market. They continue to outperform the overall housing market by about a thousand basis points every quarter, largely because high-end luxury homes continue to outgrow the overall market — the broad-based housing tracks are a little weaker, but luxury continues to outperform.

What I really like is that you don't need a big housing recovery for the thesis to play out. The more interesting side is the cost and margin story. They're still targeting $420 million of OpEx synergies through 2028, with about $150 million in the bank through 2026. They've intimated there will be upside to these synergy targets over time, though the pace will slow. A lot of these comments cut against each other, and I think management is setting themselves up for another guidance raise in the back half of the year or early 2027.

I think street OpEx looks way too high in 2027 and 2028. Management talks about core OpEx growth pre-synergies of 3% to 4% a year. Do the math on 2026 OpEx of $2.8 billion, grow it at 3.5%, subtract $120 to $150 million of synergies, and you get flat to slightly down OpEx — versus the street up 3%.

One of the interesting things is that the broader brokerage market is becoming a bit more rational, and legacy Compass gross margins are actually improving as they layer on additional one-time transaction fees for agents — even though the mix has been extremely negative because the highest-performing agents continue to outperform. Last quarter had an outsized benefit in California due to everybody getting rich on AI. They're starting to roll out more of these transaction fees, so you're getting a little more margin accretion over time.

On 2027 numbers I have about a $15 price target, and through the cycle, a bit more normalized, I get to about 100% upside or a $22 price target. I think it was bucketed as an AI loser by Citrini, and now it's turning into a winner. That's it for me.

Close — Eric Ritter

Thanks, Mitch, really appreciate that. I think that's it — it's 2:54 and I've got a bunch of ideas. Thank you everyone for being on. If you have any questions please reach out, and we'll do this again soon. Again, we'll have notes if you'd like them.

Broader Industry Discussion: Power Shortage: The industry is facing a 30GW power shortage relative to traditional sources, forcing hyperscalers to look at alternatives like Bitcoin miners for "clean," front-of-the-meter power. This is viewed as a structural, multi-year theme rather than a short-term trend.

Energy Storage: The energy storage market is projected to be 10x the size of the EV market. Companies with battery storage capabilities are becoming increasingly valuable as grid demand spikes.

Infrastructure Software Valuations: Investors are seeking comfort in high-growth companies with free cash flow yields exceeding 5%, even if valuations appear "egregious" relative to historical norms.

The "Transition Period": The group characterized the current market as being in a "messy transition"—similar to the shift from combustion engines to EVs—where legacy broadcast, traditional energy, and new streaming/AI infrastructure are competing for dominance.

Other Noted Ideas: Enphase: Potential for power conversion dominance (using gallium nitride) in data centers and grid transformers. Atlas Energy Solutions: Discussed as a potential short against competitors due to capacity issues.

events.2026-02-25-dematteo-resea-dematteo-softw:
Broader Discussion

Winner-Take-All vs. LLM Commoditization: The group debated whether the large language model (LLM) market will become a winner-take-all environment or quickly commoditize. There was a view, influenced by commentary from figures like Elon Musk, that all LLMs (frontier and open source) will be fundamentally similar and accurate within six months, making the underlying technology a commodity. Conversely, it was noted that cutting-edge technology for complex tasks (like inventing new medicines) will remain differentiated, but 99% of white-collar tasks will be commoditized, making it a "dandy" business for in-house models that are a few months behind the cutting edge.

Data Security and Model Weights: A major hurdle for mass AI deployment in regulated industries (like financial services) is the security and ownership of model weights (the probabilistic calculation logic of the AI). The Problem: While contracts ensure proprietary query data (the input) is secure, the third-party LLM provider (e.g., Anthropic) uses the model weights to train and distill models, which lowers their future compute costs. The Conflict: Customers like JP Morgan are unwilling to turn over these model weights, fearing that the probabilistic logic derived from their private data could be used to train models that benefit competitors like Goldman Sachs. This concern has led to regulated firms still not having "out of sandbox" instances for mass deployment.

The Capex Trade-Off and the Hyper-Scalers: The discussion touched on the market's skepticism toward major hyperscalers (Google, AWS, Microsoft) due to the massive increase in capital expenditure for the AI build-out. The Burden of Proof: Despite strong revenue numbers (e.g., GCP at 48%), the burden of proof has shifted to how much they can beat revenue growth by to justify the capex. The Real Long Trade: It was suggested that the best time to be long these stocks will be the first time they cut capex (e.g., late 2026 or 2027), as that moment will confirm that the underlying businesses are "phenomenal" and no longer require massive capital allocation to grow.

AI Diffusion: There was a general agreement that the full-scale diffusion of AI into the broader economy, regardless of its ultimate capability, will take a long time, countering the idea of a near-term "ghost GDP" where white-collar jobs are immediately decimated. Jobs for software engineers, for example, are currently increasing.
